docs.title: Low-Level Language Models (LLLM)
docs.text:
lllm.one

LLLM is a lightweight framework for building advanced agentic systems: the kind that decompose hard questions, call many tools, write and run code, and need to be inspected turn by turn. It is low-level on purpose. Instead of hiding the agent loop, LLLM gives you small, plain abstractions for every part of it (prompts, parsers, tool calls, exception and interrupt handling, dialog state) so research and production systems can be customised without fighting the framework.

pip install "lllm-core[native]"

from lllm import Tactic

print(Tactic.quick("What is the capital of France?").content)

docs.title: Design Ideas
docs.text:
LLLM treats an agentic system as a program. Four abstractions carry the whole design:

Tactic is the program A typed unit of work that owns a task interface and wires agents together. Tactics compose, and a tactic can be handed to another agent as a tool. Agent is the caller A model plus a call loop that handles retries, parse failures, and tool interrupts, so the program does not have to. Prompt is the function A template with a parser, tools, and exception/interrupt handlers: the full specification of one agent turn. Dialog is the mental state Each agent's own message history, kept as a tree you can fork, replay, and inspect.

Around them run a few principles:

  • Configuration as declaration. Prompts, tools, proxies, and tactics are discovered from lllm.toml and referenced by key, so a system's shape is declared rather than wired by hand.
  • Recursive by construction. A whole tactic can be exposed as a prompt-callable tool, so a single agent turn can call a high-level subsystem.
  • Programs, not just tool calls. Proxies give agents an API surface they can read and program against (query_api_doc, run_python, CALL_API), backed by a Jupyter sandbox for program synthesis.
  • Typed end to end with Pydantic. Task inputs, structured outputs, and service contracts are Pydantic models.

The architecture overview walks through each idea with code.

docs.title: The Native Runtime
docs.text:
The native runtime is LLLM's engine. A prompt, a tool, and a dialog:

from lllm.runtimes.native import Dialog, FunctionCall, Prompt, Role, tool


@tool(description="Create a display label for a project area")
def label(topic: str) -> str:
    return topic.strip().title()


task = Prompt(
    path="planner/task",
    prompt="Plan the next checkpoint for {project}.",
    function_list=[label],
)

dialog = Dialog(owner="planner")
dialog.put_prompt(task, prompt_args={"project": "LLLM"}, name="operator")

call = task.get_function("label")(
    FunctionCall(name="label", arguments={"topic": "native core"})
)
dialog.put_text(call.result_str or "", role=Role.TOOL, name="label")

retry = dialog.fork(last_n=1)  # branch the agent's state and try again
print(dialog.overview())

Agents run prompts through this state with a call loop that retries, repairs parse failures, and services tool calls. Start with the tutorials or the agent reference.

docs.title: Compatible With Pydantic
docs.text:
Pydantic is part of LLLM's contract, not an add-on:

  • Typed tasks and outputs. A tactic declares its input and output as Pydantic models (input_model/output_model, or input_type/ output_type). Inputs are validated on the way in and outputs on the way out, prompts can demand structured output with format=Model, and the JSON schemas are published with every service and tool.
  • Pydantic AI agents are tactics. Wrap a pydantic_ai.Agent with PydanticAITactic and it can be served, packaged, and composed like any other tactic, while Pydantic AI keeps owning its tools, models, and output validation.
  • Tactics are Pydantic AI tools. tactic_as_tool hands a tactic, such as a native multi-agent tactic, to a Pydantic AI agent as a typed tool.

See Runtimes and the Pydantic AI tutorial.

docs.title: One Boundary For Every Runtime
docs.text:
Tactic is both the program and the boundary. A tactic written with call() and agents, a _run() hook, a Pydantic AI agent, or a plain Python function is called, streamed, served, and packaged the same way.

from pydantic import BaseModel
from lllm import Tactic


class Question(BaseModel):
    text: str


class Answer(BaseModel):
    text: str


class Shout(Tactic[Question, Answer]):
    name = "shout"
    input_type = Question
    output_type = Answer

    def _run(self, input_value, *, context=None):
        return Answer(text=input_value.text.upper())


assert Shout().run({"text": "hello"}).text == "HELLO"

lllm serve tactics:Shout --port 8000      # FastAPI: /run, /stream, /info

Read more in The Tactic and Services.

docs.title: Beyond One Tactic
docs.text:
Packages and the hub One lllm.toml describes a package for the native runtime and the hub. Validate, publish, and browse packages at lllm.one/hub. SSSN: the network module Channels, events, artifacts, and snapshots that connect systems, plus a TacticProcessor that runs tactics over a channel. AAAX: the shell module Mount packages, tactics, and channels into one strategy and serve it as a single API. One CLI lllm create, init, serve, hub, network, and shell.

SSSN and AAAX are experimental modules: SSSN, AAAX, packages, hub, CLI.

docs.title: Where It Comes From
docs.text:
LLLM's tactic design grew out of the reusable reasoning units needed by Analytica, which decomposes complex societal, economic, political, and scientific questions into grounded subpropositions, runs specialised agents over them, and synthesises a more robust analysis. The same small boundary has since served autonomous software development in Apeiron: demand modeling, computer-use evaluation, activity tracing, and full-lifecycle application synthesis.

  • Cheng, Junyan, Kyle Richardson, and Peter Chin. "Analytica: Soft Propositional Reasoning for Robust and Scalable LLM-Driven Analysis." ICLR, 2026.
  • Cheng, Junyan, Ankit Srivastava, Jessie Zeng, Milenko Drinic, and Jack W. Stokes. "Apeiron: A Scalable LLM-agentic Framework for Autonomous Full-lifecycle Demand-optimized Application Synthesis." Findings of ACL, 2026, pp. 3868-3899.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: From install to a multi-agent program, a served API, and a package, in a few minutes.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install "lllm-core[native,server]"

The distribution is lllm-core; the import is lllm.

Extra Adds native LiteLLM (any provider) and YAML configs for the native agent runtime server FastAPI and Uvicorn for lllm serve and the service apps client httpx for RemoteTactic and RemoteStore pydantic-ai the Pydantic AI runtime adapter sandbox the Jupyter sandbox for program synthesis secure OS keyring storage for lllm setup all everything above

Set a provider key (for example OPENAI_API_KEY), or point LLLM at a local OpenAI-compatible server as shown in the quick start.

docs.title: 1. One line
docs.text:
from lllm import Tactic

print(Tactic.quick("What is the capital of France?").content)

Tactic.quick builds one agent with no configuration. Keep it with return_agent=True and continue the conversation with agent.receive(...) and agent.respond().

docs.title: 2. A program with agents
docs.text:
A tactic is the program of an agentic system. Declare the agents it needs in agent_group; every call gets fresh agents built from the config, and a call session records what they did and what it cost:

from pydantic import BaseModel
from lllm import Prompt, Tactic

TASK = Prompt(path="brief/task", prompt="Write three bullets about {topic}.")


class Topic(BaseModel):
    topic: str


class BriefTactic(Tactic):
    name = "brief"
    agent_group = ["writer", "editor"]
    input_model = Topic

    def call(self, task: Topic) -> str:
        writer, editor = self.agents["writer"], self.agents["editor"]
        writer.open("draft")
        writer.receive_prompt(TASK, {"topic": task.topic})
        draft = writer.respond().content
        editor.open("edit")
        editor.receive(f"Tighten this:\n{draft}")
        return editor.respond().content


config = {
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o-mini"},
    "agent_configs": [
        {"name": "writer", "system_prompt": "You write crisp technical briefs."},
        {"name": "editor", "system_prompt": "You cut every unnecessary word."},
    ],
}

brief = BriefTactic(config)
session = brief({"topic": "KV caches"}, return_session=True)
print(session.delivery, session.agent_call_count, session.total_cost)

Each agent keeps its own dialog. Prompts are reusable specifications of a turn; receive_prompt renders one into the dialog, and respond() runs the agent's call loop (retries, parsing, tool calls). Architecture explains the design.

docs.title: 3. Serve it
docs.text:
Every tactic is also a typed service boundary. input_model is validated on the way in and published as a JSON schema:

from lllm.services import create_tactic_app

app = create_tactic_app(brief)   # POST /run, POST /stream, GET /info

lllm serve tactics:brief --port 8000
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/run \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": {"topic": "KV caches"}}'

docs.title: 4. Make it a package
docs.text:
lllm create briefs        # lllm.toml, prompts/, configs/, tactics/, main.py, tests
cd briefs
lllm hub validate .
lllm serve .              # serves the package's primary tactic

The generated lllm.toml tells the native runtime what to discover (prompts, YAML agent configs, tactics) and tells the hub what the package is. Publish it with lllm hub publish . --local, or browse shared packages at lllm.one/hub.

docs.title: AAAX: the shell module
docs.text:
AAAX, the Advanced Autonomous Agent Executor, is the shell around an agentic system. It mounts tactics, packages, and channels into one Strategy and serves them as a single HTTP API: every tactic gets its full service surface, the strategy's channel store gets the network API, and the strategy adds a resource table and a top-level /run. In code, AAAX is lllm.shell.

AAAX is an experimental module of LLLM.

pip install "lllm-core[server,client]"   # client adds httpx, which TestClient needs

docs.title: A first strategy
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel

from lllm import Tactic
from lllm.shell import Strategy


class Text(BaseModel):
    text: str


class Shout(Tactic[Text, Text]):
    name = "shout"
    description = "Upper-case a message."
    input_type = Text
    output_type = Text

    def _run(self, input_value, *, context=None):
        return Text(text=input_value.text.upper())


strategy = Strategy("loud-desk", description="Shout at things.")
strategy.add_tactic(Shout(), ref="lllm://demo/loud-desk/tactics/shout")


@strategy.runner
async def run(input_value, *, context=None):
    first = await strategy.tactics()["shout"].arun(input_value)
    return {"once": first.text, "twice": f"{first.text}!!"}

create_strategy_app turns it into a FastAPI app:

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from lllm.shell import create_strategy_app

client = TestClient(create_strategy_app(strategy))
print(client.post("/tactics/shout/run", json={"input": {"text": "hello"}}).json()["output"])
print(client.post("/run", json={"input": {"text": "hello"}}).json())

{'text': 'HELLO'}
{'output': {'once': 'HELLO', 'twice': 'HELLO!!'}, 'strategy': 'loud-desk', 'metadata': {}}

Saved as desk.py, the same strategy runs from the shell with lllm shell serve desk.py (see CLI).

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
Strategy(name, *, description="", resources=(), runner=None, metadata=None) is a table of resources plus an optional runner. The strategy name follows the same rule as resource names, so Strategy("My Strategy") raises ValueError. Each resource is a StrategyResource:

Field Meaning name Local name, unique across the whole strategy, used in URLs. A path segment: no whitespace, /, :, \, or %, and not . or ... kind tactic, channel, service, schema, package, run, config, doc, example, snapshot, asset, or custom. ref Stable external identity, usually an lllm:// ref. entrypoint Python import target (module:attr) for package resources. description Free text. metadata Any JSON-friendly dict: runtime, schema, package, version, card.

Names are local and refs are stable: mounting the same package twice under different prefixes changes the names but keeps the refs. Add resources with the helpers strategy.tactic(), .channel(), .service(), .package(), .snapshot(), the general strategy.resource(kind, name, ...), or add_resource(StrategyResource(...)). Each takes ref, entrypoint, description, metadata, and an optional handler:

strategy.channel("log", ref="lllm://demo/loud-desk/channels/log", description="Everything shouted.")
strategy.resource("doc", "readme", ref="lllm://demo/loud-desk/docs/readme", metadata={"path": "README.md"})

for resource in strategy.resources:
    print(resource.kind, resource.name, resource.ref)

tactic shout lllm://demo/loud-desk/tactics/shout
channel log lllm://demo/loud-desk/channels/log
doc readme lllm://demo/loud-desk/docs/readme

A resource without a handler is metadata: it shows up in /strategy and /resources, and invoking it echoes the resource record, the input, and the context back. A handler makes it callable. Channels are the exception: on a strategy with a store, a channel without a handler is backed by the store (below).

docs.title: Tactics
docs.text:
add_tactic(tactic, *, name=None, ref=None, description=None, metadata=None) mounts an lllm tactic. The name defaults to tactic.info().name, the ref to the tactic's package_ref, and the runtime kind is recorded in metadata.

A plain function also works as a tactic handler. strategy.tactics() wraps it with lllm.as_tactic, so it is served like any other tactic:

def count_words(payload: dict) -> dict:
    return {"words": len(payload["text"].split())}


strategy.tactic("count", handler=count_words, description="Count words.")
print(sorted(strategy.tactics()))

['count', 'shout']

strategy.tactics() returns every tactic resource that has a handler as an lllm Tactic. Each one is mounted with create_tactic_app at /tactics/<name>/, so it gets the full service surface: run, stream, info, and any custom tactic endpoints, with the services request and error envelopes.

docs.title: Channels and stores
docs.text:
attach_store(store) backs the strategy's channels with a store and mounts the store API at /network/. Every channel resource without a handler, like log above, is backed by the store channel of the same name:

from lllm.network import LocalStore

strategy.attach_store(LocalStore(".lllm/network"))


@strategy.runner
async def run(input_value, *, context=None):
    output = await strategy.tactics()["shout"].arun(input_value)
    strategy.store.append_event({"channel": "log", "kind": "shout", "payload": output})
    return output


client = TestClient(create_strategy_app(strategy))
client.post("/run", json={"input": {"text": "hello"}})
print([event["payload"] for event in client.get("/network/events", params={"channel": "log"}).json()])
print([event["payload"] for event in client.get("/channels/log/events").json()["output"]])

[{'text': 'HELLO'}]
[{'text': 'HELLO'}]

The store creates each declared channel on first use: when the app is built or a store method is called. Channels that already exist are left as they are. strategy.store wraps the store you attached and forwards store methods to it, as the runner's append_event shows. Without a store, a channel resource is metadata like any other. Use a synchronous store, a LocalStore or a RemoteStore: the channel routes and /network/ do not work with an AsyncRemoteStore.

A strategy has one store. Attaching a different one raises ValueError instead of replacing it, so attach yours before mounting packages, which share it (below). A TacticProcessor over strategy.store is the usual way to connect a mounted tactic to a channel; Tutorial 11 does that inside a runner.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
A package folder with an lllm.toml (see The manifest) mounts in one call:

support-desk/
  lllm.toml
  tactics.py

support-desk/lllm.toml:

[package]
org = "demo"
name = "support-desk"
version = "0.1.0"
kind = "app"
description = "Triage support messages."

[tactics.triage]
entry = "tactics:triage"
description = "Assign a priority to a support message."

[channels.inbox]
description = "Support messages as they arrive."

support-desk/tactics.py:

def triage(ticket: dict) -> dict:
    urgent = "down" in ticket["text"].lower().split()
    return {"priority": "urgent" if urgent else "normal"}

from pathlib import Path

from lllm.shell import strategy_from_package

desk = strategy_from_package("support-desk")
for resource in desk.resources:
    print(resource.kind, resource.name, resource.ref)
print(desk.store.root.relative_to(Path("support-desk").resolve()))

package support-desk lllm://demo/support-desk
tactic triage lllm://demo/support-desk/tactics/triage
channel inbox lllm://demo/support-desk/channels/inbox
.lllm/network

desk had no store, so mounting the package gave it one at <package>/.lllm/network. The folder and the inbox channel are created on first use, here when the app is built, and the shortcuts work:

client = TestClient(create_strategy_app(desk))
client.post(
    "/channels/inbox/events",
    json={"input": {"kind": "message", "payload": {"text": "Checkout is down"}}},
)
events = client.get("/channels/inbox/events").json()["output"]
print([(event["kind"], event["source"], event["payload"]) for event in events])
print(client.post("/tactics/triage/run", json={"input": events[0]["payload"]}).json()["output"])

[('message', 'lllm.shell', {'text': 'Checkout is down'})]
{'priority': 'urgent'}

Packages load lazily: building or inspecting the strategy never imports package code or creates the store folder. Building the app, calling strategy.tactics(), or invoking the resource imports the code. A package tactic that declares no package_ref reports its manifest ref, lllm://demo/support-desk/tactics/triage here, in /tactics/triage/info and as the tactic_ref of the CallContext it receives.

To combine packages and your own resources, mount packages into a strategy with use_package (or add_package(strategy, path, ...)). A prefix keeps names apart:

ops = Strategy("ops", description="Support and loud desks in one API.")
ops.use_package("support-desk", prefix="support")
ops.add_tactic(Shout())
print([resource.name for resource in ops.resources])

['support.support-desk', 'support.triage', 'support.inbox', 'shout']

The prefixed tactic is served at /tactics/support.triage/run and the channel at /channels/support.inbox/events, backed by the store channel support.inbox.

Function What it does strategy_from_package(path, *, name=None, prefix=None, store=None, bind=True) A new strategy named after the package, with the package card and version in its metadata. strategy.use_package(path, *, prefix=None, store=None, bind=True) Mount a package into an existing strategy. Same as add_package(strategy, path, ...).

path is a package folder or an lllm.toml file. store picks the store folder for a strategy that has no store yet (see below). bind=False mounts metadata only: no handlers, no store, and no tactic routes.

Every manifest section becomes resources:

Manifest section Resource kind Handler when bound [package] package (named after the package) [config] config named default [schemas.<name>] schema [tactics.<name>] tactic the imported entrypoint, as a tactic [channels.<name>] channel append, query, info on the strategy's store [snapshots.<name>] snapshot [services.<name>] service its tactic's handler, when it names one [runs.<name>], [docs.<name>], [examples.<name>], [assets.<name>] run, doc, example, asset

A tactic entry loads through coerce_tactic. A Tactic instance is mounted, and a class that can be built without arguments is instantiated. A callable that takes no parameters, or that can be called without arguments and is annotated to return a Tactic, is a factory: it is called once, when the tactic loads. Any other callable, like triage, is a handler called once per input.

Things to know when mounting several packages:

  • A strategy has one store. The first package with channels gives the strategy its store, at store= or <package>/.lllm/network, unless it already has one. Later packages share it, and /network/ serves it; a later store= naming another folder raises ValueError.
  • Package channels are created in the store under their resource names (support.inbox), so a prefix keeps two packages' channels apart.
  • A package whose names clash with resources already in the strategy is rejected before anything is added; the ValueError suggests a prefix.
  • Package code is imported into the server process and stays loaded, so give packages you mount together distinct top-level module names: two packages that both ship a helpers.py share one copy of it.

docs.title: The runner
docs.text:
/run calls the strategy's runner, set with the @strategy.runner decorator or Strategy(..., runner=fn). The runner may be sync or async and is called as runner(input_value, context=...). It receives context only if it declares that parameter (or **kwargs), and the input only if it has a positional parameter besides context (or *args): def run(*, context=None) is called without the input. Handlers follow the same rules. Without a runner, /run returns the strategy name, the input, and the resources, which makes a fresh mount easy to check. desk has no runner:

output = client.post("/run", json={"input": {"q": 1}}).json()["output"]
print(output["strategy"], output["input"], [resource["name"] for resource in output["resources"]])

support-desk {'q': 1} ['support-desk', 'triage', 'inbox']

await strategy.arun(input_value, context=None) and await strategy.invoke_resource(name, input_value, context=None) do the same from Python.

docs.title: HTTP surface
Loading strategies
docs.text:
load_strategy(target) accepts:

Target Loads a directory strategy.py, else shell.py, else its lllm.toml as a package a .py file its build_strategy() factory, else its strategy object an lllm.toml file the package, as with strategy_from_package module:attr a Strategy or a no-argument factory that returns one, imported from the working directory

The CLI uses the same loader.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
lllm shell inspect TARGET [--json]
lllm shell serve TARGET [--host 127.0.0.1] [--port 8400] [--log-level info]

inspect prints the resource table without starting a server; --json prints the full StrategyInfo. With desk.py holding the strategy from the first section:

lllm shell inspect desk.py

loud-desk: Shout at things.
tactic shout lllm://demo/loud-desk/tactics/shout

serve builds the app and runs it with uvicorn; launch is an alias:

lllm shell serve desk.py --port 8400

From another terminal:

curl -s -w '\n' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8400/tactics/shout/run \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"input": {"text": "hello"}}'

{"output":{"text":"HELLO"},"request_id":"af421ae3-e594-4fc9-90af-2694b1b5d25b","tactic":"shout"}

Inspecting a package neither imports its code nor creates its store folder; serving does both.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Names and routes may change between releases. The strategy app has no authentication and handlers run in the server process, so serve it on localhost or behind your own gateway.

docs.title: Agent
docs.text:
An Agent is LLLM's "caller". It holds a system prompt, a model, and an invoker, and it runs prompts through a deterministic call loop. An agent is not a long-running process: it owns the dialogs it opens, and inside a tactic a fresh set of agents is built for every call.

agent.open("task_1", prompt_args={"topic": topic})  # create a dialog, seeded with the system prompt
agent.receive("Analyze this paper")                  # append a user turn
response = agent.respond()                           # run the call loop, return a Message

The point of the agent is control: each respond() either produces a reply that satisfies the active prompt's contract or raises. Parsing failures, tool calls, and provider errors are handled by explicit, bounded steps you can read and override.

docs.title: From configuration (inside a tactic)
docs.text:
Agents are usually declared in config and built by a Tactic that sets agent_group. A config entry says which model the agent uses, which system prompt it reads, and how its call loop behaves.

# configs/research_writer.yaml
global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  max_exception_retry: 3

agent_configs:
  - name: researcher
    system_prompt_path: research/researcher_system   # a registered prompt
    model_args:
      temperature: 0.3
      max_completion_tokens: 4000

  - name: writer
    system_prompt: "You write clear summaries of {topic}."   # inline prompt
    model_args:
      temperature: 0.7

from lllm import Tactic, resolve_config


class ResearchWriter(Tactic):
    name = "research_writer"
    agent_group = ["researcher", "writer"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        researcher = self.agents["researcher"]     # a ready Agent
        ...


tactic = ResearchWriter(resolve_config("research_writer"))

Each agent_configs entry is parsed into an AgentSpec; spec.build(runtime, invoker) produces the live Agent. Config errors (missing model_name, a system prompt path that does not resolve) surface when the tactic is constructed, before any model call. The full schema (global defaults, model_args merging, base inheritance) is in Configuration.

docs.title: Directly
docs.text:
Agent is a dataclass; build one yourself when you do not need a tactic.

from lllm import Agent, Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native.invokers import build_invoker

agent = Agent(
    name="writer",
    system_prompt=Prompt(path="writer/system", prompt="You write clear notes."),
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    llm_invoker=build_invoker({"invoker": "litellm"}),
    model_args={"temperature": 0.2},
    max_interrupt_steps=3,
)

agent.open("draft")
agent.receive("Write a short project update.")
print(agent.respond().content)
Field Default Meaning name required Agent name; also the name on its replies. system_prompt required Prompt used to seed every dialog the agent opens. model required Model id passed to the invoker (for LiteLLM: gpt-4o, anthropic/claude-..., ollama/llama3). llm_invoker required A BaseInvoker. See Invokers. stream_handler None BaseStreamHandler that receives streamed chunks. runtime default runtime Registry used to resolve prompt paths and tool refs. api_type APITypes.COMPLETION COMPLETION (Chat Completions) or RESPONSE (OpenAI Responses API). model_args {} Provider arguments (temperature, max_tokens, ...). max_exception_retry 3 Repair attempts when the reply fails to parse. max_interrupt_steps 5 Tool-call rounds per respond(). 0 means up to 100. max_llm_recall 0 Retries after a provider error (rate limits are handled separately). max_rate_limit_retries 8 Retries after rate-limit errors, with exponential backoff. context_manager None ContextManager applied before each model call. See Dialog. inference_hints None InferenceHints sent with each model call. See Serving hints.

docs.title: Quick constructor
docs.text:
For a one-off agent without config files:

from lllm import Tactic

agent = Tactic.quick(system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant.", model="gpt-4o")
agent.open("chat")
agent.receive("What is the capital of France?")
print(agent.respond().content)

reply = Tactic.quick("What is the capital of France?")              # one-shot Message
reply, agent = Tactic.quick("And of Italy?", return_agent=True)       # Message + Agent

quick(query=None, system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant.", model="gpt-4o", return_agent=False, **model_args) returns an Agent named "assistant" when query is omitted, otherwise the reply Message (and the agent with return_agent=True). Extra keyword arguments become model_args.

docs.title: LLM call vs. agent call
docs.text:
LLM call Agent call Input A flat list of chat messages. A Dialog owned by the agent, seeded with a system Prompt. Output Raw model text plus metadata. A Message, or an AgentCallSession with every invocation and retry. Responsibility The caller decides whether to retry, parse, or continue. The agent parses, repairs, runs tools, and retries within fixed budgets. Determinism Best effort. A valid next state or an explicit exception.

The goal of the agent call is to make an agent behave like a function: stable inputs, a declared output contract, and bounded side effects.

docs.title: The call loop
docs.text:
agent.respond() runs a small state machine until it reaches a final reply. In async code, await agent.arespond() does the same off the event loop (inside a tactic it is recorded in the session like respond()).

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> invoke invoke --> exception: reply fails to parse exception --> invoke: repair prompt (working dialog) exception --> [*]: max_exception_retry reached, raise invoke --> llm_recall: provider error llm_recall --> invoke: retry llm_recall --> [*]: max_llm_recall reached, raise invoke --> rate_limited: rate limit rate_limited --> invoke: back off and retry rate_limited --> [*]: max_rate_limit_retries reached, raise invoke --> interrupt: tool calls interrupt --> invoke: tool results appended invoke --> success: final reply success --> [*]

Step by step:

  1. Resolve the contract. The active prompt is dialog.top_prompt (the system prompt if nothing else was sent). String tool refs and bare Function declarations on it are resolved to executable tools, and the agent's own tools are added to it (see Where tools and parsers come from).
  2. Fork a working dialog for this step and pass it through the context_manager, if any. The canonical dialog is never pruned or edited.
  3. Invoke. The invoker calls the model with model_args (plus any per-call args) and returns an InvokeResult; the reply is appended to the working dialog.
  4. Parse failure. If invoke_result.has_errors, the error is recorded and the prompt's handler builds a repair prompt (on_exception), which is rendered with {error_message} into the working dialog. The model is called again. After max_exception_retry failures the AgentException propagates.
  5. Provider error. A rate limit (LiteLLM/OpenAI RateLimitError, HTTP 429, or a provider's "Rate limit is exceeded." / "Please wait and try again later." message) is retried with exponential backoff, waiting min(60, 2**n) seconds plus up to 1 s of jitter, up to max_rate_limit_retries times (default 8), then re-raised. Any other exception from the invoker counts as an LLM recall and is retried after 1 s, up to max_llm_recall times (default 0), then re-raised.
  6. Commit. The valid reply is appended to the canonical dialog.
  7. Tool calls. If the reply requests tools, each FunctionCall is executed against the prompt's Functions and the result is appended as a tool message through the handler's on_interrupt prompt ({call_results}). An identical repeated call gets a "already called, check previous results" message instead of running again; a tool name the prompt does not declare raises KeyError. Then the loop continues with the next step.
  8. Tool budget. After max_interrupt_steps tool rounds, the handler's on_interrupt_final prompt (no tools) asks for the final answer.
  9. Success. A plain assistant reply ends the loop; it becomes session.delivery. If the steps run out first, the session is marked "failure" and ValueError is raised.

Because repairs happen in a fork, the canonical dialog contains only the turns that succeeded: system prompt, user turns, tool calls and results, and the final reply.

docs.title: Key types
docs.text:
InvokeResult, returned by the invoker for each model call:

@dataclass
class InvokeResult:
    raw_response: Any = None                                         # raw provider response
    model_args: Dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)         # args actually sent
    execution_errors: List[Exception] = field(default_factory=list)  # parse/validation errors
    message: Optional[Message] = None                                # the conversational message

Properties: has_errors, error_message (errors joined by newlines), and cost (an InvokeCost computed from message.usage).

AgentCallSession, the full record of one respond():

class AgentCallSession(BaseModel):
    agent_name: str
    max_exception_retry: int
    max_interrupt_steps: int
    max_llm_recall: int

    exception_retries: Dict[str, List[Exception]] = {}  # parse failures, keyed by loop step
    interrupts: Dict[str, List[FunctionCall]] = {}      # tool calls per step
    llm_recalls: Dict[str, List[Exception]] = {}        # provider errors per step
    invoke_traces: Dict[str, List[InvokeResult]] = {}   # every invocation, failed ones included

    delivery: Optional[Message] = None                  # final reply on success
    state: Literal["initial", "exception", "interrupt", "llm_recall", "success", "failure"] = "initial"

Properties: exception_retries_count, llm_recalls_count, reach_max_exception_retry, reach_max_interrupt_steps, reach_max_llm_recall, and cost (summed over every invoke trace, failed attempts included).

Handlers receive this object, so a repair strategy can depend on how many retries happened and what failed.

docs.title: Where tools and parsers come from
docs.text:
Each turn is driven by dialog.top_prompt, the prompt that sent the most recent turn. The parser, format, and handlers come from it:

Call top_prompt after it agent.open(alias, prompt_args) The agent's system prompt. agent.receive_prompt(prompt, prompt_args) prompt, with its parser, format, and handler. agent.receive(text) A plain prompt for that text: no parser, so the reply is free-form. agent.receive_image(image) Unchanged. Tool results inside the loop With the default handler, a child of the current prompt that keeps its parser.

Tools are different: they are capabilities of the agent. The tools on the agent's system prompt (its function_list, including agent-config tools, proxy tools, and skills, plus MCP servers) are merged into whatever prompt drives the turn, on every turn. The turn prompt can add its own tools on top and wins on a name clash. A prompt that must be answered without the agent's tools sets agent_tools=False.

from lllm import Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import DefaultTagParser

ask = Prompt(
    path="analyst/ask",
    prompt="{question}\nAnswer inside <answer> tags.",
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["answer"]),
)

agent.open("main")
agent.receive("Remember: we report in USD.")          # plain turn, agent tools available
agent.respond()

agent.receive_prompt(ask, {"question": "What changed in Q3 revenue?"})
reply = agent.respond()                                # parser from `ask`, agent tools available
print(reply.parsed["xml_tags"]["answer"][0])

final = Prompt(path="analyst/final", prompt="Summarise in one line: {topic}", agent_tools=False)
agent.receive_prompt(final, {"topic": "Q3"})
agent.respond()                                        # no tools on this turn

docs.title: Interrupt and exception handling
docs.text:
Each Prompt carries a handler that the loop calls automatically:

  • on_exception(prompt, session) runs when parsing or validation fails. Its prompt is rendered with {error_message}. Called up to max_exception_retry times, always inside the forked working dialog.
  • on_interrupt(prompt, session) runs after each tool call. Its prompt is rendered with {call_results} and stays in the dialog as the tool message.
  • on_interrupt_final(prompt, session) runs when max_interrupt_steps is reached and asks for the final reply without tools.

The default DefaultSimpleHandler derives each of these from the active prompt with prompt.extend(...), so repair turns keep the parser (and, except for the final prompt, the tools). Custom handlers are covered in Prompts.

docs.title: respond() arguments
docs.text:
agent.respond(
    alias=None,           # dialog to respond in; default: the active dialog
    metadata=None,        # attached to the reply Message's metadata, not sent to the model
    args=None,            # per-call model args merged over model_args, e.g. {"temperature": 0}
    parser_args=None,     # keyword arguments forwarded to prompt.parse(...)
    return_session=False, # True: return the AgentCallSession instead of the Message
)

docs.title: Dialog management
docs.text:
Agents own the dialogs they create, keyed by a user-chosen alias. The alias makes code self-documenting and keeps dialogs from leaking between agents.

agent = self.agents["coder"]

# Open a dialog: seeded with the system prompt, becomes active
agent.open("task_1", prompt_args={"language": "Python"})
agent.receive("Write a sorting function")
response = agent.respond()

# Open a second dialog, then switch back
agent.open("task_2", prompt_args={"language": "Rust"})
agent.switch("task_1")
agent.receive("Now add error handling")
response = agent.respond()

# Fork for exploration: keep the system prompt + the last 2 messages, switch to it
agent.fork("task_1", "task_1_alt", last_n=2, first_k=1, switch=True)
agent.receive("Try a different algorithm")
response = agent.respond()

old = agent.close("task_2")       # detach and return the Dialog
Member Description open(alias, prompt_args=None, session_name=None, switch=True) New dialog seeded with the rendered system prompt. Raises ValueError if the alias exists. fork(alias, child_alias, last_n=0, first_k=1, switch=True) Branch alias into child_alias (see Dialog forking). switch(alias) Make alias active. close(alias) Remove the dialog and return it. receive(text, alias=None, role=Roles.USER, name="user") Append text. receive_prompt(prompt, prompt_args=None, alias=None, role=Roles.USER, name="user") Append a rendered prompt and make it the active contract. receive_image(image, caption=None, alias=None, role=Roles.USER, name="user") Append an image (path, base64 string, or PIL image). current_dialog The active Dialog. dialogs Snapshot dict of alias → Dialog. active_alias The active alias, or None.

open, fork, and switch return the agent, so calls can be chained.

For multi-agent collaboration, each agent keeps its own dialog. Information is shared explicitly by passing content between agents in the tactic:

coder.open("collab", prompt_args={"language": "Python"})
reviewer.open("collab")

coder.receive("Write a REST API")
code = coder.respond()

reviewer.receive(code.content, name=coder.name)
review = reviewer.respond()

coder.receive(review.content, name=reviewer.name)
revision = coder.respond()

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
A prompt's function_list declares the tools for one turn. Agents can also receive standing tools through config: entries in tools are appended to the agent's system prompt when the agent is built.

global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  tools:
    - shared_pkg.tools:search                # a @tool Function
    - shared_pkg.tactics:code_review         # a tactic tool
    - shared_pkg.tactics:research#summarize  # a named tactic tool method
    - shared_pkg.proxies:market_data         # a proxy (programming surface)

agent_configs:
  - name: analyst
    system_prompt_path: system/analyst

  - name: writer
    system_prompt_path: system/writer
    tools: []   # replaces the global list; writer gets none

Like skills, tools may be set globally or per agent, and a per-agent list replaces the global one. The tools live on the system prompt, so they are offered on every turn, whichever prompt drives it, unless that prompt sets agent_tools=False; see Where tools and parsers come from.

Regular tool and tactic refs stay strings until the prompt runs, then resolve through the runtime: full URLs (pkg.tools:name) are exact, while bare names and pkg:name shorthand resolve relative to the system prompt's package before the runtime's default namespace. Proxy refs must be explicit (pkg.proxies:name); they are resolved when the agent is built because they inject query_api_doc, run_python, and an API directory into the system prompt. See Proxies & Sandbox.

Config stores references, not live objects, so there are no definition cycles. Keep tool modules declarative at import time: define @tool functions and BaseProxy classes there, and build or load any agent a tool needs inside the tool function body.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
LLLM supports agent skills following the agentskills.io standard: reusable, self-contained capability folders that you attach to an agent through config instead of baking them into the system prompt. The spec is young and evolving, so treat this surface as experimental.

global:
  model_name: claude-sonnet-4-6
  skills: [pdf, commit, skill_01abc, https://example.com/skills/review/SKILL.md]

docs.title: When to use skills
docs.text:
Use skills instead of system-prompt text when:

  • the capability is reusable across agents or projects ("how to fill a PDF form", "commit message conventions");
  • you want to version and share capabilities independently of prompts;
  • you need provider-hosted tool grants that must be declared server-side;
  • the instructions are long and only some agents need them.

Keep persona and role instructions in the system prompt, and per-call values (user name, date) in prompt template variables.

docs.title: Entry types
docs.text:
Each entry in skills is classified by its format:

Format Example Mechanism Local name pdf Found in the standard skill directories; catalog entry injected into the system prompt. Works with any model. Anthropic skill ID skill_01abc123 Sent to the API as skills=[{"id": ...}] with the anthropic-beta: skills-2025-10-02 header. Anthropic models only. URL https://example.com/skills/review/SKILL.md Downloaded when the agent is built; catalog entry injected. Works with any model. "*" skills: "*" Every locally discovered skill.

docs.title: Config examples
docs.text:
Same skills for all agents:

global:
  model_name: claude-sonnet-4-6
  skills: [pdf, commit, review-pr]

agent_configs:
  - name: coder
    system_prompt_path: system/coder
  - name: reviewer
    system_prompt_path: system/reviewer

Per-agent override (a per-agent list replaces the global list):

global:
  model_name: claude-sonnet-4-6
  skills: [commit]

agent_configs:
  - name: coder
    system_prompt_path: system/coder
    skills: [commit, pdf]

  - name: reviewer
    system_prompt_path: system/reviewer
    # inherits skills: [commit]

Mixed entry types:

agent_configs:
  - name: analyst
    system_prompt_path: system/analyst
    skills:
      - data-analysis                              # local skill
      - skill_01abc123def                          # Anthropic-hosted skill
      - https://acme.com/skills/forecast/SKILL.md  # remote skill

docs.title: Local skill discovery
docs.text:
Local names are resolved by scanning these directories in order; the first match wins, so project skills override user skills:

<cwd>/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
<cwd>/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md

A missing name logs a warning and is skipped.

docs.title: Creating a local skill
docs.text:
A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md:

.agents/skills/
└── pdf/
    ├── SKILL.md          # frontmatter + instructions
    ├── scripts/          # optional helpers
    └── references/       # optional reference documents

---
name: pdf
description: Extract PDF text, fill forms, merge files. Use when handling PDFs.
allowed-tools: computer_20250124 text_editor_20250124
---

# PDF Skill

## Extracting text

Run `scripts/extract_text.py <input.pdf>` and pipe the output to your analysis step.

LLLM reads three frontmatter fields:

Field Description name Skill name. Defaults to the directory name. description What the skill does and when to use it; the only text the model sees before activating it. allowed-tools Tool requirements, as a space-separated string or a YAML list.

docs.title: How skills reach the model
docs.text:
When the agent is built, local and URL skills follow the agentskills.io progressive-disclosure model.

Tier 1: catalog. Only names and descriptions are appended to the system prompt, and an activate_skill tool is added to its function_list. The block is brace-escaped, so braces in a description reach the model as written when the prompt renders with the default str.format renderer:

<system prompt text>

When a task matches a skill's description, call the `activate_skill` tool with that skill's name to load its full instructions before proceeding.

<available_skills>
  <skill name="pdf">
    <description>Extract PDF text, fill forms, merge files. Use when handling PDFs.</description>
  </skill>
</available_skills>

Tier 2: activation. activate_skill(name="pdf") returns the SKILL.md body, the skill directory, and a listing of bundled files:

<skill_content name="pdf">
# PDF Skill
...

Skill directory: /path/to/.agents/skills/pdf
Relative paths in this skill resolve against the skill directory.

<skill_resources>
  <file>scripts/extract_text.py</file>
</skill_resources>

Note: This skill declares tool requirements: computer_20250124 text_editor_20250124. Ensure the agent has access to these tools.
</skill_content>

Tier 3: resources. The model reads referenced files with whatever file tools you gave it, only when the instructions call for them.

Anthropic-hosted IDs skip the tiers. When the agent is built, this patch is deep-merged into its model_args, so it is sent on every call:

{
    "skills": [{"id": "skill_01abc"}],
    "extra_headers": {"anthropic-beta": "skills-2025-10-02"},
}

Create hosted skills with Anthropic's Skills API, then put the returned skill_... ID in the list.

docs.title: allowed-tools
docs.text: For hosted skills, allowed-tools grants are applied by Anthropic. For local and URL skills the field is informational: activate_skill includes a note listing the requirements, but the agent does not receive those tools. Add them to the agent's prompt yourself, or use a hosted skill for API-level tool grants.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Rely on progressive disclosure. Many installed skills cost only a catalog line each until one is activated.
  • Write description as a trigger, not a title. "Extract PDF text, fill forms, merge files. Use when handling PDFs." beats "PDF utilities".
  • Keep SKILL.md short and move long reference material into files the model can load on demand.
  • Scope skills to the agents that need them. Per-agent lists replace the global list.
  • Commit .agents/skills/ next to your prompts and configs.
  • Cache remote skills. A tactic rebuilds its agents on every call, so URL skills are fetched again each time (and local directories rescanned). An unreachable URL logs a warning and the skill is skipped.

docs.title: Context management
docs.text: Set context_manager (or context_manager: in config) to prune or rewrite the working dialog before each model call; the canonical dialog keeps growing untouched. The built-in DefaultContextManager truncates old messages to fit the model's context window. See Dialog.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
Give the agent a BaseStreamHandler to receive chunks while the full InvokeResult is still assembled at the end:

from lllm.runtimes.native.invokers.base import BaseStreamHandler


class PrintStream(BaseStreamHandler):
    def handle_chunk(self, chunk_content: str, chunk_response):
        print(chunk_content, end="", flush=True)


agent.stream_handler = PrintStream()
message = agent.respond()

See Invokers.

docs.title: Serving hints
docs.text:
An agent knows things a model server cannot see from a single request: which calls belong to the same dialog, which dialog was forked from which (a shared prompt prefix), and how urgent a call is. inference_hints turns that into request fields for serving stacks with KV-cache-aware routing and priority scheduling:

agent_configs:
  - name: planner
    system_prompt_path: planner/system
    inference_hints:
      profile: vllm          # "openai" (default) | "dynamo" | "vllm" | "sglang"
      priority: 5            # higher is more urgent
      session_prefix: run-42

from lllm import InferenceHints

agent.inference_hints = InferenceHints(profile="dynamo", priority=2)

The session id is the dialog id being answered (prefixed with session_prefix), and a forked dialog also sends its parent's id. Each profile maps these to its own headers and body fields (x-session-id, x-dynamo-session-id, nvext.agent_hints, vLLM priority and cache_salt), merged into model_args as extra_headers / extra_body without overriding values you set yourself. Servers ignore headers they do not use, so the default openai profile is always safe.

Inference Hints covers every profile and field, the server-side flags for Dynamo, vLLM, and SGLang, and what a server receives.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
Pass return_session=True to get the full AgentCallSession:

from lllm import Tactic


class ResearchTactic(Tactic):
    name = "research"
    agent_group = ["researcher"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        agent = self.agents["researcher"]
        agent.open("research", prompt_args={"topic": task})

        session = agent.respond(return_session=True)

        print(session.state)                          # "success"
        print(session.delivery.parsed)                # parser output
        print(session.cost)                           # tokens and dollars, all attempts
        print(session.exception_retries_count)        # repairs needed
        print(len(session.interrupts))                # tool rounds
        print(agent.current_dialog.tree_overview())   # dialog tree incl. working forks

        return session.delivery.content

Inside a tactic, every respond() is also recorded on the tactic's TacticCallSession; see Tactics.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
LLLM stands for Low-Level Language Model. At its core is a small, readable framework for building advanced agentic systems: program synthesis loops, neuro-symbolic pipelines, multi-agent research systems, anything where you need to see and steer every turn an agent takes. That framework is the native runtime, lllm.runtimes.native.

"Low-level" here means control and transparency. It does not mean boilerplate.

  • Every turn is a declared contract. A Prompt bundles the template, the parser that defines a valid reply, the tools the model may call, and the handlers that decide what to say when parsing fails or a tool returns.
  • The loop that enforces it is short enough to read. Agent.respond() calls the model, parses the reply, runs tools, and routes failures through your handlers, with explicit retry caps.
  • State is explicit. Each agent's conversation is a Dialog, a tree you can fork, inspect, serialize, and replay.
  • Everything is typed with Pydantic: prompts, messages, call sessions, and tactic inputs and outputs.
  • It comes with research tooling: an in-process Python interpreter and a Jupyter sandbox for agents that run code, proxies for agents that need many API endpoints, agent skills, and access to 100+ model providers through LiteLLM.
pip install "lllm-core[native]"     # LiteLLM-backed agents
pip install "lllm-core[sandbox]"    # optional Jupyter sandbox

docs.title: The four abstractions
docs.text:
LLLM organises an agentic system into four layers, each with a single responsibility.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Tactic                        │  ← "the program"
│  (orchestrates agents, owns the task interface)  │
├────────────────┬────────────────┬────────────────┤
│    Agent A     │    Agent B     │    Agent C     │  ← "the callers"
│  (model+loop)  │  (model+loop)  │  (model+loop)  │
├────────────────┴────────────────┴────────────────┤
│               Prompts (functions)                │  ← "the calls"
│  template · parser · tools · handlers            │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│               Dialogs (state)                    │  ← "mental state"
│  per-agent message history, fork-able tree       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Abstraction Role Class Tactic The program. Takes a task, wires agents together, returns a result. Tactic (set agent_group to get agents) Agent The caller. A system prompt, a model, and the call loop. Agent Prompt The function. One turn's template, output contract, tools, and handlers. Prompt Dialog The agent's mental state. Append-only messages in a fork-able tree. Dialog

All four import from the top-level package:

from lllm import Agent, Dialog, Prompt, Tactic, tool

lllm exports the native vocabulary (Tactic, Prompt, Agent, Dialog, Message, Function, tool, tactictool, Runtime, load_runtime, resolve_config, build_tactic, BaseProxy, ...). lllm.runtimes.native holds the same objects plus the parser and handler classes (DefaultTagParser, BaseParser, BaseHandler, DefaultSimpleHandler, ...); import those from there, because lllm.DefaultTagParser is the runtime-agnostic parser, whose tags are optional.

lllm.Tactic is also LLLM's protocol tactic: the same class you serve, package, and compose with other runtimes. See How native fits into the rest of LLLM.

docs.title: An agentic system is a program
docs.text:
A tactic's call() is ordinary Python. Agents are called like functions, and the control flow (sequencing, branching, loops, parallelism) is code you write and can debug.

from lllm import Tactic


class DraftAndReview(Tactic):
    name = "draft_and_review"
    agent_group = ["writer", "reviewer"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        writer, reviewer = self.agents["writer"], self.agents["reviewer"]

        writer.open("draft", prompt_args={"topic": task})
        draft = writer.respond().content

        reviewer.open("review")
        reviewer.receive(draft, name="writer")
        return reviewer.respond().content


config = {
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o-mini"},
    "agent_configs": [
        {"name": "writer", "system_prompt": "Write a one-paragraph brief about {topic}."},
        {"name": "reviewer", "system_prompt": "Tighten the draft you receive."},
    ],
}

tactic = DraftAndReview(config)
session = tactic("dialog trees", return_session=True)
print(session.delivery)
print(session.summary())          # agent calls, cost, state

Why it matters. A tactic is stateless: every call gets fresh agents and fresh dialogs, so concurrent calls (tactic.bcall(tasks)) never share mutable state. Each call returns or records a TacticCallSession with every agent call and its cost. See Tactics.

docs.title: A prompt is a function signature
docs.text:
The agent is the function and the Prompt is its type signature. The invoker reads the parser, output format, and handlers from the prompt that sent the latest turn, and the agent loop keeps going until the reply satisfies it. Plain text sent with agent.receive() has no parser; send a Prompt with agent.receive_prompt() when the turn needs a contract. Tools combine: the agent's own tools (those on its system prompt) are offered on every turn, alongside the turn prompt's.

from lllm import Prompt, tool
from lllm.runtimes.native import DefaultTagParser


@tool(description="Evaluate an arithmetic expression", prop_desc={"expr": "e.g. 2*(3+4)"})
def calc(expr: str) -> str:
    return str(eval(expr, {"__builtins__": {}}))   # demo only


solve = Prompt(
    path="math/solve",
    prompt="Solve: {question}\nShow work in <work> and the result in <answer>.",
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["work", "answer"]),
    function_list=[calc],
)

print(solve(question="What is 17 * 23?"))
print(solve.parse("<work>17*23</work><answer>391</answer>")["xml_tags"]["answer"])

With an agent, the same prompt becomes one validated call:

agent.open("main")
agent.receive_prompt(solve, {"question": "What is 17 * 23?"})
reply = agent.respond()                      # tool calls and repairs happen inside
answer = reply.parsed["xml_tags"]["answer"][0]

Why it matters. Parse failures become repair turns ("Error: {error_message}. Please fix." by default) in a forked working dialog, so the canonical history only records the valid reply. Retries are capped (max_exception_retry), and failure surfaces as an exception rather than a silently malformed answer. The handler is a replaceable object, so the repair strategy is yours. See Prompts and Agent.

docs.title: A dialog is the agent's mental state
docs.text:
A dialog is what one agent has seen: not a shared global chat log. Agents share information only by passing content explicitly. Dialogs are append-only and fork into trees.

from lllm import Dialog, Prompt, Role

system = Prompt(path="planner/system", prompt="You are a {style} planner.")

dialog = Dialog(owner="planner")
dialog.put_prompt(system, {"style": "careful"}, role=Role.SYSTEM, name="system")
dialog.put_text("Plan the next release.", name="user")

branch = dialog.fork(last_n=1, first_k=1)    # keep system prompt + last message
branch.put_text("Assume the deadline moved up a week.", name="user")

print(dialog.tree_overview())
print(branch.parent is dialog, len(branch.messages))

Why it matters. Forking gives you speculation, alternative strategies, and context-window management without mutating history. Every dialog carries a DialogTreeNode (ids and split points only), so the full tree can be reconstructed from logs. The agent loop itself forks a working dialog at every step of a call. See Dialog.

docs.title: Configuration is declaration
docs.text:
What exists (prompts, tools, proxies, tactics, configs) is declared in an lllm.toml package; how agents are wired is declared in YAML. Python code refers to resources by namespaced URL instead of import paths.

# lllm.toml
[package]
name = "research_kit"

[prompts]
paths = ["prompts"]

[tactics]
paths = ["tactics"]

# tools/, proxies/, configs/, assets/ are discovered by default when present

# configs/default.yaml
tactic_type: draft_and_review
global:
  model_name: gpt-4o-mini
  tools: [research_kit.tools:search]
agent_configs:
  - name: writer
    system_prompt_path: research_kit:briefs/writer
  - name: reviewer
    system_prompt_path: research_kit:briefs/reviewer

from lllm import build_tactic, load_runtime, resolve_config

load_runtime()                                   # discover ./lllm.toml
tactic = build_tactic(resolve_config("default"))

lllm create my-app generates exactly this shape: lllm.toml, prompts/, configs/default.yaml, tactics/, a main.py, and an offline smoke test.

Why it matters. The system's shape is inspectable, diffable, and reproducible; swapping a model or prompt is a config change. Packages are namespaced (research_kit.prompts:briefs/writer), so you can depend on other people's prompts and tactics like libraries. Because configs hold references, not live objects, tool modules never have to build agents at import time. See Configuration and Package Discovery.

docs.title: Declaring a tool is separate from implementing it
docs.text:
A prompt can carry a bare Function declaration, a header that tells the model what it may call. The implementation is a normal @tool function in the same package. At run time LLLM binds them by exact name.

# prompts/notes.py: what the model sees
from lllm import Function, Prompt

save_note = Function(
    name="save_note",
    description="Save a research note.",
    properties={"title": {"type": "string"}, "content": {"type": "string"}},
    required=["title", "content"],
)
system = Prompt(path="system", prompt="Take notes as you go.", function_list=[save_note])

# tools/save_note.py: how it runs
from lllm import tool


@tool(name="save_note", description="Save a research note.")
def save_note(title: str, content: str) -> str:
    ...
    return f"saved {title!r}"

Why it matters. Prompts stay declarative and versionable as interfaces; implementations stay testable Python. A name mismatch fails loudly instead of silently binding the wrong callable. When declaration and implementation belong together, pass the @tool function directly instead. See Prompts.

docs.title: Tactics are tools: the recursive abstraction graph
docs.text:
A tactic is the top of the stack, yet a prompt can call one. Decorate a tactic method with @tactictool and reference the tactic by URL in a function_list; one model turn can then invoke a whole agentic subsystem.

from pydantic import BaseModel
from lllm import Prompt, Tactic, tactictool


class CodeInput(BaseModel):
    code: str


class CodeReview(Tactic):
    """Review code and list concrete issues."""
    name = "code_review"
    agent_group = ["reviewer"]

    @tactictool("code_review", config="shared_pkg:review")
    def call(self, task: CodeInput) -> str:
        reviewer = self.agents["reviewer"]
        reviewer.open("review")
        reviewer.receive(task.code)
        return reviewer.respond().content


planner = Prompt(
    path="planner/system",
    prompt="Plan the change. Request a code review before finishing.",
    function_list=["shared_pkg.tactics:code_review"],
)

Why it matters. Reusable capabilities ship as tactics, and any agent can use them as tools without knowing how many agents or prompts sit inside. The CodeInput model becomes the tool's JSON schema. See Tactics.

docs.title: Tool calling as programming: proxies
docs.text:
When an agent needs dozens of related endpoints, one function schema per endpoint does not scale. A proxy exposes an API surface as a programming environment: the agent reads endpoint docs with query_api_doc and writes Python that calls CALL_API(...) through run_python, keeping variables between calls.

import os

from lllm import BaseProxy, ProxyRegistrator


@ProxyRegistrator(path="weather", name="Weather API", description="Current conditions.")
class WeatherProxy(BaseProxy):
    base_url = "https://api.example.com/v1"   # requests go to <base_url>/<endpoint>
    api_key_name = "appid"                    # the key is sent as ?appid=<api_key>
    api_key = os.getenv("WEATHER_API_KEY")

    @BaseProxy.endpoint(
        category="current",
        endpoint="current",
        description="Current temperature for a city.",
        params={"city*": (str, "Paris")},
        response={"city": "Paris", "temp": 21.5},
    )
    def current(self, params: dict) -> dict:
        return params          # shape or validate the request parameters here

The agent writes CALL_API("weather/current", {"city": "Oslo"}) inside run_python, and LLLM sends GET https://api.example.com/v1/current?city=Oslo&appid=....

agent_configs:
  - name: analyst
    system_prompt_path: analyst/system
    tools: [my_pkg.proxies:weather]    # injects query_api_doc + run_python

Why it matters. The model composes calls, filters results, and computes with Python instead of shuttling raw JSON through the context window. See Proxies & Sandbox.

docs.title: Composing with Pydantic
docs.text:
Pydantic is the type system across the native runtime.

Typed tactic inputs and outputs. Set input_type and output_type (or input_model / output_model). The tactic validates every call, so dicts are coerced into models, and tactic.info() exports both JSON schemas.

from pydantic import BaseModel
from lllm import Tactic


class BriefIn(BaseModel):
    topic: str
    audience: str = "engineers"


class BriefOut(BaseModel):
    title: str


class Brief(Tactic):
    name = "brief"
    input_type = BriefIn
    output_type = BriefOut

    def call(self, task: BriefIn) -> BriefOut:
        return BriefOut(title=f"{task.topic} for {task.audience}")


print(Brief()({"topic": "Dialogs"}))                      # dict -> BriefIn
print(Brief().info().input_schema["required"])            # ['topic']

Structured output. Prompt(format=MyModel) asks the provider for JSON that matches the model (Chat Completions API). The reply's message.parsed holds the decoded dict:

class Report(BaseModel):
    title: str
    sources: list[str]


report_prompt = Prompt(path="report", prompt="Report on {topic}.", format=Report)

agent.open("main")
agent.receive_prompt(report_prompt, {"topic": "dialog trees"})
report = Report.model_validate(agent.respond().parsed)

Validation with repair. A parser can validate with Pydantic and raise ParseError; the agent loop then sends Pydantic's error message back to the model and asks for a fix, up to max_exception_retry times.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError
from lllm import Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import BaseParser, ParseError, find_md_blocks


class Verdict(BaseModel):
    label: str = Field(pattern="^(approve|reject)$")
    confidence: float = Field(ge=0, le=1)


class ModelParser(BaseParser):
    """Validate a ```json block against a Pydantic model."""

    def __init__(self, model: type[BaseModel]):
        self.model = model

    def parse(self, content: str, **runtime_args) -> dict:
        blocks = find_md_blocks(content, "json")
        if not blocks:
            raise ParseError("Reply with one ```json block.")
        try:
            return {"value": self.model.model_validate_json(blocks[0])}
        except ValidationError as exc:
            raise ParseError(f"The JSON does not match the schema:\n{exc}")


review = Prompt(
    path="review/verdict",
    prompt="Review this diff:\n{diff}\nReply with a ```json block matching {schema}.",
    parser=ModelParser(Verdict),
)
print(review.parse('```json\n{"label": "approve", "confidence": 0.9}\n```')["value"])

Typed tactic tools. A @tactictool method whose parameter is a BaseModel uses that model as the tool's JSON schema, and a BaseModel return value is sent back to the calling model as JSON.

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text: sequenceDiagram   participant C as Caller   participant T as Tactic.call()   participant A as Agent   participant D as Dialog   participant I as Invoker   participant F as Tools    C->>T: tactic(task)   T->>A: open(alias, prompt_args)   A->>D: system prompt   T->>A: receive(...) / receive_prompt(...)   A->>D: user turn (sets top_prompt)   T->>A: respond()   loop until a valid final reply     A->>D: fork working dialog     A->>I: call(working dialog, model, model_args)     I-->>A: InvokeResult (message, parse errors)     alt parse error       A->>D: repair prompt (working dialog only)     else tool calls       A->>F: execute Function(s)       A->>D: tool results     end   end   A->>D: append final reply   A-->>T: Message   T-->>C: result (or TacticCallSession)

docs.title: How native fits into the rest of LLLM
docs.text:
The native runtime is where agents are built. The rest of LLLM is the outer interface that lets a native system be served, packaged, and mixed with other runtimes, and a native tactic plugs into it directly: lllm.Tactic is both the program class and the protocol tactic.

flowchart LR N["lllm.Tactic<br/>call() · agents · prompts · dialogs"] --> P["protocol surface<br/>run / arun / info"] P --> S["FastAPI service<br/>create_tactic_app · lllm serve"] P --> H["lllm.toml package<br/>hub resources"] O["Other tactics<br/>(Pydantic AI, Python, remote)"] -->|tactic_as_function| N
  • Protocol. Every tactic has validated run() / arun(), accepts a CallContext (passed to call(context=...) when call takes it), and describes itself with info(); runtime_kind is "native" for tactics that write call(). See Tactics and Tactic protocol.
  • Services. Pass the tactic to lllm.create_tactic_app, or point lllm serve at it or at a factory that builds it (lllm serve my_pkg.tactics:build; see Factories and handlers). See Services.
  • Packages. The same lllm.toml that drives native discovery also carries hub metadata. See Package Manifest and Hub.
  • Other runtimes. tactic_as_function(tactic) turns any protocol tactic into a native Function a prompt can call; tactic.as_tool() turns a tactic into a plain Python callable for other agent frameworks. NativeTacticAdapter remains for objects that only look like tactics (a class with call() or run() that does not subclass Tactic).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The native runtime uses two configuration formats: lllm.toml declares the package (where prompts, tools, proxies, configs, and tactics live), and YAML files declare the agents. Together they wire up an entire agentic system without hardcoding paths or model choices in Python. Configuration is declaration: the shape of the system is data you can read, diff, and swap.

docs.title: lllm.toml: the package manifest
docs.text:
Place lllm.toml at the project root. lllm create my-app (templates minimal, the default, plus pipeline, proxy, research, service, or a folder containing lllm-template.toml) generates a project with this file, prompts/, configs/default.yaml, tactics/, a main.py that calls load_runtime(), and an offline smoke test.

[package]
name = "my_system"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Research assistant"

[prompts]
paths = ["prompts"]

[tools]
paths = ["tools"]

[proxies]
paths = ["proxies"]

[configs]
paths = ["configs"]

[tactics]
paths = ["tactics"]

[dependencies]
packages = ["./packages/shared_lib"]

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
Section Purpose Default folder [package] name, version, description. Every resource is namespaced under name (default: the folder name). — [prompts] Folders scanned for Prompt objects. prompts/ [tools] Folders scanned for @tool Function objects; other files there are registered as lazy data resources. tools/ [proxies] Folders scanned for BaseProxy subclasses. proxies/ [configs] Folders of YAML agent configs, loaded lazily. configs/ [tactics] Folders scanned for Tactic subclasses with a name. tactics/ [assets] Folders of data files, loaded lazily. assets/ [services] Folders of service files: module-level ASGI apps (FastAPI/Starlette) and service spec files (.json, .yaml, .toml) loaded as data. services/ [dependencies] packages = [...]: other packages to load, each into its own namespace. —

A section's paths replace its default folder; a section you omit falls back to the default folder if it exists. Paths are relative to the lllm.toml. Any other table with paths is a custom section for packaging data files. Entries accept under prefixes ("./vendor/prompts under vendor") and dependencies accept as aliases ("./pkgs/shared as shared"). The full rules (keys, namespaces, aliases, re-exports, custom sections) are in Package Discovery.

The same file can also describe the package for the LLLM hub: [package] keys such as org and kind, and named resources such as [tactics.brief] with an entry. Native discovery reads only [package] name/version/description, [dependencies] packages, each section's paths, and custom sections. It ignores hub sections (schemas, channels, snapshots, runs, config, docs, examples, requirements, card) unless one sets paths, which makes it a custom section like any other. See Package Manifest and Hub.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
Nothing is loaded at import time. Load the package into the default runtime at startup:

from lllm import load_runtime

runtime = load_runtime()                    # nearest lllm.toml, searching upward from cwd
runtime = load_runtime("path/to/lllm.toml") # explicit file (or folder)

load_runtime() looks for $LLLM_CONFIG first, then lllm.toml, .lllm.toml, or LLLM.toml in the working directory and its parents. It also loads drop-in packages from lllm_packages/ and ~/.lllm/packages/. See Runtime & Registries.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Purpose LLLM_CONFIG Path to an lllm.toml file or to a folder containing one; overrides the search.

docs.title: Multiple environments
docs.text: LLLM_CONFIG=lllm.prod.toml python main.py

docs.title: Agent YAML configs
docs.text: Agent config files live in configs/ and describe how a tactic's agents are built. They are loaded lazily, only when load_config() or resolve_config() reads them.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
base: ...              # optional: inherit from another config (no .yaml suffix)

tactic_type: analytica # optional: which registered tactic build_tactic() creates

global:                # defaults merged into every agent in this file
  model_name: gpt-4o
  api_type: completion
  model_args:
    temperature: 0.1
  max_exception_retry: 3
  max_interrupt_steps: 5
  max_llm_recall: 3
  tools:
    - shared_pkg.tools:search
    - shared_pkg.tactics:code_review
    - shared_pkg.proxies:market_data

agent_configs:
  - name: analyzer
    system_prompt_path: analytica/analyzer_system
    model_args:
      max_completion_tokens: 20000

  - name: synthesizer
    model_name: gpt-4o-mini            # overrides global
    system_prompt: "You are a synthesizer."
    model_args:
      temperature: 0.3                 # overrides global

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text:
Key Read by Meaning base resolve_config Parent config name to inherit from. tactic_type build_tactic Registered tactic name to build when name= is not given. global Tactic with agent_group Defaults deep-merged into every agent entry. agent_configs Tactic with agent_group List of agent entries, each with a name. invoker Tactic with agent_group Invoker name (default "litellm"); see Invokers. invoker_config Tactic with agent_group Dict passed to the invoker builder (default: the whole config). max_workers Tactic Default thread-pool size for bcall / ccall (default 4).

Anything else at the top level is yours to read in call() via self.config.

docs.title: Per-agent fields
docs.text:
Field Required Description name Yes Agent name; must match an entry in the tactic's agent_group. model_name Yes (or from global) Model id, e.g. gpt-4o, anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5, ollama/llama3. system_prompt One of Inline system prompt string (may contain {variables}). system_prompt_path these two Registered prompt, e.g. analytica/system or my_pkg:analytica/system. api_type No "completion" (default) or "response" (OpenAI Responses API). model_args No Provider arguments (temperature, max_tokens, ...). Deep-merged with global. max_exception_retry No Repair attempts after parse failures. Default 3. max_interrupt_steps No Tool-call rounds per respond(). Default 5. max_llm_recall No Retries after provider errors. Default 0. max_rate_limit_retries No Retries after rate-limit errors, with exponential backoff up to 60 s. Default 8. tools No Tool, tactic-tool, or proxy refs added to the system prompt. proxy No Proxy settings; see Proxies & Sandbox. skills No Skill entries; see Agent. context_manager No {type: ..., max_tokens: ...}; no type means the default manager, type: null disables it. See Dialog. inference_hints No Serving hints sent with each call; see Inference Hints. extra_settings No Free-form dict kept on the AgentSpec for your own code.

Unrecognized keys are added to model_args, with a warning that names them, so typos are visible.

docs.title: Global merge
docs.text:
global provides defaults for every agent and each entry overrides it. The merge is deep: dicts merge recursively, while lists and scalars are replaced. So you can set temperature globally and override only max_tokens per agent:

global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  model_args:
    temperature: 0.1

agent_configs:
  - name: creative_writer
    system_prompt: "You are a creative writer."
    model_args:
      temperature: 0.9        # overrides global
      max_tokens: 4000        # added to global model_args

Result: creative_writer gets model_name: gpt-4o and model_args: {temperature: 0.9, max_tokens: 4000}.

For list fields such as tools and skills, a per-agent list replaces the global list, so one agent can opt into a different capability surface. proxy and context_manager blocks are dicts, so they merge.

docs.title: Agent tools
docs.text:
tools attaches package resources to an agent:

global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  tools:
    - shared_pkg.tools:search
    - shared_pkg.tactics:code_review
    - shared_pkg.tactics:research#summarize
    - shared_pkg.proxies:market_data

agent_configs:
  - name: analyst
    system_prompt_path: system/analyst

  - name: writer
    system_prompt_path: system/writer
    tools: []   # replaces the global tools; writer gets none
Entry Becomes shared_pkg.tools:search A regular Function created with @tool. shared_pkg.tactics:code_review The tactic's default @tactictool. shared_pkg.tactics:research#summarize A named tactic-tool method. shared_pkg.proxies:market_data A proxy: adds query_api_doc, run_python (interpreter mode), and an API directory to the system prompt.

This is the config-level form of the decoupled tool style: the config declares what belongs to the agent's surface, and the implementations come from package resources. Regular tool and tactic refs stay strings when the agent is built and are resolved only when the prompt runs; bare names and pkg:name shorthand resolve relative to the system prompt's package, then the default namespace. Proxy refs must be explicit (pkg.proxies:name) because they are resolved at build time to inject the proxy block.

Keep tool modules declarative at import time: define @tool functions and BaseProxy classes there, and construct any agent a tool needs inside the tool function body. See Agent for when these tools are offered to the model.

docs.title: Inheritance via base
docs.text:
Configs inherit with base. Inheritance is recursive and uses a deep merge: dict values merge, lists and scalars replace.

configs/
  base.yaml
  experiments/
    ablation.yaml
    full.yaml

# base.yaml
global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  model_args:
    temperature: 0.1
agent_configs:
  - name: analyzer
    system_prompt_path: research/system

# experiments/ablation.yaml
base: base                      # inherits configs/base.yaml
global:
  model_args:
    max_tokens: 500             # added to base's model_args
agent_configs:                  # replaces base's list (lists replace, dicts merge)
  - name: analyzer
    system_prompt_path: research/system_no_cot

# experiments/full.yaml
base: experiments/ablation      # chain: full -> ablation -> base
global:
  model_name: o4-mini           # overrides all the way up

from lllm import resolve_config

config = resolve_config("experiments/full")
config["global"]["model_name"]                  # 'o4-mini'
config["global"]["model_args"]["temperature"]   # 0.1  (from base)
config["global"]["model_args"]["max_tokens"]    # 500  (from ablation)

The result has no base key. Circular inheritance raises ValueError.

base names are resolved like any config ref: a bare name looks in the runtime's default namespace (the root package). A config that ships in a package meant to be used as a dependency should name its parent with the package prefix (base: shared_pkg:common) so it resolves from any root.

docs.title: Recommended layout
docs.text:
configs/
├── default.yaml            # main config
├── experiments/
│   ├── fast.yaml           # base: default, swaps to smaller models
│   └── ablation.yaml       # base: default, swaps prompts
└── vendor/                 # pinned dependency configs
    └── A.yaml              # base: "A:default" plus overrides

docs.title: Managing dependency configs
docs.text: When your package depends on other packages, keep the model simple: each package configures its own agents. Your config declares your agents and may point at prompts from dependencies by namespaced path.

docs.title: Assembly config
docs.text:
# configs/default.yaml
global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  model_args:
    temperature: 0.1

agent_configs:
  - name: orchestrator
    system_prompt_path: my_pkg:orchestrator/system

  - name: analyzer
    system_prompt_path: A:analysis/system        # prompt from dependency A
    model_args:
      max_completion_tokens: 20000

  - name: searcher
    system_prompt_path: B:search/system          # prompt from dependency B
    model_name: gpt-4o-mini

Prompt references point into dependencies, like importing a function. Configuration decisions (model, temperature, retries) stay yours.

docs.title: Vendoring configs for sub-tactics
docs.text:
