When you compose a dependency's tactic, pull its config and apply your overrides with vendor_config:

from lllm import get_default_runtime
from lllm.runtimes.native.core.config import vendor_config

cfg = vendor_config("A:default", {
    "global": {
        "model_name": "gpt-4o",
        "model_args": {"temperature": 0.05},
    },
})

get_default_runtime().register_config("vendor/A", cfg, namespace="my_pkg.configs")

Or as a YAML file:

# configs/vendor/A.yaml
base: "A:default"
global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  model_args:
    temperature: 0.05

vendor_config(source, overrides=None, *, runtime=None, registry=None) resolves the full base chain, deep-merges your overrides, and returns a standalone dict with no base key:

cfg = vendor_config("A:default")                                         # resolve only
cfg = vendor_config("A:default", {"global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o-mini"}})

import yaml
with open("configs/vendor/A.yaml", "w") as f:
    yaml.dump(cfg, f)                                                    # save to disk

docs.title: Loading configs in Python
docs.text:
from lllm import build_tactic, load_config, resolve_config

cfg = load_config("default")                    # raw, no inheritance
cfg = load_config("my_pkg:experiments/fast")    # package-qualified

cfg = resolve_config("experiments/full")        # with the base chain (recommended)

tactic = build_tactic(resolve_config("default"))

Configs can also be plain dicts or Pydantic models passed straight to a tactic: MyTactic({"global": {...}, "agent_configs": [...]}).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A Dialog is one agent's internal view of a conversation: its mental state. It holds an ordered, append-only list of Message objects, tracks which Prompt governs the next model turn (top_prompt), and forks into branches.

Each dialog is owned by one agent and carries a DialogTreeNode that records its position in a dialog tree. That is what makes branching, speculation, and session reconstruction from logs possible.

A Message is a clean record of one turn. Per-invocation diagnostics (raw provider responses, retries, the model args actually sent) live on InvokeResult and AgentCallSession, not on the message.

from lllm import Dialog, Message, Prompt, Role

docs.title: Message
docs.text:
A Message captures what was said in one turn.

Field Type Description role Roles SYSTEM, USER, ASSISTANT, TOOL, TOOL_CALL content str \| List[Dict] Text, a base64 image, or multipart content name str Sender: "user", "system", an agent name, a tool name function_calls List[FunctionCall] Tool calls requested by the model modality Modalities TEXT or IMAGE (also AUDIO, FUNCTION_CALL) logprobs List[TokenLogprob] Token log probabilities, when the provider returns them parsed Dict[str, Any] Output of the prompt's parser (or decoded format JSON) model str \| None Model that produced the message usage Dict[str, Any] Provider token usage plus LLLM's cost fields metadata Dict[str, Any] Arbitrary metadata (tool_call_id, dialog_id, caption, ...) api_type APITypes COMPLETION or RESPONSE vectors List[float] Placeholder for embedding vectors

Computed properties:

message.cost              # InvokeCost: token counts and dollar costs from usage
message.is_function_call  # True if the model requested tool calls
message.sanitized_name    # name safe for provider APIs (alphanumerics, _ and -, max 64 chars)

InvokeCost has token fields (prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens, cached_prompt_tokens, reasoning_tokens, audio tokens), per-token rates, and dollar fields (prompt_cost, completion_cost, cost). Costs add with +; str(cost) prints a readable summary.

Messages are Pydantic models: message.to_dict() / Message.from_dict(d) round-trip every field. Roles.SYSTEM is sent to providers with the "developer" role.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
Inside an agent, dialogs are created by Agent.open(), which builds the dialog, seeds it with the rendered system prompt, and registers it under an alias:

agent.open("planning", prompt_args={"language": "Python"}, session_name="run_001")

You can also build one directly, which is useful for tests, offline dataset generation, or replaying a conversation:

from lllm import Dialog, Prompt, Role

system = Prompt(path="assistant/system", prompt="You are {style}.")

dialog = Dialog(owner="assistant", session_name="demo")
dialog.put_prompt(system, {"style": "concise"}, role=Role.SYSTEM, name="system")
dialog.put_text("Explain dialog trees in one sentence.")

Dialog(session_name=None, top_prompt=None, runtime=None, owner=None): the session name defaults to a timestamp, and the runtime to the default runtime (used to resolve prompt paths).

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text: Every dialog is owned by the agent that created it. owner records the agent name, and the system message is always that agent's persona. Do not hand one agent's dialog to another: the second agent would answer under the first one's system prompt. Pass content between agents instead.

docs.title: The top_prompt calling convention
docs.text:
top_prompt is the active calling convention: the Prompt whose parser, format, tools, and handler govern the next model turn.

Operation top_prompt after it put_prompt(prompt, ...) prompt put_text(text, ...) A fresh plain prompt for that text (no parser, no tools of its own) put_image(image, ...) Unchanged fork() Inherited by the child

When the agent loop starts and top_prompt is None, it uses the agent's system prompt. It then adds the agent's own tools (those on its system prompt) to the top prompt unless that prompt sets agent_tools=False, so a plain-text turn still has the agent's tools; see Agent. During the loop, tool results are appended with put_prompt using the handler's interrupt prompt, so the contract (tools, parser) carries through the tool rounds.

docs.title: Appending messages
docs.text:
Three primitives cover all cases.

put_prompt(prompt, prompt_args=None, name="user", metadata=None, role=Roles.USER) is stateful: it renders the template, appends the message, and advances top_prompt. Use it for any message that carries a calling convention. A string is resolved as a prompt path through the dialog's runtime.

dialog.put_prompt(my_prompt, {"task": task_str}, name="user")
dialog.put_prompt("my_pkg.prompts:research/agent", {"topic": "transformers"})

put_text(text, name="user", metadata=None, role=Roles.USER) appends raw text, for unstructured input.

dialog.put_text("What is the capital of France?")

put_image(image, caption=None, name="user", metadata=None, role=Roles.USER) appends an image message. It accepts a file path (str or Path), a PIL Image, or a base64 string of a PNG, JPEG, WebP, or GIF; the caption is stored in metadata["caption"].

dialog.put_image("screenshot.png", caption="Current state of the UI")

All three return the new Message and go through dialog.append(message), which stamps metadata["dialog_id"].

docs.title: Inspection
docs.text:
dialog.tail        # last Message, or None
dialog.head        # first Message (the system prompt), or None
dialog.messages    # the message list (treat as read-only)
dialog.cost        # InvokeCost summed over all messages
dialog.overview()  # one line per message, contents truncated to 100 chars
dialog.dialog_id   # this dialog's id (from its tree node)

[0. system (developer)]: You are concise.

[1. user (user)]: Explain dialog trees in one sentence.

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
data = dialog.to_dict()
restored = Dialog.from_dict(data, runtime=runtime)

to_dict() records the messages, session_name, owner, the tree node, the child dialogs (recursively), and the top prompt both as data (top_prompt) and as a registry key (top_prompt_path). The result is JSON-safe: the top prompt's tools are stored as schemas (implementations are not included) and a Pydantic format model as its import path plus JSON schema; see Prompts.

import json

json.dumps(dialog.to_dict())       # ready to store

from_dict() rebuilds the tree and restores top_prompt from the embedded data, falling back to looking up top_prompt_path in the runtime (with a warning if it is missing). Tool implementations are re-bound by name to registered @tool resources when the prompt next runs. Loading never imports code: a saved format model is used only when its module is already imported, and its stored JSON schema otherwise.

docs.title: DialogTreeNode
docs.text:
Every Dialog owns exactly one DialogTreeNode, a lightweight record of its position in the tree. Nodes hold ids and structure only, no message payloads, so the topology can be rebuilt from a flat log store.

Field Type Description dialog_id str Globally unique hex UUID owner str \| None Agent that owns the dialog parent_id str \| None Parent's dialog_id (None for a root) split_point int \| None Number of messages copied into this child last_n int \| None Trailing messages kept from the parent first_k int \| None Leading messages kept from the parent children_ids List[str] Direct children's ids

Nodes also keep live in-process _parent / _children references for fast traversal.

node = dialog.tree_node
node.is_root        # True if no parent
node.depth          # number of forks from the root
node.subtree_ids()  # BFS over live children: all reachable ids, self included
node.to_dict()      # serializable form; DialogTreeNode.from_dict(d) restores it

On the dialog itself: dialog.parent, dialog.children, dialog.is_root, and dialog.depth.

docs.title: Forking
docs.text:
fork(last_n=0, first_k=1) creates a child dialog. It deep-copies the selected messages, links a new DialogTreeNode to the parent's, wires the live parent/child references, and inherits session_name, owner, runtime, and top_prompt.

child = dialog.fork()                    # full copy
child = dialog.fork(last_n=3, first_k=1) # first message (system prompt) + last 3
child = dialog.fork(last_n=5, first_k=2) # first 2 + last 5

last_n / first_k are for context-window management: keep the system prompt and the recent conversation, drop the middle. first_k only applies when last_n > 0, and a last_n that covers every message gives a full copy. The parent is never modified.

The agent loop forks a working dialog at the start of each step, so repair prompts and failed replies stay out of the canonical dialog; only the successful reply is appended to it.

docs.title: Visualizing the tree
docs.text:
print(dialog.tree_overview())

[a1b2c3d4] owner=coder msgs=5 split@None
  └─ [e5f6a7b8] owner=coder msgs=5 split@5
  └─ [c9d0e1f2] owner=coder msgs=3 split@3 (last_n=2, first_k=1)

After an agent call, the working forks show up here, which is a quick way to see how many repair attempts a turn needed.

docs.title: Agent-level dialog access
docs.text:
Most code works with dialogs through the agent's alias system:

agent.open("planning")             # create and activate
agent.receive("What's the plan?")  # append to the active dialog
response = agent.respond()         # run the agent loop

agent.open("execution")            # second dialog
agent.switch("planning")           # switch back

agent.fork("planning", "planning_alt", last_n=2, switch=True)

agent.current_dialog               # the active Dialog
agent.dialogs                      # dict of alias -> Dialog
agent.active_alias                 # current alias

See Agent for the full API.

docs.title: Example: a complete single-agent turn
docs.text:
from lllm import Tactic


class Summarizer(Tactic):
    name = "summarizer"
    agent_group = ["assistant"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        agent = self.agents["assistant"]

        # 1. Open a dialog (the system prompt goes in automatically)
        agent.open("summarize", prompt_args={"persona": "helpful assistant"})

        # 2. Send the user's task
        agent.receive(task)

        # 3. Run the agent loop
        response = agent.respond()

        # 4. Inspect
        print(agent.current_dialog.cost)          # total token cost
        print(agent.current_dialog.overview())    # readable message log

        return response.content

tactic = Summarizer({
    "agent_configs": [
        {"name": "assistant", "model_name": "gpt-4o-mini",
         "system_prompt": "You are a {persona}. Summarise what you are given."},
    ],
})
print(tactic("LLLM dialogs are append-only trees of messages..."))

docs.title: Context manager
docs.text:
A ContextManager is a hook the agent applies to the working dialog before each model call. It can truncate, compress, or rewrite the dialog without touching the canonical history.

[canonical dialog] --fork--> [working dialog] --context_manager--> [pruned dialog] --> model

The canonical dialog grows monotonically; the pruned copy is never written back.

docs.title: Contract
docs.text:
ContextManager and DefaultContextManager live in lllm.runtimes.native.core.dialog.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from typing import ClassVar


class ContextManager(ABC):
    name: ClassVar[str]   # registry key: set it on every concrete subclass

    @abstractmethod
    def __call__(self, dialog: Dialog) -> Dialog:
        """Return a dialog that is safe to send to the model."""

__call__ may return the same dialog unchanged or a new one (typically dialog.fork(...)).

docs.title: DefaultContextManager
docs.text:
The built-in truncator. It uses litellm.token_counter (install lllm-core[native]) to measure the dialog and drops or truncates old messages until it fits the model's context window.

  1. The first message (the system prompt) is always kept.
  2. Messages are kept from the tail (most recent) inward.
  3. The border message, the oldest one that partly fits, is character-truncated and prefixed with [...earlier content truncated...].
  4. A SAFETY_BUFFER of 5,000 tokens is subtracted from the limit so calls never land at the edge of the window.
from lllm import Agent
from lllm.runtimes.native.core.dialog import DefaultContextManager

cm = DefaultContextManager("gpt-4o")                     # window size from LiteLLM's model table
cm = DefaultContextManager("gpt-4o", max_tokens=32000)   # explicit cap

agent = Agent(..., context_manager=cm)

In config:

global:
  context_manager:
    type: default        # built-in, no registration needed
    max_tokens: 128000   # optional; looked up from LiteLLM if omitted

agent_configs:
  - name: cheap_agent
    model_name: gpt-4o-mini
    context_manager:     # deep-merged with global
      max_tokens: 16000

  - name: no_prune_agent
    model_name: gpt-4o
    context_manager:
      type: null         # disabled for this agent

A context_manager block without type means the default manager, so {max_tokens: 16000} alone is enough; type: null (or no block at all) disables pruning. When the model is unknown to LiteLLM and max_tokens is not set, the window defaults to 4,096 tokens.

docs.title: Writing a custom ContextManager
docs.text:
1. Subclass ContextManager and set name.
  2. Accept model_name and max_tokens keyword arguments; the config layer constructs the class with both.
  3. Register the class on the runtime and reference it by name in config.
from lllm import Dialog
from lllm.runtimes.native.core.dialog import ContextManager


class KeepLastTurns(ContextManager):
    """Keep the system prompt and the last `n` messages."""

    name = "keep_last"

    def __init__(self, model_name: str, max_tokens: int | None = None, n: int = 8):
        self.model_name = model_name
        self.max_tokens = max_tokens
        self.n = n

    def __call__(self, dialog: Dialog) -> Dialog:
        if len(dialog.messages) <= self.n + 1:
            return dialog
        return dialog.fork(last_n=self.n, first_k=1)

runtime.register_context_manager(KeepLastTurns)   # key comes from KeepLastTurns.name

global:
  context_manager:
    type: keep_last

register_context_manager raises ValueError if the class has no name.

docs.title: Inference Hints
docs.text:
An agent knows things an inference server cannot see from a single request: which calls belong to the same reasoning chain, which chains were forked from which (and so share a prompt prefix), how urgent a call is, and roughly how long the answer will be. Serving stacks with KV-cache-aware routing and priority scheduling can use exactly that: keep a chain on the worker that already holds its prefix, warm the cache for the next turn, and schedule urgent work first.

InferenceHints lets a native agent send that knowledge with every model call. Hints are off unless you configure them.

docs.title: Turn them on
docs.text:
On an agent:

from lllm import Agent, InferenceHints, Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native.invokers import build_invoker

agent = Agent(
    name="planner",
    system_prompt=Prompt(path="planner/system", prompt="You plan."),
    model="hosted_vllm/Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct",
    llm_invoker=build_invoker({"invoker": "litellm"}),
    model_args={"api_base": "http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", "max_tokens": 512},
    inference_hints=InferenceHints(profile="dynamo", priority=5, speculative_prefill=True),
)

Or in an agent config, so every agent of a tactic gets them:

global:
  model_name: hosted_vllm/Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
  model_args:
    api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1
  inference_hints:
    profile: dynamo
    priority: 5
    speculative_prefill: true

agent_configs:
  - name: planner
    system_prompt: You plan.

docs.title: Session identity comes from dialogs
docs.text:
A dialog is one reasoning chain, so it is one session: every turn of an agent's dialog carries the same session id. A dialog created with agent.fork(...) names its parent, which tells the server that the child starts from the parent's prefix.

agent.open("main")
agent.receive("Draft a plan.")
agent.respond()                  # session = main dialog
agent.fork("main", "retry")      # child dialog shares main's prefix
agent.respond()                  # session = retry, parent = main

Session ids are the dialogs' ids. Set session_prefix (for example a run id) to get run-42:<dialog id>, or session=False to send no identity.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Profile Session identity Body fields dynamo x-dynamo-session-id, x-dynamo-parent-session-id nvext.agent_hints: priority, strict_priority, osl, speculative_prefill vllm x-session-id, x-parent-session-id priority, cache_salt sglang x-session-id, x-parent-session-id priority openai (default) x-session-id, x-parent-session-id none Field Meaning priority Higher is more urgent. The vllm profile converts it to vLLM's order, where lower runs first. strict_priority Dynamo router queue tier; higher tiers always go first. osl Expected output tokens (Dynamo). Defaults to the agent's max_tokens or max_completion_tokens. speculative_prefill Ask Dynamo to prefill the predicted next-turn prefix after this turn. cache_salt vLLM prefix-cache salt, to keep tenants' cached prefixes apart.

Unset fields are not sent. The openai profile only adds headers, which servers that do not use them ignore, so it is safe against any endpoint; send priority to vLLM or SGLang only when priority scheduling is enabled there, because they reject it otherwise. Explicit extra_headers or extra_body in model_args always win over hints.

docs.title: Server side
docs.text:
Hints change behavior only where the serving stack is configured to use them:

Stack What to enable NVIDIA Dynamo KV-aware routing; --router-queue-threshold for priority queueing; --router-track-output-blocks to use osl vLLM --scheduling-policy priority for priority; prefix caching for shared prefixes SGLang --enable-priority-scheduling; --radix-eviction-policy priority for priority-aware cache eviction

Session headers matter for routers with session affinity, which keep a chain on one worker so its KV cache is reused. Dynamo also accepts the generic x-session-id headers that the other profiles send.

docs.title: Ending a session
docs.text:
Dynamo can release per-session state as soon as a chain is finished. Build a minimal request with final_request_fields:

hints = InferenceHints(profile="dynamo")
fields = hints.final_request_fields(agent.dialogs["main"].tree_node.dialog_id)
# {"extra_headers": {"x-dynamo-session-id": "...", "x-dynamo-session-final": "true"}}

docs.title: What the server receives
docs.text:
Against a local OpenAI-compatible server, the two calls above arrive as:

{"headers": {"x-dynamo-session-id": "run-1:714fa934..."},
 "nvext": {"agent_hints": {"priority": 5, "osl": 24, "speculative_prefill": true}}}
{"headers": {"x-dynamo-session-id": "run-1:be2272f7...",
             "x-dynamo-parent-session-id": "run-1:714fa934..."},
 "nvext": {"agent_hints": {"priority": 5, "osl": 24, "speculative_prefill": true}}}

and with InferenceHints(profile="vllm", priority=2, cache_salt="tenant-a"):

{"headers": {"x-session-id": "08b7512d..."}, "priority": -2, "cache_salt": "tenant-a"}

The second Dynamo request carries the forked dialog's shared prefix (four messages) and names its parent: the structure a KV-aware router reuses.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
InferenceHints(profile="openai", session=True, session_prefix=None, priority=None, strict_priority=None, osl=None, speculative_prefill=None, cache_salt=None)

  • request_fields(*, dialog_id=None, parent_dialog_id=None, model_args=None) returns {"extra_headers": ..., "extra_body": ...} for one call.
  • final_request_fields(dialog_id) adds Dynamo's end-of-session header.
  • session_ids(dialog_id, parent_dialog_id=None) returns the ids that would be sent.

See Agent for where hints sit in the call loop, and the quick start for pointing agents at a local server.

docs.title: Invokers
docs.text:
Invokers are the execution engines of the native runtime. An invoker takes the state of a Dialog, calls a model API, and turns the response into the next Message. Keeping the invoker that small is what lets the agent loop stay provider-agnostic: retries, parsing policy, and tool execution live in the agent, while the invoker only talks to the provider.

The default invoker is built on LiteLLM, which reaches 100+ providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Vertex AI, Azure, Bedrock, local models through Ollama or vLLM, and more) through one interface.

pip install "lllm-core[native]"

docs.title: The BaseInvoker interface
docs.text:
Every invoker subclasses BaseInvoker and implements one method, call:

class BaseInvoker(ABC):
    def __init__(self, config: Dict[str, Any]):
        self.config = config

    @abstractmethod
    def call(
        self,
        dialog: Dialog,
        model: str,
        model_args: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
        parser_args: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
        responder: str = "assistant",
        metadata: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
        api_type: APITypes = APITypes.COMPLETION,
        stream_handler: Optional[BaseStreamHandler] = None,
    ) -> InvokeResult:
        ...

BaseInvoker and BaseStreamHandler live in lllm.runtimes.native.invokers.base.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description dialog The working dialog. The invoker reads dialog.top_prompt for tools, MCP servers, format, and parser. model Model id, e.g. "gpt-4o" or "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5". model_args Provider arguments (temperature, max_tokens, api_base, ...), already merged by the agent. parser_args Keyword arguments for the prompt's parser. responder Name of the agent replying; becomes the reply's name. metadata Tracking data attached to the reply's metadata; not sent to the model. api_type APITypes.COMPLETION (Chat Completions) or APITypes.RESPONSE (OpenAI Responses API). stream_handler Optional BaseStreamHandler for real-time chunks.

docs.title: Return value: InvokeResult
docs.text:
@dataclass
class InvokeResult:
    raw_response: Any = None                                         # raw provider response
    model_args: Dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)         # args actually sent
    execution_errors: List[Exception] = field(default_factory=list)  # parse/validation errors
    message: Optional[Message] = None                                # the conversational message

InvokeResult bundles the clean Message that goes into the dialog with the diagnostics the loop needs. The agent uses has_errors to decide whether to repair, and appends message to the dialog:

invoke_result = invoker.call(dialog, model, model_args, ...)
if invoke_result.has_errors:
    raise AgentException(invoke_result.error_message)   # -> exception handler
dialog.append(invoke_result.message)

docs.title: The invoker contract
docs.text:
An invoker should:

  • read tools and the output contract from dialog.top_prompt;
  • return a message with role ASSISTANT for a final reply, or TOOL_CALL with function_calls when the model asks for tools;
  • run the prompt's parser on final replies (prompt.parse(content, **parser_args)) and put any parser exception in execution_errors instead of raising, so the agent can send a repair prompt;
  • fill message.usage (token counts, and response_cost, prompt_cost, completion_cost when known) so costs aggregate;
  • raise on provider failures (network, auth, rate limits). The agent retries rate limits (an exception named RateLimitError, one with status_code == 429, or a known rate-limit message) with backoff, and treats other errors as LLM recalls.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
Streaming uses a callback so dialog state stays clean and synchronous. Subclass BaseStreamHandler:

from lllm.runtimes.native.invokers.base import BaseStreamHandler


class ConsoleStreamer(BaseStreamHandler):
    def handle_chunk(self, chunk_content: str, chunk_response):
        print(chunk_content, end="", flush=True)


agent.stream_handler = ConsoleStreamer()              # used by every respond()
invoke_result = invoker.call(dialog, "gpt-4o", stream_handler=ConsoleStreamer())

The invoker streams text chunks to the handler as they arrive and still returns a complete InvokeResult at the end. chunk_response is the raw chunk (a Chat Completions chunk or a Responses API event), for anything beyond text.

docs.title: The LiteLLM invoker
docs.text:
from lllm.runtimes.native.invokers import build_invoker

invoker = build_invoker({"invoker": "litellm"})
# equivalently:
from lllm.runtimes.native.invokers.litellm import LiteLLMInvoker
invoker = LiteLLMInvoker({})

A Tactic with agent_group builds this invoker for you unless its config names another one.

docs.title: 1. Model names
docs.text:
LiteLLM routes by model prefix:

  • OpenAI: gpt-4o or openai/gpt-4o
  • Anthropic: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5
  • Google: gemini/gemini-2.5-pro
  • Ollama (local): ollama/llama3
  • Azure: azure/my-gpt4-deployment

See the LiteLLM providers for every supported model.

docs.title: 2. API keys
docs.text:
LiteLLM reads the standard environment variables:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
export GEMINI_API_KEY="..."

When the module is imported, LLLM checks provider groups that need several variables and raises ValueError for a partial setup: Vertex AI (VERTEXAI_PROJECT, VERTEXAI_LOCATION), NVIDIA NIM (NVIDIA_NIM_API_KEY, NVIDIA_NIM_API_BASE), and Azure (AZURE_API_KEY, AZURE_API_BASE, AZURE_API_VERSION). If no known provider variable is set it logs a warning, which you can ignore for Ollama.

docs.title: 3. Provider arguments (model_args)
docs.text:
Pass standard or provider-specific arguments through model_args (in config or on the agent):

model_args = {
    "temperature": 0.2,
    "max_tokens": 4096,
    "api_base": "http://localhost:11434",   # local deployments
}

The invoker always sends drop_params=True, so an argument a provider does not support (say presence_penalty on Anthropic) is dropped instead of failing the call. Request token log probabilities with {"logprobs": True, "top_logprobs": 5}; they land on message.logprobs. See LiteLLM's completion input and responses input for every argument.

docs.title: 4. Errors
docs.text: LiteLLM maps provider errors to OpenAI-style exceptions (RateLimitError, ContextWindowExceededError, AuthenticationError, APIConnectionError). The invoker lets them propagate and the agent decides: a rate limit (RateLimitError or HTTP 429) is retried with exponential backoff, min(60, 2**n) seconds plus up to 1 s of jitter, up to max_rate_limit_retries times (default 8); other errors are retried up to max_llm_recall times (default 0) before being re-raised. Parse failures never raise from the invoker; they arrive as execution_errors and go to the prompt's exception handler. Malformed JSON in tool-call arguments is reported the same way.

docs.title: 5. Costs
docs.text: For every response the invoker records token usage plus dollar figures from LiteLLM's pricing table (response_cost, prompt_cost, completion_cost, and the per-token rates) on message.usage, which message.cost, session.cost, and dialog.cost aggregate.

docs.title: 6. Chat Completions vs. Responses API
docs.text:
api_type selects the API (per agent, or api_type: in config):

  • APITypes.COMPLETION (default) uses Chat Completions.
    • Prompt.format enables structured output: a Pydantic class is sent as response_format, a dict requests {"type": "json_object"}, and the reply is decoded with json.loads into message.parsed.
    • Function tools and MCP servers from the prompt are sent as tools.
  • APITypes.RESPONSE uses OpenAI's Responses API.
    • Prompt.format is rejected (ValueError).
    • addon_args={"web_search": True} adds {"type": "web_search_preview"}, and addon_args={"computer_use": {...}} adds a computer_use_preview tool (display size and environment from the dict, defaulting to 1280×800 "browser").
    • max_output_tokens comes from max_output_tokens or max_completion_tokens in model_args (default 32000); truncation and tool_choice default to "auto".
    • Reasoning summaries, when present, are stored in message.metadata["reasoning"].

Both go through the same agent loop; only the wire format differs.

docs.title: Custom invokers
docs.text:
Any class that honours the contract can drive agents: a different SDK, a local model server, a cache, or a scripted model for tests.

from lllm import Message, Role
from lllm.runtimes.native import InvokeResult
from lllm.runtimes.native.invokers.base import BaseInvoker


class EchoInvoker(BaseInvoker):
    """Offline invoker: answers by echoing the last message."""

    def call(self, dialog, model, model_args=None, parser_args=None,
             responder="assistant", metadata=None, api_type=None, stream_handler=None):
        prompt = dialog.top_prompt
        content = f"echo: {dialog.tail.content}"
        errors, parsed = [], {}
        if prompt.parser is not None:
            try:
                parsed = prompt.parse(content, **(parser_args or {}))
            except Exception as exc:          # hand parse errors to the agent loop
                errors.append(exc)
        message = Message(
            role=Role.ASSISTANT,
            name=responder,
            content=content,
            parsed=parsed,
            model=model,
            metadata=dict(metadata or {}),
        )
        return InvokeResult(message=message, model_args=dict(model_args or {}),
                            execution_errors=errors)

Use it directly:

from lllm import Agent, Prompt

agent = Agent(
    name="tester",
    system_prompt=Prompt(path="test/system", prompt="You are a test double."),
    model="echo",
    llm_invoker=EchoInvoker({}),
)
agent.open("main")
agent.receive("ping")
print(agent.respond().content)   # echo: ping

Or register a builder and select it from tactic config:

from lllm import register_invoker

register_invoker("echo", lambda invoker_config: EchoInvoker(invoker_config))

invoker: echo
invoker_config:        # optional; passed to the builder (default: the whole config)
  latency_ms: 0
agent_configs:
  - name: tester
    model_name: echo
    system_prompt: You are a test double.

register_invoker(name, builder, *, overwrite=False) raises if the name is taken unless overwrite=True; build_invoker(config) looks up config["invoker"] (default "litellm") and calls the builder with config.get("invoker_config", config). Scripted invokers like this are the easiest way to unit-test tactics without network access.

docs.title: Logging & Sessions
docs.text:
The native runtime gives you two orthogonal systems:

  • Session records. Every tactic call produces a TacticCallSession holding every agent call, every model invocation, every repair and tool round, and the cost. Dialogs keep the full message trees. Attach an observer to persist them wherever you like.
  • Terminal logging. Internal diagnostics go through Python's standard logging module under the lllm.runtimes.native logger hierarchy.

docs.title: Session records
docs.text:
One tactic call is the unit of record. From the top down:

TacticCallSession                 one tactic(task) call
├── delivery / error / error_traceback / state
├── agent_sessions[agent_name] -> [AgentCallSession, ...]      one per respond()
│   ├── delivery                  the final Message
│   ├── exception_retries         parse failures per loop step
│   ├── interrupts                tool calls per loop step
│   ├── llm_recalls               provider errors per loop step
│   └── invoke_traces[step] -> [InvokeResult, ...]
│       ├── raw_response          the provider's response object
│       ├── model_args            what was actually sent
│       ├── execution_errors
│       └── message               the Message produced
└── sub_tactic_sessions[name] -> [TacticCallSession, ...]   tactics called during this one

Alongside the session, each agent's dialogs (agent.dialogs) hold the message trees, including the working forks the loop created for repairs; see Dialog. Together they contain enough to reconstruct what every agent saw and said on every turn, with the exact model arguments and costs.

session = tactic("Analyze this paper", return_session=True)

session.state                  # "success" | "failure"
session.total_cost             # InvokeCost (tokens and dollars), sub-tactics included
for agent_name, calls in session.agent_sessions.items():
    for call in calls:
        print(agent_name, call.state, call.cost.cost, call.exception_retries_count)
        print(call.delivery.content)

On failure the exception is re-raised; to inspect the failed session, persist it from an observer (below), which receives it with state="failure", error, and error_traceback filled in.

docs.title: Tactic identity: the stable pkg::name key
docs.text:
Every session records which tactic produced it in session.tactic_path, in the form:

{package_name}::{tactic_name}

for example my_pkg::researcher.

A runtime path such as my_pkg.tactics:v2/researcher encodes where a tactic lives inside a package, including folders and under prefixes. That is useful for lookup but a poor storage key, because restructuring would orphan old records. The pkg::name form only uses the package name and Tactic.name:

Change tactic_path Move the tactic file to another folder Stable Add or change an under prefix Stable Rename [package] name Changes Rename Tactic.name Changes

The last two are semantic changes and should be deliberate. Treat [package] name as a permanent identity, like a Python distribution name.

How it is set:

  • build_tactic(config, name=...) looks the tactic up and records "<package>::<name>", where the package is the first segment of the namespace it was found in. Building through an alias (build_tactic(cfg, name="p1:researcher")) records the alias, so build through the canonical package name when you key records on tactic_path.
  • A tactic constructed directly with a registry looks up its own name in that registry's default namespace and falls back to the bare Tactic.name.
  • Pass tactic_path="my_pkg::researcher" (or TacticContext(tactic_path=...)) to set it explicitly.

docs.title: Persisting sessions with an observer
docs.text:
A tactic accepts an observer: any object with some of these methods. All are optional and called with keyword arguments.

Method When Arguments observe_tactic(...) Before call() (or the hook) runs. Return a context manager (or None); the value it yields is passed to the callbacks as span. tactic, session, task, session_name, tags, metadata on_tactic_success(...) After call() (or the hook) returns and the output validates. tactic, session, task, result, span, tags, metadata on_tactic_failure(...) When call(), the hook, or validation raises. tactic, session, task, exception, span, tags, metadata

For a call() program, tactic is the per-call copy, so tactic.agents holds this call's agents and their dialogs; for a protocol hook it is the tactic itself. An exception inside an observer is logged as a warning and never breaks the tactic call. The observer sees every call that runs in a session: tactic(task), acall, bcall, and ccall on any tactic, run() / arun() on tactics that write call(), and every stream from an overridden sync events() or stream() (on_tactic_success gets result=None when the stream ends; a stream closed early leaves its session "cancelled" with no callback). A tactic that only implements the _run() or _arun() hook runs it directly from run() / arun(), without a session.

docs.title: Example: a JSON Lines session log
docs.text:
import json
import time
from contextlib import contextmanager
from pathlib import Path


class JsonlSessionLog:
    """Append one JSON record per tactic call."""

    def __init__(self, path: str):
        self.path = Path(path)

    @contextmanager
    def observe_tactic(self, *, tactic, session, task, session_name, tags, metadata):
        yield {"session_name": session_name, "started": time.time()}

    def on_tactic_success(self, *, tactic, session, task, result, span, tags, metadata):
        self._write(tactic, session, span, tags, metadata)

    def on_tactic_failure(self, *, tactic, session, task, exception, span, tags, metadata):
        self._write(tactic, session, span, tags, metadata)

    def _write(self, tactic, session, span, tags, metadata):
        dialogs = {}
        for agent_name, agent in getattr(tactic, "agents", {}).items():
            for alias, dialog in agent.dialogs.items():
                dialogs[f"{agent_name}/{alias}"] = dialog.to_dict()   # JSON-safe
        record = {
            "session_name": span["session_name"],
            "tactic": session.tactic_path,
            "state": session.state,
            "tags": tags or {},
            "metadata": metadata or {},
            "cost_usd": session.total_cost.cost,
            "agent_calls": session.agent_call_count,
            "latency_s": round(time.time() - span["started"], 3),
            "error": session.error,
            "traceback": session.error_traceback,
            "delivery": session.delivery if session.state == "success" else None,
            "dialogs": dialogs,
        }
        with self.path.open("a") as fh:
            fh.write(json.dumps(record, default=str) + "\n")

Attach it at construction, or through build_tactic, which forwards keyword arguments to the constructor:

log = JsonlSessionLog("runs/sessions.jsonl")

tactic = MyTactic(config, observer=log)
tactic = build_tactic(resolve_config("default"), observer=log)

Every call is now recorded, with the tags and metadata you pass:

result = tactic(
    task,
    tags={"experiment": "exp-001", "dataset": "arxiv-2024", "split": "val"},
    metadata={"user": "alice", "git_sha": "abc1234"},
)

Reading it back is ordinary Python:

import json

records = [json.loads(line) for line in open("runs/sessions.jsonl")]

failures = [r for r in records if r["state"] == "failure"]
exp = [r for r in records if r["tags"].get("experiment") == "exp-001"]
total = sum(r["cost_usd"] for r in exp)
print(f"{len(exp)} sessions, ${total:.4f}")
for r in failures:
    print(r["tactic"], r["error"])
    print(r["traceback"])

Swap the file for SQLite, a document store, or an experiment tracker by changing _write.

docs.title: Example: OpenTelemetry spans
docs.text:
For production tracing, have observe_tactic return a span:

from opentelemetry import trace

tracer = trace.get_tracer("my-app")


class OTelObserver:
    def observe_tactic(self, *, tactic, session, task, session_name, tags, metadata):
        attributes = {"lllm.session_name": session_name}
        attributes.update({f"lllm.tag.{k}": v for k, v in (tags or {}).items()})
        return tracer.start_as_current_span(f"tactic {session.tactic_name}", attributes=attributes)

    def on_tactic_success(self, *, span, session, **_):
        span.set_attribute("lllm.agent_calls", session.agent_call_count)
        span.set_attribute("lllm.cost_usd", session.total_cost.cost)

    def on_tactic_failure(self, *, span, exception, **_):
        span.record_exception(exception)

When a tactic that writes call() is called through the protocol (run(), arun(), or a FastAPI service), the per-call copy passed to the observer carries the request's CallContext as tactic.call_context (request id, trace id, refs, tags, metadata), so service traces and native sessions line up:

class TraceIdObserver:
    def on_tactic_success(self, *, tactic, session, **_):
        ctx = tactic.call_context                  # None for plain tactic(task) calls
        if ctx is not None:
            print(session.tactic_path, ctx.request_id, ctx.trace_id, ctx.tags)

docs.title: Tags and metadata
docs.text: tags are short str -> str values meant for filtering; metadata is richer context you want to keep but not filter on. Both are passed through to the observer untouched.

docs.title: Recommended vocabulary
docs.text:
# Experiment / run tracking
tags = {"experiment": "ablation-001", "run": "run-003", "variant": "no-retrieval"}

# Dataset splits
tags = {"dataset": "pubmed-2024", "split": "test", "subset": "cardiology"}

# Multi-stage pipelines
tags = {"pipeline": "document-qa", "stage": "extraction", "doc_id": "doc-00127"}

# Production / CI
tags = {"env": "prod", "version": "v2.3.1", "requester": "user-alice"}

docs.title: Composing tags
docs.text:
Build tags incrementally so every level can be filtered on:

BASE = {"project": "doc-qa", "model": "gpt-4o"}

for experiment in ["baseline", "rag-v1", "rag-v2"]:
    for doc_id in document_ids:
        tactic(make_task(doc_id), tags={**BASE, "experiment": experiment, "doc_id": doc_id})

docs.title: Tags vs. metadata
docs.text:
tactic(
    task,
    tags={"experiment": "exp-001", "split": "val"},
    metadata={"git_sha": "abc1234", "input_file": "/data/val.jsonl", "config": config},
)

bcall, acall, and ccall accept tags and metadata too and apply them to every task.

docs.title: Terminal logging
docs.text:
Every native module logs through logging.getLogger(__name__), so all loggers live under lllm.runtimes.native:

Logger Covers lllm.runtimes.native Everything below lllm.runtimes.native.core.tactic Tactic start, completion with cost, and failure, one line each (INFO), the failure traceback (DEBUG), observer errors (WARNING) lllm.runtimes.native.core.prompt Repair retries and LLM recalls (WARNING), tool calls and their arguments (DEBUG), an agent call that uses up its tool rounds without a final reply (ERROR) lllm.runtimes.native.core.agent Loop configuration warnings lllm.runtimes.native.core.native_config Unknown agent config keys, missing or unreachable skills lllm.runtimes.native.core.config Discovery registration problems lllm.runtimes.native.core.runtime Package install, export, removal; resource overwrites (DEBUG) lllm.runtimes.native.core.dialog Context truncation (DEBUG), unresolved prompts when restoring dialogs lllm.runtimes.native.core.resource Lazy resources that fail to load lllm.runtimes.native.invokers.litellm Provider environment checks lllm.runtimes.native.proxies.base Proxy registration lllm.runtimes.native.sandbox.jupyter Notebook server and kernel lifecycle lllm.runtimes.native.tools.cua Computer-use agent events

Package discovery problems (a missing folder, a module that fails to import, a dependency without lllm.toml) are reported with warnings.warn(..., RuntimeWarning) rather than logging, so they show up even without logging configured.

docs.title: Quick setup
docs.text:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)-8s %(name)s: %(message)s")
logging.getLogger("lllm.runtimes.native").setLevel(logging.INFO)

docs.title: Level guide
docs.text:
Level What you see WARNING Repair retries with the parse error, LLM recalls, unknown config keys, missing skills INFO Plus tactic start and completion with cost and agent-call counts, one line per tactic failure, package installs DEBUG Plus every tool call with arguments, successful agent calls, tactic failure tracebacks, context truncation, resource overwrites

A failed tactic call raises, and its session records the error and traceback, so the log keeps the failure to one INFO line and the traceback at DEBUG. An agent call that runs out of repair retries, LLM recalls, or rate-limit retries raises its last error without an ERROR line, so inside a tactic it shows up as that INFO line.

docs.title: Fine-grained control
docs.text:
import logging

logging.getLogger("lllm.runtimes.native").setLevel(logging.WARNING)
logging.getLogger("lllm.runtimes.native.core.tactic").setLevel(logging.INFO)   # just tactic summaries
logging.getLogger("lllm.runtimes.native.core.prompt").setLevel(logging.ERROR)  # mute retry noise

handler = logging.FileHandler("lllm.log")
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s"))
logging.getLogger("lllm.runtimes.native").addHandler(handler)

Silence everything with logging.getLogger("lllm.runtimes.native").setLevel(logging.CRITICAL + 1).

docs.title: Prompts
docs.text:
A Prompt is the complete behavioural definition for one agent turn. It bundles four concerns into one object:

  1. Template: the text sent to the model, with {variable} placeholders.
  2. Output contract: a parser (or a structured-output format) that defines what a valid reply looks like. The agent loop keeps repairing until it gets one, within its retry budget.
  3. Tool surface: the Function and MCP objects the model may call during this turn.
  4. Handler strategy: a BaseHandler that decides what to send back when a tool result arrives or when parsing fails.

The key design principle: the agent is a function, and the Prompt is its type signature. The invoker reads the parser, format, and handler from dialog.top_prompt, the prompt that sent the latest turn (agent.open() for the system prompt, agent.receive_prompt() for a user turn). The turn's tools are that prompt's function_list plus the agent's own tools (those on its system prompt), unless the prompt sets agent_tools=False. This is what gives you turn-level control: every turn declares exactly what it accepts and how failure is handled.

docs.title: Anatomy of a prompt
docs.text:
from lllm import Prompt, tool
from lllm.runtimes.native import DefaultTagParser


@tool(
    description="Get current weather for a city",
    prop_desc={"location": "City name, e.g. San Francisco, CA"},
)
def get_weather(location: str, units: str = "celsius") -> str:
    return f"Sunny, 22 degrees ({units}) in {location}"


weather_prompt = Prompt(
    path="weather/bot",
    prompt=(
        "You are a weather assistant.\n"
        "Answer the user's question: {question}\n"
        "Put your answer inside <answer> tags."
    ),
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["answer"]),
    function_list=[get_weather],
    metadata={"author": "team-weather", "version": "1.0"},
)
Field Type Purpose path str Identifier and registry key, e.g. runtime.get_prompt(path). prompt str Template, rendered by renderer (default: str.format). metadata dict Tracking info: version, author, experiment name. parser object with parse(), a callable, or None Defines a valid reply. None = free-form. format Pydantic model class, JSON-schema dict, or None Structured output (Chat Completions API). function_list list[Function \| str] Tools for this turn. Strings are package refs resolved when the prompt runs. mcp_servers_list list[MCP] MCP server declarations. agent_tools bool Also offer the agent's own tools on this turn. Default True; False for a turn that must answer without them. addon_args dict Provider features such as web search or computer use. handler BaseHandler Exception and tool-interrupt strategy. Default: DefaultSimpleHandler(). renderer BaseRenderer Template renderer. Default: StringFormatterRenderer().

Read-only helpers: functions (name → Function), mcp_servers, template_vars, allow_web_search, computer_use_config.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
Calling a prompt renders it:

from lllm import Prompt

prompt = Prompt(path="greeter", prompt="Hello {name}, welcome to {place}!")

prompt(name="Alice", place="Wonderland")   # 'Hello Alice, welcome to Wonderland!'
prompt.template_vars                        # {'name', 'place'}
prompt.validate_args({"name": "Alice"})     # ['place'] (missing variables)

template_vars is read from the current template text, so a copy made with prompt.model_copy(update={"prompt": ...}) reports its own variables. Every variable must be supplied; a missing one raises ValueError before anything is sent. Templates are always formatted, so literal braces are written doubled ({{ and }}) and come out single, whether or not the template has variables:

from lllm import Prompt

Prompt(path="json/hint", prompt='Reply as {{"answer": ...}}')()   # 'Reply as {"answer": ...}'

Dialog.put_prompt() and Agent.receive_prompt() render the prompt with the prompt_args you pass.

docs.title: Custom renderer
docs.text:
Subclass BaseRenderer to change how values are rendered:

from lllm import Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import BaseRenderer


class BulletRenderer(BaseRenderer):
    """Render list values as bullet lists, everything else with str.format."""

    def render(self, prompt: str, **kwargs) -> str:
        def fmt(value):
            if isinstance(value, (list, tuple)):
                return "\n".join(f"- {item}" for item in value)
            return value

        return prompt.format(**{key: fmt(value) for key, value in kwargs.items()})


report = Prompt(
    path="report/items",
    prompt="Summarise these findings:\n{items}",
    renderer=BulletRenderer(),
)

print(report(items=["apples", "bananas", "cherries"]))

The renderer runs for every render, with or without variables. Required variables are still detected with str.format field syntax before it runs, and each {name} field must be supplied, so a renderer should keep {name} fields for its variables. Engines with their own syntax (Jinja's {% %} blocks) do not fit this contract.

docs.title: Parsing
docs.text: The parser defines the return type of the turn. The invoker runs it on the reply; any exception it raises becomes a parse error, and the agent loop sends a repair prompt until the reply parses or retries run out.

docs.title: No parser: free-form
docs.text:
prompt = Prompt(path="chat", prompt="Say hello to {name}.")
# reply.content is the text; reply.parsed == {}

prompt.parse(text) on a parser-less prompt returns {"raw": text}.

docs.title: Tag parser: XML and Markdown blocks
docs.text:
from lllm import Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import DefaultTagParser

prompt = Prompt(
    path="analyst/report",
    prompt=(
        "Analyse the following text: {text}\n\n"
        "Respond with:\n"
        "<reasoning>your step-by-step reasoning</reasoning>\n"
        "<answer>your final answer</answer>\n"
        "End with <DONE> when complete."
    ),
    parser=DefaultTagParser(
        xml_tags=["reasoning", "answer"],   # extracted; each must appear
        signal_tags=["DONE"],               # presence check only
    ),
)

parsed = prompt.parse(
    "<reasoning>step 1 ...</reasoning><answer>The answer is 42.</answer> <DONE>"
)
# {
#     "raw": "...",
#     "xml_tags": {"reasoning": ["step 1 ..."], "answer": ["The answer is 42."]},
#     "md_tags": {},
#     "signal_tags": {"DONE": True},
# }

DefaultTagParser fields:

Field Behaviour xml_tags <tag>...</tag> blocks to extract. A listed tag that never appears is a parse error. md_tags Fenced blocks to extract (```python ... ```). A listed tag that never appears is a parse error. required_xml_tags / required_md_tags Also extracted, and also errors when missing. Use them when you only list required tags. signal_tags True/False for whether <TAG> occurs anywhere. parser_args Free-form dict for subclasses.

Each extracted entry is a list, because a tag may occur several times. Missing tags raise ParseError with a message such as No answer tags found, it should be provided as <answer>...</answer>, and that message is what the model sees in the repair prompt. The native ParseError subclasses lllm.ParseError, so except lllm.ParseError catches both.

parser = DefaultTagParser(md_tags=["python"])
parser.parse("Here:\n```python\nprint('hi')\n```")["md_tags"]   # {'python': ["print('hi')"]}

If you need optional tags, the runtime-agnostic lllm.DefaultTagParser has the same fields but only enforces the required_* lists. Any object with a parse(content, **kwargs) method works as a prompt parser.

docs.title: Structured output: Pydantic model
docs.text:
For JSON-mode replies use format instead of parser:

from pydantic import BaseModel


class ResearchReport(BaseModel):
    title: str
    summary: str
    confidence: float
    sources: list[str]


prompt = Prompt(
    path="researcher/report",
    prompt="Research the following topic and return a structured report: {topic}",
    format=ResearchReport,
)

# reply.parsed == {"title": "...", "summary": "...", "confidence": 0.9, "sources": [...]}
# report = ResearchReport.model_validate(reply.parsed)

With a Pydantic class, the LiteLLM invoker sends it as response_format; with a dict it requests {"type": "json_object"}. The reply is decoded with json.loads (invalid JSON triggers a repair turn) and the parser is not run. format is not supported with the Responses API (api_type="response").

To validate the decoded object against the model and get repair turns with Pydantic's error message, use a validating parser instead; see Composing with Pydantic.

docs.title: Custom parser
docs.text:
Subclass DefaultTagParser to add domain validation on top of tag extraction:

from lllm import Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import DefaultTagParser, ParseError


class GraphParser(DefaultTagParser):
    """Parse an edge list in <graph> tags and reject cycles."""

    def parse(self, content: str, **kwargs) -> dict:
        parsed = super().parse(content, **kwargs)
        edges = [
            tuple(part.strip() for part in line.split("->"))
            for line in parsed["xml_tags"]["graph"][0].strip().splitlines()
            if "->" in line
        ]
        if has_cycle(edges):
            raise ParseError(
                "The graph you returned contains a cycle. "
                "Please revise so all edges point forward."
            )
        parsed["edges"] = edges
        return parsed


def has_cycle(edges) -> bool:
    graph = {}
    for a, b in edges:
        graph.setdefault(a, []).append(b)
    seen, stack = set(), set()

    def visit(node):
        if node in stack:
            return True
        if node in seen:
            return False
        seen.add(node)
        stack.add(node)
        cyclic = any(visit(nxt) for nxt in graph.get(node, []))
        stack.discard(node)
        return cyclic

    return any(visit(node) for node in list(graph))


prompt = Prompt(
    path="planner/dag",
    prompt="Build a dependency graph for: {task}. Return edges like 'a -> b' in <graph> tags.",
    parser=GraphParser(xml_tags=["graph"]),
)

A parser can also be a plain function. A non-dict return value is wrapped as {"value": ...}, and "raw" is always added:

def word_count(content: str, **kwargs) -> int:
    return len(content.split())


Prompt(path="wc", prompt="Write a haiku.", parser=word_count).parse("an old silent pond")
# {'value': 4, 'raw': 'an old silent pond'}

parser_args passed to agent.respond(parser_args={...}) arrive as keyword arguments to parse().

docs.title: Defining tools
docs.text:
LLLM has one regular tool type, Function, and two ways to program against it:

  • Coupled declaration and implementation: @tool turns a Python function into a Function that carries both schema and implementation. Pass it directly in function_list, or reference the package resource by URL.
  • Decoupled declaration and implementation: put a bare Function declaration in the prompt, like a header file, and provide a package @tool(name=...) implementation with the same name. LLLM binds them by exact name when the prompt runs.

Tactic tools and proxies are built on top of this model: a tactic tool is a generated Function backed by a tactic method, and a proxy exposes many endpoints through query_api_doc, run_python, and CALL_API. See Tactics and Proxies & Sandbox.

docs.title: @tool: coupled tools
docs.text:
The decorator builds the JSON schema from type hints:

from lllm import Prompt, tool


@tool(
    description="Search the web for current information",
    prop_desc={
        "query": "The search query string",
        "max_results": "Maximum number of results to return",
    },
)
def web_search(query: str, max_results: int = 5) -> str:
    return f"{max_results} results for {query!r}"   # call a real API here


@tool(description="Evaluate an arithmetic expression")
def calculator(expression: str) -> str:
    return str(eval(expression, {"__builtins__": {}}))   # demo only


prompt = Prompt(
    path="research/agent",
    prompt="Answer the following question using your tools: {question}",
    function_list=[web_search, calculator],
)

tool(description=None, prop_desc=None, *, name=None, strict=None, processor=...):

  • Parameter schemas follow the annotations, through Pydantic: list[str] gives an array with string items, Literal["fast", "deep"] an enum, a BaseModel a nested object, Optional[...] a nullable value. Unannotated parameters are strings.
  • Nested models are inlined, since tool schemas have no $defs. A recursive model is spelled out once; references back into it become its type and title, such as {"type": "object", "title": "Node"}.
  • Parameters without defaults are required; defaults are added to the property description.
  • strict=None (the default) turns on strict tool schemas when every parameter is required and flat (a string, number, boolean, enum, or a list of these), which is what OpenAI-style strict mode accepts. An object parameter, such as a model or a dict, keeps it off, because strict mode needs additionalProperties: false on every object. Pass strict=True or strict=False to decide yourself.
  • description defaults to the docstring, name to the function name. Names may not contain whitespace, /, :, \, ;, or %.
  • Function.from_callable(fn, ...) does the same without the decorator.
from typing import Literal

from lllm import tool


@tool(description="Search the archive")
def archive_search(query: str, tags: list[str], mode: Literal["fast", "deep"]) -> str:
    return f"{mode} search for {query!r} in {tags}"


archive_search.properties["mode"]   # {'enum': ['fast', 'deep'], 'type': 'string'}
archive_search.strict               # True: every parameter required, all flat

When the model calls a tool, the loop runs the implementation with the call's arguments. An exception inside the tool does not crash the loop: the model receives Error: <message> as the result and can recover.

from lllm import FunctionCall

call = web_search(FunctionCall(name="web_search", arguments={"query": "LLLM"}))
call.result       # '5 results for ...'
call.result_str   # formatted text the model sees

Package-discovered tools can be referenced by URL instead of imported:

prompt = Prompt(
    path="research/agent",
    prompt="Answer the following question using your tools: {question}",
    function_list=[
        "shared_pkg.tools:web_search",
        "shared_pkg.tactics:code_review",
    ],
)

String refs are resolved when the prompt runs. Full URLs are exact; bare names and pkg:name shorthand resolve relative to the prompt's own package, then the runtime's default namespace. A ref that matches both a tool and a tactic is an error; use the full URL. Proxy refs are not allowed in function_list; put pkg.proxies:name in the agent config tools instead.

docs.title: Function declarations: schema and implementation apart
docs.text:
Useful when the prompt file should define what tools exist and a tool module defines how they run:

# prompts/research.py: declaration, versioned with the prompt
from lllm import Function, Prompt

search_schema = Function(
    name="search",
    description="Search an internal knowledge base",
    properties={
        "query": {"type": "string", "description": "Search query"},
        "top_k": {"type": "integer", "description": "Number of results"},
    },
    required=["query"],
)

research = Prompt(path="system", prompt="Use search when needed.", function_list=[search_schema])

# tools/search.py: implementation
from lllm import tool


@tool(name="search", description="Search internal documents.")
def search(query: str, top_k: int = 5) -> str:
    return my_retriever.search(query, top_k=top_k)

When the prompt runs, search_schema binds to the tool registered under <package>.tools:search: the declaration keeps its own schema and borrows the implementation. The implementation's registered key must equal the declared name, so give a decoupled tool its own module named after it (tools/search.py), or register it explicitly with runtime.register_tool("search", search, namespace="pkg.tools"). If no implementation matches, resolution fails instead of silently binding the wrong callable. Calling an unbound declaration directly raises RuntimeError.

docs.title: Custom result formatting
docs.text:
By default a tool result reaches the model as:

Return of calling function <name> with arguments <args>:
---
<result>
---

Override it per tool with a processor(result, function_call) -> str:

def compact_processor(result, function_call) -> str:
    return str(result)


@tool(
    description="Get stock price",
    prop_desc={"ticker": "Stock ticker symbol, e.g. AAPL"},
    processor=compact_processor,
)
def get_stock_price(ticker: str) -> str:
    return f"$123.45 ({ticker})"

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text:
from lllm import MCP, Prompt

prompt = Prompt(
    path="docs/search",
    prompt="Search the docs when needed.",
    mcp_servers_list=[
        MCP(
            server_label="docs",
            server_url="https://example.com/mcp",
            require_approval="never",       # "never" | "manual" | "auto"
            allowed_tools=["search"],
        )
    ],
)

MCP.to_tool() produces the {"type": "mcp", ...} entry the LiteLLM invoker sends next to function tools.

docs.title: Agent tools and agent_tools
docs.text:
A prompt's function_list is the tool surface specific to its turn. When an agent runs the prompt, it adds its own tools: everything on its system prompt, including agent-config tools, proxy tools (query_api_doc, run_python), and activate_skill. A user-turn prompt therefore never has to repeat them, and a tool on the turn prompt wins over an agent tool with the same name. Set agent_tools=False for a turn that must be answered without the agent's tools:

from lllm import Prompt

summary = Prompt(
    path="analyst/summary",
    prompt="Summarise the findings so far in three bullets.",
    agent_tools=False,       # answer from the conversation only
)

The handler's final prompt, sent when the tool budget runs out, has no tools either.

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text: When the loop meets a parse error or a tool result, it asks dialog.top_prompt.on_exception(session) or on_interrupt(session) for the next prompt. The handler field is the object that answers. All three methods receive the active prompt and the current AgentCallSession and return a Prompt.

docs.title: What the default handler does
docs.text:
Event Message sent to the model Inherits tools? Parse error "Error: {error_message}. Please fix." Yes Tool result "{call_results}" Yes Tool budget exhausted "You are reaching the limit of tool calls. Provide the final response." No

Each message is wrapped in a child prompt via extend(), so it keeps the parent's parser. The messages are fields, so simple changes need no subclass:

from lllm import Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import DefaultSimpleHandler, DefaultTagParser

strict = Prompt(
    path="analyst/strict",
    prompt="Analyse {topic}. Put your answer in <answer> tags.",
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["answer"]),
    handler=DefaultSimpleHandler(
        exception_msg="That reply was not valid: {error_message}\nResend it in the required format.",
        interrupt_final_msg="Stop calling tools and give your final answer now.",
    ),
)

docs.title: Custom handler: rule-based
docs.text:
from lllm import Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import AgentCallSession, BaseHandler, DefaultTagParser


class RetryWithHintHandler(BaseHandler):
    """First failure: a gentle hint. Later failures: a strict format reminder."""

    def on_exception(self, prompt: Prompt, session: AgentCallSession) -> Prompt:
        retry = session.exception_retries_count
        if retry <= 1:
            msg = "Your response had a formatting error: {error_message}. Please try again."
        else:
            msg = (
                f"Formatting error (attempt {retry}): {{error_message}}\n"
                "You MUST wrap your answer in <answer> tags. No other format is accepted."
            )
        return prompt.extend(path=f"__{prompt.path}_exception_{retry}", prompt=msg)

    def on_interrupt(self, prompt: Prompt, session: AgentCallSession) -> Prompt:
        return prompt.extend(path=f"__{prompt.path}_interrupt", prompt="{call_results}")

    def on_interrupt_final(self, prompt: Prompt, session: AgentCallSession) -> Prompt:
        return prompt.extend(
            path=f"__{prompt.path}_interrupt_final",
            prompt=f"You have used all {session.max_interrupt_steps} tool rounds. Answer now.",
            function_list=[],
            mcp_servers_list=[],
            addon_args={},
        )


prompt = Prompt(
    path="analyst/strict",
    prompt="Analyse {topic}. Put your answer in <answer> tags.",
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["answer"]),
    function_list=[web_search],
    handler=RetryWithHintHandler(),
)

The exception prompt is rendered with {error_message} and the interrupt prompt with {call_results}, so keep exactly those placeholders (and escape other braces).

docs.title: Custom handler: agentic
docs.text:
The handler gets the full session, so it can call another agent:

from lllm import Agent, Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import AgentCallSession, BaseHandler, DefaultSimpleHandler


class FixerHandler(BaseHandler):
    """Ask a second agent how to repair a failed reply."""

    def __init__(self, fixer: Agent):
        self.fixer = fixer
        self.fallback = DefaultSimpleHandler()

    def on_exception(self, prompt: Prompt, session: AgentCallSession) -> Prompt:
        step = max(session.exception_retries)                 # latest loop step
        errors = "\n".join(str(e) for e in session.exception_retries[step])
        alias = f"fix_{id(session)}_{session.exception_retries_count}"

        self.fixer.open(alias)
        self.fixer.receive(
            f"A reply failed validation:\n{errors}\n\n"
            f"Original instructions:\n{prompt.prompt}\n\n"
            "Write one short repair instruction for the author."
        )
        advice = self.fixer.respond().content
        self.fixer.close(alias)

        safe = advice.replace("{", "{{").replace("}", "}}")
        return prompt.extend(path=f"__{prompt.path}_fix", prompt=safe + "\n\nParser said: {error_message}")

    def on_interrupt(self, prompt, session):
        return self.fallback.on_interrupt(prompt, session)

    def on_interrupt_final(self, prompt, session):
        return self.fallback.on_interrupt_final(prompt, session)

docs.title: Prompt composition
docs.text:
extend() creates a child prompt that inherits every field, with overrides. A new path is required.

base = Prompt(
    path="base/analyst",
    prompt="You are a research analyst.\n\nTask: {task}",
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["reasoning", "answer"]),
    function_list=[web_search, calculator],
)

# Specialise the persona, keep everything else
finance_analyst = base.extend(
    path="finance/analyst",
    prompt="You are a financial research analyst.\n\nTask: {task}",
)

# Strip tools for a lightweight summary turn
summariser = base.extend(
    path="base/summariser",
    prompt="Summarise the following research: {research}",
    function_list=[],
)

# Require an extra tag
strict_analyst = base.extend(
    path="base/analyst_strict",
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["reasoning", "answer", "confidence"]),
)

extend() copies field values directly rather than serializing, so custom parsers, renderers, and handler instances carry over.

docs.title: Provider capabilities
docs.text:
Provider-specific features live in addon_args, so new provider features never need new Prompt fields:

# OpenAI web search
search_prompt = Prompt(
    path="web/searcher",
    prompt="Research this question using web search: {question}",
    addon_args={"web_search": True},
)

# Computer use
cua_prompt = Prompt(
    path="browser/agent",
    prompt="Complete the following browser task: {task}",
    addon_args={
        "computer_use": {"display_width": 1280, "display_height": 800, "environment": "browser"}
    },
)

search_prompt.allow_web_search      # True
cua_prompt.computer_use_config      # {'display_width': 1280, ...}

The LiteLLM invoker turns these into native tools on the Responses API (api_type: response): web_search adds {"type": "web_search_preview"} and computer_use adds a computer_use_preview tool. On the default Chat Completions API they are ignored. See Invokers.

docs.title: Organization and discovery
docs.text:
Prompts are Python objects at module scope in .py files. lllm.toml names the folders, and discovery registers every Prompt it finds:

# lllm.toml
[package]
name = "my_pkg"

[prompts]
paths = ["prompts"]

The registry key is the file path (without .py) plus the prompt's own path. A prompt with path="system" in prompts/weather/bot.py registers as my_pkg.prompts:weather/bot/system:

prompts/
├── weather/
│   └── bot.py          # system, analysis
├── finance/
│   └── analyst.py      # research, summary
└── coding/
    └── agent.py        # planner, executor, reviewer

Register without discovery:

from lllm import register_prompt

register_prompt(my_prompt)          # default runtime, key = my_prompt.path, overwrites
# register_prompt(my_prompt, overwrite=False) raises ValueError if the key exists

runtime.register_prompt(my_prompt, namespace="my_pkg.prompts")   # a specific runtime

Retrieve:

from lllm import load_prompt

prompt = load_prompt("weather/bot/system")               # default package
prompt = load_prompt("my_pkg:weather/bot/system")        # package-qualified
prompt = runtime.get_prompt("my_pkg.prompts:weather/bot/system")

A registered prompt remembers its package, which is what lets bare tool refs and Function declarations on it resolve inside that package. See Package Discovery.

docs.title: Metadata and tracking
docs.text:
metadata accepts any JSON-like dict. info_dict() produces a snapshot for experiment tracking:

prompt = Prompt(
    path="analyst/v2",
    prompt="Analyse {topic}.",
    metadata={"author": "junyan", "experiment": "ablation-no-cot", "version": "2.1"},
)

prompt.info_dict()
# {
#     "path": "analyst/v2",
#     "prompt_hash": "...",            # first 12 hex chars of SHA-256 of the template
#     "metadata": {"author": "junyan", "experiment": "ablation-no-cot", "version": "2.1"},
#     "functions": [],
#     "mcp_servers": [],
#     "addon_args": {},
#     "has_parser": False,
#     "has_format": False,
# }

prompt_hash changes whenever the template text changes, which makes prompt drift across experiments easy to detect.

to_dict() returns a JSON-safe snapshot: tools are stored as their schemas (implementations are not included; they are re-bound by name to registered @tool implementations when the prompt next runs), a Pydantic format model is stored as {"model": "module:Qualname", "schema": {...}}, and the parser, handler, and renderer are left out. Prompt.from_dict() rebuilds the prompt without importing code: it uses the format model class only when its module is already imported, and the stored JSON schema otherwise.

docs.title: Complete example: a prompt file
docs.text:
A real prompt module. Discovery registers every module-level Prompt, prefixed with the file path.

# prompts/research/agent.py
#
# Registered keys (package "research_pkg"):
#   research_pkg.prompts:research/agent/system
#   research_pkg.prompts:research/agent/task
#   research_pkg.prompts:research/agent/summarise

from lllm import Function, Prompt, tool
from lllm.runtimes.native import DefaultTagParser, ParseError


# -- Tools -------------------------------------------------------------------

@tool(
    description="Search the web for current information on a topic",
    prop_desc={"query": "Search query string"},
)
def web_search(query: str) -> str:
    return f"[Search results for: {query}]"   # call a real search API here


@tool(description="Fetch the full text of a URL", prop_desc={"url": "The URL to fetch"})
def fetch_url(url: str) -> str:
    return f"[Content of: {url}]"


# Declared here for the model; implemented by tools/save_note.py in this package.
save_note = Function(
    name="save_note",
    description="Save a research note to the session store",
    properties={
        "title": {"type": "string", "description": "Note title"},
        "content": {"type": "string", "description": "Note content"},
    },
    required=["title", "content"],
)


# -- Parser ------------------------------------------------------------------

class ResearchParser(DefaultTagParser):
    """Tag extraction plus a range check on <confidence>."""

    def parse(self, content: str, **kwargs) -> dict:
        parsed = super().parse(content, **kwargs)
        raw = parsed["xml_tags"]["confidence"][0].strip()
        try:
            confidence = float(raw)
        except ValueError:
            raise ParseError(f"<confidence> must be a number, got {raw!r}")
        if not 0.0 <= confidence <= 1.0:
            raise ParseError(f"<confidence> must be between 0 and 1, got {confidence}")
        parsed["confidence"] = confidence
        return parsed


# -- Prompts -----------------------------------------------------------------

system = Prompt(
    path="system",
    prompt=(
        "You are a careful research assistant with access to web search.\n"
        "Verify claims with at least two sources before concluding.\n"
        "Current date: {date}"
    ),
    metadata={"role": "system"},
)

task = Prompt(
    path="task",
    prompt=(
        "Research the following question thoroughly: {question}\n\n"
        "Use your tools, then respond with:\n"
        "<reasoning>your research process</reasoning>\n"
        "<answer>your final, sourced answer</answer>\n"
        "<confidence>a number between 0 and 1</confidence>"
    ),
    parser=ResearchParser(xml_tags=["reasoning", "answer", "confidence"]),
    function_list=[web_search, fetch_url, save_note],
    metadata={"version": "1.2"},
)

summarise = task.extend(
    path="summarise",
    prompt=(
        "Summarise these findings in 2-3 sentences: {findings}\n\n"
        "<answer>your summary</answer>"
    ),
    function_list=[],
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["answer"]),
)

# tools/save_note.py
from lllm import tool

NOTES: list[tuple[str, str]] = []


@tool(name="save_note", description="Save a research note to the session store")
def save_note(title: str, content: str) -> str:
    NOTES.append((title, content))
    return f"Note {title!r} saved."

And a tactic that uses these prompts:

# tactics/researcher.py
import datetime

from lllm import Tactic


class Researcher(Tactic):
    name = "researcher"
    agent_group = ["researcher"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        agent = self.agents["researcher"]
        agent.open("research", prompt_args={"date": datetime.date.today().isoformat()})

        agent.receive_prompt(agent.runtime.get_prompt("research/agent/task"), {"question": task})
        response = agent.respond()
        answer = response.parsed["xml_tags"]["answer"][0]

        if response.parsed["confidence"] < 0.5:
            # Low confidence: consolidate in a tool-free summary turn.
            agent.receive_prompt(
                agent.runtime.get_prompt("research/agent/summarise"), {"findings": answer}
            )
            answer = agent.respond().parsed["xml_tags"]["answer"][0]
        return answer

# configs/default.yaml
tactic_type: researcher
global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  model_args:
    temperature: 0.2
agent_configs:
  - name: researcher
    system_prompt_path: research/agent/system

from lllm import build_tactic, load_runtime, resolve_config

load_runtime("research_pkg/lllm.toml")
tactic = build_tactic(resolve_config("default"))
print(tactic("What architecture do modern LLMs use?"))

docs.title: Proxies & Sandbox
docs.text:
LLLM treats API access and code execution as first-class capabilities. Proxies standardize how agents reach external APIs; execution environments let agents run the Python they write.

A proxy is not just another way to define a function tool. It is the programming-based tool surface: the agent reads endpoint docs with query_api_doc, writes small Python programs with run_python, and calls registered endpoints through CALL_API. Use proxies when an agent needs many related endpoints, stateful analysis, or a small sandbox; use @tool functions when the model only needs a few direct schemas.

The native runtime ships two execution environments:

  • Interpreter: an in-process exec() with a persistent namespace. Zero start-up cost and safe to run many agents in parallel. Best for fast data retrieval and computation.
  • Jupyter: a real kernel driven through JupyterSession, producing .ipynb artifacts and supporting plots. Install lllm-core[sandbox].

Both are optional, and any object with a "run this code, return output" method can take Jupyter's place; see Custom execution environments.

from lllm import BaseProxy, ProxyManager, ProxyRegistrator
from lllm.runtimes.native.proxies import AgentInterpreter, load_builtin_proxies

docs.title: Overview: execution modes
docs.text:
When an agent has a proxy: block or a proxy ref in its config tools, it gets API awareness automatically. exec_env decides how it uses the APIs:

exec_env Tools injected What the agent does Who runs code "interpreter" (default) query_api_doc + run_python Calls run_python with Python LLLM's AgentInterpreter, in process "jupyter" query_api_doc Writes <python_cell> tags Your tactic, through JupyterSession null (or any other string) query_api_doc Uses the API directory for awareness Nobody (or your own runner)

Every mode appends an API directory block to the system prompt and adds query_api_doc to its tools. Like all of an agent's tools, they are offered on every turn.

docs.title: Proxy config reference
docs.text:
Set under proxy: in an agent entry, or under global: for all agents. Per-agent values deep-merge over global ones, so an agent can change one field (exec_env, say) without repeating the rest.

proxy:
  activate_proxies: [fmp, fred]        # which proxies to load; empty = every registered proxy
  deploy_mode: false                   # passed to proxy instances
  cutoff_date: "2024-01-01"            # ISO date passed to proxies (data cutoff)
