  exec_env: interpreter                # "interpreter" | "jupyter" | null
  max_output_chars: 5000               # truncate run_python output (0 = no limit)
  truncation_indicator: "... (truncated)"
  timeout: 60.0                        # seconds per run_python call
  prompt_template: null                # replace the injected system-prompt block

For one packaged proxy with default settings, a tools ref is enough:

global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  tools:
    - market_pkg.proxies:fmp

Proxy refs in tools must be explicit (pkg.proxies:name). They are added to activate_proxies (merged with any proxy: block). Use proxy: when you need to tune exec_env, timeouts, truncation, or the cutoff date.

global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  proxy:
    activate_proxies: [fmp, fred]
    exec_env: interpreter

agent_configs:
  - name: researcher
    system_prompt_path: research/system
    # inherits the global proxy block

  - name: notebook_analyst
    system_prompt_path: analyst/notebook
    proxy:
      exec_env: jupyter       # this agent writes notebook cells instead

  - name: macro_analyst
    system_prompt_path: analyst/macro
    proxy:
      activate_proxies: [fred]
      timeout: 30.0

A custom prompt_template is formatted with {api_directory}, {max_output_chars}, and {truncation_indicator}; double any other braces. The defaults are DEFAULT_PROXY_PROMPT_TEMPLATE (interpreter) and DEFAULT_PROXY_PROMPT_NO_PYTHON_TEMPLATE (other modes) in lllm.runtimes.native.proxies.

Agents are rebuilt for every tactic call, so each call gets a fresh ProxyManager and a fresh interpreter namespace.

docs.title: Interpreter mode (default)
docs.text: The agent calls run_python with code. LLLM executes it in a persistent namespace and returns what the code printed. Variables survive from one call to the next within the agent.

docs.title: Why not Jupyter?
docs.text:
For most API work the interpreter is the better default:

  • No overhead: no subprocess, no kernel start, no files.
  • Parallel-safe: each agent has its own namespace, so bcall over many tasks works.
  • Instant: no kernel boot per agent.

Use Jupyter when you need notebook files, plots, or a cell-by-cell record of the work.

docs.title: What gets injected
docs.text:
When the agent is built, LLLM appends a block to the system prompt explaining the interpreter, CALL_API, printing, and truncation, followed by the API directory, and adds two tools:

  • query_api_doc(proxy_name): full endpoint docs for one proxy.
  • run_python(code): execute Python in the persistent interpreter.

The agent writes code like:

obs = CALL_API("fred/series/observations", {"series_id": "GDP", "limit": 4})
print(obs)

CALL_API("<proxy>/<endpoint path>", params) takes the proxy key followed by an endpoint path exactly as the API directory lists it (see How a call is made). Params can also be passed as keyword arguments: CALL_API("fred/series/observations", series_id="GDP").

Only stdout comes back, so code must print() what matters. Exceptions come back as tracebacks. Output longer than max_output_chars is cut and the indicator appended. A call that runs past timeout returns Error: Code execution timed out after ...; the namespace keeps whatever the code changed before the timeout.

The interpreter uses exec() in your process: it is meant for trusted agent code that calls APIs and processes data; it does not isolate that code from your process.

docs.title: Using the interpreter directly
docs.text:
from lllm import BaseProxy, ProxyManager, ProxyRegistrator
from lllm.runtimes.native.proxies import AgentInterpreter


@ProxyRegistrator(path="calc", name="Calculator", description="Local arithmetic.")
class CalcProxy(BaseProxy):          # no base_url: endpoints return their own result
    @BaseProxy.endpoint(
        category="math",
        endpoint="add",
        description="Add two numbers.",
        params={"a*": (float, 1.0), "b*": (float, 2.0)},
        response={"sum": 3.0},
    )
    def add(self, params: dict) -> dict:
        return {"sum": params["a"] + params["b"]}


interpreter = AgentInterpreter(
    ProxyManager(activate_proxies=["calc"]),
    max_output_chars=2000,
    timeout=10.0,
)

print(interpreter.run('r = CALL_API("calc/add", {"a": 2, "b": 3})\nprint(r)'))
print(interpreter.run("print(r['sum'] * 10)"))   # state persists
interpreter.reset()                               # clear variables, keep CALL_API

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
from lllm import Prompt

analyst_system = Prompt(
    path="analyst/system",
    prompt="You are a financial analyst. Answer the user's question with data.",
)

global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  model_args:
    temperature: 0.1

agent_configs:
  - name: analyst
    system_prompt_path: analyst/system
    proxy:
      activate_proxies: [fmp]
      max_output_chars: 8000

The analyst agent now has run_python and query_api_doc on its system prompt, and they are offered on every turn, whichever prompt drives it (unless a prompt sets agent_tools=False); no tactic-level wiring is needed. See Agent.

docs.title: Jupyter mode
docs.text:
In Jupyter mode the agent writes <python_cell> and <markdown_cell> tags in its reply. Your tactic extracts the cells, runs them in a JupyterSession, and feeds the output back.

Use it when you want notebooks as artifacts, matplotlib/plotly figures, cell-level error recovery, or a reproducible record of the analysis.

pip install "lllm-core[native,sandbox]"

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
proxy:
  activate_proxies: [fred]
  exec_env: jupyter    # no run_python; the agent writes cell tags

Only query_api_doc is injected. The API directory block is still appended (a shorter version without interpreter instructions), and your system prompt explains the notebook interface.

docs.title: System prompt and parser
docs.text:
from lllm import Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import ParseError
from lllm.runtimes.native.utils import find_all_xml_tags_sorted

NOTEBOOK_SYSTEM = """
You are an expert analyst working in a Jupyter notebook.

Every response must contain one or more cells:
1. Python cells: wrap code in <python_cell>...</python_cell>.
2. Markdown cells: wrap notes in <markdown_cell>...</markdown_cell>.

Rules:
- Cells run in order; variables persist across turns.
- If a cell fails you will see the error; fix that cell only.
- When the analysis is complete, reply with <TERMINATE_NOTEBOOK> alone.

CALL_API(api_path, params) is available in Python cells.
Call query_api_doc before using a new endpoint.
"""


def notebook_parser(message: str, **kwargs):
    matches = find_all_xml_tags_sorted(message)
    terminate = "<TERMINATE_NOTEBOOK>" in message
    cells = [(m["tag"], m["content"]) for m in matches if m["tag"] in ("python_cell", "markdown_cell")]
    if not cells and not terminate:
        raise ParseError(
            "No cells found. Wrap code in <python_cell>...</python_cell> "
            "or notes in <markdown_cell>...</markdown_cell>."
        )
    return {"cells": cells, "terminate": terminate}


notebook_turn = Prompt(path="analyst/notebook_turn", prompt="{content}", parser=notebook_parser)

The system prompt (NOTEBOOK_SYSTEM, registered as analyst/notebook) sets the interface; notebook_turn carries the parser, so every turn the tactic sends with it is validated and repaired by the agent loop.

docs.title: Tactic wiring with JupyterSession
docs.text:
The tactic drives the notebook loop. JupyterSandbox(config) manages session folders (under ~/.lllm/sandbox/<name>/sessions/ by default) and new_session() creates a notebook. Cells are appended with append_code_cell() / append_markdown_cell(), which return the cell index, and executed with run_cell(index), which starts the kernel on first use and returns True on success. Outputs are stored on the notebook cell.

from lllm import Tactic
from lllm.runtimes.native.sandbox import JupyterSandbox

SETUP_CELL = """\
from lllm.runtimes.native.proxies import ProxyManager, load_builtin_proxies
load_builtin_proxies()                      # or import / load your own proxy package
CALL_API = ProxyManager(activate_proxies=["fred"]).__call__
"""


def cell_text(session, index: int) -> str:
    parts = []
    for out in session.cells[index].outputs:
        if out.output_type == "stream":
            parts.append(out.text)
        elif out.output_type in ("execute_result", "display_data"):
            parts.append(out.data.get("text/plain", ""))
        elif out.output_type == "error":
            parts.append(f"{out.ename}: {out.evalue}")
    return "".join(parts)


class NotebookAnalysis(Tactic):
    name = "notebook_analysis"
    agent_group = ["analyst"]

    def call(self, task: str, max_turns: int = 10) -> str:
        sandbox = JupyterSandbox({"name": "analysis", "project_root": ".", "activate_proxies": []})
        session = sandbox.new_session()
        session.run_cell(session.append_code_cell(SETUP_CELL))

        agent = self.agents["analyst"]
        turn = agent.runtime.get_prompt("analyst/notebook_turn")
        agent.open("main")
        content = task
        try:
            for _ in range(max_turns):
                agent.receive_prompt(turn, {"content": content})
                parsed = agent.respond().parsed
                if parsed["terminate"]:
                    break
                outputs = []
                for tag, code in parsed["cells"]:
                    if tag == "markdown_cell":
                        session.append_markdown_cell(code)
                        continue
                    index = session.append_code_cell(code)
                    ok = session.run_cell(index)
                    status = "ok" if ok else "error"
                    outputs.append(f"[cell {index}: {status}]\n{cell_text(session, index)}")
                content = "\n\n".join(outputs) or "No code cells were run."
        finally:
            session.shutdown()
        return session.notebook_file

JupyterSession reserves cell 0 for an init cell it writes itself: it builds CALL_API from a ProxyManager with the session's activate_proxies. A fresh kernel has no proxy classes registered, so that manager starts empty; register your proxies in the kernel (as the setup cell does) and build CALL_API after they are registered. Other useful members: cells, n_cells, get_cells(indices), run_all_cells(stop_on_error=True), delete_cells(indices), launch_server() (open the notebook in a browser), and shutdown().

docs.title: Custom execution environments
docs.text: Nothing forces you to use the built-in sandboxes. The tactic-drives-execution pattern works with any code runner, because the runner is just an object in your tactic's call().

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
The agent side (prompt + parser) stays the same wherever code runs:

  1. The agent writes <python_cell> / <markdown_cell> tags.
  2. The tactic reads parsed["cells"].
  3. The tactic runs each code cell and feeds the output back.
  4. Repeat until parsed["terminate"] is True.

Only step 3 changes when you swap sandboxes.

docs.title: Example: remote execution service
docs.text:
import httpx

from lllm import Tactic


class RemoteSandbox:
    """Execute cells on a remote code runner."""

    def __init__(self, base_url: str, session_id: str):
        self.base_url = base_url
        self.session_id = session_id
        self.last_cell_failed = False

    def run_cell(self, code: str) -> str:
        resp = httpx.post(
            f"{self.base_url}/execute",
            json={"session_id": self.session_id, "code": code},
            timeout=60,
        )
        result = resp.json()
        self.last_cell_failed = result.get("error", False)
        return result.get("output", "")


class RemoteAnalysis(Tactic):
    name = "remote_analysis"
    agent_group = ["analyst"]

    def call(self, task: str, **kwargs) -> str:
        agent = self.agents["analyst"]
        turn = agent.runtime.get_prompt("analyst/notebook_turn")
        sandbox = RemoteSandbox("https://runner.example.com", session_id="abc123")

        agent.open("main")
        content = task
        for _ in range(10):
            agent.receive_prompt(turn, {"content": content})
            parsed = agent.respond().parsed
            if parsed["terminate"]:
                break
            outputs = []
            for tag, code in parsed["cells"]:
                if tag == "python_cell":
                    output = sandbox.run_cell(code)
                    label = "failed" if sandbox.last_cell_failed else "output"
                    outputs.append(f"[{label}]\n{output}")
            content = "\n\n".join(outputs) or "No code cells were run."

        return agent.current_dialog.tail.content

Any executor that takes code and returns output works: Docker containers, WebAssembly runtimes, database query runners, or a fake sandbox in tests. The prompt and parser stay identical.

docs.title: When to use each option
docs.text: Interpreter Jupyter (built-in) Custom sandbox Setup None Kernel start (seconds) You provide it Proxy integration Automatic (CALL_API injected) A setup cell defines CALL_API Inject it yourself Parallel agents Safe Heavy Depends on your implementation Visualizations No Yes (matplotlib/plotly) Depends Output artifact None .ipynb notebook Whatever you return Best for Fast API orchestration Exploratory analysis, charts Isolation, testing, non-Python runtimes

docs.title: Writing a proxy
docs.text:
A proxy is a BaseProxy subclass. Each endpoint is a method decorated with @BaseProxy.endpoint, and the class says where requests go:

import os

from lllm import BaseProxy, ProxyRegistrator


@ProxyRegistrator(path="fmp", name="Financial Modeling Prep", description="Market data API.")
class FMPProxy(BaseProxy):
    base_url = "https://financialmodelingprep.com/stable"
    api_key_name = "apikey"                 # sent as ?apikey=<api_key>

    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.api_key = os.getenv("FMP_API_KEY")

    @BaseProxy.endpoint(
        category="search",
        endpoint="search-symbol",
        description="Search tickers by company name or symbol.",
        params={"query*": (str, "AAPL"), "limit": (int, 10)},
        response=[{"symbol": "AAPL", "name": "Apple Inc."}],
    )
    def search_symbol(self, params: dict) -> dict:
        params.setdefault("limit", 10)      # validate, add defaults, rename keys
        return params

    @BaseProxy.endpoint(
        category="company",
        endpoint="profile",
        description="Company profile for a ticker.",
        params={"symbol*": (str, "AAPL")},
        response=[{"symbol": "AAPL", "companyName": "Apple Inc."}],
    )
    def profile(self, params: dict) -> dict:
        return params

CALL_API("fmp/search-symbol", {"query": "AAPL"}) sends GET https://financialmodelingprep.com/stable/search-symbol?query=AAPL&limit=10&apikey=... and returns the decoded JSON.

@BaseProxy.endpoint(category, endpoint, description, params, response, name=None, sub_category=None, remove_keys=None, dt_cutoff=None, method="GET") records the endpoint:

  • endpoint is the path under base_url, and the name the API directory and CALL_API use. It may contain /, hyphens, and {name} placeholders (series/{series_id}/observations); any placeholder name works, {series-id} included.
  • params maps each parameter to (type, example); a trailing * marks it required. response is an example response.
  • method is "GET" or "POST"; remove_keys lists keys to drop from the response.

ProxyRegistrator(path, name, description, runtime=None, *, registry=None) registers the class (in the default runtime unless you pass one) and sets the key path that activate_proxies and CALL_API use.

lllm create my-proxy --template proxy starts a project whose proxies/sample_proxy.py follows these conventions without the decorator: it sets _proxy_path = "sample", its endpoint methods take the params dict, and account_id* marks a required parameter. python main.py --catalog prints its API docs.

docs.title: How a call is made
docs.text:
CALL_API(endpoint, params) is ProxyManager.__call__, which hands the call to the proxy's call(path, params):

  1. Pick the proxy. The manager matches the longest loaded proxy key that starts the endpoint string (fmp in fmp/search-symbol, acme/notes in acme/notes/notes) and passes on the rest as the path.
  2. Resolve the endpoint. The path is matched against the endpoints' endpoint values, exactly as listed in the API directory, then against {name} templates, whose values are taken from the path. As a fallback the Python method name works too ("fmp.search_symbol"). Only decorated endpoints are reachable; other attributes of the proxy never are.
  3. Shape the params. The endpoint method receives the params (path values included) and returns the params to send.
  4. Build the request. With a base_url, the URL is <base_url>/<endpoint> with templates filled in, and the instance's api_key is added: as a query parameter named api_key_name, or as a header when the name starts with * (api_key_name = "*x-api-key" sends header x-api-key). Each {name} takes its value out of the params, URL-encoded as exactly one path segment ({"ticker": "BRK/A"} fills companies/{ticker} as companies/BRK%2FA), so pass raw values, not encoded ones. A missing or empty value, ., or .. raises ValueError before anything is sent.
  5. Send it. _call_api(url, params, endpoint_info, headers) performs the request. The default sends GET or POST by the endpoint's method, raises on HTTP errors and on JSON responses carrying an error key, drops remove_keys, and caches responses on disk while use_cache is true (the default; under ~/.lllm/.cache/, or $TMP_DIR/.cache/). Override _call_api for APIs that answer in plain text or need custom authentication.

A proxy with neither a base_url nor its own _call_api returns whatever the endpoint method returns, which suits local computation (the CalcProxy above). One that overrides _call_api without a base_url, such as an SDK client (the built-in exa), gets the filled-in endpoint path instead of a URL, with the same placeholder rules. Tactic-backed endpoints always return the tactic's result.

You can call a proxy without a manager: FMPProxy().call("search-symbol", {"query": "AAPL"}), and resolve_endpoint(path) returns the method, its metadata, and the path values. endpoint_directory(), api_directory(), and auto_test() (a metadata check) read the decorators.

docs.title: A plain-text API
docs.text:
Wolfram Alpha's LLM API answers in text, so this proxy overrides _call_api:

import os

import requests

from lllm import BaseProxy, ProxyRegistrator


@ProxyRegistrator(
    path="wolfram",
    name="Wolfram Alpha",
    description="Computations and factual answers from Wolfram Alpha.",
)
class WolframProxy(BaseProxy):
    base_url = "https://www.wolframalpha.com/api/v1"
    api_key_name = "appid"

    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.api_key = os.getenv("WA_API_DEV")

    def _call_api(self, url, params, endpoint_info, headers):
        resp = requests.get(url, params=params, headers=headers, timeout=30)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        return {"response": resp.text}

    @BaseProxy.endpoint(
        category="query",
        endpoint="llm-api",
        name="Wolfram Alpha LLM API",
        description="Natural-language query; returns a text answer.",
        params={"input*": (str, "10 densest elemental metals"), "assumption": (str, None)},
        response={"response": "Input interpretation: ..."},
    )
    def query(self, params: dict) -> dict:
        return params

Key points:

  • __init__ receives cutoff_date, activate_proxies, deploy_mode, and the runtime through **kwargs; pass them on to super().__init__, which also accepts use_cache.
  • Read API keys from the environment, and fail with a clear message when one is required and missing.
  • The endpoint method is the place for per-endpoint logic; _call_api is the place for transport.

docs.title: Three ways proxies enter the registry
1. @ProxyRegistrator at import time
docs.text:
@ProxyRegistrator(path="wa", name="Wolfram Alpha API", description="...")
class WAProxy(BaseProxy):
    ...
# registered under the key "wa" in the default runtime

docs.title: 2. Package discovery
docs.text:
[package]
name = "my_system"

[proxies]
paths = ["proxies"]

Discovery imports every .py file in the folder and registers each BaseProxy subclass as my_system.proxies:<path>: the class's _proxy_path, which @ProxyRegistrator sets and a class may also declare itself, else <file>/<ClassName>.

docs.title: 3. load_builtin_proxies()
docs.text:
LLLM bundles proxies for research data APIs. Importing them registers them in the default runtime:

from lllm.runtimes.native.proxies import load_builtin_proxies

loaded, errors = load_builtin_proxies()
print("Loaded:", loaded)
print("Failed (missing deps):", errors)       # e.g. exa_proxy needs exa_py

load_builtin_proxies(["lllm.runtimes.native.proxies.builtin.wa_proxy"])   # selective
Key API API key variable fmp Financial Modeling Prep FMP_API_KEY fred Federal Reserve Economic Data FRED_API_KEY exa Exa search (needs exa_py) EXA_API_KEY gt Google Trends through SearchApi SEARCH_API_KEY msd Main Street Data MSD_API_KEY wa Wolfram Alpha LLM API WA_API_DEV

BUILTIN_PROXY_MODULES lists the module paths. Use them as ready proxies, or as worked examples of base_url, header and query-parameter keys, cutoff-date handling, and _call_api overrides.

docs.title: ProxyManager
docs.text:
ProxyManager instantiates registered proxies and dispatches calls:

from lllm import ProxyManager

pm = ProxyManager(activate_proxies=["fmp", "calc"], cutoff_date=None, deploy_mode=False)

pm.available()                   # ['calc', 'fmp']
pm.retrieve_api_docs()           # human-readable docs for every loaded proxy
pm.retrieve_api_docs("calc")     # one proxy (what query_api_doc returns)
pm.api_catalog()                 # {name: api_directory()} structured metadata
pm.get_api_directory("calc")

pm("calc/add", {"a": 1, "b": 2})       # same as CALL_API
pm("calc.add", {"a": 1, "b": 2})       # method-name form
pm("calc/add", a=1, b=2)               # keyword params
pm.register("custom/my_api", MyAPIProxy)   # add or replace at runtime

ProxyManager(activate_proxies=None, cutoff_date=None, deploy_mode=False, runtime=None, registry=None) reads proxies from the given registry (default runtime) when it is created. A proxy is loaded if any entry of activate_proxies equals its qualified key (my_system.proxies:fmp), its bare key (fmp), or its @ProxyRegistrator path. An empty list loads every registered proxy. Loaded proxies are addressed by their bare key.

docs.title: Tactic-backed endpoints
docs.text:
A proxy endpoint can run a tactic:

class SharedProxy(BaseProxy):
    code_review = BaseProxy.tactic_endpoint(
        "shared_pkg.tactics:code_review",
        config="shared_pkg:default",
    )


SharedProxy.register_tactic("shared_pkg.tactics:review", endpoint="review", config="shared_pkg:default")

The endpoint's params and response schema come from the tactic's tool schema, so it shows up in query_api_doc like any endpoint and runs through CALL_API. See Tactics.

docs.title: Related utilities
docs.text:
• Computer use. lllm.runtimes.native.tools.cua is an experimental browser-automation agent built on the OpenAI computer-use API and Playwright (pip install "lllm-core[tools]"). For provider-side computer use inside a normal agent turn, see addon_args in Prompts.
  • Protocol wrappers. lllm.proxy_tactic (call recording) and lllm.sandbox_tactic (timeouts and payload limits) wrap protocol tactics when you serve them. They are unrelated to native API proxies and code sandboxes.

docs.title: Runtime & Registries
docs.text:
Most code only needs load_runtime()

Call load_runtime() once at startup to load your package, then refer to resources by name. Read on if you write tests with isolated registries, run parallel experiments with separate runtimes, or embed LLLM in a system that manages its own package loading.

A runtime is a registry: one store of ResourceNode objects keyed by namespaced URLs. It is where prompts, tools, proxies, tactics, configs, assets, and context managers are looked up by name.

from lllm import Runtime   # Runtime is an alias of Registry

docs.title: Loading a package
docs.text:
Nothing is loaded when you import lllm. Populate the default runtime explicitly:

from lllm import load_runtime

runtime = load_runtime()   # finds lllm.toml, loads the package tree, sets it as default

Projects generated by lllm create my-app do this in main.py. Looking up a resource in a runtime that nothing has been loaded into raises a KeyError that says to call lllm.load_runtime().

load_runtime(toml_path=None, name=None, *, discover_cwd=True, discover_shared_packages=True):

  1. Find the manifest. With toml_path, that file (or the lllm.toml in that folder). Otherwise $LLLM_CONFIG if set, then the first lllm.toml, .lllm.toml, or LLLM.toml in the working directory or its parents (a template/ subfolder at each level is checked too).
  2. Load the package tree: the package, its dependencies (recursively, with cycle detection), and every resource section. See Package Discovery.
  3. No manifest? With discover_cwd=True, the working directory is scanned for the standard folders (prompts/, tools/, proxies/, configs/, tactics/, assets/, services/). If any exist they are loaded as a package named after the directory, with a RuntimeWarning suggesting you add an lllm.toml. Otherwise the runtime stays empty. Pass discover_cwd=False for a strict, deterministic boot.
  4. Shared packages. With discover_shared_packages=True, every sub-folder with an lllm.toml in <project root>/lllm_packages/ and ~/.lllm/packages/ is loaded too.
  5. Store it. name=None makes the new runtime the default; a name stores it as a named runtime and leaves the default alone.

docs.title: The default runtime
docs.text:
A process-wide default runtime exists from import time, empty and without side effects. Everything that takes runtime= / registry= falls back to it: Agent, Dialog, Tactic, ProxyManager, ProxyRegistrator, register_prompt, and the load_* helpers.

from lllm import get_default_runtime, set_default_runtime

runtime = get_default_runtime()
print(runtime.keys("prompt"))   # qualified keys of every prompt
print(runtime.default_namespace)  # root package name, used for bare keys

docs.title: Named runtimes
docs.text:
For parallel experiments or tests, keep separate runtimes:

from lllm import get_runtime, load_runtime

load_runtime("experiment_a/lllm.toml", name="exp_a")
load_runtime("experiment_b/lllm.toml", name="exp_b")

rt_a = get_runtime("exp_a")
rt_b = get_runtime("exp_b")

tactic_a = MyTactic(config, registry=rt_a)

Each runtime has its own registry. get_runtime() with no name returns the default; an unknown name raises KeyError.

docs.title: Internal architecture
docs.text:
All resources are ResourceNode objects in one _resources dict, keyed by qualified key ("my_pkg.prompts:greet/hello"). A _type_index maps resource types to keys for fast filtered iteration.

Registry
├── _resources: Dict[str, ResourceNode]    # "pkg.section:key" -> node
├── _type_index: Dict[str, Set[str]]       # "prompt" -> {"pkg.prompts:a", ...}
├── packages: Dict[str, PackageInfo]       # "pkg_name" (or alias) -> metadata
├── _loaded_package_paths: Set[str]        # cycle detection
└── _default_namespace: Optional[str]      # root package name

PackageInfo(name, version, description, base_dir, alias) describes a loaded package; effective_name is the alias if set.

docs.title: Resource resolution
docs.text:
runtime.get(key, resource_type=None) and the typed helpers resolve keys in this order:

  1. Exact match: key is a qualified key in the store.
  2. Default namespace: for a key without :, try <default>.<section>:<key> for the requested type's section (prompt -> prompts, proxy -> proxies, ...), then each built-in section in order: tactics, services, configs, assets, prompts, tools, proxies.
  3. Package shorthand: for pkg:key with no . in the package part and a requested type, try pkg.<section>:key.

So:

  • get_prompt("greet/hello") tries my_system.prompts:greet/hello
  • get_prompt("child_pkg:greet/hello") tries child_pkg.prompts:greet/hello
  • get("my_pkg.prompts:greet/hello") is an exact match

A miss raises KeyError listing the closest registered keys (or, in a runtime nothing has been loaded into, suggesting lllm.load_runtime()).

docs.title: Through discovery
docs.text:
from lllm import load_package

load_package("path/to/lllm.toml", runtime=runtime)
# every prompt, tool, proxy, tactic, config, and asset is now registered

load_package(config_path=None, *, runtime=None, registry=None) loads one package tree into an existing runtime without the shared-package scan. The first package loaded into a runtime becomes its default namespace.

docs.title: Typed methods
docs.text:
from lllm import Prompt, Runtime, tool

runtime = Runtime()

# Prompt: key is prompt.path
runtime.register_prompt(Prompt(path="test/greeting", prompt="Hello {name}!"), namespace="my_pkg.prompts")


# Tool: the key's last segment must equal the tool's name
@tool(description="Search documents.")
def search(query: str) -> str:
    return query


runtime.register_tool("search", search, namespace="my_pkg.tools")

# Proxy and tactic classes
runtime.register_proxy("search/web", WebProxy, namespace="my_pkg.proxies")
runtime.register_tactic("analytica", Analytica, namespace="my_pkg.tactics")

# Config: eager, or lazy with a loader
runtime.register_config("default", {"global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o"}}, namespace="my_pkg.configs")
runtime.register_config("heavy", loader=lambda: yaml.safe_load(open("heavy.yaml")),
                        namespace="my_pkg.configs")

# Context manager class: key is cls.name
runtime.register_context_manager(KeepLastTurns)

register_tool rejects a key whose last segment differs from tool.name; that exact-name rule is what binds prompt Function declarations to implementations. register_proxy and register_tactic default to overwrite=False and raise ValueError on a duplicate key; the other typed methods overwrite by default. Registering a prompt, tool, proxy, or tactic also records its qualified key and namespace on the object, which is how bare refs on a prompt resolve inside its own package.

Decorators that register at import time, such as @ProxyRegistrator without a runtime=, write to the default runtime.

docs.title: Low-level API
docs.text:
from lllm.runtimes.native.core.resource import ResourceNode

node = ResourceNode.eager("logo.png", image_bytes, namespace="my_pkg.assets", resource_type="asset")
runtime.register(node)

# Lazy: the loader runs on first .value access, then the result is cached
node = ResourceNode.lazy("big_data", loader=lambda: load_parquet("data.parquet"),
                         namespace="my_pkg.datasets", resource_type="dataset")
runtime.register(node)

ResourceNode is a wrapper, not a base class: Prompt, Function, Tactic, and BaseProxy do not inherit from it. Extra keyword arguments to eager / lazy land in node.metadata (discovered files store file_path there). node.category is "platform" for tactics, services, configs, and assets, "native" for prompts, tools, proxies, and context managers, and "custom" otherwise.

docs.title: Retrieving resources
docs.text:
# Typed (section inferred)
prompt = runtime.get_prompt("greet/hello")
tool_fn = runtime.get_tool("my_pkg:search")
tactic_cls = runtime.get_tactic("analytica")
proxy_cls = runtime.get_proxy("my_pkg.proxies:search/web")
config = runtime.get_config("default")          # triggers the lazy load
asset = runtime.get_asset("my_pkg:logo.png")
proxy_cls = runtime.get_proxy("my_pkg:search/web")  # package shorthand works for every type

# Generic
value = runtime.get("my_pkg.assets:logo.png")
node = runtime.get_node("my_pkg.assets:logo.png")
runtime.has("my_pkg.prompts:greet/hello")       # True / False

# Module-level helpers (default runtime unless runtime=/registry= is given)
from lllm import load_config, load_prompt, load_proxy, load_resource, load_tactic, load_tool
from lllm.runtimes.native.core.resource import load_asset, load_service_ref

prompt = load_prompt("child_pkg:greet/hello")
config = load_config("experiments/ablation", runtime=runtime)
asset = load_resource("my_pkg.assets:logo.png")

load_resource requires a : and accepts "pkg.section:key" or "section:key" (the section is looked up in the default package). A typed lookup that finds a resource of another type raises TypeError.

docs.title: Isolated runtimes for testing
docs.text:
from lllm import Prompt, Runtime


def test_my_tactic():
    runtime = Runtime()
    runtime.register_prompt(Prompt(path="test/prompt", prompt="Hi {name}"), namespace="test.prompts")
    tactic = MyTactic(config, registry=runtime)
    result = tactic("hello")
    assert runtime.has("test.prompts:test/prompt")

Pair this with a scripted invoker (see Invokers) to test tactics without network access.

runtime.reset() clears every registry and the default namespace:

import pytest

from lllm import get_default_runtime


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def clean_runtime():
    yield
    get_default_runtime().reset()

docs.title: Registry / Runtime
docs.text: Member Description register(node, overwrite=True) Register any ResourceNode. get(key, resource_type=None) Resolve a key and return the node's value. get_node(key, resource_type=None) Resolve a key and return the ResourceNode. has(key) Whether a key resolves. keys(resource_type=None) Sorted qualified keys, optionally filtered by type. iter_items(resource_type=None) / iter_nodes(...) Deterministic iteration over (key, node) pairs / nodes. register_prompt(prompt, overwrite=True, namespace="") Register a prompt under prompt.path. get_prompt(path) Typed lookup. register_tool(name, tool, overwrite=True, namespace="") Register a Function; the key's last segment must equal tool.name. get_tool(path) Typed lookup. register_proxy(name, proxy_cls, overwrite=False, namespace="") Register a proxy class. get_proxy(path) Typed lookup. register_tactic(tactic_type, tactic_cls, overwrite=False, namespace="") Register a tactic class. get_tactic(name) Typed lookup. register_config(name, config_data=None, overwrite=True, namespace="", loader=None) Register a config, eager or lazy. get_config(path) Typed lookup (runs a lazy loader). get_asset(path) Typed lookup for [assets] files. register_service(name, service, overwrite=True, namespace="", loader=None) / get_service(path) Service resources (ASGI apps, service spec files). register_context_manager(cm_cls, overwrite=True, namespace="") Register a ContextManager class under cm_cls.name. get_context_manager(name) Typed lookup. register_package(pkg) Record a PackageInfo. packages Dict of loaded packages (aliases included). default_namespace Root package name used for bare keys. discovery_done True after load_runtime finished. loaded_package_paths Frozen set of loaded package folders. reset() Clear all state.

docs.title: Module-level helpers
docs.text:
Importable from lllm (defined in lllm.runtimes.native.core.runtime):

Function Description get_default_runtime() The process-wide default runtime. set_default_runtime(rt) Replace the default. get_runtime(name=None) A named runtime (None = default). load_runtime(toml_path=None, name=None, *, discover_cwd=True, discover_shared_packages=True) Create, populate, and store a runtime.

get_default_registry, set_default_registry, get_registry, and load_registry (in lllm.runtimes.native.core.runtime) are aliases.

docs.title: Package management
docs.text:
Also importable from lllm; see Package Discovery for the workflow.

Function Description install_package(zip_path, *, alias=None, scope="user", load=True, runtime=None) Install a package zip into ~/.lllm/packages/ (scope="user") or <project root>/lllm_packages/ (scope="project"). alias renames the package namespace; load=False skips loading it. Returns the installed folder. export_package(package_name, output_path, *, bundle_deps=False, runtime=None) Zip a loaded package (.zip is appended to the path if missing). bundle_deps=True packs its transitive dependencies under lllm_packages/ inside the zip. Returns the zip path. list_packages(scope=None, *, runtime=None) Dicts with name, version, description, scope, path for installed packages, plus packages loaded in the runtime from elsewhere (scope="unknown"). remove_package(name, *, scope=None, runtime=None) Delete an installed package and unregister it. Raises ValueError if it exists in both scopes and no scope is given.

docs.title: Design notes
docs.text:
• Creating a runtime has no side effects. No scanning, no imports; it is an empty container until something registers into it.
  • One store, smart resolution. Each resource is stored once under its qualified key. Bare keys and package shorthand are resolved at read time, not stored as duplicates (aliases are the exception: an aliased dependency is registered again under its alias namespace).
  • Not thread-safe for concurrent registration. The normal pattern (load once at startup, read many times during agent calls) has no contention. If you register concurrently, use a lock or separate runtimes.

docs.title: Tactics
docs.text:
A tactic is the top-level abstraction of the native runtime: the "program" that wires agents (callers) to prompts (functions). It is the uppermost building block of an agentic system and is designed to be local, functional, and composable.

How it relates to the rest of the runtime:

  • Prompts define what an agent can do on one turn: template, parser, tools, handler.
  • Agents execute prompts through the call loop, managing dialogs and retries.
  • Tactics define how a group of agents collaborates on a task.

A tactic accepts a str or a Pydantic model and returns a str or a Pydantic model; subclasses narrow these types for their interface.

lllm.Tactic is one class with two faces. As a program, you write call() and, if you need agents, declare agent_group. As a protocol tactic, every Tactic has validated run() / arun() and info(), so it can be served, packaged, and composed with tactics from other runtimes without an adapter.

from lllm import Tactic   # the same object as lllm.runtimes.native.Tactic

docs.title: Defining a tactic
docs.text:
Subclass Tactic, set name and agent_group, implement call():

from lllm import Tactic


class Analytica(Tactic):
    name = "analytica"
    agent_group = ["analyzer", "synthesizer"]

    def call(self, task: str, **kwargs) -> str:
        analyzer = self.agents["analyzer"]
        synthesizer = self.agents["synthesizer"]

        analyzer.open("work", prompt_args={"task": task})
        analysis = analyzer.respond()

        synthesizer.open("synth", prompt_args={"analysis": analysis.content})
        return synthesizer.respond().content

config = {
    "global": {"model_name": "o4-mini", "model_args": {"max_completion_tokens": 20000}},
    "agent_configs": [
        {"name": "analyzer", "system_prompt_path": "analytica/analyzer_system"},
        {"name": "synthesizer", "system_prompt_path": "analytica/synthesizer_system"},
    ],
}

tactic = Analytica(config)
result = tactic("Analyze this paper")

With agent_group set, the tactic builds a fresh, configured Agent for each name every time it runs call() (or streams), and puts them in self.agents. Without it, call() is plain Python: deterministic steps, or orchestration over other tactics, tools, and runtimes.

docs.title: call() or a protocol hook
docs.text:
A tactic writes one program: call(), or the protocol hook _run() (or _arun() for async-only code). The native entry points (tactic(task), acall, bcall, ccall) run whichever one the class writes, inside a TacticCallSession:

from lllm import Tactic


class Upper(Tactic):
    name = "upper"

    def _run(self, input_value, *, context=None):
        return input_value.upper()


upper = Upper()
upper("hi")       # 'HI', recorded in a TacticCallSession
upper.run("hi")   # 'HI'
  • run() and arun() run that program too.
  • call() runs on a per-call copy of the tactic with fresh agents (the v1 design), whichever entry point starts it. A hook runs on the tactic itself, like any protocol tactic, so it should not keep per-call state on self. Agents are built fresh only for call() programs and streams, so a class that declares agent_group but writes only a hook gets a warning: write call() instead.
  • A hook always receives a CallContext as context= (a fresh one when the caller passes none).
  • A hook-only tactic has no call(): upper.call("hi") raises TacticUnsupportedError and points to tactic(task), run(), and arun(). A hook that hands its call back, through super()._run() or self.call(), raises the same error at once instead of recursing.
  • An _arun()-only tactic also gets run() and tactic(task), which run the hook to completion.
  • call() may be async def. The async entry points (acall, arun, ccall, and a service's /run) await it on the caller's event loop, so it must not block: call agents with await agent.arespond(), sub-tactics with await sub.acall(...). The sync entry points (tactic(task), run(), bcall) run it on the calling thread's own event loop, kept for that thread's later calls (a forked process starts a fresh one), so clients it keeps between calls stay usable. A sync call made from async code runs the program on a separate thread while the caller waits.
  • A tactic that writes neither raises TacticUnsupportedError when called.

NativeTactic is a thin subclass that only insists on agent_group (raising AssertionError without it), kept for code that subclasses it.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
Tactic(config=None, runtime=None, registry=None, tactic_path=None, context=None, observer=None,
       *, name=None, description=None, package_ref=None, service_ref=None, examples=None, metadata=None)
Argument Meaning config Dict or Pydantic model. With agent_group: global, agent_configs, and optionally invoker, invoker_config, max_workers. registry / runtime Registry used to resolve prompts, tools, and configs (the same object; pass one). Defaults to the default runtime. tactic_path Stable identity recorded on sessions, e.g. "my_pkg::analytica". context A TacticContext(registry=..., tactic_path=..., observer=..., metadata=...) bundling the above. observer Object with tactic lifecycle hooks; see Logging. name, description, package_ref, service_ref, examples, metadata Override what info() publishes. The description defaults to the class docstring. A name is one path segment (no /, :, \, ;, or %); an Enum member stands for its value.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
A tactic class must be in a registry for build_tactic, config tactic_type, or tactic refs such as my_pkg.tactics:analytica to find it.

  • Package discovery ([tactics] paths in lllm.toml) imports the modules and registers every Tactic subclass that defines name, under that name.

  • At class definition, by passing a registry as a class keyword:

    from lllm import Runtime, Tactic

registry = Runtime()


class Analytica(Tactic, runtime=registry):   # or registry=registry
    name = "analytica"
    agent_group = ["analyzer", "synthesizer"]
    ...

  • Explicitly, with lllm.register_tactic_class(Analytica, runtime=registry).

Defining a subclass without one of these does not register it anywhere.

docs.title: Building from config
docs.text:
from lllm import build_tactic, resolve_config

tactic = build_tactic(resolve_config("experiment"), name="analytica")
result = tactic("Analyze this paper")

Or let the config name the tactic:

# configs/experiment.yaml
tactic_type: analytica

agent_configs:
  - name: analyzer
    model_name: o4-mini
    system_prompt_path: analytica/analyzer_system
  - name: synthesizer
    model_name: o4-mini
    system_prompt_path: analytica/synthesizer_system

tactic = build_tactic(resolve_config("experiment"))   # reads tactic_type

build_tactic(config, name=None, runtime=None, *, registry=None, **kwargs) looks the class up in the registry, sets the stable tactic_path to "<package>::<name>" for package-discovered tactics, and passes extra keyword arguments (for example observer=) to the constructor.

docs.title: Agent initialization
docs.text:
agent_group lists the agent names the tactic needs. At construction, the tactic reads global and agent_configs from the config, merges each entry over global, and parses it into an AgentSpec:

global:
  model_name: o4-mini
  model_args:
    temperature: 0.1

agent_configs:
  - name: analyzer
    system_prompt_path: analytica/analyzer_system
    max_completion_tokens: 20000        # unknown key -> model_args (with a warning)
  - name: synthesizer
    system_prompt: "Synthesize this analysis: {analysis}"

AgentSpec separates config parsing from agent construction. Known keys (model_name, system_prompt, system_prompt_path, api_type, model_args, the retry budgets, tools, proxy, skills, context_manager, inference_hints, extra_settings) are extracted; anything else is merged into model_args. A missing agent, a missing model_name, or a prompt path that does not resolve raises before any model call.

The constructor also builds the invoker (LiteLLM unless the config sets invoker), so constructing a tactic with agent_group needs lllm-core[native] installed. See Configuration for every key.

docs.title: Stateless execution and per-call isolation
docs.text:
A tactic holds no per-call state. Each call of a call() program, whatever the entry point, runs on a shallow copy with fresh agents:

result_a = tactic("Analyze this paper")        # call 1
result_b = tactic("Analyze this other paper")  # call 2: no interference

For each call, __call__:

  1. copies the tactic (copy.copy), sharing the config, registry, invoker, and agent specs;
  2. builds fresh Agents from the specs, each with no dialogs, and wraps them in _TrackedAgent proxies that record every respond();
  3. validates the task against the input type, runs call() (awaiting it if it is async), validates the result against the output type;
  4. marks the TacticCallSession as "success" or "failure" (re-raising the exception).

Concurrent calls (bcall, threads) never share mutable state: each gets its own agents, dialogs, and session. Streams from an overridden sync events() or stream() get the same treatment, one copy per stream. Protocol hooks (_run(), _arun()) and async astream()/aevents() overrides run on the instance itself, like any protocol tactic: keep per-call state out of self there (an agent_group tactic that overrides them warns).

docs.title: Session tracking
docs.text:
Every agent.respond() inside call() is recorded into a TacticCallSession. You write normal agent code; tracking is invisible:

def call(self, task: str, **kwargs) -> str:
    analyzer = self.agents["analyzer"]
    analyzer.open("work", prompt_args={"task": task})
    result = analyzer.respond()      # recorded into the TacticCallSession
    return result.content

Ask for the session with return_session=True:

session = tactic("Analyze this paper", return_session=True)

print(session.state)              # "success"
print(session.delivery)           # the return value of call()
print(session.total_cost)         # InvokeCost across agents and sub-tactics
print(session.agent_call_count)   # number of agent.respond() calls
print(session.summary())          # compact dict

tactic(task, session_name=None, tags=None, metadata=None, return_session=False, **kwargs): extra keyword arguments are passed to call() (or the hook). session_name defaults to "<name>_<task hash>_<timestamp>"; it, tags, and metadata are handed to the tactic's observer, which is how sessions get persisted (see Logging).

docs.title: TacticCallSession
docs.text:
Field Type Description tactic_name str The tactic's name: the constructor's name=, else Tactic.name, else the class name tactic_path str \| None Stable identity, "<package>::<name>" when known state str "initial", "running", "success", or "failure" agent_sessions Dict[str, List[AgentCallSession]] Per-agent call records sub_tactic_sessions Dict[str, List[TacticCallSession]] Sessions of tactics called during this call delivery Any Return value of call() (or the hook) on success error str \| None "ExcType: message" on failure error_traceback str \| None Full traceback on failure

Properties:

session.agent_cost             # cost from this tactic's agents
session.sub_tactic_cost        # cost from sub-tactic sessions
session.total_cost             # agent_cost + sub_tactic_cost (recursive)
session.agent_call_count       # agent.respond() calls
session.sub_tactic_call_count  # sub-tactic calls

docs.title: Sub-tactic composition
docs.text:
Tactics compose like nn.Module children. Assign a tactic as an attribute and it is tracked in sub_tactics:

from lllm import Tactic


class ResearchTactic(Tactic):
    name = "research"
    agent_group = ["planner"]

    def __init__(self, config, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(config, **kwargs)
        self.analyzer = Analytica(config, registry=self.context.registry)
        self.searcher = Searcher(config, registry=self.context.registry)

    def call(self, task: str, **kwargs) -> str:
        planner = self.agents["planner"]
        planner.open("plan", prompt_args={"task": task})
        plan = planner.respond()

        # Sub-tactic calls: each runs with its own fresh agents
        analysis = self.analyzer(plan.content)
        search = self.searcher(task)

        planner.receive(f"Analysis: {analysis}\nSearch: {search}")
        return planner.respond().content


tactic.sub_tactics      # {'analyzer': Analytica(...), 'searcher': Searcher(...)}

Sessions roll up automatically. Any tactic called while another tactic is running records its session into the caller's, under its name (session.sub_tactic_sessions["analytica"], or the name= it was constructed with), so sub-tactic agent calls and cost reach the parent's total_cost. This tracks the call, not the attribute: a tactic created inside call() is recorded too, and so are calls made through acall, bcall, and ccall, whose worker threads carry the caller's context.

docs.title: Tactic inheritance
docs.text: Concrete tactics subclass like any Python class, so you can build reusable pipeline bases and extend them.

docs.title: Extending a concrete tactic
docs.text:
class WritingPipeline(Tactic):
    """Reusable base: outline, then draft."""
    name = "writing_pipeline"
    agent_group = ["outliner", "writer"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        outliner = self.agents["outliner"]
        writer = self.agents["writer"]

        outliner.open("outline")
        outliner.receive(f"Create a concise outline about: {task}")
        outline = outliner.respond().content

        writer.open("write")
        writer.receive(f"Expand this outline:\n\n{outline}")
        return writer.respond().content


class EditedWritingPipeline(WritingPipeline):
    """Adds an editing stage on top of the base pipeline."""
    name = "edited_writing_pipeline"
    agent_group = ["outliner", "writer", "editor"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        draft = super().call(task)        # reuse outline -> draft

        editor = self.agents["editor"]
        editor.open("edit")
        editor.receive(f"Polish this draft:\n\n{draft}")
        return editor.respond().content

super().call(task) works because agents are built for every name in the subclass's agent_group before call() runs.

docs.title: Abstract bases with register=False
docs.text:
register=False keeps a helper base out of the registry even when a registry is passed:

class BasePipeline(Tactic, register=False):
    """Shared helpers; never registered."""

    def _run_stage(self, agent_name: str, alias: str, message: str) -> str:
        agent = self.agents[agent_name]
        agent.open(alias)
        agent.receive(message)
        return agent.respond().content


class SummaryPipeline(BasePipeline):
    name = "summary_pipeline"
    agent_group = ["extractor", "writer"]

    def call(self, text: str) -> str:
        facts = self._run_stage("extractor", "extract", f"Extract key facts:\n{text}")
        return self._run_stage("writer", "write", f"Summarise:\n{facts}")

docs.title: Typed I/O inheritance
docs.text:
Subclasses can tighten the output type:

class BaseAnalysis(Tactic, register=False):
    agent_group = ["analyzer"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        agent = self.agents["analyzer"]
        agent.open("analyze")
        agent.receive(task)
        return agent.respond().content


class StructuredAnalysis(BaseAnalysis):
    name = "structured_analysis"
    output_type = AnalysisOutput

    def call(self, task: str) -> AnalysisOutput:
        return AnalysisOutput.model_validate_json(super().call(task))

A type the subclass declares itself wins over an inherited one under either spelling: an output_model set on the subclass replaces an inherited output_type, and input_model likewise replaces input_type.

docs.title: Batch and concurrent execution
docs.text: Model calls are I/O-bound, so tactics fan out on thread pools. Each task gets its own agents; there is no lock contention.

docs.title: Synchronous batch
docs.text:
tasks = ["Analyze paper A", "Analyze paper B", "Analyze paper C"]
results = tactic.bcall(tasks, max_workers=3)   # results[i] belongs to tasks[i]

bcall(tasks, max_workers=None, fail_fast=True, tags=None, metadata=None, return_sessions=False, **kwargs) returns results in input order. With fail_fast=True the first failure raises; with fail_fast=False exceptions are returned in place of results.

docs.title: Async single
docs.text:
result = await tactic.acall("Analyze this paper")

acall awaits an async def call() on the caller's loop and runs a sync call() in the default executor, so neither blocks the event loop (as long as the async one does not block itself; see above).

docs.title: Async concurrent (fastest first)
docs.text:
async for idx, result in tactic.ccall(tasks, max_workers=3):
    print(f"Task {idx} finished: {result}")

Yields (index, result) pairs as tasks complete, not in input order. Async programs run as concurrent tasks on the caller's loop, sync ones on up to max_workers threads.

All three accept return_session(s)=True to get TacticCallSession objects. max_workers defaults to the config's max_workers key (4 if unset).

docs.title: Typed I/O with Pydantic
docs.text:
For shareable tactics, declare the input and output types so callers can validate against them and services can publish schemas:

from pydantic import BaseModel
from lllm import Tactic


class AnalysisInput(BaseModel):
    topic: str
    depth: int = 3


class AnalysisOutput(BaseModel):
    reasoning: str
    conclusion: str
    confidence: float


class Analytica(Tactic):
    name = "analytica"
    input_type = AnalysisInput
    output_type = AnalysisOutput
    agent_group = ["analyzer"]

    def call(self, task: AnalysisInput) -> AnalysisOutput:
        analyzer = self.agents["analyzer"]
        analyzer.open("work", prompt_args={"topic": task.topic, "depth": task.depth})
        parsed = analyzer.respond().parsed          # prompt uses DefaultTagParser
        tags = parsed["xml_tags"]
        return AnalysisOutput(
            reasoning=tags["reasoning"][0],
            conclusion=tags["answer"][0],
            confidence=float(tags["confidence"][0]),
        )


tactic({"topic": "attention", "depth": 2})   # the dict is validated into AnalysisInput

input_type / output_type (or the aliases input_model / output_model) accept any type Pydantic's TypeAdapter can validate. The tactic validates the task before call() and the result after it, and tactic.info() publishes both as JSON schema, which is what a service's /info returns.

Simple tactics can stay str in, str out.

docs.title: Tactics as tools
docs.text:
Tactic tools make the abstraction graph recursive. A Tactic is the top-level orchestration unit and a Prompt is the low-level contract for one turn; exposing a tactic as a tool lets a turn call back into a complete agentic subsystem. A planner prompt can invoke a code-review tactic, that tactic runs its own agents and prompts, and the result returns through the normal tool loop.

Mechanically, a tactic tool is a generated Function backed by a decorated tactic method. Use @tool when a plain function is enough; use @tactictool when the implementation needs config, agents, prompts, or several turns.

docs.title: Exposing a method
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel
from lllm import Tactic, tactictool


class CodeInput(BaseModel):
    code: str
    language: str = "python"


class CodeReviewTactic(Tactic):
    """Review code and return concrete issues."""
    name = "code_review"
    agent_group = ["reviewer"]

    @tactictool("code_review", description="Review code and list issues.", config="shared_pkg:default")
    def call(self, task: CodeInput) -> str:
        reviewer = self.agents["reviewer"]
        reviewer.open("review", prompt_args={"language": task.language})
        reviewer.receive(task.code)
        return reviewer.respond().content

tactictool(name, *, description=None, input_model=None, output_model=None, config=None):

  • name is required and is the tool name the model sees.
  • Input schema: a BaseModel parameter (or input_model=) becomes the tool's JSON schema; the model's arguments are validated into it. Otherwise annotated parameters are mapped to JSON types, and unannotated ones become strings with a warning.
  • Description: the decorator's description, else the method docstring, else the class docstring, else a generated one (with a warning).
  • Result: a BaseModel return value is sent as JSON, anything else with str().
  • config is required for refs: the URL identifies the class, not the config to instantiate it with. Pass a config ref (resolved relative to the tactic's package, base inheritance applied) or an inline dict.

Each tool call instantiates the tactic with that config and calls the method directly.

docs.title: Referencing tactic tools
docs.text:
Put the tactic's URL in a prompt's function_list:

from lllm import Prompt

prompt = Prompt(
    path="agent/system",
    prompt="Use the available tools when useful.",
    function_list=["shared_pkg.tactics:code_review"],
)

Full URLs (shared_pkg.tactics:code_review) are canonical; package shorthand (shared_pkg:code_review) and bare names resolve relative to the prompt's package, then the runtime's default namespace.

A tactic can expose several tools. Select one with a URL fragment:

from lllm import Prompt, Tactic, tactictool


class ReviewTactic(Tactic):
    name = "review"
    agent_group = ["reviewer"]

    @tactictool("review_code", config="shared_pkg:default")
    def call(self, task: CodeInput) -> str:
        ...

    @tactictool("summarize", config="shared_pkg:default")
    def summarize_review(self, task: SummaryInput) -> str:
        ...


Prompt(path="lead/system", prompt="...", function_list=[
    "shared_pkg.tactics:review",            # the decorated call()
    "shared_pkg.tactics:review#summarize",  # a named method (tool name or method name)
])

Selection rules: a decorated call() is the default; a tactic with exactly one decorated method uses it; with several decorated methods and no decorated call(), a fragment is required. A tactic with no decorated methods falls back to call() with a warning, which only works for callers that pass a config explicitly, such as a proxy endpoint.

docs.title: Proxy endpoints
docs.text:
The same tactic can be exposed as a proxy endpoint:

from lllm import BaseProxy, ProxyRegistrator


@ProxyRegistrator(path="shared", name="Shared tools", description="Shared tactic endpoints.")
class SharedProxy(BaseProxy):
    code_review = BaseProxy.tactic_endpoint(
        "shared_pkg.tactics:code_review",
        config="shared_pkg:default",
    )

Tactic-backed endpoints appear in query_api_doc (their params come from the tactic's schema) and run through CALL_API like any other endpoint. SharedProxy.register_tactic("shared_pkg.tactics:review", endpoint="review", config=...) adds one imperatively.

docs.title: Agent-level tool config
docs.text:
To give every turn of an agent access, list the refs in config:

global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  tools:
    - shared_pkg.tools:search
    - shared_pkg.tactics:code_review
    - shared_pkg.proxies:market_data

agent_configs:
  - name: reviewer
    system_prompt_path: system/reviewer

See Agent for how agent tools reach the model.

This design is reference-based to avoid definition cycles: configs name tools by URL instead of importing and building agents while a tool module loads. Regular tool and tactic refs stay lazy until the prompt runs.

docs.title: The other direction: tactics as plain callables
docs.text:
fn = tactic.as_tool()                         # plain callable: fn(task) -> tactic.run(task)
fn = tactic.as_tool(parameter_mode="kwargs")  # fn(**fields), validated into input_type

as_tool() hands a tactic to other agent frameworks (Pydantic AI or anything that accepts Python callables). To give a native prompt any protocol tactic (a Tactic from another package, a Pydantic AI tactic, a remote tactic), wrap it as a Function:

from lllm import Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import tactic_as_function

lookup = tactic_as_function(search_tactic, parameter_mode="kwargs")
prompt = Prompt(path="research/answer", prompt="Use tools when needed.", function_list=[lookup])

The tool publishes the tactic's input schema: in the default "task" mode as one task parameter holding the whole input, and with parameter_mode="kwargs" as the input model's fields, one parameter each. An input without fields, such as str, keeps the single task parameter in either mode. Nested models are inlined as for @tool. The tool's description is the tactic's description.

docs.title: Quick constructor
docs.text:
For prototyping without config files:

from lllm import Tactic

agent = Tactic.quick(system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant.", model="gpt-4o")
agent.open("chat")
agent.receive("What is the capital of France?")
print(agent.respond().content)

This returns a plain Agent, the same object a tactic builds internally. Pass a query as the first argument to get the reply directly; see Agent.

docs.title: Serving and the protocol
docs.text:
Because Tactic is a protocol tactic, the same object you call in Python is the one you serve:

Surface What it does tactic(task, ...), acall, bcall, ccall Native calls; return the result or a TacticCallSession. tactic.run(value, context=None, return_trace=False) Protocol call: validates input and output; return_trace=True returns a CallResult with a CallTrace. await tactic.arun(value, context=None) Async protocol call. tactic.info() TacticInfo: name, description (the class docstring unless overridden), input/output JSON schemas, capabilities, runtime_kind. tactic.events(task) Override it to stream: aevents() and a service's /stream route serve what it yields, as TacticEvents. Each stream runs like call(): on a per-call copy with fresh agents and its own observed session. It is pulled one item at a time on a worker thread, so a slow stream never blocks the event loop and nothing runs ahead of the reader; closing the stream (or a client disconnecting) closes the generator. Overriding the protocol's sync stream() works the same way.

runtime_kind is "native" for tactics that write call() (or declare agent_group) and "python" for ones that only implement _run() or _arun(). A runtime_kind set on a class is inherited by its subclasses.

run() and arun() accept a CallContext (request id, trace id, refs, tags, metadata). It is passed to call() as context= when call accepts a context keyword (or **kwargs), and the per-call copy also exposes it as self.call_context:

from lllm import CallContext, Tactic


class Brief(Tactic):
    """Write a short brief."""
    name = "brief"
    agent_group = ["writer"]

    def call(self, task: str, *, context=None, tone: str = "plain") -> str:
        writer = self.agents["writer"]
        writer.open("draft", prompt_args={"tone": tone})
        writer.receive(task)
        return writer.respond().content


tactic = Brief(config)
tactic.run("Summarize the release", context=CallContext(trace_id="trace-1"))
tactic.info().runtime_kind      # 'native'

A _run() or _arun() hook always receives the CallContext as context=.

docs.title: Serving over HTTP
docs.text:
Pass the tactic to create_tactic_app:

# research_kit/service.py
from lllm import build_tactic, create_tactic_app, load_runtime, resolve_config


def build_public_tactic():
    load_runtime()
    return build_tactic(resolve_config("default"))


app = create_tactic_app(build_public_tactic())

uvicorn research_kit.service:app
# or let the CLI build it (run from the project folder):
lllm serve research_kit.service:build_public_tactic --port 8000

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/run \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": {"topic": "attention"}}'

lllm serve module:attr accepts a tactic instance, a Tactic subclass it can construct with no arguments, a factory, or a plain function; point it at a factory when the tactic needs a loaded runtime and config. It imports from the working directory, so no PYTHONPATH setup is needed. See Tactic protocol and Services.

docs.title: Factories and handlers
docs.text:
lllm serve module:attr, lllm inspect module:attr, and a package tactic's entry = "module:attr" tell a factory from a handler by one rule:

  • A factory is called once, with no arguments, when the entry is loaded, and returns the tactic. A function is a factory when it takes no parameters, or when it can be called without arguments and its return annotation is a Tactic.
  • Any other function is a handler: it is wrapped with lllm.as_tactic and called once per input.
from lllm import Tactic, build_tactic, load_runtime, resolve_config


def build_public_tactic():                       # factory: no parameters
    load_runtime()
    return build_tactic(resolve_config("default"))


def build_named(config_name: str = "default") -> Tactic:   # factory: annotated
    load_runtime()
    return build_tactic(resolve_config(config_name))


def greet(name: str = "world") -> str:            # handler: runs on every input
    return f"Hello {name}"

Without its -> Tactic annotation, build_named would be a handler and receive each input as config_name. An annotation that cannot be evaluated at load time, such as a class imported only under TYPE_CHECKING, counts when the class name ends in Tactic.

docs.title: Objects that only look like tactics
docs.text:
NativeTacticAdapter wraps an object that has call() or run() but does not subclass Tactic (a class from older code, say) as a protocol tactic:

from lllm import NativeTacticAdapter

public = NativeTacticAdapter(legacy_brief, description="Write a brief.", run_kwargs={"tone": "precise"})
public.run("Summarize the release")

It reads the name and types from the object, passes run_kwargs to every call, forwards the CallContext as context= when the object's method accepts it, and with include_context_metadata=True passes safe call metadata (lllm_request_id, lllm_trace_id, refs, endpoint, tags) as metadata=. A Tactic does not need it.

docs.title: Design notes
docs.text:
• Tactics are stateless. Per-call data lives on TacticCallSession, not on the tactic, so tactics are safe to call concurrently.
  • Agents are per call. Each call() and each stream builds fresh agents from specs. The expensive objects (invoker, registry, prompts) are shared; only the Agent shells and their dialogs are new. Protocol hooks run on the tactic itself and do not get agents of their own (see call() or a protocol hook).
  • Tracking is transparent. _TrackedAgent intercepts respond() without changing the agent API, and nested tactic calls record themselves into the running session.
  • Threads, not processes. Model calls are I/O-bound; threads share the invoker and avoid pickling.
  • One class for the program and the protocol. A tactic you can call in a notebook is the tactic you serve, package, and use as a tool.

docs.title: Package Discovery
docs.text:
A single script with one agent is fine for experiments. As a system grows (several prompts, several agents, tactics you want to reuse across projects) you need a way to organise and find resources without hardcoding import paths everywhere.

The native package system is that organisational layer. A package is a folder with an lllm.toml manifest that declares where its prompts, tools, proxies, configs, and tactics live. LLLM discovers them, namespaces them, and loads data lazily.

The jump looks like this:

# Stage 1: everything inline
from lllm import Tactic

agent = Tactic.quick(system_prompt="You are a research assistant.", model="gpt-4o")

# Stage 3: resources discovered from a package, no paths in Python code
from lllm import build_tactic, load_runtime, resolve_config

load_runtime()                                   # reads ./lllm.toml
tactic = build_tactic(resolve_config("research_writer"))
result = tactic("Analyze transformer architectures")

Your Tactic and Prompt code does not change; you add lllm.toml and the folder structure, and LLLM wires everything together. You can always use LLLM purely as a library, but separating resources into a package is the recommended shape for anything beyond a single script.

docs.title: Package layout
docs.text:
package_name/
├── lllm.toml       # package metadata and resource declarations
├── prompts/        # Prompt objects
├── tools/          # @tool Function implementations
├── proxies/        # BaseProxy subclasses
├── configs/        # agent config YAML files
├── tactics/        # Tactic subclasses
├── assets/         # data files (optional)
└── services/       # ASGI apps and service spec files (optional)

lllm create my-app generates a working package in this shape (lllm.toml, prompts/, configs/default.yaml, tactics/, a main.py that calls load_runtime(), and an offline smoke test). Pick another starting point with --template pipeline|proxy|research|service, or point --template at a folder containing lllm-template.toml.

A typical project:

project_name/
├── lllm.toml               # root package
├── lllm_packages/          # drop-in third-party packages (auto-loaded)
│   ├── finance-toolkit/
│   └── data-utils/
└── ...                     # application code, data, etc.

Conceptually, LLLM keeps one registry of resources, indexed by URLs of the form <package>.<section>:<resource_path>. Tactics find agent configs by key, prompts in the prompt registry, tools in the tool registry, and proxies in the proxy registry.

docs.title: Loading packages
docs.text:
Loading is explicit. Call load_runtime() at startup:

from lllm import load_prompt, load_runtime

load_runtime()                          # or load_runtime("path/to/lllm.toml")
prompt = load_prompt("research/system")

load_runtime() uses $LLLM_CONFIG if set, otherwise the nearest lllm.toml (or .lllm.toml, LLLM.toml) in the working directory or its parents. It loads that package and its dependency tree into a fresh runtime and makes it the default.

If there is no manifest, it scans the working directory for the standard folders (prompts/, tools/, proxies/, configs/, tactics/, assets/, services/), loads any it finds as a package named after the directory, and emits a RuntimeWarning recommending an lllm.toml. If none exist, the runtime stays empty. Pass discover_cwd=False to disable the scan.

After the main package, load_runtime() also loads shared packages from the standard drop-in folders; see Sharing packages. For isolated or named runtimes, see Runtime & Registries.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
There are seven built-in resource types (prompts, tools, proxies, configs, tactics, assets, services), and custom sections add your own.

Every resource is wrapped in a ResourceNode that manages its qualified key, namespace, lazy loading, and metadata. ResourceNode is a wrapper, not a base class: Prompt, Function, Tactic, and BaseProxy do not inherit from it.

Python resources (prompts, tools, proxies, tactics, service apps) are registered eagerly when discovery imports their modules. File resources (configs, assets, service specs, custom sections, data files in tools/) are registered lazily: the node holds a loader and the file is read on first access, then cached.

docs.title: lllm.toml for native discovery
docs.text:
[package]
name = "my_system"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Research assistant"

[prompts]
paths = ["prompts"]

[tools]
paths = ["tools"]

[proxies]
paths = ["proxies"]

[configs]
paths = ["configs"]

[tactics]
paths = ["tactics"]

[assets]
paths = ["assets"]

[services]
paths = ["services"]

[dependencies]
packages = ["./packages/child_pkg"]
  • [package]: identity. All resources from this manifest are namespaced under name (default: the folder name).
  • [prompts], [tools], [proxies], [configs], [tactics], [assets], [services]: paths lists folders relative to the manifest. Without paths, the same-named subfolder is used if it exists; otherwise the section is empty. A listed path that does not exist is skipped with a RuntimeWarning.
  • [dependencies]: packages lists other package folders. Each loads into its own namespace only.
  • Any other table is a custom section, with the same paths and fallback rules.

The same manifest can also carry hub metadata (org, kind, named resources such as [tactics.brief] with an entry). Native discovery reads only the keys above. It skips the hub-declared sections (schemas, channels, snapshots, runs, config, docs, examples, requirements, card) unless one sets paths, which makes it a custom section. The hub cannot load most of those sections with paths, and lllm hub validate does not check paths in config or card, the two it does load, so give custom sections their own names. One file serves both:

[package]
name = "research-kit"
org = "acme"
version = "0.2.0"

[prompts]
paths = ["prompts"]

[tactics]
paths = ["tactics"]          # native discovery

[tactics.brief]              # hub resource
entry = "research_kit.tactics:build_tactic"
runtime = "native"

See Package Manifest and Hub for the hub side.

docs.title: Resource URLs and keys
docs.text:
Resources are indexed by <package_name>.<section_name>:<resource_path>, with exactly one :. The resource path depends on the type:

Section Resource path prompts <file path without .py>/<prompt.path> tools <file path> when the tool's name equals the file name, else <file path>/<tool name>; other files: <file path with extension> proxies The @ProxyRegistrator path, else <file path>/<ClassName> tactics Tactic.name (the file path is not part of the key) configs <file path without .yaml/.yml> services Module-level ASGI apps (FastAPI/Starlette): <file path>/<attribute>; spec files (.json, .yaml, .toml): <file path with extension>, loaded as data assets, custom sections <file path with extension>

File paths are relative to the declared folder, so the folder itself is stripped, and several paths entries merge into one flat namespace. An under prefix is prepended to every key from that entry. Files whose names start with _ (and data files starting with .) are skipped, as is __pycache__.

When two entries produce the same key, the later one wins (logged at debug level). Use under to keep them apart.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Given [prompts] paths = ["prompts_1", "prompts_2"] in package my_pkg:

prompts_1/
├── greet.py          # Prompt objects with path "hello" and "goodbye"
└── sub/
    └── deep.py       # path "analyzer"

prompts_2/
└── tools.py          # path "searcher"

The URLs are:

  • my_pkg.prompts:greet/hello
  • my_pkg.prompts:greet/goodbye
  • my_pkg.prompts:sub/deep/analyzer
  • my_pkg.prompts:tools/searcher

docs.title: Convenience access
docs.text:
load_resource takes a URL with a section:

from lllm import load_prompt, load_resource

load_resource("my_pkg.prompts:greet/hello")
load_resource("prompts:greet/hello")          # section only: default package

Typed helpers infer the section:

load_prompt("my_pkg:greet/hello")             # package-qualified
load_prompt("greet/hello")                    # bare: default package
load_prompt("my_pkg.prompts:greet/hello")     # full URL

The default package is the first one loaded into the runtime (the root package). Package shorthand (pkg:key) works for every typed helper, including load_proxy("my_pkg:weather").

docs.title: Dependency-only loading
docs.text:
[package]
name = "my_system"

[dependencies]
packages = ["./packages/child_pkg", "../shared/shared_pkg"]

Each dependency's resources live in its own namespace:

load_prompt("child_pkg:greet/hello")
load_prompt("shared_pkg:tools/searcher")

Nothing is registered under my_system unless you re-export it. Dependencies load recursively, each package folder is loaded once (cycles are detected), and a dependency folder without a manifest is skipped with a RuntimeWarning.

docs.title: Re-exporting into the current namespace
docs.text:
List a dependency's folders in your own sections to include them in your namespace as well:

[package]
name = "my_system"

[prompts]
paths = ["./packages/child_pkg/prompts", "../shared/shared_pkg/prompts"]

[dependencies]
packages = ["./packages/child_pkg", "../shared/shared_pkg"]

load_prompt("greet/hello")             # via my_system (the default package)
load_prompt("child_pkg:greet/hello")   # via the dependency's namespace

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
Two mechanisms resolve name collisions:

  • as on dependencies registers an additional namespace for the package. The original name keeps working.
  • under on resource paths adds a virtual folder prefix inside the importing package's namespace.

Both have a string form and an equivalent TOML table form:

# String keyword form
packages = ["./packages/child_pkg as cp"]
paths = ["./some/path under vendor"]

# Table form
packages = [{path = "./packages/child_pkg", alias = "cp"}]
paths = [{path = "./some/path", prefix = "vendor"}]

# The table form also accepts the keyword names
packages = [{path = "./packages/child_pkg", as = "cp"}]
paths = [{path = "./some/path", under = "vendor"}]

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
[package]
name = "my_system"

[tactics]
paths = ["./pkg1/tactics under v1", "./pkg2/tactics under v2"]

[prompts]
paths = ["./pkg1/prompts", "./pkg2/prompts under vendor"]

[dependencies]
packages = ["./pkg1 as p1", "./pkg2 as p2"]

from lllm import load_prompt, load_tactic

# Tactics from pkg1, re-exported into my_system with the v1 prefix
load_tactic("v1/my_tactic")              # default namespace
load_tactic("my_system:v1/my_tactic")    # explicit

# The same tactic through pkg1's own namespace (no prefix)
load_tactic("p1:my_tactic")              # alias
load_tactic("pkg1:my_tactic")            # original name

# Prompts from pkg2 with the vendor prefix
load_prompt("vendor/my_file/my_prompt")  # default namespace
load_prompt("p2:my_file/my_prompt")      # alias, no prefix

under changes how resources appear in the importing package's namespace, not in the source package's own namespace. A re-exported module is imported once per namespace it appears in.

docs.title: Custom sections
docs.text: Beyond the built-in sections, any table with paths packages arbitrary files: images, model weights, JSON schemas, datasets.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Custom sections use the same paths and under rules. Discovery walks the folders and registers every file as a lazy ResourceNode; nothing is read until first access, so a package with 500 MB of weights costs nothing at load time.
