Extension Loaded as .json json.load → dict / list .yaml, .yml yaml.safe_load → dict / list .toml tomllib.load → dict anything else raw bytes

Keys include the file extension (unlike Python sections, where .py is dropped), because logo.png and logo.svg are different resources. The [assets] section behaves the same way and also has a typed helper, load_asset.

Keep Python modules in the built-in sections (prompts/, tools/, proxies/, tactics/); use custom sections for data files.

docs.title: Declaring custom sections
docs.text:
[package]
name = "my_toolkit"

[models]
paths = ["models"]

[datasets]
paths = ["datasets"]

my_toolkit/
├── lllm.toml
├── assets/
│   ├── logo.png
│   └── templates/
│       └── email.html
├── models/
│   └── classifier.pt
└── datasets/
    └── labels.json

docs.title: Accessing custom resources
docs.text:
from lllm import load_resource
from lllm.runtimes.native.core.resource import load_asset

logo = load_resource("my_toolkit.assets:logo.png")          # bytes
labels = load_resource("my_toolkit.datasets:labels.json")   # parsed JSON

# Section only, when my_toolkit is the default package
html = load_resource("assets:templates/email.html")        # bytes
weights = load_resource("models:classifier.pt")            # bytes

logo = load_asset("my_toolkit:logo.png")

docs.title: Getting the file path
docs.text:
For large files or formats the default loader does not suit (a PyTorch checkpoint, say), take the path from the node:

from lllm import get_default_runtime

node = get_default_runtime().get_node("my_toolkit.models:classifier.pt")
file_path = node.metadata["file_path"]      # absolute path

import torch
model = torch.load(file_path)

docs.title: under prefixes
docs.text:
[assets]
paths = [
    "./icons under ui",
    "./photos under content",
]

load_resource("assets:ui/check.svg")
load_resource("assets:content/hero.jpg")

docs.title: Resource access reference
docs.text: All types share the URL scheme and the ResourceNode store; they differ in how they enter the registry and how you use them.

docs.title: Prompts
docs.text:
Python Prompt objects at module scope.

Registration:

  1. Discovery: folders in [prompts]; every module-level Prompt is registered.
  2. Manually: runtime.register_prompt(prompt, namespace="pkg.prompts"), or register_prompt(prompt) for the default runtime.
# prompts/research.py
from lllm import Prompt

system = Prompt(path="system", prompt="You are a research analyst. Analyze {topic}.")
followup = Prompt(path="followup", prompt="Suggest next steps for {topic}.")

With [prompts] paths = ["prompts"] in package my_pkg, these register as my_pkg.prompts:research/system and my_pkg.prompts:research/followup.

from lllm import load_prompt

prompt = load_prompt("research/system")               # bare (default package)
prompt = load_prompt("my_pkg:research/system")        # package-qualified
prompt = load_prompt("my_pkg.prompts:research/system")  # full URL

In agent configs, reference prompts by path:

agent_configs:
  - name: analyst
    system_prompt_path: research/system      # or my_pkg:research/system

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Function objects, usually created with @tool. Two package-friendly styles:

  • Coupled: the decorated function is both declaration and implementation. Import it in local code, or reference its URL from a prompt or config.
  • Decoupled: a prompt declares a Function schema and the package provides an @tool(name=...) implementation registered under exactly that name, like a header file plus an implementation file.

Registration:

  1. Discovery: folders in [tools]; every module-level Function is registered. Other files in those folders are registered as lazy data resources.
  2. Manually: runtime.register_tool("name", fn, namespace="pkg.tools").
# tools/search.py
from lllm import tool


@tool(name="search", description="Search internal documents.")
def search(query: str, top_k: int = 5) -> str:
    return f"Top {top_k} results for {query}"

With [tools] paths = ["tools"] in package my_pkg, this registers as my_pkg.tools:search, because the tool's name matches its file. A module with several tools nests them under the module path: tools/math.py with square and cube gives my_pkg.tools:math/square and my_pkg.tools:math/cube.

A decoupled declaration binds to the tool whose key is exactly its name, so give each such implementation its own module named after it (tools/search.py) or register it explicitly.

from lllm import Prompt

Prompt(
    path="research/system",
    prompt="Use tools when needed.",
    function_list=["my_pkg.tools:search"],
)

In agent configs, tools can mix regular tools, tactic tools, and proxies:

global:
  tools:
    - my_pkg.tools:search
    - shared_pkg.tactics:code_review
    - market_pkg.proxies:prices

docs.title: Proxies
docs.text:
BaseProxy subclasses, usually decorated with @ProxyRegistrator, dispatched at run time by ProxyManager.

Registration:

  1. @ProxyRegistrator: registers the class into the default runtime at import time (or the runtime you pass) and sets _proxy_path, the bare key.
  2. Discovery: folders in [proxies]; importing the modules registers each BaseProxy subclass as pkg.proxies:<_proxy_path>.
  3. load_builtin_proxies(): imports LLLM's bundled proxy modules.
# proxies/weather.py
import os

from lllm import BaseProxy, ProxyRegistrator


@ProxyRegistrator(path="weather", name="OpenWeather API", description="Current weather and forecasts")
class OpenWeatherProxy(BaseProxy):
    base_url = "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5"
    api_key_name = "appid"

    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.api_key = os.getenv("OPENWEATHER_API_KEY")

    @BaseProxy.endpoint(
        category="current",
        endpoint="weather",
        description="Get current weather for a city",
        params={"q*": (str, "London"), "units": (str, "metric")},
        response={"main": {"temp": 15.2}, "weather": [{"description": "cloudy"}]},
    )
    def current_weather(self, params: dict) -> dict:
        params.setdefault("units", "metric")
        return params

from lllm import ProxyManager, load_proxy

proxy_cls = load_proxy("my_pkg:weather")
proxy = ProxyManager(activate_proxies=["weather"])
result = proxy("weather/weather", {"q": "London"})   # GET <base_url>/weather?q=London&units=metric&appid=...

See Proxies & Sandbox for the full proxy system.

docs.title: Tactics
docs.text:
Tactic subclasses with a name.

Registration:

  1. Discovery: folders in [tactics]; every Tactic subclass with a name is registered under that name.
  2. At class definition: class MyTactic(Tactic, runtime=registry).
  3. Manually: register_tactic_class(MyTactic, runtime=registry).
# tactics/research.py
from lllm import Tactic


class ResearchTactic(Tactic):
    name = "researcher"
    agent_group = ["analyst"]

    def call(self, task: str, **kwargs) -> str:
        analyst = self.agents["analyst"]
        analyst.open("work", prompt_args={"topic": task})
        return analyst.respond().content

from lllm import build_tactic, resolve_config

tactic = build_tactic(resolve_config("default"), name="researcher")
result = tactic("Analyze transformer architectures")

Tactics built this way record the stable identity my_pkg::researcher on their sessions; see Logging.

docs.title: Configs
docs.text:
YAML files from [configs] folders, loaded lazily.

from lllm import load_config, resolve_config

cfg = load_config("default")                 # no inheritance
cfg = resolve_config("experiments/fast")     # with base inheritance (recommended)

See Configuration for global merging, base inheritance, and vendor_config.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Files from [services] folders. Module-level ASGI apps (FastAPI or Starlette instances; names starting with _ are skipped) register as pkg.services:<file path>/<attribute>, and service spec files (.json, .yaml, .toml) as pkg.services:<file path with extension>, loaded as data:

from lllm.runtimes.native.core.resource import load_service_ref

app = load_service_ref("my_pkg:app/app")        # services/app.py, attribute `app`
spec = load_service_ref("my_pkg:api.yaml")      # services/api.yaml, parsed

How services are launched is covered in Services.

docs.title: Assets and custom sections
docs.text: Files from [assets] or any custom section, loaded lazily by extension; see Custom sections.

docs.title: Sharing packages
docs.text: A package is a folder with an lllm.toml, so sharing one is sharing that folder: through git, a zip, or anything else. The consumer drops it into a standard location and it is loaded with no config changes.

docs.title: Drop-in folders
docs.text:
load_runtime() loads every package found in:

Folder Scope <project root>/lllm_packages/<pkg>/ Project: shared with everyone using the repo ~/.lllm/packages/<pkg>/ User: available in all your projects

The project root is the folder containing the project's lllm.toml (or the working directory if there is none). Each sub-folder must contain an lllm.toml; it is loaded exactly like an explicit dependency, into its own namespace. A package that fails to load produces a RuntimeWarning instead of stopping startup.

To use a published package:

git clone https://github.com/acme/finance-toolkit lllm_packages/finance-toolkit
# or
unzip finance-toolkit-v1.2.zip -d lllm_packages/

On the next load_runtime() it is live:

from lllm import load_prompt, resolve_config

prompt = load_prompt("finance-toolkit:analysis/system")
config = resolve_config("finance-toolkit:research")

Commit lllm_packages/ so the team gets the same packages; keep ~/.lllm/packages/ for personal ones.

docs.title: Installing, exporting, listing, removing
docs.text:
from lllm import export_package, install_package, list_packages, remove_package

# Export a loaded package to a zip (a top-level folder named after the package)
export_package("finance-toolkit", "dist/finance-toolkit-1.2.zip")
export_package("finance-toolkit", "dist/finance-toolkit-1.2-full.zip", bundle_deps=True)

# Install (user scope by default) and load it into the current runtime
install_package("dist/finance-toolkit-1.2.zip")
install_package("dist/finance-toolkit-1.2.zip", alias="ft", scope="project")

for pkg in list_packages():
    print(pkg["name"], pkg["version"], pkg["scope"], pkg["path"])

remove_package("ft", scope="project")
Scope Location Visibility user (default) ~/.lllm/packages/<name>/ All your projects project <project root>/lllm_packages/<name>/ This repo (commit it)
  • install_package expects a zip with lllm.toml at the top level or in exactly one top-level folder. It refuses to overwrite an installed package (FileExistsError); install under another name with alias, which renames the folder and rewrites name in its lllm.toml (lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens). load=False installs without loading.
  • export_package skips hidden files and __pycache__. With bundle_deps=True, every transitive dependency from [dependencies] is packed under lllm_packages/ inside the zip, so recipients get everything in one install. .zip is appended to the output path if it has another suffix.
  • remove_package deletes the installed folder and unregisters the package; with no scope it raises ValueError if the name exists in both scopes.

docs.title: Explicit dependency
docs.text:
For tighter control (pinning a path, aliasing the namespace, re-exporting into your own namespace) declare the package as a dependency:

[dependencies]
packages = [
    "./lllm_packages/finance-toolkit",
    "./lllm_packages/data-utils as du",
]

Explicit and drop-in loading can be combined. A package folder that appears in both is loaded once.

docs.title: Packages vs. skills
docs.text:
Both packages and agent skills are shareable, drop-in, version-controlled folders. Choose by what you are sharing:

Agent skills LLLM packages Contains SKILL.md instructions, scripts, reference files Prompts, tactics, tools, proxies, agent configs Drop-in path .agents/skills/<name>/ lllm_packages/<name>/ Consumed by Any agentskills-compatible agent LLLM Use when Sharing task instructions and workflows Sharing complete agent infrastructure Activated On demand, by the model via activate_skill When the runtime loads

They are complementary: a package can ship prompts and tactics and a skills/ folder for agents that prefer skills.

docs.title: Writing a package for sharing
docs.text:
Use a unique, stable package name. name becomes the namespace prefix of every resource and part of every session's tactic_path. Pick something specific (acme-finance, not finance) and never rename it after publishing.

[package]
name = "acme-finance"
version = "1.2.0"
description = "Financial data prompts and analysis tactics"

Qualify references in configs. Bare names resolve against the root package's namespace, which is not yours when your package is a dependency. Use package-qualified prompt paths and base names in configs you ship:

base: acme-finance:common              # not: base: common
agent_configs:
  - name: analyst
    system_prompt_path: acme-finance:analysis/system   # not: analysis/system

Inside prompts, bare tool refs and Function declarations already resolve within the prompt's own package. In your README, always show fully qualified names (load_prompt("acme-finance:analysis/system")).

Declare requirements. Document the environment variables your tactics and proxies need, and fail with a clear message when one is missing instead of letting the error surface mid-call.

Declare your own dependencies in [dependencies], and either document them or bundle them with export_package(..., bundle_deps=True).

Version releases, not just the manifest. Consumers usually pin a commit or a release zip. Tag releases, keep a changelog, and treat renamed resources and removed tactics as breaking changes.

Keep prompts and tactics portable. The most reusable packages work with any model and agent config: no hardcoded model names, no assumptions about the consumer's proxies. Ship example configs (configs/examples/) for consumers to copy.

Provide a minimal example. A short README with the three lines needed to load the package and run a tactic.

docs.title: The Hub
docs.text:
The hub is how LLLM packages are shared: validated, published, rendered as cards for people and agents, downloaded, and served. Browse the public hub at lllm.one/hub.

The hub works on lllm.toml packages and comes in three forms:

What it is Use it for Local hub A folder (.lllm/hub by default) managed by lllm hub Publishing and fetching packages on one machine or a shared drive Hub API lllm hub serve, a FastAPI app over a local hub Sharing a hub on a network Static hub lllm hub index, a catalog plus zips any web server can host Read-only public listings

docs.title: Validate and publish
docs.text:
lllm hub validate ./briefs
lllm hub publish ./briefs --local          # copies the package into .lllm/hub
lllm hub list

ok
acme/briefs@0.1.0
acme/briefs@0.1.0

Publishing validates first and refuses packages with errors, such as a raw api_key in metadata (see Validation). Secrets and build leftovers (.env, .git, __pycache__, *.egg-info, ...) are never copied. Use --hub DIR (before the command) to work with another hub folder:

lllm hub --hub /shared/lllm-hub publish ./briefs --local

docs.title: Read a package
docs.text:
lllm hub card acme/briefs             # Markdown card for people
lllm hub agent-card acme/briefs       # operating notes and refs for coding agents
lllm hub config-template acme/briefs  # a starting .lllm/config.toml
lllm hub get acme/briefs --dest ./vendor

Cards are generated from the manifest: description, [card] summary and tags, declared resources with their refs and entrypoints, API-key requirements, and example calls. The agent card is written for coding agents that will use the package: it lists every ref and says how to run the package.

docs.title: Run a downloaded package
docs.text:
lllm setup ./vendor/briefs        # store the API keys the package declares
lllm serve ./vendor/briefs        # serve its primary resource over FastAPI

lllm serve checks [requirements.api_keys] before starting, reading keys from the environment, a local .env.local, or the OS keyring (the secure extra). See Services for the HTTP API.

Native packages can also be installed as runtime dependencies: a package archive installed with lllm.install_package("briefs.zip") lands in ~/.lllm/packages/ (or ./lllm_packages/ with scope="project"), and lllm.load_runtime() loads it alongside your project. See Discovery.

docs.title: Serve a hub
docs.text:
lllm hub serve --port 8787
Method and path Purpose GET /health Liveness POST /validate Validate a package folder on the server POST /publish Publish a package folder on the server GET /packages List packages GET /packages/{org}/{name} Package record (?version= for a specific one) GET /packages/{org}/{name}/card Package card GET /packages/{org}/{name}/agent-card Agent card GET /packages/{org}/{name}/config-template Local config template GET /packages/{org}/{name}/download Package zip

lllm.one/hub is its own website, built on the same package format: the lllm-hub repository adds a web app, authenticated uploads, and object storage.

docs.title: Publish a static hub
docs.text:
lllm hub --hub .lllm/hub index ./site/hub

site/hub/
  data/catalog.json
  packages/acme/briefs/0.1.0.zip

The catalog holds each package's latest version: summary, resources, card, agent card, config template, README, and download link. Like cards and the hub API, it drops secret-shaped metadata keys. Like cards, it also drops them inside JSON schemas, which the hub API returns unchanged (see Hub Metadata). A README that is not valid UTF-8 is read with U+FFFD replacement characters instead of failing the build.

Each zip holds the package files at its root, like GET /packages/{org}/{name}/download, so unzip 0.1.0.zip -d briefs leaves lllm.toml in briefs/, ready for lllm setup briefs and lllm serve briefs.

To make the folder browsable, add the hub web app with lllm-hub --export-web ./site/hub (from the lllm-hub repository); any static host can then serve the folder.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
from lllm.hub import LocalHub, build_catalog, init_package, validate_package

init_package("briefs", org="acme")          # writes briefs/lllm.toml
report = validate_package("briefs")
assert report.ok, report.issues

hub = LocalHub(".lllm/hub")
record = hub.publish("briefs")
print(record.key, [resource.ref for resource in record.resources])
print(hub.card("acme/briefs"))
build_catalog(hub, "site/hub")

lllm.hub.tactic_resource(tactic) and lllm.network.channel_resource(channel) export metadata for tactics and channels you want to describe in a manifest.

docs.title: The lllm.toml Manifest
docs.text:
A package is a folder with an lllm.toml. The same file has two readers:

  • the native runtime reads it to discover resources: prompts, tools, proxies, tactics, YAML configs, and package dependencies (see Discovery);
  • the hub reads it to identify, validate, render, publish, and serve the package (see The Hub).

Neither reader needs the other's sections, so a package can start as a handful of discovery paths and grow hub metadata later. lllm create writes a manifest that already serves both, and lllm init writes a minimal one.

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text:
[package]
org = "acme"
name = "briefs"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Writes and reviews technical briefs."
primary = "tactics.brief"

# --- native discovery -------------------------------------------------
[prompts]
paths = ["prompts"]

[configs]
paths = ["configs"]

[tactics]
paths = ["tactics"]

[dependencies]
packages = ["./vendor/style-guide as style"]

# --- declared resources (hub) ------------------------------------------
[schemas.brief_input]
entry = "briefs.schemas:BriefInput"

[schemas.brief_output]
entry = "briefs.schemas:BriefOutput"

[tactics.brief]
entry = "main:create_tactic"
input = "brief_input"
output = "brief_output"
description = "Plan, draft, and review a brief."

[services.api]
tactic = "brief"
transport = "fastapi"

[requirements.api_keys]
OPENAI_API_KEY = "Model access for the writer and reviewer agents."

[card]
summary = "Technical briefs with a writer and a reviewer agent."
tags = ["writing", "multi-agent"]

[docs.readme]
path = "README.md"
title = "README"

[tactics] holds both kinds of entry at once: paths tells the native runtime which folder to scan, and [tactics.brief] declares one tactic by name for the hub. The same split works in [services] and [assets].

docs.title: [package]
docs.text: Field Default Meaning name folder name (the hub requires it) Package name; the namespace prefix for discovered resources org "local" Owner; the identifier is org/name version "0.1.0" Package version description "" One line about the package primary none The resource lllm serve <package> launches, e.g. tactics.brief kind "mixed" tactic, channel, service, app, library, or mixed license, authors none Optional metadata manifest_version "0.1" Manifest format version

docs.title: Native discovery
docs.text:
Discovery sections name folders to scan. Each entry is a path, optionally with a virtual prefix:

[prompts]
paths = ["./prompts", "./shared/prompts under shared"]  # or {path = ..., prefix = ...}
Section Discovers [prompts] Prompt objects in Python modules [tools] @tool functions (plus metadata files) [proxies] BaseProxy subclasses [tactics] (paths) Tactic subclasses with a name [configs] YAML configs (.yaml/.yml: agent configs, with base inheritance) [services] (paths) ASGI apps in Python modules; spec files as data [assets] (paths) any files, loaded lazily any other table a custom section: files and Python resources

A section without paths falls back to a folder with the section's name, if one exists. The native runtime does this for all seven built-in sections, even with no table. Validation checks that the following stay inside the package:

  • the paths or fallback folder of [prompts], [tools], [proxies], [configs], and custom sections;
  • the paths of [tactics], [services], and [assets].

It does not check the fallback folder of [tactics], [services], or [assets] without paths, or of a built-in section with no table. The native runtime treats the hub's own tables ([schemas], [docs], [card], ...) as custom sections only when they set paths. The hub cannot load most of them with paths. It does load [config] and [card] with paths, but validation does not check those paths. Give custom sections their own names.

Resources are keyed package.section:path, for example briefs.prompts:writer/system. [dependencies] packages = ["./pkg as alias"] loads other packages first, under an optional alias.

Discovery covers keys, aliases, shared packages, and installing package archives.

docs.title: Declared resources
docs.text:
Declared resources are named tables the hub indexes. Each gets a ref, lllm://org/package/<section>/<name>.

Table Key fields [schemas.<name>] entry (a module:Model), description [tactics.<name>] entry, input, output (schema names), runtime, description, examples [services.<name>] tactic or tactics, entry, transport, subscribes, publishes [channels.<name>] schema, form (log, ...), description [snapshots.<name>] schema, channel [runs.<name>] services, tactics, channels, snapshots that make up one run; lllm serve launches a run that lists exactly one service [config] schema and defaults for package settings [docs.<name>] path, title [examples.<name>] path or command [assets.<name>] path, media_type [requirements.api_keys] NAME = "why it is needed", checked by lllm setup and lllm serve [card] summary, tags, safety, latency, suggested_commands

The named resource tables, [config], and [card] also accept metadata = {...}. The package ships lllm.toml as written, so validation rejects raw secret-shaped keys (api_key, token, clientSecret, ...) in metadata, nested maps included, and in extra keys written directly in those tables. References such as api_key_ref are allowed. Validation does not look inside maps under JSON-schema keys (schema, input_schema, output_schema, or forms such as inputSchema), since a schema may name a field api_key. It does not check [config] defaults or tactic examples either. Keep secret values out of all of these: the package zip keeps them, and the hub API shows schema maps unchanged. Hub Metadata lists the key shapes and what cards, the hub API, and the catalog drop.

docs.title: Entrypoints
docs.text:
Entrypoints are module:attribute, imported relative to the package folder. A tactic entry may name a Tactic class or instance, a factory, or a handler. A factory is called once, with no arguments, when the package loads; a handler is wrapped with as_tactic and called once per input. lllm serve and AAAX package tactics tell them apart by one rule:

  • Any other class is a factory when it can be constructed without arguments.
  • Any other callable is a factory when it takes no parameters, like main:create_tactic in generated projects, or when it can be called without arguments and is annotated to return a Tactic or a FastAPI or Starlette app.
  • Everything else is a handler: def greet(name="world") answers each input instead of being called once at load.

A return annotation that cannot be evaluated at runtime, such as a class imported only under TYPE_CHECKING, counts when its class name ends in Tactic or is FastAPI or Starlette. A [services.<name>] entry has no handler form: it names an app, or a callable that can be called without arguments and builds a FastAPI or Starlette app, a tactic, or a data payload. Anything else is a launch error.

Serving keeps a package's modules imported, and packages served in one process share sys.modules. A module that a tactic imports when it is called needs a top-level name no other served package uses.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
lllm hub validate .

Validation imports declared entrypoints without calling them, checks refs and schema links, checks that declared files and the discovery folders listed in Native discovery stay inside the package, and rejects secret-shaped metadata keys. It reports errors (the package cannot be published) and warnings. The main codes:

Code Level Meaning manifest_load_failed error lllm.toml does not parse or fit the manifest, for example a primary that is not section.name, or paths in [schemas] entrypoint_import_failed error A declared entry could not be imported primary_missing error primary names a resource the manifest does not declare schema_ref_missing error A tactic's input/output names no schema metadata_secret_key error metadata or an extra table key holds a raw secret-shaped key outside a JSON schema discovery_path_absolute, discovery_path_outside_package error A checked discovery path or fallback folder is absolute, escapes the package, or goes through a symlink discovery_path_missing warning A checked discovery path does not exist discovery_section_empty warning A checked section has no paths and no folder: often a typo such as [tactic.x] dependency_manifest_missing warning A dependency folder has no lllm.toml card_metadata_missing, card_summary_missing, readme_missing, readme_doc_missing warning The hub page will be sparse

docs.title: Local configuration
docs.text:
Bindings that depend on where a package runs (service URLs, channel stores, settings) live outside the package, in .lllm/config.toml:

[refs."lllm://acme/briefs/tactics/brief"]
url = "http://127.0.0.1:8000"

[refs."lllm://acme/briefs/channels/events"]
store = ".lllm/network"

lllm hub config-template acme/briefs renders a starting point, and lllm.Resolver reads it.

docs.title: Refs and Composition
docs.text:
A ref is a stable name for a package resource:

lllm://demo/shout/tactics/shout

A ref says what a resource is, not where it runs. Local config decides whether it resolves to an object in your process, a service on another host, or a channel store. Code that calls tactics by ref keeps working when one of them moves from a notebook into a service.

docs.title: Ref shape
docs.text:
Refs have the form lllm://ORG/PACKAGE/SECTION/NAME, where SECTION is one of the package sections:

Section Names tactics A tactic. services A service. channels, snapshots An SSSN channel or snapshot. schemas, runs, configs, docs, examples, assets Other package resources.

A package gives each resource a ref built from its [package] org and name: [tactics.shout] in package demo/shout is lllm://demo/shout/tactics/shout (see The lllm.toml manifest).

from lllm import TacticRef, TacticRefError
from lllm.protocol.refs import parse_resource_ref

ref = TacticRef("lllm://demo/shout/tactics/shout")
print(ref.org, ref.package, ref.resource_kind, ref.name)

print(parse_resource_ref("lllm://demo/shout/channels/events").resource_kind)

try:
    TacticRef("lllm://demo/shout/channels/events")
except TacticRefError as exc:
    print(exc)

demo shout tactics shout
channels
Tactic ref must point at /tactics/, got /channels/: lllm://demo/shout/channels/events

Each segment must be a plain path segment: no whitespace, percent escapes, . or .., and none of /, \, :, ;. Unknown sections are rejected. A tactic's package_ref is a tactic ref; its service_ref is a /services/ ref or an http(s) URL.

docs.title: lllm.Resolver
docs.text: lllm.Resolver turns refs into live objects: tactics (in-process or remote), channel stores, and project settings.

docs.title: Register in-process tactics
docs.text:
from lllm import Resolver, Tactic

LOWER = "lllm://demo/text/tactics/lower"


class Lower(Tactic):
    """Lowercase the text."""

    name = "lower"

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        return task.lower()


resolver = Resolver()
resolver.register(LOWER, Lower())

print(resolver.run(LOWER, "QUIET PLEASE"))
print(resolver.tactic(LOWER).package_ref)

quiet please
lllm://demo/text/tactics/lower

Registering a tactic also sets its package_ref, so the ref appears in its info() and, once served, in the tactic_ref of every request context.

docs.title: Bind refs in .lllm/config.toml
docs.text:
A project keeps its bindings in .lllm/config.toml. This one points the tactic ref at the service from Services and gives a channel ref a local store:

[refs."lllm://demo/shout/tactics/shout"]
url = "http://127.0.0.1:8000"

[refs."lllm://demo/shout/tactics/shout".metadata]
owner = "docs"
api_key_ref = "openai.default"

[refs."lllm://demo/shout/channels/events"]
store = ".lllm/network"

[settings]
region = "us"

Resolver.from_config() reads the file once:

from lllm import Resolver

resolver = Resolver.from_config(".")

shout = resolver.tactic("lllm://demo/shout/tactics/shout")
print(type(shout).__name__, shout.tactic_name, shout.url)
print(shout.run({"text": "via config"}))
print(shout.info().metadata)

store = resolver.store("lllm://demo/shout/channels/events")
print(type(store).__name__)
print(resolver.setting("region"), resolver.setting("timeout", 30))
print(resolver.refs())

RemoteTactic shout http://127.0.0.1:8000/run
{'text': 'VIA CONFIG', 'trace_id': None}
{'owner': 'docs', 'api_key_ref': 'openai.default', 'ref': 'lllm://demo/shout/tactics/shout', 'url': 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/run'}
LocalStore
us 30
('lllm://demo/shout/channels/events', 'lllm://demo/shout/tactics/shout')

The rules:

  • from_config(path) takes a project folder (and reads PATH/.lllm/config.toml) or the path of the file itself.
  • A tactic ref binds to url: an absolute http(s) service URL, either the service base or .../tactics/NAME inside a multi-tactic app. It resolves to a RemoteTactic named after the ref, with the ref as its package_ref. It has no input_type or output_type, so it returns JSON as-is.
  • A channel or snapshot ref binds to store, a relative path resolved against the project folder (a LocalStore; opening it creates the folder), or to url, an SSSN store service (a RemoteStore).

  • Each binding declares exactly one target. A tactic ref bound to anything but a url is rejected:

    TacticRefError: Tactic URL binding must declare a url target, got store: lllm://demo/shout/tactics/shout

  • The metadata table (and any extra keys) becomes binding metadata, which a remote tactic reports in info().metadata next to ref and url. Raw secrets are refused; point at credentials with a reference such as api_key_ref instead:

    TacticRefError: Tactic URL binding metadata must not include raw secret key 'api_key': lllm://demo/shout/tactics/shout

  • Refs to other sections, such as /services/, may sit in the same file for other tools. The resolver validates their shape and otherwise leaves them alone.

  • [settings] is free-form; setting(key, default=None) reads it.
  • register() replaces a config binding for the current process, which is handy in tests.

lllm hub config-template renders a starting config for a published package (The Hub).

docs.title: Resolver reference
docs.text:
Method Does Resolver() An empty resolver; register tactics yourself. Resolver.from_config(path=".") Load bindings and settings from .lllm/config.toml. register(ref, tactic) Bind a tactic ref to an in-process tactic. tactic(ref) The tactic bound to a /tactics/ ref. Raises TacticRefError when unbound. store(ref) The LocalStore or RemoteStore behind a /channels/ or /snapshots/ ref. resolve(ref) tactic() or store(), chosen by the ref's section. run(ref, value, *, context=None, **kwargs), await arun(...) Resolve a tactic ref and call it. setting(key, default=None) A value from [settings]. refs() Every bound tactic and channel ref.

Its parts are attributes: resolver.tactics is a TacticResolver (also importable from lllm) whose bind_url(ref, url, **kwargs) binds a ref to a service in code, passing extra keywords such as input_type or timeout to RemoteTactic. resolver.channels is the ChannelResolver from lllm.network, and resolver.config holds the parsed file.

docs.title: Call tactics by ref
docs.text:
A tactic that holds a resolver can call other tactics without knowing where they run:

from lllm import CallContext, Resolver, Tactic

SHOUT = "lllm://demo/shout/tactics/shout"
LOWER = "lllm://demo/text/tactics/lower"


class Contrast(Tactic):
    """Say it loud, then say it quietly."""

    name = "contrast"
    output_type = dict

    def __init__(self, resolver: Resolver, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.resolver = resolver

    def call(self, task: str, *, context=None) -> dict:
        loud = self.resolver.run(SHOUT, {"text": task}, context=context)
        quiet = self.resolver.run(LOWER, task, context=context)
        return {"loud": loud["text"], "quiet": quiet, "trace_id": loud["trace_id"]}


resolver = Resolver.from_config(".")  # SHOUT is bound to the service
resolver.register(LOWER, Lower())     # LOWER runs in this process

contrast = Contrast(resolver)
print(contrast.run("Hello There", context=CallContext(trace_id="trace-7")))

session = contrast("Hello There", return_session=True)
print(list(session.sub_tactic_sessions))

{'loud': 'HELLO THERE', 'quiet': 'hello there', 'trace_id': 'trace-7'}
['lower']
  • Contrast does not know that SHOUT is remote. Moving LOWER behind a service means binding its ref to a url in .lllm/config.toml instead of registering it; Contrast stays the same.
  • Passing context along carries the trace_id across the HTTP hop: the remote tactic received trace-7 and echoed it back.
  • In-process tactics that run in a session, such as the call() program Lower, are recorded in the caller's session (lower above). The remote call is an HTTP request, so the service keeps its own record of it.
  • To serve a tactic that takes constructor arguments, point lllm serve at a factory, such as def build(): return Contrast(Resolver.from_config(".")), which it calls once at load (Loading entrypoints).

docs.title: Sub-tactics
docs.text: Inside one program, assigning a tactic to an attribute in __init__ makes it a sub-tactic: it is listed in self.sub_tactics, and its calls roll up into the parent's session and cost. See Sessions for call() programs.

docs.title: Test against an in-process service
docs.text:
bind_url accepts httpx transports, so a test can exercise the full HTTP path (envelope, context, errors) without opening a port:

import asyncio

import httpx
from lllm import Resolver, create_tactic_app

resolver = Resolver()
app = create_tactic_app(Lower())
resolver.tactics.bind_url(LOWER, "http://testserver", async_transport=httpx.ASGITransport(app=app))

print(type(resolver.tactic(LOWER)).__name__)
print(asyncio.run(resolver.arun(LOWER, "OVER HTTP")))

RemoteTactic
over http

httpx.ASGITransport is async-only, so call arun(); for synchronous run(), pass a synchronous transport as transport=.

docs.title: Tactics as tools
docs.text: Any tactic, local or bound by ref, can be handed to an agent as a tool. See Tactics as Pydantic AI tools.

docs.title: Tactics over channels
docs.text:
A channel ref resolves to a store, and a TacticProcessor runs a tactic over a channel's events, appending each output to another channel:

from lllm import Resolver
from lllm.network import TacticProcessor

resolver = Resolver.from_config(".")
store = resolver.store("lllm://demo/shout/channels/events")

store.create_channel({"name": "inbox"})
store.create_channel({"name": "outbox"})
store.append_event({"channel": "inbox", "payload": "HELLO THERE"})

processor = TacticProcessor(Lower(), store, source="inbox", sink="outbox")
for event in processor.process():
    print(event.kind, event.payload, event.parent_ids != ())
print(processor.process())

result hello there True
[]

The processor reads through a named subscription, so a second process() picks up only new events. Each output event links back to its source through parent_ids, and the tactic receives a CallContext naming the channel and event. Channels, stores, and processors are covered in SSSN; mounting several packages and channels behind one API is AAAX.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• The Tactic: the boundary every ref resolves to.
  • Services: the HTTP side of a url binding.
  • Runtimes: what can sit behind a tactic.

docs.title: Runtimes
docs.text:
A runtime is whatever executes behind the tactic boundary: LLLM's native agent engine, ordinary Python, a Pydantic AI agent, or a service on another machine. Callers cannot tell which. Every runtime is reached through run(), arun(), stream(), and info(), served by the same service adapter, and listed in packages the same way.

Runtime You write runtime_kind Native an lllm.Tactic subclass with a call() program native Plain Python an lllm.Tactic subclass with _run(), or as_tactic(fn) python Pydantic AI PydanticAITactic(agent) pydantic-ai Remote RemoteTactic(url) http

docs.title: Native
docs.text:
The native runtime is LLLM's own engine for agentic systems. Prompts declare a turn's template, parser, tools, and failure handlers. Agents run prompts through a short, readable call loop. Dialogs are forkable trees, and tactics are the programs that wire agents together. The Architecture overview walks through the design.

A native tactic is an lllm.Tactic with a call() program, and there is no adapter step: the class you write is the one that gets served, packaged, and handed to other runtimes as a tool. Agent-backed programs (agent_group, agent configs, sessions with cost) are shown in The Tactic and covered fully in the Tactic reference and the Agent reference.

  • lllm.Tactic is the same class as lllm.runtimes.native.Tactic. The rest of the native vocabulary (Agent, Prompt, Dialog, Message, tool, Runtime, and so on) imports from either lllm or lllm.runtimes.native, and the package loaders (load_runtime, build_tactic, resolve_config) from lllm.
  • NativeTactic is a Tactic that insists on agent_group and raises AssertionError without one. Existing subclasses keep working.

docs.title: Wrapping native-style objects
docs.text:
NativeTacticAdapter is for objects that are not tactics but have the native call shape: a run() or call() method, and optionally arun()/acall() and stream(). Subclasses of lllm.Tactic do not need it.

from pydantic import BaseModel
from lllm import CallContext, NativeTacticAdapter


class Summary(BaseModel):
    words: int
    tone: str


class WordCounter:
    """Count the words in a text."""

    name = "word-counter"
    output_model = Summary

    def call(self, task, *, tone="neutral", metadata=None):
        return Summary(words=len(task.split()), tone=tone)


tactic = NativeTacticAdapter(WordCounter(), input_type=str, run_kwargs={"tone": "brisk"})
print(repr(tactic.run("three short words", context=CallContext(trace_id="t-1"))))
print(tactic.info().name, "|", tactic.info().description)

Summary(words=3, tone='brisk')
word-counter | Count the words in a text.

The adapter calls run() if the object has one, else call(), and uses arun()/acall() for async calls when they exist (otherwise a worker thread). It takes the types from the object's input_type/input_model and output_type/output_model unless you pass them, adds run_kwargs to every call, and passes context= when the method accepts it. When the method accepts metadata, it also receives the context's metadata plus lllm_request_id and lllm_trace_id (turn this off with include_context_metadata=False).

docs.title: as_tactic
docs.text:
Any function becomes a tactic:

from pydantic import BaseModel
from lllm import as_tactic


class Order(BaseModel):
    sku: str
    quantity: int


class Quote(BaseModel):
    sku: str
    total: float


def quote(order: Order) -> Quote:
    """Price an order at 2.50 per unit."""
    return Quote(sku=order.sku, total=order.quantity * 2.5)


tactic = as_tactic(quote)
print(tactic.info().name, "|", tactic.info().description)
print(repr(tactic.run({"sku": "A-1", "quantity": 4})))

quote | Price an order at 2.50 per unit.
Quote(sku='A-1', total=10.0)
  • The input type comes from the first parameter's annotation (ignoring one named context) and the output type from the return annotation. Override either with input_type= or output_type=.
  • The name comes from the function name and the description from its docstring. as_tactic also takes name, description, package_ref, service_ref, examples, and metadata, and returns a CallableTactic.
  • A function that accepts context (or **kwargs) receives the CallContext.
  • Async functions work with both arun() and run(). run() drives them with asyncio.run(), so inside a running event loop use arun().
from lllm import CallContext, as_tactic


def label(text: str, *, context=None) -> dict:
    return {"text": text, "trace_id": context.trace_id if context else None}


async def slug(title: str) -> str:
    return title.lower().replace(" ", "-")


print(as_tactic(label).run("hello", context=CallContext(trace_id="trace-1")))
print(as_tactic(slug).run("Typed Tactics"))

{'text': 'hello', 'trace_id': 'trace-1'}
typed-tactics

When the tactic needs configuration, several methods, streaming, or custom endpoints, subclass lllm.Tactic and implement _run() instead (The Tactic).

docs.title: Loading entrypoints
docs.text:
lllm serve, lllm inspect, and package loading turn an imported module:attribute into a tactic with coerce_tactic(value, name=None). It accepts, in order:

  1. a Tactic subclass (instantiated, with name= if its constructor takes it) or instance;
  2. a factory that returns any of these shapes, called once when the value is loaded;
  3. an object with a run method;
  4. any other callable: a handler, wrapped with as_tactic and called once per input.

A class is a factory when it can be constructed without arguments. Any other callable is a factory when it takes no parameters, or when it can be called without arguments and is annotated to return a Tactic or an ASGI app (FastAPI or Starlette). A return annotation that cannot be evaluated at runtime, such as a class imported only under TYPE_CHECKING, counts when the class name ends in Tactic or is FastAPI or Starlette. Everything else is a handler.

from lllm import CallableTactic
from lllm.runtimes import coerce_tactic


class Reverser:
    def run(self, value: str) -> str:
        return value[::-1]


def make_quote_tactic(name: str = "bulk-quote") -> CallableTactic:
    return as_tactic(quote, name=name)


def greet(name: str = "world") -> str:
    return f"Hello {name}"


print(type(coerce_tactic(quote)).__name__)
print(coerce_tactic(make_quote_tactic).info().name)
print(coerce_tactic(Reverser(), name="reverse").run("abc"))
print(coerce_tactic(greet).run("Ada"))

CallableTactic
bulk-quote
cba
Hello Ada

make_quote_tactic can be called without arguments and is annotated to return a tactic, so it is a factory. greet can be called without arguments too, but it takes a parameter and is not annotated to return a tactic, so it is a handler: it answers each input instead of being called once at load.

docs.title: Pydantic AI
docs.text:
Pydantic runs through LLLM in both directions:

  • Pydantic models are the I/O types of every tactic. They are validated on the way in and out, exported as JSON Schema by info() and /info, and serialized by services. Whatever runtime is behind a tactic, its contract is written in Pydantic.
  • A Pydantic AI agent becomes a tactic with PydanticAITactic, and is then served, packaged, composed, and streamed like any other.
  • A tactic becomes a Pydantic AI tool, including a native multi-agent program, so a Pydantic AI agent can call LLLM systems.

Pydantic AI keeps owning what it is good at: models, tools, dependencies, model settings, output validation, streaming, and instrumentation. Install it with pip install "lllm-core[pydantic-ai]". The examples below use Pydantic AI's TestModel, which runs offline and fills outputs with placeholder values.

docs.title: Pydantic AI agents as tactics
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.models.test import TestModel
from lllm import PydanticAITactic


class Brief(BaseModel):
    title: str
    bullets: list[str]


# TestModel runs offline. For live calls use a model name, e.g. Agent("openai:gpt-4o-mini", ...).
agent = Agent(TestModel(), output_type=Brief, name="brief-writer")
tactic = PydanticAITactic(agent, description="Write a short brief.")

print(repr(tactic.run("typed tactic boundaries")))
info = tactic.info()
print(info.name, info.runtime_kind, info.capabilities)
print(info.output_schema["title"], info.output_schema["required"])

Brief(title='a', bullets=['a'])
brief-writer pydantic-ai ('arun', 'events', 'run', 'stream')
Brief ['title', 'bullets']

The tactic takes its name from agent.name, its output type from agent.output_type, and its published output schema from the agent. The description comes from description=, else the agent's own description, else a description or docstring on your subclass of PydanticAITactic, else your own agent class's docstring. Pydantic AI's class docstrings are never used, so without any of these the description is empty. run() calls agent.run_sync(), arun() calls agent.run(), and both return result.output.

docs.title: Typed input
docs.text:
Give the tactic an input_type to validate input and publish its schema:

class BriefRequest(BaseModel):
    topic: str
    audience: str = "engineers"


typed = PydanticAITactic(agent, input_type=BriefRequest, description="Write a short brief.")
print(repr(typed.run({"topic": "refs"})))
print(typed.info().input_schema["required"])

Brief(title='a', bullets=['a'])
['topic']

input_mode decides what the agent receives when the validated input is a Pydantic model:

input_mode The agent receives auto (default), json The model as JSON text, e.g. {"topic":"refs","audience":"engineers"}. dict model.model_dump(mode="json"). python The model instance. text str(value).

For anything else, pass input_mapper= (a function from the validated input to the agent's prompt) and, on the way back, output_mapper= (a function from the run result to the output).

docs.title: Run settings and context
docs.text:
run_kwargs are passed to every agent run, and keyword arguments given to run() or arun() are merged on top, so Pydantic AI's own options such as model_settings, deps, usage_limits, and message_history pass straight through. The CallContext arrives as the run's metadata, with lllm_request_id and lllm_trace_id added:

from pydantic_ai import RunContext
from lllm import CallContext

probe = Agent(TestModel(), name="probe")
seen = {}


@probe.tool
def record(ctx: RunContext[None]) -> str:
    """Record what the run received."""
    seen.update(model_settings=ctx.model_settings, metadata=ctx.metadata)
    return "recorded"


probe_tactic = PydanticAITactic(
    probe,
    input_type=str,
    output_type=str,
    run_kwargs={"model_settings": {"temperature": 0}},
)
probe_tactic.run("hi", context=CallContext(trace_id="trace-1", metadata={"user": "ada"}))
print(seen["model_settings"])
print(seen["metadata"]["user"], seen["metadata"]["lllm_trace_id"])

{'temperature': 0}
ada trace-1

An explicit metadata= argument wins over the context. Turn the forwarding off with include_context_metadata=False.

docs.title: The full result
docs.text:
result_mode="result" returns Pydantic AI's run result instead of result.output. Without an output_type, the output type is then Any, so the result comes back unvalidated:

full = PydanticAITactic(agent, result_mode="result")
result = full.run("typed tactic boundaries")
print(type(result).__name__, repr(result.output))

AgentRunResult Brief(title='a', bullets=['a'])

Keep this mode for in-process callers. info() still publishes the agent's output schema, and a served result would carry the run's private state, including the agent's instructions and message history.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
stream() and astream() use run_stream_sync() and run_stream() and yield the agent's output as it builds up:

print(list(tactic.stream("typed tactic boundaries")))
print(list(typed.stream({"topic": "refs"})))

[Brief(title='a', bullets=['a']), Brief(title='a', bullets=['a'])]
[Brief(title='a', bullets=['a']), Brief(title='a', bullets=['a'])]
  • stream_mode="text" yields from Pydantic AI's stream_text(), "response" yields ModelResponse objects from stream_response(), and "raw" yields Pydantic AI's stream object itself.
  • The streaming methods validate the input the way run() does, so the dict above becomes a BriefRequest first, and bad input raises SchemaError before the agent runs.
  • aevents() reads run_stream_events() and wraps each Pydantic AI event in a TacticEvent, which is what /stream sends.

Each event's kind is Pydantic AI's event_kind, its metadata names the event class, and its data is the event as JSON-safe data:

import asyncio


async def show_events():
    async for event in typed.aevents({"topic": "refs"}):
        print(event.kind, event.metadata)


asyncio.run(show_events())

part_start {'event_type': 'PartStartEvent'}
final_result {'event_type': 'FinalResultEvent'}
part_end {'event_type': 'PartEndEvent'}
output_tool_call {'event_type': 'OutputToolCallEvent'}
output_tool_result {'event_type': 'OutputToolResultEvent'}
agent_run_result {'event_type': 'AgentRunResultEvent'}

docs.title: Tactics as Pydantic AI tools
docs.text:
A tactic is a typed callable, so handing one to a Pydantic AI agent takes one small function over tactic.run(). Pydantic AI builds the tool's schema from the function's annotations and validates the model's arguments into Term:

from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.models.test import TestModel
from lllm import Tactic


class Term(BaseModel):
    word: str


class Definition(BaseModel):
    word: str
    meaning: str


class Glossary(Tactic):
    """Look up a term in the team glossary."""

    name = "glossary"
    input_type = Term
    output_type = Definition
    entries = {"tactic": "a typed unit of work"}

    def call(self, task: Term) -> Definition:
        return Definition(word=task.word, meaning=self.entries.get(task.word, "not in the glossary"))


glossary = Glossary()


def lookup(term: Term) -> Definition:
    """Look up a term in the team glossary."""
    return glossary.run(term)


agent = Agent(TestModel(), tools=[lookup])
result = agent.run_sync("What does 'tactic' mean here?")
print(result.output)

{"lookup":{"word":"a","meaning":"not in the glossary"}}

TestModel calls every tool once with placeholder arguments (word="a") and reports what came back; a real model chooses the arguments. Any tactic works here, including a native program with its own agents or a RemoteTactic. A tactic that runs a Pydantic AI agent itself needs an async tool, covered below.

tactic_as_tool(tactic) and the method tactic.as_tool() build such a function for you: named after the tactic, documented with its description, and signed task: InputType -> OutputType, or with one keyword argument per model field when parameter_mode="kwargs":

import inspect
from lllm import tactic_as_tool

tool = tactic_as_tool(glossary)
print(tool.__name__, inspect.signature(tool))
print(tool({"word": "tactic"}))

define = glossary.as_tool(name="define", parameter_mode="kwargs")
print(define.__name__, inspect.signature(define))
print(define(word="tactic"))

glossary (task: __main__.Term) -> __main__.Definition
word='tactic' meaning='a typed unit of work'
define (*, word: str) -> __main__.Definition
word='tactic' meaning='a typed unit of work'

The functions' annotations match these signatures, and Pydantic AI reads a tool's parameter types from its annotations, so both register as they are:

agent = Agent(TestModel(), tools=[tool, define])
print(agent.run_sync("What does 'tactic' mean here?").output)

{"glossary":{"word":"a","meaning":"not in the glossary"},"define":{"word":"a","meaning":"not in the glossary"}}

These tools are synchronous and call tactic.run(). Pydantic AI does not allow Agent.run_sync() inside a synchronous tool, so a PydanticAITactic around a real agent, such as typed above, needs an async def tool that awaits arun():

async def write_brief(request: BriefRequest) -> Brief:
    """Write a short brief about a topic."""
    return await typed.arun(request)


planner = Agent(TestModel(), tools=[write_brief])
print(planner.run_sync("Plan a talk about refs.").output)

{"write_brief":{"title":"a","bullets":["a"]}}

docs.title: Remote tactics
docs.text:
RemoteTactic is a tactic backed by an LLLM service. It sends the request envelope to /run, reads /stream as server-sent events, and fetches /info:

from lllm import RemoteTactic

remote = RemoteTactic("http://127.0.0.1:8000", name="shout")
print(remote.run({"text": "hello"}))

{'text': 'HELLO', 'trace_id': None}

With input_type and output_type, its run() and arun() validate locally and return models; its stream methods do not validate. Its URL, error handling, and test transports are covered in Services. Usually you don't construct one directly: an lllm:// ref bound to a URL in .lllm/config.toml resolves to a RemoteTactic (Refs and Composition).

docs.title: Picking a runtime
docs.text:
• Native when you are building the agentic system itself: you want to see and steer every agent turn, fork dialogs, parse and repair outputs, run code in a sandbox, or orchestrate several agents with sessions and cost tracking.
  • Plain Python for deterministic steps (parsing, scoring, lookups, glue) and for adapting code that has nothing to do with agents.
  • Pydantic AI when an agent is already written for Pydantic AI, or you want its model and tool ecosystem and its instrumentation. Wrap it once and it joins services, packages, and channels.
  • Remote when the tactic runs elsewhere: another team's service, a GPU host, or a process you scale separately.

The choice is local to one tactic. A native program can call a Pydantic AI tactic, which can use a native tactic as a tool, and any of them can move behind a service without its callers changing.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Services: serve a tactic and call it over HTTP.
  • Refs and Composition: wire tactics together by lllm:// ref.
  • Tutorials: step-by-step walkthroughs, including wrapping, serving, and packaging a Pydantic AI agent.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Any tactic can be served over HTTP with the contract it has in Python. A request carries the input and a CallContext, a response carries the validated output, and /info publishes the schemas. RemoteTactic turns a service back into a tactic, so calling code does not change when a tactic moves to another process or machine.

pip install "lllm-core[server]"   # FastAPI and Uvicorn, for serving
pip install "lllm-core[client]"   # httpx, for RemoteTactic

docs.title: Serve a tactic
docs.text:
Put a tactic in a module, tactics.py:

from pydantic import BaseModel
from lllm import Tactic, TacticEvent


class Question(BaseModel):
    text: str


class Answer(BaseModel):
    text: str
    trace_id: str | None = None


class Shout(Tactic):
    """Shout the question back."""

    name = "shout"
    input_type = Question
    output_type = Answer

    def call(self, task: Question, *, context=None) -> Answer:
        trace_id = context.trace_id if context else None
        return Answer(text=task.text.upper(), trace_id=trace_id)

    def stream(self, task: Question, *, context=None):
        for word in task.text.split():
            yield word.upper()
        yield TacticEvent.result(self.run(task, context=context))

Serve it from the same folder:

lllm serve tactics:Shout --port 8000

INFO:     Started server process [3940928]
INFO:     Waiting for application startup.
INFO:     Application startup complete.
INFO:     Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000 (Press CTRL+C to quit)

Call it:

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/run \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": {"text": "hello"}, "context": {"trace_id": "trace-1"}}'

{"output":{"text":"HELLO","trace_id":"trace-1"},"request_id":"fba55530-a1a1-4f28-abfa-535817256e08","tactic":"shout"}

The module:attribute can name a tactic class or instance, a factory that returns one, an object with a run method, or a handler function. A factory is called once at load and a handler once per input; the rule that tells them apart is in Loading entrypoints. --host defaults to 127.0.0.1, --port to 8000, and --log-level to info.

To build the app in code, use create_tactic_app and any ASGI server:

# app.py
from lllm import create_tactic_app
from tactics import Shout

app = create_tactic_app(Shout())

uvicorn app:app --port 8000

create_tactic_app(tactic, *, title=None, description=None) returns a FastAPI app titled with the tactic's name and description unless you pass your own.

docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
Route Purpose GET /health {"ok": true, "tactics": [...]} GET /info The tactic's TacticInfo. POST /run Run once and return the output. POST /stream Stream events as server-sent events. GET /tactics TacticInfo for every tactic in the app. GET /tactics/{name}/info One tactic's TacticInfo. POST /tactics/{name}/run Run one tactic. POST /tactics/{name}/stream Stream one tactic.

create_tactic_app mounts all of them. FastAPI's own /docs and /openapi.json are there as usual. /info publishes the tactic's input and output schemas, and /openapi.json shows the same schemas as the input of the /run and /stream request envelopes and the output of the /run response. The /tactics/{name}/... routes are listed without them.

docs.title: Several tactics in one app
docs.text:
create_service_app serves a list of tactics (routed by name) or a mapping of route names to tactics. It mounts /health and the /tactics/... routes:

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from lllm import as_tactic, create_service_app
from tactics import Shout


def word_count(text: str) -> int:
    """Count the words in a text."""
    return len(text.split())


app = create_service_app([Shout(), as_tactic(word_count)], title="Text tools")
client = TestClient(app)

print(client.get("/health").json())
print(client.post("/tactics/word_count/run", json={"input": "one two three"}).json())

{'ok': True, 'tactics': ['shout', 'word_count']}
{'output': 3, 'request_id': 'e518af99-f181-4587-9fcd-a1fef116b8fa', 'tactic': 'word_count'}

Route names must be unique, plain path segments. Pass expose_single_tactic_routes=True to also mount /info, /run, and /stream when the app holds exactly one tactic.

docs.title: Requests and responses
docs.text:
POST /run takes an envelope with the input and an optional context:

{
  "input": {"text": "hello"},
  "context": {
    "request_id": "req-1",
    "trace_id": "trace-1",
    "caller": "cli",
    "tags": {"env": "dev"},
    "metadata": {"user": "ada"}
  }
}

The context object has the shape of a CallContext: request_id, trace_id, span_id, caller, tags, metadata, package_ref, service_ref, and tactic_ref. The service generates a request_id when there is none, sets endpoint to the route ("run", "stream", or a custom endpoint's name), defaults tactic_ref to the tactic's package_ref, and ignores keys it does not know. This is the context the tactic receives:

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from lllm import Tactic, create_tactic_app


class ShowContext(Tactic):
    name = "show-context"
    output_type = dict

    def call(self, task, *, context=None):
        return context.model_dump(exclude_none=True)


app = create_tactic_app(ShowContext(package_ref="lllm://demo/debug/tactics/show-context"))
response = TestClient(app).post("/run", json={
    "input": "hi",
    "context": {"request_id": "req-1", "trace_id": "trace-1", "caller": "cli",
                "tags": {"env": "dev"}, "metadata": {"user": "ada"}, "region": "eu"},
})
print(response.json())

{'output': {'request_id': 'req-1', 'caller': 'cli', 'trace_id': 'trace-1', 'tactic_ref': 'lllm://demo/debug/tactics/show-context', 'endpoint': 'run', 'tags': {'env': 'dev'}, 'metadata': {'user': 'ada'}}, 'request_id': 'req-1', 'tactic': 'show-context'}

A successful /run returns {"output": ..., "request_id": ..., "tactic": ...}.

Two looser forms are accepted for clients you cannot change: task works in place of input, and a body that is not an envelope is taken as the input itself, so {"text": "hello"} works too. (An envelope is a JSON object with input or task and no keys besides input, task, and context.) New clients should send the envelope; it is the only form that carries a context.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
POST /stream responds with text/event-stream. Each event is one data: line holding a TacticEvent as JSON:

curl -s -N -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/stream \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": {"text": "hello world"}}'

data: {"id": "52f5acbc-174f-4d6f-bdb9-f52ddcefaecb", "timestamp": 1793845808.4317925, "kind": "message", "data": "HELLO", "metadata": {}}

data: {"id": "34f98b46-3109-4105-bcdb-5bfe20faf471", "timestamp": 1793845808.4319072, "kind": "message", "data": "WORLD", "metadata": {}}

data: {"id": "8e506315-e940-4dd2-bb34-5a5c063a77b5", "timestamp": 1793845808.432171, "kind": "result", "data": {"text": "HELLO WORLD", "trace_id": null}, "metadata": {}}

The route sends what tactic.aevents() yields. For a tactic that implements stream(), that path validates the input before stream() runs (Streaming and events). Once the response has started, a failure (including invalid input) arrives as a final error event while the HTTP status stays 200:

data: {"id": "458cf822-a0f0-4a81-b345-a02520feec00", "timestamp": 1793845812.2663333, "kind": "error", "data": {"message": "Value does not match schema Question: 1 validation error for Question\ntext\n  Field required [type=missing, input_value={'txt': 'hello'}, input_type=dict]\n    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.14/v/missing"}, "metadata": {"error_type": "SchemaError", "tactic": "shout", "endpoint": "stream", "request_id": "req-7"}}

A tactic that supports neither stream nor events gets a 400 TacticUnsupportedError before any event is sent. Event metadata passes through the same secret filter as /info.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Failures return a stable JSON body under FastAPI's detail key:

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/run \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": {"text": 5}, "context": {"request_id": "req-42"}}'

{
  "detail": {
    "error": {
      "type": "SchemaError",
      "message": "Value does not match schema Question: 1 validation error for Question\ntext\n  Input should be a valid string [type=string_type, input_value=5, input_type=int]\n    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.14/v/string_type",
      "tactic": "shout",
      "endpoint": "run",
      "request_id": "req-42",
      "metadata": {}
    }
  }
}
Status error.type When 400 SchemaError Invalid input or output, or a malformed envelope or context. 400 TacticUnsupportedError /stream on a tactic that does not stream. 404 TacticNotFound /tactics/{name}/... with an unknown name. 500 the exception's class name Anything else the tactic raises; message is str(exc).

RemoteTactic turns this body back into a RemoteTacticError (below). See also the Service API reference.

docs.title: Custom endpoints
docs.text:
A tactic can mount its own routes next to the standard ones. Decorate a method with endpoint.post, endpoint.get, endpoint.put, endpoint.patch, or endpoint.delete:

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from pydantic import BaseModel
from lllm import Tactic, TacticEvent, create_tactic_app, endpoint


class Ticket(BaseModel):
    text: str


class Route(BaseModel):
    queue: str
    urgent: bool


class Triage(Tactic):
    """Route a support ticket to a queue."""

    name = "triage"
    input_type = Ticket
    output_type = Route

    def call(self, task: Ticket) -> Route:
        urgent = "outage" in task.text.lower()
        return Route(queue="oncall" if urgent else "support", urgent=urgent)

    @endpoint.post("/triage/explain", description="Route a ticket and say why.")
    def explain(self, ticket: Ticket, *, context=None) -> dict:
        route = self.run(ticket, context=context)
        reason = "mentions an outage" if route.urgent else "routine request"
        return {"queue": route.queue, "reason": reason, "endpoint": context.endpoint}

    @endpoint.post("/triage/steps", mode="stream")
    def steps(self, ticket: Ticket, *, context=None):
        yield {"step": "read", "chars": len(ticket.text)}
        yield TacticEvent.result(self.run(ticket, context=context))


client = TestClient(create_tactic_app(Triage()))
print(client.post("/triage/explain", json={"input": {"text": "Total outage in eu-west"}}).json())
print(client.post("/triage/steps", json={"input": {"text": "Printer jam"}}).text)

{'queue': 'oncall', 'reason': 'mentions an outage', 'endpoint': 'explain'}
data: {"step": "read", "chars": 11}

data: {"id": "2011ecab-0a65-4527-9946-c563d23cdef4", "timestamp": 1793845911.8305802, "kind": "result", "data": {"queue": "support", "urgent": false}, "metadata": {}}

How custom endpoints behave:

  • The signature is endpoint.post(path, *, name=None, mode="run", description="", tags=()). name defaults to the method name and becomes context.endpoint; the description defaults to the docstring.
  • The method receives the request's input, read from the same envelope as /run and validated against the tactic's input_type, plus context= when it accepts one. Sync and async methods both work.
  • endpoint.get and endpoint.delete routes may be called without a body. The method then receives the query parameters as a dict of strings (a repeated key gives a list), or None when there are none, without validation. A request that sends a body is read and validated as above.
  • With mode="run" the return value is the JSON response, with no envelope around it. With mode="stream" or mode="events", each yielded item becomes one data: line: events as TacticEvent JSON, anything else as plain JSON.
  • Routes may not shadow the standard routes (/run, /stream, /info, /tactics/...), and each method and path pair must be unique across the app. Both are checked when the app is built.
  • lllm inspect module:attr --json lists the endpoints with their method, path, mode, description, and tags.

docs.title: Calling a service from Python
docs.text:
RemoteTactic is a tactic whose implementation is an HTTP service. With the service from Serve a tactic running:

from lllm import CallContext, RemoteTactic
from tactics import Answer, Question

remote = RemoteTactic(
    "http://127.0.0.1:8000",
    name="shout",
    input_type=Question,
    output_type=Answer,
)

print(repr(remote.run({"text": "hello"}, context=CallContext(trace_id="trace-1"))))
print(list(remote.stream({"text": "hello world"})))
print(remote.fetch_info().capabilities)

Answer(text='HELLO', trace_id='trace-1')
['HELLO', 'WORLD', {'text': 'HELLO WORLD', 'trace_id': None}]
('acall', 'arun', 'call', 'run', 'stream')
Method HTTP call run(), await arun() POST {url}/run with the envelope; returns output. stream(), astream() POST {url}/stream; yields each event's data. aevents() POST {url}/stream; yields TacticEvents. fetch_info(), await afetch_info() GET {url}/info; returns the service's TacticInfo.

Things to know:

  • The URL is the service base (http://host:8000), or a tactic inside a multi-tactic app (http://host:8000/tactics/shout). A URL that already ends in /run, /stream, or /info is normalized.
  • Without name=, the name comes from the URL: its last path segment (ignoring a trailing /run, /stream, or /info), such as shout in .../tactics/shout, or else the host and port, so http://127.0.0.1:8000 is named 127.0.0.1-8000.
  • run() and arun() validate the input against input_type before anything is sent, and validate the response into output_type; without output_type you get the JSON as-is. stream(), astream(), and aevents() send the input as given and do not validate what comes back. Bad input fails on the service and arrives as its error event (Streaming): stream() and astream() yield that event's data like any other item, and aevents() yields the event with kind="error".
  • The context travels in the envelope, so ids, tags, and metadata reach the remote tactic.
  • info() is local (runtime_kind is "http"); fetch_info() asks the service.
  • timeout defaults to 30 seconds. transport= and async_transport= take httpx transports, which is how tests call an app in-process; see Refs and Composition.

An error response (status 400 or above) raises RemoteTacticError, with the structured fields as attributes:

from lllm import RemoteTacticError

untyped = RemoteTactic("http://127.0.0.1:8000", name="shout")
try:
    untyped.run({"text": 5})
except RemoteTacticError as exc:
    print(exc.status_code, exc.error_type, exc.tactic, exc.endpoint)

400 SchemaError shout run

RemoteTacticError also carries message, request_id, and the raw detail. It subclasses TacticServiceError.

docs.title: lllm serve
docs.text:
lllm serve module:attribute [--host 127.0.0.1] [--port 8000] [--log-level info]
lllm serve PATH [--resource SECTION.NAME] [--port N] [--skip-key-check]

Given a package folder (or its lllm.toml), lllm serve launches the package's primary resource ([package] primary), or the one named with --resource, such as tactics.shout or services.api. The port comes from --port, else the resource's metadata.port (for a tactic without one, the port of a service that declares it as its tactic), else 8000. Here is a package folder holding the tactics.py above and this manifest:

[package]
org = "demo"
name = "shout"
version = "0.1.0"
primary = "tactics.shout"

[requirements.api_keys]
OPENAI_API_KEY = "Model access for the agents."

[tactics.shout]
entry = "tactics:Shout"
description = "Shout the question back."

[tactics.shout.metadata]
port = 8100

Before starting, lllm serve checks the API keys the package declares, in [requirements.api_keys] or a resource's required_api_keys metadata. It looks in the environment, the --env-file (default .env.local), and the OS keyring (skip it with --no-keyring). In a terminal it prompts for missing keys; otherwise it stops:

usage: lllm [-h] [--version] COMMAND ...
lllm: error: missing required API key(s):
- OPENAI_API_KEY - Model access for the agents.

Run `lllm setup .` or set the missing names in your environment.

lllm setup . stores keys in the OS keyring or .env.local. It also works for a package with nothing to launch, such as a library, from its [requirements.api_keys]. --skip-key-check starts without checking. The manifest format is covered in The lllm.toml manifest.

A tactic entry loads by the same rule as a module:attribute target. A service entry has no handler form: it names a FastAPI or Starlette app, or something that can be called without arguments, which is called once to build an app, a tactic, or an object with a run method. If that call returns plain data instead (a mapping, list, tuple, string, int, float, or bool), a service that declares tactic serves that tactic, and a service without one serves the data from a fixed JSON app: GET /health, plus POST /run, which returns the data as output. Any other entry stops lllm serve with an error that names the cause, instead of serving the service's tactic without its auth or middleware. That includes an entry that fails to import, raises while building, names a tactic instance, or returns an app wrapped in raw ASGI middleware, None, or a coroutine:

usage: lllm [-h] [--version] COMMAND ...
lllm: error: service api entry service:create_app failed: NameError: name 'add_auth' is not defined

Only services, tactics, channels, and runs resources can be launched. Naming another kind, such as config.default, as the primary or with --resource is an error that lists what can be launched:

usage: lllm [-h] [--version] COMMAND ...
lllm: error: resource config.default cannot be launched; launchable resources: tactics.shout

A served package keeps its modules loaded and its folder on sys.path for the life of the process, so its code can import the package's own modules when it is called. Packages served in one process, such as the packages of an AAAX strategy, share sys.modules, so give their top-level modules distinct names.

docs.title: lllm inspect
docs.text:
lllm inspect shows what a target is without starting anything. For an entrypoint it prints the tactic's contract:

lllm inspect tactics:Shout

shout (native)
Shout the question back.
capabilities: acall, arun, call, run, stream

--json prints the full contract: name, description, runtime, capabilities, endpoints, input_schema, output_schema, package_ref, service_ref, examples, and metadata, with secret-shaped metadata keys removed. For a package it shows what lllm serve would launch, the state of each declared key, and the routes:

lllm inspect .

demo/shout:tactics.shout (tactic)
port: 8100
api keys:
  OPENAI_API_KEY: missing - Model access for the agents.
GET /health
GET /info
GET /tactics
GET /tactics/{name}/info
GET,HEAD /docs
GET,HEAD /docs/oauth2-redirect
GET,HEAD /openapi.json
GET,HEAD /redoc
POST /run
POST /stream
POST /tactics/{name}/run
POST /tactics/{name}/stream
