  • A model: an API key for a hosted provider (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ...) or a local OpenAI-compatible server such as vLLM, SGLang, or NVIDIA Dynamo. Lesson 1 shows both.

docs.title: How to read them
docs.text: Each lesson builds on the previous one, and every code block is runnable. Lessons that call a model say so; everything else runs offline. When you want the full detail behind a lesson, each one links to its reference page.

docs.title: 1. Quick Start
docs.text:
Goal: talk to a model in one line, keep the conversation going with an agent, point LLLM at a local model, and generate a project to grow into.

You need: pip install "lllm-core[native]" and either a provider key (for example OPENAI_API_KEY) or a local OpenAI-compatible server.

docs.title: Step 1: one line
docs.text:
from lllm import Tactic

response = Tactic.quick("What is the capital of France?")
print(response.content)  # Paris

Tactic.quick() is the zero-config entry point: it builds a prompt from the default system prompt, creates one agent with a LiteLLM invoker, sends your message, and returns the reply as a Message. .content is the text.

docs.title: Step 2: choose the model and the persona
docs.text:
response = Tactic.quick(
    "What is 2 + 2?",
    system_prompt="You are a patient math teacher.",
    model="claude-opus-4-6",  # any LiteLLM model string
)

Any LiteLLM model identifier works: gpt-4o, claude-opus-4-6, mistral/mistral-large, gemini/..., and so on, with the provider's usual environment variable for the key.

docs.title: Step 3: keep the agent
docs.text:
Pass return_agent=True to get the agent back, or call quick() without a query to get an agent you drive yourself:

response, agent = Tactic.quick("Hi!", return_agent=True)
print(agent.name)  # assistant

agent = Tactic.quick(system_prompt="You are terse.")
agent.open("chat")                      # 1. open a dialog
agent.receive("Name a color.")          # 2. put a message in it
print(agent.respond().content)          # 3. run the agent's call loop

open → receive → respond is the pattern everything in LLLM builds on. The dialog belongs to the agent: it is the agent's mental state, and Lesson 2 shows how to branch it, inspect it, and run several of them side by side.

docs.title: Step 4: run against a local model
docs.text:
Extra keyword arguments to quick() become model arguments, so any OpenAI-compatible server works, including vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA Dynamo:

local = {
    "model": "hosted_vllm/Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct",
    "api_base": "http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1",
    "api_key": "local",
    "max_tokens": 64,
}
print(Tactic.quick("What is the capital of France? One word.", **local).content)

Self-hosted serving stacks can do more when they know what an agent is doing: which calls belong to one reasoning chain, which dialogs were forked from which, and how urgent a call is. Agents can send that as inference hints for KV-cache-aware routing and priority scheduling.

docs.title: Step 5: generate a project
docs.text:
When the one-liner grows into a system, let LLLM lay out the project:

lllm create my-app            # native project, template "minimal"
cd my-app
pip install -e ".[dev]"
python main.py "Say hello in one sentence."
pytest                        # offline smoke test, no model calls

my-app/
  lllm.toml            # the package: what to discover, and hub metadata
  prompts/assistant.py # Prompt objects, discovered by key
  configs/default.yaml # agents declared in YAML
  tactics/assistant.py # the program: a Tactic with agent_group
  main.py
  tests/test_smoke.py

Other templates: --template pipeline (planner, writer, reviewer), proxy (an API surface for agents), research (batch experiments), and service (served over HTTP). The tactic in the minimal template is a whole program in a few lines:

from lllm import Tactic


class AssistantTactic(Tactic):
    name = "assistant"
    agent_group = ["assistant"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        assistant = self.agents["assistant"]
        assistant.open("chat")
        assistant.receive(task)
        return assistant.respond().content

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
You want Use One question, one answer Tactic.quick("...") A conversation quick(return_agent=True) or quick(), then open → receive → respond A local or self-hosted model model=..., api_base=... A project to grow into lllm create my-app

Next: 2. Agents and Dialogs

docs.title: 2. Agents and Dialogs
docs.text:
Goal: build a native Agent, hold multi-turn conversations, run several dialogs on one agent, branch them with fork(), inspect and save them, and keep long conversations inside the model's context window.

Every interaction in LLLM's native runtime is built from two primitives:

  • An Agent owns an LLM identity: a name, a system prompt, a model, and the invoker that talks to the provider.
  • A Dialog is that agent's mental state: an append-only, forkable message history. An agent can hold many named dialogs at once.

This is the low-level control LLLM is built around. Nothing is hidden in a framework loop: you decide which dialog a message goes into, when the model is called, and where a conversation branches. That is what research workflows need when they retry from an earlier point, explore alternatives side by side, or replay a transcript later.

Where Pydantic fits: every message is a Pydantic model (Message), and so are the per-call diagnostics (AgentCallSession) and costs (InvokeCost). A transcript is typed data you can dump to JSON and load back.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Start with Lesson 1 if you are new to LLLM. The native runtime needs the native extra and a key for your model provider:

pip install "lllm-core[native]"
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...   # or the key for any LiteLLM provider you use

Steps that call respond() send requests to your model provider. Building agents, opening, forking, inspecting, and saving dialogs run locally.

docs.title: Step 1: Build an agent
docs.text:
from lllm import Agent, Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native.invokers import build_invoker

system = Prompt(path="assistant/system", prompt="You are a helpful assistant.")
invoker = build_invoker({"invoker": "litellm"})

agent = Agent(
    name="assistant",
    system_prompt=system,
    model="gpt-4o",
    llm_invoker=invoker,
)
  • Prompt is LLLM's prompt object. Here it is just a template; the next lesson gives it parsers, tools, and handlers.
  • build_invoker({"invoker": "litellm"}) returns the LiteLLM invoker, so model accepts any LiteLLM model string: OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, local Ollama models, and more.

Agent is a dataclass. The fields you will use most:

Field Default Meaning name required The agent's role, used as the responder name on its messages system_prompt required The Prompt that seeds every dialog the agent opens model required Model identifier passed to the invoker llm_invoker required The invoker that calls the provider model_args {} Extra model arguments, such as temperature max_exception_retry 3 Retries when the reply fails parsing (Lesson 3) max_interrupt_steps 5 Tool-call rounds allowed per respond() (Lesson 4) max_llm_recall 0 Retries when the provider call raises an error other than a rate limit max_rate_limit_retries 8 Retries after rate-limit errors, waiting exponentially longer (up to 60 seconds) context_manager None Trims the dialog before each call (Step 10)

For a quick experiment, Tactic.quick() from Lesson 1 builds the same kind of agent in one line:

from lllm import Tactic

agent = Tactic.quick(system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant.", model="gpt-4o")

Without a query, quick() returns the agent; with one, it opens a dialog, sends the query, and returns the reply.

In larger projects you declare agents in configuration instead of constructing them by hand; Lesson 5 shows how.

docs.title: Step 2: Run one turn: open, receive, respond
docs.text:
agent.open("chat")                                 # 1. create a named dialog
agent.receive("What is the capital of France?")   # 2. append a user message
response = agent.respond()                         # 3. call the model, append its reply
print(response.content)
  1. open(alias) creates a dialog owned by the agent, seeds it with the system prompt, and makes it the active dialog. The alias ("chat") is your name for this conversation; opening an alias that already exists raises ValueError.
  2. receive(text) appends a user message to the active dialog.
  3. respond() sends the dialog to the model, appends the reply, and returns it as a Message. .content holds the reply text.

docs.title: Step 3: Hold a multi-turn conversation
docs.text:
agent.receive("And what language do they speak there?")
print(agent.respond().content)

Each receive / respond cycle appends to the same dialog, and the whole history is sent on every call, so the model answers the follow-up with the earlier turn in context.

docs.title: Step 4: Run several dialogs on one agent
docs.text:
An agent can hold several named dialogs and switch between them:

agent.open("topic_a")               # opening also switches to the new dialog
agent.receive("Tell me about black holes.")
agent.respond()

agent.open("topic_b")
agent.receive("Tell me about cats.")
agent.respond()

agent.switch("topic_a")             # back to the first conversation
agent.receive("How massive is Sagittarius A*?")
agent.respond()

print(agent.active_alias)           # topic_a
print(sorted(agent.dialogs))        # ['chat', 'topic_a', 'topic_b']

receive() and respond() also take alias= to target a dialog without switching to it, for example agent.respond(alias="topic_b").

docs.title: Step 5: Inspect a dialog
docs.text:
dialog = agent.current_dialog

for message in dialog.messages:
    print(f"[{message.name}] {message.content[:80]}")

print(dialog.overview())   # condensed, numbered view
print(dialog.cost)         # token counts and dollar cost so far

overview() returns one entry per message, truncated to 100 characters:

[0. system (developer)]: You are a helpful assistant.

[1. user (user)]: Tell me about black holes.

[2. assistant (assistant)]: ...

dialog.head is the first message (the system prompt) and dialog.tail is the last one (usually the latest reply). dialog.cost sums the usage the provider reported for every message.

docs.title: Step 6: Fork a dialog
docs.text:
Forking creates a child dialog that starts with a copy of the parent's history and then evolves independently. Use it to explore "what if" branches without touching the main thread:

agent.open("main")
agent.receive("You are interviewing a candidate for a backend role.")
agent.respond()

agent.fork("main", "strict_branch")   # copy "main" and switch to the copy
agent.receive("Explain recursion.")
strict_reply = agent.respond()

agent.fork("main", "lenient_branch")  # "main" itself was never changed
agent.receive("Tell me something interesting about yourself.")
lenient_reply = agent.respond()

print(len(agent.dialogs["main"].messages))           # 3
print(len(agent.dialogs["strict_branch"].messages))  # 5

fork(alias, child_alias, last_n=0, first_k=1) copies the whole history by default. With last_n > 0 the child keeps only the first first_k messages plus the last last_n, which is handy for retrying from a clean point:

agent.fork("main", "retry", last_n=1, first_k=1)   # system prompt + last message

Every dialog records its lineage. Print the tree from any dialog:

print(agent.dialogs["main"].tree_overview())

[a033d03f] owner=assistant msgs=3 split@None
  └─ [29cd695c] owner=assistant msgs=3 split@2
  └─ [6a89279f] owner=assistant msgs=5 split@3
    └─ [25480008] owner=assistant msgs=5 split@4
  └─ ...

Your named forks appear in the tree, and so do the short-lived working copies that respond() makes for each model call (see "How it works" below). The ids differ on every run.

docs.title: Step 7: Close a dialog
docs.text:
old_dialog = agent.close("chat")   # remove it from the agent and return it
print(len(old_dialog.messages))

Closing returns the Dialog object so you can archive or inspect it. If the closed dialog was active, the agent has no active dialog until you open() or switch() again.

docs.title: Step 8: Read the reply Message
docs.text:
respond() returns a Message:

agent.receive("Give me one more fact about cats.", alias="topic_b")
message = agent.respond(alias="topic_b")

message.content            # str: the reply text
message.role               # Roles.ASSISTANT
message.name               # "assistant" (the agent's name)
message.model              # the model used for the call
message.usage              # dict of token counts reported by the provider
message.cost               # InvokeCost: tokens and dollar cost for this reply
message.is_function_call   # True when the model asked for tools (Lesson 4)
message.parsed             # parser output (Lesson 3); {} when no parser ran
message.to_dict()          # JSON-ready dict

For diagnostics about the whole call, including parse retries and tool rounds, ask for the session instead:

agent.receive("And one more, please.", alias="topic_b")
session = agent.respond(alias="topic_b", return_session=True)
print(session.state)                    # "success"
print(session.delivery.content)         # the same Message respond() would return
print(session.exception_retries_count)  # 0 when the first reply parsed cleanly

Lesson 7 covers sessions in detail.

docs.title: Step 9: Save and restore a dialog
docs.text:
Dialogs serialize to JSON-ready dictionaries that include their message history, lineage, child dialogs, and the latest prompt (tools are stored as their schemas):

import json
from lllm import Dialog

with open("main_dialog.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(agent.dialogs["main"].to_dict(), f)

with open("main_dialog.json") as f:
    restored = Dialog.from_dict(json.load(f))

print(len(restored.messages), len(restored.children))
print(restored.overview())

Use saved dialogs to review runs, build datasets, or compare branches offline. Single messages round-trip the same way with message.to_dict() and Message.from_dict(data).

docs.title: Step 10: Manage the context window
docs.text: Long conversations can outgrow a model's context window. A ContextManager trims what is sent to the model before each call without touching the dialog itself.

docs.title: Use the built-in truncator
docs.text:
from lllm.runtimes.native.core.dialog import DefaultContextManager

cm = DefaultContextManager("gpt-4o")                     # window size from LiteLLM
cm = DefaultContextManager("gpt-4o", max_tokens=32000)   # or an explicit cap

agent = Agent(
    name="assistant",
    system_prompt=system,
    model="gpt-4o",
    llm_invoker=invoker,
    context_manager=cm,
)

Before each model call, DefaultContextManager counts tokens with LiteLLM and, when the dialog is too long:

  • always keeps the first message (the system prompt);
  • keeps messages from the most recent backwards until the budget runs out;
  • cuts the oldest kept message to fit, prefixed with [...earlier content truncated...];
  • reserves a 5,000-token safety buffer below the limit.

docs.title: Write your own policy
docs.text:
Subclass ContextManager, set name, and implement __call__. It receives a working copy of the dialog and returns the dialog to send:

from typing import Optional

from lllm import Dialog
from lllm.runtimes.native.core.dialog import ContextManager


class RollingWindowManager(ContextManager):
    name = "rolling_window"

    def __init__(self, model_name: str, max_tokens: Optional[int] = None, keep_last: int = 10):
        self.model_name = model_name
        self.keep_last = keep_last

    def __call__(self, dialog: Dialog) -> Dialog:
        if len(dialog.messages) <= self.keep_last + 1:
            return dialog                                       # short enough
        return dialog.fork(last_n=self.keep_last, first_k=1)   # system prompt + recent turns


agent.context_manager = RollingWindowManager("gpt-4o", keep_last=6)

Keep the model_name and max_tokens parameters even if you ignore them: agents built from configuration construct context managers with those two keyword arguments.

docs.title: Declare it in configuration
docs.text:
When agents are built from a tactic config (Lesson 5), context management is a config key. A global default applies to every agent and each agent can override it:

global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  context_manager:
    type: default          # DefaultContextManager
    max_tokens: 128000

agent_configs:
  - name: small_agent
    model_name: gpt-4o-mini
    system_prompt: You answer briefly.
    context_manager:
      type: default
      max_tokens: 16000    # tighter cap for the smaller model

  - name: full_history_agent
    system_prompt: You keep every detail.
    context_manager:
      type: null           # disabled: always send the full dialog

  - name: rolling_agent
    system_prompt: You chat casually.
    context_manager:
      type: rolling_window # a registered custom policy

Custom types are looked up in the runtime registry the tactic uses, so register the class there first:

from lllm import Runtime

runtime = Runtime()
runtime.register_context_manager(RollingWindowManager)   # registered under its `name`
# then build the tactic with registry=runtime (Lesson 5)

docs.title: How it works: dialogs as mental state
docs.text:
LLLM treats a dialog as an agent's internal mental state. It is:

  • Append-only. Messages are added with put_* methods and never edited in place.
  • Owned by one agent. The agent that opens a dialog seeds it with its system prompt and records itself as the owner.
  • Forkable. Branching happens through fork(), which records the parent, the split point, and the children.

respond() builds on these rules. For every model call it forks a working copy of the dialog, applies the context manager to that copy, and sends it. Failed attempts and repair messages stay in the working copy; your dialog receives only accepted replies (plus, when tools are used, the tool calls and their results). That keeps the canonical history clean and is why working copies show up in tree_overview().

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Concept API Build an agent Agent(name, system_prompt, model, llm_invoker) One-line agent Tactic.quick(system_prompt=..., model=...) Create a dialog agent.open(alias) Append a user message agent.receive(text) Call the model agent.respond() returns a Message Switch dialogs agent.switch(alias) Branch a dialog agent.fork(alias, child_alias, last_n=0, first_k=1) Remove a dialog agent.close(alias) returns the Dialog Inspect dialog.messages, dialog.overview(), dialog.cost, dialog.tree_overview() Save and load dialog.to_dict(), Dialog.from_dict(data) Call diagnostics agent.respond(return_session=True) Trim context DefaultContextManager(model, max_tokens=...) or a ContextManager subclass

See the Agent reference and the Dialog reference for every method and field.

Next: 3. Prompts and Structured Output

docs.title: 3. Prompts and Structured Output
docs.text:
Goal: write prompt templates, attach output parsers that turn replies into structured data, watch the agent repair a malformed reply on its own, get Pydantic-typed output, and reuse prompts through inheritance and a registry.

In LLLM a Prompt is more than a string. It is the complete behavior contract for one agent turn:

  1. Template: the text sent to the model, with {variable} placeholders.
  2. Output contract: a parser (or a structured-output format) that turns the reply into data.
  3. Tools: functions and MCP servers offered during the turn, on top of the agent's own tools (Lesson 4).
  4. Handlers: the messages used to recover from errors and to feed tool results back.

This is what makes LLLM agents reliable enough for program synthesis and other research pipelines. When a reply breaks the output contract, the agent sends the error back to the model and asks again, automatically, and only the corrected reply is kept in the dialog.

Where Pydantic fits: Prompt(format=MyModel) asks the provider for JSON that matches a Pydantic model, and a parser can validate replies with Pydantic so that validation errors drive the same repair loop. Prompts and parsers are Pydantic models themselves.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Finish Lesson 2. The examples reuse its agent; any agent works. Everything except the respond() calls runs locally, so you can try prompts and parsers without an API key.

docs.title: Step 1: Create a prompt
docs.text:
from lllm import Prompt

greet = Prompt(
    path="greet/system",
    prompt="You are a friendly assistant. Greet the user warmly.",
)

print(greet())   # render the template

path is the prompt's identifier. It shows up in logs and is the key under which the prompt is registered (Step 11), so keep it unique.

docs.title: Step 2: Use template variables
docs.text:
Placeholders use Python str.format() syntax. Calling the prompt renders it:

analyst = Prompt(
    path="analyst/system",
    prompt="You are an expert in {domain}. Today's date is {date}.",
)

print(analyst(domain="machine learning", date="2026-03-17"))
# You are an expert in machine learning. Today's date is 2026-03-17.

print(sorted(analyst.template_vars))                     # ['date', 'domain']
print(sorted(analyst.validate_args({"domain": "ml"})))   # ['date']: still missing

Rendering with a missing variable raises a ValueError that names the missing variables, so a forgotten argument fails loudly instead of reaching the model.

Literal braces are always written doubled, whether or not the template has variables:

json_hint = Prompt(
    path="json/system",
    prompt='Reply with JSON like {{"answer": "..."}} about {topic}.',
)
print(json_hint(topic="cats"))   # Reply with JSON like {"answer": "..."} about cats.

plain = Prompt(path="json/plain", prompt='Reply with JSON like {{"answer": "..."}}.')
print(plain())                   # Reply with JSON like {"answer": "..."}.

docs.title: Step 3: Use prompts in a dialog
docs.text:
There are two places a prompt enters a dialog:

agent.system_prompt = analyst
agent.open("session", prompt_args={"domain": "finance", "date": "2026-03-17"})
print(agent.current_dialog.head.content)
# You are an expert in finance. Today's date is 2026-03-17.
  • agent.open(alias, prompt_args=...) renders the agent's system prompt with those arguments.
  • agent.receive_prompt(prompt, prompt_args) renders any prompt and appends it as the next user message. You will use it in the next step.

This distinction matters because of one rule worth remembering:

The most recent prompt put into a dialog drives the next respond(). Its parser, format, and handlers decide how the reply is checked and repaired, and any tools it declares are offered on top of the agent's own tools. receive(text) puts a plain prompt with no parser, so the reply comes back as free text.

So when a turn needs structured output, send it with receive_prompt().

docs.title: Step 4: Parse XML tags
docs.text:
Attach a DefaultTagParser to the prompt for the turn:

from lllm import Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import DefaultTagParser

extract = Prompt(
    path="extractor/task",
    prompt="""Extract the people and organizations mentioned in the text.
Answer in exactly this format:

<people>comma-separated names</people>
<organizations>comma-separated organization names</organizations>

Text: {text}""",
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["people", "organizations"]),
)

You can test the output contract without a model by parsing a sample reply:

from pprint import pprint

pprint(
    extract.parse("<people>Alice, Bob</people><organizations>Acme Corp</organizations>"),
    sort_dicts=False,
)

{'raw': '<people>Alice, Bob</people><organizations>Acme Corp</organizations>',
 'xml_tags': {'people': ['Alice, Bob'], 'organizations': ['Acme Corp']},
 'md_tags': {},
 'signal_tags': {}}

Each tag maps to a list because a tag can appear more than once. Now run it on a real turn:

agent.receive_prompt(extract, {"text": "Alice and Bob met the Acme Corp board in Paris."})
message = agent.respond()
print(message.parsed["xml_tags"]["people"])

message.parsed holds the same dictionary shape, built from the model's reply.

With this native parser, every tag listed in xml_tags (and in required_xml_tags) must appear in the reply, otherwise parsing fails and the repair loop in Step 7 kicks in. If a tag is optional, use the portable parser, which only enforces the required_* lists:

from lllm.parsers import DefaultTagParser as PortableTagParser

lenient = PortableTagParser(xml_tags=["organizations"], required_xml_tags=["people"])
print(lenient.parse("<people>Alice</people>")["xml_tags"])
# {'organizations': [], 'people': ['Alice']}

Native prompts accept either parser. Note that from lllm import DefaultTagParser imports this portable parser; the native one lives in lllm.runtimes.native.

docs.title: Step 5: Parse fenced code blocks
docs.text:
md_tags extracts fenced Markdown blocks by their language tag:

coder = Prompt(
    path="coder/task",
    prompt="Write a Python function that {goal}. Put the code in a ```python block.",
    parser=DefaultTagParser(md_tags=["python"]),
)

parsed = coder.parse("Here it is:\n```python\ndef add(a, b):\n    return a + b\n```")
print(parsed["md_tags"]["python"])   # ['def add(a, b):\n    return a + b']

docs.title: Step 6: Detect signal tags
docs.text:
Signal tags let the model raise a flag. They are reported as booleans and never fail parsing:

review = Prompt(
    path="classifier/task",
    prompt="Is this review positive? If it is, include <POSITIVE> in your reply.\n\nReview: {review}",
    parser=DefaultTagParser(signal_tags=["POSITIVE"]),
)

print(review.parse("Clearly happy with the product. <POSITIVE>")["signal_tags"])  # {'POSITIVE': True}
print(review.parse("Mixed feelings.")["signal_tags"])                             # {'POSITIVE': False}

docs.title: Step 7: Watch the repair loop
docs.text:
When the parser raises, the agent does not fail right away. It shows the model its own reply plus an error message and asks again, up to the agent's max_exception_retry (default 3):

strict = Prompt(
    path="math/answer",
    prompt="Compute {expression}. Put only the final number in <answer> tags.",
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["answer"]),
)

agent.receive_prompt(strict, {"expression": "17 * 23"})
session = agent.respond(return_session=True)

print(session.delivery.parsed["xml_tags"]["answer"])
print(session.exception_retries_count)   # how many repairs were needed

If a reply has no <answer> tag, the next request the model sees ends with its bad reply followed by this message from the prompt's default handler:

Error: Parsing errors:
No answer tags found, it should be provided as <answer>...</answer>. Please fix.

Repairs happen on a working copy of the dialog, so your dialog keeps only the accepted reply. When retries run out, respond() raises AgentException with the last parsing error. You can reword the repair message per prompt with handler=DefaultSimpleHandler(exception_msg="..."); Lesson 8 shows custom handlers.

docs.title: Step 8: Write a custom parser
docs.text:
Subclass DefaultTagParser and override parse() to add your own validation. Raise ParseError with a message the model can act on:

from lllm.runtimes.native import DefaultTagParser, ParseError


def has_cycle(edges):
    graph = {}
    for src, dst in edges:
        graph.setdefault(src, []).append(dst)
    visiting, done = set(), set()

    def visit(node):
        if node in done:
            return False
        if node in visiting:
            return True
        visiting.add(node)
        if any(visit(nxt) for nxt in graph.get(node, [])):
            return True
        visiting.discard(node)
        done.add(node)
        return False

    return any(visit(node) for node in list(graph))


class DagParser(DefaultTagParser):
    """Parse 'a -> b' lines inside <edges> and reject cyclic graphs."""

    def parse(self, content: str, **kwargs) -> dict:
        parsed = super().parse(content, **kwargs)
        edges = [
            tuple(part.strip() for part in line.split("->"))
            for line in parsed["xml_tags"]["edges"][0].strip().splitlines()
        ]
        if has_cycle(edges):
            raise ParseError("The graph contains a cycle. Return an acyclic graph.")
        parsed["edges"] = edges
        return parsed


dag = DagParser(xml_tags=["edges"])
print(dag.parse("<edges>\nload -> clean\nclean -> train\n</edges>")["edges"])
# [('load', 'clean'), ('clean', 'train')]

Attach it with Prompt(..., parser=DagParser(xml_tags=["edges"])). A cyclic reply now goes back to the model with "The graph contains a cycle" until it returns a valid graph. The native ParseError is a subclass of lllm.ParseError, so except lllm.ParseError catches failures from either parser.

A parser can also be a plain function parser(content, **kwargs) -> dict. Whatever it returns is stored in message.parsed: a dict is kept as is (non-dict values are wrapped as {"value": ...}), and "raw" is set to the reply text unless the dict already has that key. Any exception it raises triggers the repair loop. Extra keyword arguments come from agent.respond(parser_args={...}).

docs.title: Step 9: Get Pydantic-typed output
docs.text: There are two ways to get typed output.

docs.title: Validate with Pydantic inside a parser
docs.text:
This works with any model. Validation errors become repair messages, so the model is told exactly which field is missing or malformed:

from pydantic import BaseModel

from lllm import Prompt, find_md_blocks


class Summary(BaseModel):
    headline: str
    key_points: list[str]
    sentiment: str


def summary_parser(content: str, **kwargs) -> dict:
    blocks = find_md_blocks(content, "json")        # accept ```json fences too
    text = blocks[0] if blocks else content
    return Summary.model_validate_json(text).model_dump()


summarize = Prompt(
    path="summarizer/task",
    prompt=(
        "Summarize the article as a JSON object with the keys "
        "headline, key_points (a list of strings), and sentiment.\n\n{article}"
    ),
    parser=summary_parser,
)

article = "LLLM adds parsers and repair loops so agent outputs stay structured."
agent.receive_prompt(summarize, {"article": article})
summary = Summary.model_validate(agent.respond().parsed)
print(summary.headline, summary.key_points)

docs.title: Ask the provider for structured output
docs.text:
format= passes the model class to the provider's structured-output mode, so the model is constrained to emit matching JSON:

structured = Prompt(
    path="summarizer/structured",
    prompt="Summarize the following article:\n\n{article}",
    format=Summary,
)

agent.receive_prompt(structured, {"article": article})
message = agent.respond()
summary = Summary.model_validate(message.parsed)   # parsed holds the decoded JSON dict

Things to know about format:

  • It needs a model and provider that support structured output, and the default completion API (api_type="completion").
  • message.parsed is the decoded JSON as a dict; call Summary.model_validate() to get the model instance.
  • The prompt's parser is not run when format is set. Invalid JSON still triggers the repair loop.

docs.title: Step 10: Extend a prompt
docs.text:
extend() copies every field (template, parser, tools, handler, format) and applies your overrides. A new path is required:

base = Prompt(
    path="base/system",
    prompt="You are a helpful assistant working on {topic}.",
)

python_expert = base.extend(
    path="python_expert/system",
    prompt="You are a senior Python engineer working on {topic}. Always include type hints.",
)

print(python_expert(topic="a CLI tool"))

Calling extend() without path raises ValueError, because two prompts with the same path would collide in the registry.

docs.title: Step 11: Register prompts and load them by path
docs.text:
Prompts can live in a registry and be fetched by path anywhere in your code:

from lllm import Prompt, load_prompt, register_prompt

register_prompt(Prompt(
    path="greeter/system",
    prompt="You are a warm, friendly assistant. The user's name is {name}.",
))

greeter = load_prompt("greeter/system")
print(greeter(name="Ada"))

register_prompt() adds the prompt to the default runtime registry. Dialogs accept registered paths directly, so agent.receive_prompt("extractor/task", {...}) works once extractor/task is registered.

In a project you rarely register prompts by hand: an LLLM package declares its prompt folders in lllm.toml (a prompts/ folder is picked up by default), and every Prompt defined in those files is registered when the package loads. lllm create sets this up for you (Lesson 1), and Lesson 6 covers packages.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Feature How Template variables {variable} in the template; literal braces always as {{ }} Render manually prompt(var=value) Check variables prompt.template_vars, prompt.validate_args(args) Send a structured turn agent.receive_prompt(prompt, prompt_args) XML tags DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=[...]) from lllm.runtimes.native Markdown blocks DefaultTagParser(md_tags=[...]) Signal flags DefaultTagParser(signal_tags=[...]) Optional tags lllm.parsers.DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=[...], required_xml_tags=[...]) Custom validation Subclass DefaultTagParser or pass a function; raise ParseError Repair budget Agent(max_exception_retry=N) Pydantic output Validate in a parser, or Prompt(format=MyModel) + MyModel.model_validate(message.parsed) Inheritance prompt.extend(path=..., ...) Registry register_prompt(prompt), load_prompt(path)

See the Prompts reference for every field.

Next: 4. Tools, Proxies, and Sandbox

docs.title: 4. Tools, Proxies, and Sandbox
docs.text:
Goal: give an agent Python tools and watch the tool-call loop, control that loop, declare tools separately from their implementations, expose a whole tactic or an MCP server as a tool, connect research data APIs through proxies, and run agent-written code in a sandbox you control.

LLLM gives you three levels of capability, each with more autonomy:

  • Tools: Python functions the model can call during a turn. LLLM runs the tool-call loop for you, and you decide which tools are on offer, how results are reported, and how many rounds are allowed.
  • Proxies: whole data APIs (dozens of endpoints) behind a small programming surface. Instead of one schema per endpoint, the agent reads the API's documentation and calls endpoints from Python with CALL_API; the proxy adds credentials and sends the requests. This is how LLLM agents work with research data sources such as financial statements or economic series.
  • Sandboxes: the agent writes code cells and your tactic decides where and how they run.

Where Pydantic fits: tool schemas are generated from type annotations, including lists, Literal choices, and nested Pydantic models. Tool schemas (Function) and tool invocations (FunctionCall) are Pydantic models themselves, and when a tactic is used as a tool, its arguments are validated against the tactic's input_type (Lesson 5).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Finish Lesson 3, in particular Step 3: the most recent prompt put into a dialog drives the next respond(). Steps that call respond() or run a tactic need a model provider key; defining tools, proxies, and sandboxes and calling them directly runs locally.

docs.title: Step 1: Define a tool with @tool
docs.text:
from lllm import tool


@tool(
    description="Get the current weather for a city",
    prop_desc={
        "city": "The city name, e.g. 'Paris'",
        "unit": "Temperature unit: 'celsius' or 'fahrenheit'",
    },
)
def get_weather(city: str, unit: str = "celsius") -> str:
    # Replace with a real weather API call.
    return f"Sunny, 22 degrees {unit} in {city}"

@tool turns the function into a Function: the schema the model sees plus the implementation. It builds the JSON Schema from the signature:

import json

print(json.dumps(get_weather.to_tool(), indent=2))

{
  "type": "function",
  "function": {
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Get the current weather for a city",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "city": {
          "type": "string",
          "description": "The city name, e.g. 'Paris'"
        },
        "unit": {
          "type": "string",
          "description": "Temperature unit: 'celsius' or 'fahrenheit' (default: 'celsius')"
        }
      },
      "required": [
        "city"
      ],
      "additionalProperties": false
    },
    "strict": false
  }
}
  • Parameters without defaults are required; defaults are noted in the description.
  • Without description, the function's docstring is used.
  • strict is chosen for you: a schema is marked strict when every parameter is required and flat (a string, number, boolean, enum, or a list of these), which is what strict function calling (for example OpenAI's) accepts. An object parameter, such as a model or a dict, keeps it off. Pass strict=True or strict=False to decide yourself.

Annotations map to JSON Schema, including containers, choices, and models; unannotated parameters become strings:

from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Point(BaseModel):
    x: float
    y: float


@tool(description="Draw a line through the points")
def draw(points: list[Point], color: Literal["red", "blue"]) -> str:
    return f"Drew {len(points)} points in {color}"


print(json.dumps(draw.properties["color"]))   # {"enum": ["red", "blue"], "type": "string"}
print(draw.properties["points"]["type"], draw.properties["points"]["items"]["required"])  # array ['x', 'y']
print(draw.strict)                            # False: the points are nested objects
Annotation JSON Schema str, int, float, bool string, integer, number, boolean list[str] an array of strings dict[str, int] an object with integer values Literal["red", "blue"] a string enum Optional[int] anyOf integer or null a Pydantic model the model's object schema, inlined a recursive model inlined once; references back into it become its type and title, e.g. {"type": "object", "title": "Node"}

docs.title: Step 2: Call a tool yourself
docs.text:
A tool is called with a FunctionCall, exactly as the agent loop does:

from lllm import FunctionCall

call = get_weather(FunctionCall(name="get_weather", arguments={"city": "Paris"}))
print(call.result)       # Sunny, 22 degrees celsius in Paris
print(call.result_str)

result_str is what the model reads back:

Return of calling function get_weather with arguments {'city': 'Paris'}:
---
Sunny, 22 degrees celsius in Paris
---

docs.title: Step 3: Decide where tools live
docs.text:
Tools are declared on prompts, in one of two places:

  • The agent's system prompt. These are the agent's own tools, offered on every turn, whether the turn was sent with receive(text) or with a prompt.
  • The prompt for one turn, sent with receive_prompt(). Its tools are offered on that turn in addition to the agent's own; if both declare a tool with the same name, the turn's version wins. Set agent_tools=False on a turn prompt to offer only that prompt's tools (or none).
from lllm import Prompt

weather_system = Prompt(
    path="weather_bot/system",
    prompt="You are a weather assistant.",
    function_list=[get_weather],
)
print(sorted(weather_system.functions))   # ['get_weather']

docs.title: Step 4: Run the tool loop
docs.text:
from lllm import Agent
from lllm.runtimes.native.invokers import build_invoker

agent = Agent(
    name="weather_bot",
    system_prompt=weather_system,
    model="gpt-4o",
    llm_invoker=build_invoker({"invoker": "litellm"}),
    max_interrupt_steps=3,   # at most 3 rounds of tool calls per respond()
)

agent.open("chat")
agent.receive("What is the weather in Paris and Tokyo?")
response = agent.respond()
print(response.content)

for message in agent.current_dialog.messages:
    print(f"{message.role.value:>9} | {message.name}")

A typical run leaves this in the dialog (the model may request both lookups in one round, as here, or one per round):

   system | system
     user | user
tool_call | weather_bot
     tool | get_weather
     tool | get_weather
assistant | weather_bot

What respond() did:

  1. The model saw the question and the get_weather schema, and replied with tool calls instead of text.
  2. LLLM ran each requested function and appended the results as tool messages.
  3. The model was called again with the results and wrote the final answer.
  4. respond() returned that final Message.

A turn prompt can add a tool for one turn, or switch the agent's tools off:

@tool(description="Convert a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit")
def to_fahrenheit(celsius: float) -> float:
    return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32


convert = Prompt(path="weather_bot/convert", prompt="{question}", function_list=[to_fahrenheit])
agent.receive_prompt(convert, {"question": "How warm is Paris today in Fahrenheit?"})
print(agent.respond().content)    # get_weather and to_fahrenheit are both offered

recap = Prompt(path="weather_bot/recap", prompt="Summarize our conversation in one sentence.", agent_tools=False)
agent.receive_prompt(recap)
print(agent.respond().content)    # no tools are offered on this turn

docs.title: Step 5: Control the loop
docs.text:
@tool(description="Divide two numbers")
def divide(a: float, b: float) -> str:
    if b == 0:
        raise ValueError("Division by zero")
    return str(a / b)


print(divide(FunctionCall(name="divide", arguments={"a": 1, "b": 0})).result_str)
# Error: Division by zero

The loop is governed by a few rules:

  • Round limit. max_interrupt_steps (default 5) caps tool-call rounds per respond(). When the cap is reached, LLLM appends "You are reaching the limit of tool calls. Provide the final response." and calls the model once more without tools. 0 means up to 100 rounds and logs a warning; always set a cap.
  • Tool errors. An exception inside a tool becomes the result Error: <message>, as above, so the model can retry with other arguments.
  • Repeated calls. If the model repeats a call with identical arguments in the same respond(), LLLM does not run it again and tells the model to use the earlier result.
  • Unknown tools. A call to a tool that is not offered on the turn raises KeyError.

To see the rounds of one call, ask for its session:

agent.receive("And in Berlin?")
session = agent.respond(return_session=True)

for step, rounds in session.interrupts.items():
    for calls in rounds:
        print(step, [(call.name, call.arguments) for call in calls])

docs.title: Step 6: Format tool results
docs.text:
The default result text is the "Return of calling function ..." block from Step 2. Pass a processor(result, function_call) -> str to change it:

def short_result(result, function_call):
    return f"[{function_call.name}] {result}"


@tool(description="Get the current weather for a city", processor=short_result)
def weather_brief(city: str) -> str:
    return f"Sunny in {city}"


print(weather_brief(FunctionCall(name="weather_brief", arguments={"city": "Paris"})).result_str)
# [weather_brief] Sunny in Paris

docs.title: Step 7: Declare a tool separately from its implementation
docs.text:
Sometimes the prompt should own the interface while the implementation lives elsewhere, like a header file and its source. Declare the schema as a Function without an implementation:

from lllm import Function

search_decl = Function(
    name="web_search",
    description="Search the web for information",
    properties={"query": {"type": "string", "description": "Search query"}},
    required=["query"],
)

Then register an implementation under the same name in a runtime registry:

from lllm import Runtime


@tool(name="web_search", description="Search the web for information")
def web_search(query: str) -> str:
    return f"Top results for {query!r}"   # call your search API here


runtime = Runtime()
runtime.register_tool("web_search", web_search)

An agent resolves declarations against its runtime when a turn starts:

researcher = Agent(
    name="researcher",
    system_prompt=Prompt(
        path="research_bot/system",
        prompt="You research questions carefully.",
        function_list=[search_decl],
    ),
    model="gpt-4o",
    llm_invoker=build_invoker({"invoker": "litellm"}),
    runtime=runtime,
)

researcher.open("main")
researcher.receive("What is the LLLM framework?")
print(researcher.respond().content)

Binding is by exact name. If nothing named web_search is registered, respond() raises KeyError naming the missing tool. A plain string works as well, function_list=["web_search"], and a prompt can mix live Function objects, declarations, and strings in one list. Inside an LLLM package, tools defined in the package's tool folders are registered automatically and can be referenced by package refs such as "my_pkg.tools:web_search" (Lesson 6 explains how refs are formed).

docs.title: Step 8: Use a tactic as a tool
docs.text:
A tool can be a whole agentic workflow. tactic_as_function() turns a tactic into a Function whose single task argument is passed to the tactic:

from lllm import Prompt, Tactic
from lllm.runtimes.native import tactic_as_function


class CodeReviewTactic(Tactic):
    """Review a Python snippet and list concrete problems."""

    name = "code_review"
    agent_group = ["reviewer"]
    input_type = str
    output_type = str

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        reviewer = self.agents["reviewer"]
        reviewer.open("review")
        reviewer.receive(f"Review this code and list concrete problems:\n\n{task}")
        return reviewer.respond().content


review_tool = tactic_as_function(CodeReviewTactic({
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o"},
    "agent_configs": [{"name": "reviewer", "system_prompt": "You are a strict Python reviewer."}],
}))

print(review_tool.name, review_tool.required)   # code_review ['task']
print(review_tool.description)                  # the tactic's docstring

ask_dev = Prompt(path="dev/ask", prompt="{request}", function_list=[review_tool])

With parameter_mode="kwargs", a tactic whose input is a Pydantic model publishes the model's fields as separate parameters instead. An input without fields, like the str here, keeps the single task parameter.

Tactics are covered in Lesson 5. Tactics can also mark individual methods as tools with @tactictool("name", ...) and be referenced by package ref, for example "my_pkg.tactics:code_review".

docs.title: Step 9: Connect MCP servers
docs.text:
Tools served over the Model Context Protocol are declared with MCP and attached with mcp_servers_list, on the system prompt (every turn) or on a turn prompt:

from lllm import MCP, Prompt

docs_server = MCP(
    server_label="docs",
    server_url="https://example.com/mcp",
    require_approval="never",
    allowed_tools=["search", "fetch_url"],
)

ask_docs = Prompt(path="docs_bot/ask", prompt="{question}", mcp_servers_list=[docs_server])
print(docs_server.to_tool())

The provider calls MCP servers itself; LLLM passes the declaration along as a {"type": "mcp", ...} tool. Whether that is accepted depends on the provider and API. For example, OpenAI exposes remote MCP servers through its Responses API, which you select with api_type=APITypes.RESPONSE on the agent (import APITypes from lllm.runtimes.native).

docs.title: Step 10: Declare agent tools in configuration
docs.text:
When agents are built from configuration (Lesson 5), a tools key lists capabilities for an agent, or for all agents under global. The refs are added to the agent's system prompt, resolved from the tactic's registry, and offered on every turn like any other agent tool:

from lllm import Runtime, Tactic

runtime = Runtime()
runtime.register_tool("web_search", web_search)


class AnalystTactic(Tactic):
    name = "analyst"
    agent_group = ["analyst"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        analyst = self.agents["analyst"]
        analyst.open("main")
        analyst.receive(task)
        return analyst.respond().content


config = {
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o", "tools": ["web_search"]},
    "agent_configs": [{"name": "analyst", "system_prompt": "You are a research analyst."}],
}

analyst = AnalystTactic(config, registry=runtime)
print(analyst("Find recent work on program synthesis with LLMs."))

Supported tools entries are registered tool names or pkg.tools:name refs, tactic tools (pkg.tactics:name, or pkg.tactics:name#tool to pick one method), and proxies (pkg.proxies:name), which add the proxy tools described next.

docs.title: Part 2: Proxies
docs.text:
When an agent needs many endpoints, one function schema per endpoint bloats the tool list and still cannot express multi-step data work. A proxy wraps an API surface instead: the agent reads the API's documentation and works with it from Python, through two tools:

  • query_api_doc(proxy_name) returns a proxy's endpoint documentation.
  • run_python(code) runs Python in a persistent interpreter where CALL_API(path, params) is already available.

The agent then fetches, joins, and computes over the data in ordinary Python, in a few tool rounds.

docs.title: Step 11: Define a proxy
docs.text:
from lllm import BaseProxy, ProxyRegistrator


@ProxyRegistrator(
    path="weather",
    name="Weather API",
    description="Current weather and forecasts for any city.",
)
class WeatherProxy(BaseProxy):

    @BaseProxy.endpoint(
        category="current",
        endpoint="current/{city}",
        description="Current temperature and conditions for a city.",
        params={
            "city*": (str, "London"),     # * marks a required parameter
            "units": (str, "celsius"),
        },
        response={"temperature": 18, "condition": "cloudy"},
    )
    def current(self, params: dict) -> dict:
        return {"city": params["city"], "temperature": 18, "condition": "cloudy"}

    @BaseProxy.endpoint(
        category="forecast",
        endpoint="forecast/daily",
        description="Daily forecast for a city.",
        params={
            "city*": (str, "London"),
            "days": (int, 5),
        },
        response=[{"day": 1, "high": 20, "low": 12}],
    )
    def daily_forecast(self, params: dict) -> list:
        days = params.get("days", 5)
        return [{"day": i + 1, "high": 18 + i, "low": 10 + i} for i in range(days)]
  • @ProxyRegistrator registers the class in the default runtime under path, the name you activate and the first segment of every CALL_API path.
  • endpoint is the path the agent calls, exactly as the documentation lists it: CALL_API("weather/forecast/daily", {"city": "Tokyo"}). Paths can contain slashes, hyphens, and {name} placeholders, which are filled from the path: CALL_API("weather/current/Tokyo", {}) passes city="Tokyo".
  • Only methods decorated with @BaseProxy.endpoint can be called.
  • This proxy has no base_url, so each endpoint method computes the response itself. Step 12 proxies a real HTTP API.
  • In params, the tuple is (type, example value). response is an example response. Both appear in the documentation the agent reads.

docs.title: Step 12: Proxy an HTTP API
docs.text:
For a web API, declare where it lives and how to authenticate, and let each endpoint method prepare the request parameters:

import os

from lllm import BaseProxy, ProxyRegistrator


@ProxyRegistrator(
    path="weather_api",
    name="Weather HTTP API",
    description="Current weather from a JSON web API.",
)
class WeatherHTTPProxy(BaseProxy):
    base_url = "https://api.example.com/weather"
    api_key_name = "api_key"   # sent as a query parameter; "*X-Api-Key" would send a header

    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.api_key = os.getenv("WEATHER_API_KEY")

    @BaseProxy.endpoint(
        category="current",
        endpoint="current/{city}",
        description="Current weather for a city.",
        params={"city*": (str, "London"), "units": (str, "metric")},
        response={"temperature": 18.2, "condition": "cloudy"},
    )
    def current(self, params: dict) -> dict:
        params.setdefault("units", "metric")   # validate or adjust the request here
        return params

With a base_url, an endpoint method returns the parameters to send, and the proxy makes the request: CALL_API("weather_api/current/Tokyo", {}) sends GET https://api.example.com/weather/current/Tokyo?units=metric&api_key=....

  • {name} placeholders in the endpoint path are filled in the URL, each value URL-encoded as one path segment (BRK/A becomes BRK%2FA). A missing or empty value, ., or .. raises ValueError before anything is sent.
  • The key is added under api_key_name; a name starting with * sends it as a header instead.
  • Endpoints declared with method="POST" send a JSON body.
  • Responses are cached on disk under ~/.lllm by default; pass use_cache=False to super().__init__() to turn that off.
  • Override _call_api(url, params, endpoint_info, headers) for APIs that need extra request fields or response post-processing.

The proxies that ship with LLLM (Step 15) are written this way.

docs.title: Step 13: Call proxies from Python
docs.text:
ProxyManager loads activated proxies and dispatches calls; it is exactly what the agent's CALL_API uses:

from lllm import ProxyManager
from lllm.runtimes.native.proxies import AgentInterpreter

proxies = ProxyManager(activate_proxies=["weather"])
print(proxies.available())                                   # ['weather']
print(proxies("weather/current/Tokyo", {}))
print(proxies("weather/forecast/daily", {"city": "Tokyo", "days": 2}))
print(proxies.retrieve_api_docs("weather"))                  # what query_api_doc returns

## Weather API (weather)
Current weather and forecasts for any city.
- **current/{city}** [GET] – Current temperature and conditions for a city.
    - `city*` (str) e.g. London
    - `units` (str) e.g. celsius
- **forecast/daily** [GET] – Daily forecast for a city.
    - `city*` (str) e.g. London
    - `days` (int) e.g. 5

AgentInterpreter is the interpreter behind run_python. Its namespace persists across calls, like a live REPL:

interpreter = AgentInterpreter(proxies, max_output_chars=5000, timeout=60)

print(interpreter.run('tokyo = CALL_API("weather/current/Tokyo", {})\nprint(tokyo["temperature"])'))
print(interpreter.run('print("Tokyo is", tokyo["condition"])'))   # `tokyo` is still defined
print(interpreter.run("1 / 0").splitlines()[-1])                  # ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
  • Only what the code prints is returned; the last expression is not echoed.
  • Exceptions come back as formatted tracebacks, so the agent can fix its code without losing state.
  • Output longer than max_output_chars is cut and "... (truncated)" appended.
  • Code running longer than timeout seconds raises TimeoutError, which the tool loop reports to the model as an error.
  • interpreter.reset() clears everything except CALL_API.

docs.title: Step 14: Give an agent the proxy
docs.text:
Add a proxy block to an agent's configuration. LLLM then builds a ProxyManager and an AgentInterpreter for the agent, appends the API directory and usage instructions to its system prompt, and adds the query_api_doc and run_python tools, which are offered on every turn:

from lllm import Tactic


class WeatherTactic(Tactic):
    name = "weather"
    agent_group = ["weather_analyst"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        analyst = self.agents["weather_analyst"]
        analyst.open("main")
        analyst.receive(task)
        return analyst.respond().content


config = {
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o", "model_args": {"temperature": 0.1}},
    "agent_configs": [{
        "name": "weather_analyst",
        "system_prompt": "You are a weather analyst. Use the Weather API to answer questions.",
        "proxy": {
            "activate_proxies": ["weather"],
            "exec_env": "interpreter",
            "max_output_chars": 5000,
            "timeout": 60.0,
        },
    }],
}

tactic = WeatherTactic(config)
print(sorted(tactic.agents["weather_analyst"].system_prompt.functions))
# ['query_api_doc', 'run_python']

The same configuration in YAML, with a global default that agents override field by field:

global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  proxy:
    activate_proxies: [weather]
    exec_env: interpreter

agent_configs:
  - name: weather_analyst
    system_prompt: You are a weather analyst. Use the Weather API to answer questions.

  - name: quick_analyst
    system_prompt: You answer weather questions in one sentence.
    proxy:
      timeout: 30.0          # only this field changes; the rest is inherited

Every key of the proxy block:

proxy:
  activate_proxies: [weather]      # proxies to load; empty means all registered proxies
  deploy_mode: false               # passed to each proxy instance
  cutoff_date: "2024-01-01"        # ISO date passed to proxies that restrict data by date
  exec_env: interpreter            # "interpreter" adds run_python; any other value (or null) does not
  max_output_chars: 5000           # truncate run_python output; 0 disables truncation
  truncation_indicator: "... (truncated)"
  timeout: 60.0                    # seconds per run_python call
  prompt_template: null            # custom instruction block; null selects the built-in one

With exec_env set to anything other than interpreter (for example jupyter or null), the agent still gets the API directory and query_api_doc, but no run_python: your tactic executes code itself, as in Part 3.

The built-in instruction block includes the API directory: every endpoint of every activated proxy, with its parameters. For large APIs that is a lot of system-prompt text. To keep it short, set prompt_template to your own instructions without the {api_directory} placeholder; the agent then reads documentation only through query_api_doc. A custom template may use {max_output_chars} and {truncation_indicator}, and must double any literal braces. Set it before building the tactic:

config["agent_configs"][0]["proxy"]["prompt_template"] = (
    "\n\nCall query_api_doc(name) before using a data API, then run Python with "
    "run_python, calling CALL_API(path, params). Output longer than "
    "{max_output_chars} characters is truncated."
)
tactic = WeatherTactic(config)

docs.title: Step 15: Run it
docs.text:
print(tactic("What is the current weather in Tokyo and Paris?"))

The agent typically:

  1. calls query_api_doc("weather") to read the endpoint details;
  2. calls run_python with code that runs CALL_API("weather/current/Tokyo", {}) and CALL_API("weather/current/Paris", {}) and prints the results;
  3. calls run_python again, reusing those variables, to compare or format;
  4. writes the final answer.

Each tactic call builds fresh agents, so every call starts with a fresh interpreter.

LLLM also ships ready-made proxies for research data, registered by load_builtin_proxies() from lllm.runtimes.native.proxies: Financial Modeling Prep (fmp), FRED (fred), Exa search (exa), Google Trends (gt), Wolfram Alpha (wa), and Main Street Data (msd). Each reads its API key from the environment. Lesson 8 combines several of them.

docs.title: Part 3: Sandbox
docs.text: Interpreter mode runs the agent's code for you. When you want to own execution, to intercept every cell, keep a notebook-style record, or run code somewhere else, let the agent write code cells and run them in your tactic.

docs.title: Step 16: Let the agent write cells and run them yourself
docs.text:
The agent writes <python_cell> and <markdown_cell> tags; a parser extracts them; the tactic runs the code in a sandbox and sends the outputs back:

import re

from lllm import ProxyManager, Prompt, Tactic
from lllm.runtimes.native import ParseError
from lllm.runtimes.native.proxies import AgentInterpreter

NOTEBOOK_SYSTEM = """You are a data analyst working in a Python notebook.

- Write code in <python_cell>...</python_cell> tags and notes in <markdown_cell>...</markdown_cell> tags.
- Cells run in order and variables persist between turns. Use print() to see values.
- Call the data APIs listed below with CALL_API(path, params).
- When you are done, write a final <markdown_cell> summary followed by <TERMINATE_NOTEBOOK>.

{api_directory}"""

CELL = re.compile(r"<(python_cell|markdown_cell)>(.*?)</\1>", re.DOTALL)


def notebook_parser(content: str, **kwargs) -> dict:
    cells = [(kind, body.strip()) for kind, body in CELL.findall(content)]
    has_code = any(kind == "python_cell" for kind, _ in cells)
    terminate = "<TERMINATE_NOTEBOOK>" in content and not has_code
    if not cells and not terminate:
        raise ParseError(
            "No cells found. Wrap code in <python_cell>...</python_cell>, "
            "or reply with <TERMINATE_NOTEBOOK> when you are done."
        )
    return {"cells": cells, "terminate": terminate}


task_turn = Prompt(path="notebook/task", prompt="{task}", parser=notebook_parser)
results_turn = Prompt(path="notebook/results", prompt="Cell outputs:\n\n{outputs}", parser=notebook_parser)


class NotebookAnalysisTactic(Tactic):
    name = "notebook_analysis"
    agent_group = ["analyst"]

    def call(self, task: str, max_steps: int = 8) -> str:
        proxies = ProxyManager(activate_proxies=["weather"])
        sandbox = AgentInterpreter(proxies, timeout=60)   # CALL_API is pre-loaded
        notebook = []

        analyst = self.agents["analyst"]
        analyst.open("main", prompt_args={"api_directory": proxies.retrieve_api_docs()})
        analyst.receive_prompt(task_turn, {"task": task})

        for _ in range(max_steps):
            parsed = analyst.respond().parsed
            outputs = []
            for kind, source in parsed["cells"]:
                notebook.append(f"<{kind}>\n{source}\n</{kind}>")
                if kind == "python_cell":
                    try:
                        output = sandbox.run(source)
                    except Exception as exc:          # e.g. a timeout
                        output = f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
                    outputs.append(output or "(no output)")
            if parsed["terminate"]:
                break
            analyst.receive_prompt(results_turn, {"outputs": "\n---\n".join(outputs) or "(no code cells)"})
        return "\n\n".join(notebook)


config = {
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o", "model_args": {"temperature": 0.1}},
    "agent_configs": [{"name": "analyst", "system_prompt": NOTEBOOK_SYSTEM}],
}

print(NotebookAnalysisTactic(config)("Compare the 3-day forecast for Tokyo and Paris."))

Notice how the pieces from earlier lessons fit together:

  • Both turn prompts carry notebook_parser, because every turn's reply must be parsed (the rule from Lesson 3).
  • A reply without cells fails parsing, so the model is asked again with the ParseError message before your loop ever sees it.
  • A failing cell returns its traceback as output, so the agent sees the error on the next turn and can rewrite the cell.

docs.title: Step 17: Bring your own sandbox
docs.text:
The tactic only needs an object with run(code) -> str. Swap the sandbox and nothing else changes. This one runs each cell in a fresh Python process:

import subprocess
import sys


class SubprocessSandbox:
    """Run each cell in a fresh Python process: no shared state, no CALL_API."""

    def __init__(self, timeout: float = 30.0):
        self.timeout = timeout

    def run(self, code: str) -> str:
        result = subprocess.run(
            [sys.executable, "-c", code],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            timeout=self.timeout,
        )
        return result.stdout + result.stderr


print(SubprocessSandbox().run("print(sum(range(10)))"))   # 45

Use it by replacing sandbox = AgentInterpreter(...) in the tactic. The same shape fits a container, a remote execution service, or a database query runner.

AgentInterpreter runs code with exec() inside your process. That suits trusted analysis code calling your own APIs, but it is not isolation. For untrusted code, put real isolation (a container, VM, or remote sandbox) behind the run() method.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Concept API Define a tool @tool(description=..., prop_desc={...}) Call a tool directly fn(FunctionCall(name=..., arguments={...})) Agent tools (every turn) system prompt function_list=[...], or config tools: [...] Tools for one turn Prompt(function_list=[...]) + agent.receive_prompt(prompt, args) Turn without agent tools Prompt(..., agent_tools=False) Cap tool rounds Agent(max_interrupt_steps=N) Inspect tool rounds agent.respond(return_session=True).interrupts Custom result text @tool(processor=fn) Declaration + implementation Function(name=..., properties=...) + runtime.register_tool(name, impl) Tactic as a tool tactic_as_function(tactic) MCP server Prompt(mcp_servers_list=[MCP(...)]) Define a proxy @ProxyRegistrator(path=...) + @BaseProxy.endpoint(endpoint="a/{b}", ...) HTTP-backed proxy base_url, api_key_name, api_key; endpoint methods return the params Use a proxy in Python ProxyManager(activate_proxies=[...])("proxy/path", params), AgentInterpreter(manager) Give an agent proxies config proxy: {activate_proxies: [...], exec_env: interpreter} Own code execution <python_cell> parser + any object with run(code) -> str

See the Proxies and Sandbox reference and the Prompts reference for every option.

Next: 5. Native Tactics

docs.title: 5. Native Tactics
docs.text:
Goal: write a program of agents as a Tactic, declare its agents in configuration, type its input and output with Pydantic, inspect per-call sessions, compose and extend tactics, run them in batches, and finally serve one over HTTP.

A tactic is LLLM's unit of agentic work: the program. A Tactic subclass:

  • implements call() with full control over every agent turn, using the open / receive / respond primitives from the earlier lessons;
  • declares the agents it needs in agent_group, and gets those agents built from a config dictionary, so models, prompts, tools, proxies, and limits are declared as data rather than wired in code;
  • runs every call on fresh agents and records a session with each agent call, retry, tool round, sub-tactic call, and cost.

Think of it as an nn.Module for agents: composable, isolated between calls, and easy to test. Every tactic is also a typed, service-ready unit, so the same class can be served over HTTP (Step 11).

Where Pydantic fits: input_type and output_type declare what a tactic takes and returns. Every call validates the task before call() runs and the result after it returns, and the same types describe the tactic when it is served.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Finish Lesson 4. Calling a tactic sends requests to your model provider; defining tactics and building them from config does not.

docs.title: Step 1: Define a tactic
docs.text:
from lllm import Tactic


class SummarizerTactic(Tactic):
    name = "summarizer"
    agent_group = ["writer"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        writer = self.agents["writer"]
        writer.open("session")
        writer.receive(f"Summarize this text in 3 bullet points:\n\n{task}")
        return writer.respond().content

A native tactic defines:

  • name: a unique identifier used for registration, sessions, and logs;
  • agent_group: the agent names it needs, each of which must appear in the config;
  • call(task, ...): the orchestration logic. self.agents maps each name in agent_group to a ready-to-use Agent.

A tactic without agent_group is plain Python: call() can do anything, and it still gets typing, sessions, composition, and serving. NativeTactic is a subclass of Tactic that only adds a check that agent_group is set.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure the agents
docs.text:
A tactic receives a config dictionary when it is constructed:

config = {
    "global": {
        "model_name": "gpt-4o",
        "model_args": {"temperature": 0.2},
    },
    "agent_configs": [
        {
            "name": "writer",
            "system_prompt": "You are a concise technical writer.",
            "model_args": {"max_completion_tokens": 1000},
        },
    ],
}

tactic = SummarizerTactic(config)
print(tactic)                                # SummarizerTactic(name='summarizer', agents=['writer'])
print(tactic.agents["writer"].model_args)    # {'temperature': 0.2, 'max_completion_tokens': 1000}

global holds defaults that are deep-merged into every entry of agent_configs: nested dictionaries such as model_args merge key by key, and the agent's own values win. The same config in YAML:

global:
  model_name: gpt-4o
  model_args:
    temperature: 0.2

agent_configs:
  - name: writer
    system_prompt: You are a concise technical writer.
    model_args:
      max_completion_tokens: 1000

Keys an agent entry understands:

Key Meaning name Agent name, matched against agent_group model_name Model string (required, usually set under global) system_prompt Inline system prompt text system_prompt_path Path of a registered prompt, used instead of system_prompt model_args Model arguments such as temperature api_type completion (default) or response max_exception_retry, max_interrupt_steps, max_llm_recall Loop limits (Lesson 2) context_manager Context-window policy (Lesson 2, Step 10) tools, proxy Agent tools and proxies (Lesson 4) skills Agent skills to expose to the model inference_hints Serving hints for self-hosted model servers

Unknown keys are passed to the model as extra arguments, with a warning that lists the known keys, so typos are easy to spot. At the top level, invoker selects the invoker (default "litellm") and max_workers sets the default thread count for batch calls (Step 8).

docs.title: Step 3: Call the tactic
docs.text:
result = tactic("Large language models are increasingly used as components of larger programs ...")
print(result)

Each call:

  1. makes a per-call copy of the tactic and builds fresh agents from the config, wrapped so that every respond() is recorded;
  2. validates the task against input_type, if declared (Step 5);
  3. runs call();
  4. validates the result against output_type, if declared;
  5. records the outcome, agent calls, sub-tactic calls, costs, and any error with its traceback in a TacticCallSession;
  6. returns the result, or re-raises the exception.

Because agents are rebuilt for every call, nothing leaks from one task into the next, and concurrent calls are safe.

docs.title: Step 4: Coordinate several agents
docs.text:
class ResearchTactic(Tactic):
    name = "researcher"
    agent_group = ["finder", "synthesizer"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        finder = self.agents["finder"]
        synthesizer = self.agents["synthesizer"]

        # Stage 1: gather raw facts
        finder.open("gather")
        finder.receive(f"List 5 key facts about: {task}")
        facts = finder.respond().content

        # Stage 2: synthesize them
        synthesizer.open("synthesize")
        synthesizer.receive(f"Facts:\n{facts}\n\nWrite a short paragraph.")
        return synthesizer.respond().content


research_config = {
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o"},
    "agent_configs": [
        {"name": "finder", "system_prompt": "You gather accurate factual information."},
        {"name": "synthesizer", "system_prompt": "You write clear, concise summaries."},
    ],
}

researcher = ResearchTactic(research_config)
print(researcher("quantum error correction"))

Each agent keeps its own dialogs, and call() decides exactly what flows between them.

docs.title: Step 5: Type the task and the result
docs.text:
Declare Pydantic types and the tactic validates both ends of every call:

from pydantic import BaseModel


class BriefInput(BaseModel):
    topic: str
    audience: str = "engineers"


class BriefOutput(BaseModel):
    title: str
    bullets: list[str]


class BriefTactic(Tactic):
    name = "brief"
    agent_group = ["writer"]
    input_type = BriefInput
    output_type = BriefOutput

    def call(self, task: BriefInput) -> BriefOutput:
        writer = self.agents["writer"]
        writer.open("brief")
        writer.receive(f"Write three one-line bullet points about {task.topic} for {task.audience}.")
        lines = writer.respond().content.splitlines()
        bullets = [line.lstrip("-* ").strip() for line in lines if line.strip()]
        return BriefOutput(title=task.topic.title(), bullets=bullets)


brief = BriefTactic({
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o"},
    "agent_configs": [{"name": "writer", "system_prompt": "You write crisp technical briefs."}],
})

print(brief({"topic": "package refs"}))   # a dict is validated into BriefInput

brief({"audience": "managers"}) raises lllm.SchemaError before any agent runs, because topic is required; the Pydantic validation error is attached as its cause. Validation uses Pydantic's TypeAdapter, so plain types such as str or list[str] work too.

To make the model's own output typed, combine this with the parsers and format= from Lesson 3.

docs.title: Step 6: Inspect the call session
docs.text:
session = tactic("Some text to summarize ...", return_session=True)

print(session.state)              # "success"
print(session.delivery)           # the value call() returned
print(session.agent_call_count)   # number of respond() calls
print(session.total_cost.cost)    # dollar cost reported by the provider
print(session.summary())          # compact overview dict

session.agent_sessions maps each agent name to the AgentCallSession of every respond() it made, with its parse retries, tool rounds, and cost. Lesson 7 shows how to log and persist sessions.

docs.title: Step 7: Compose tactics
docs.text:
Tactics can call other tactics like functions:

class PipelineTactic(Tactic):
    name = "pipeline"
    agent_group = ["coordinator"]

    def __init__(self, config, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(config, **kwargs)
        self.researcher = ResearchTactic(config)   # tracked in self.sub_tactics

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        research = self.researcher(task)

        coordinator = self.agents["coordinator"]
        coordinator.open("plan")
        coordinator.receive(f"Based on this research:\n{research}\n\nCreate an action plan.")
        return coordinator.respond().content


pipeline_config = {
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o"},
    "agent_configs": research_config["agent_configs"] + [
        {"name": "coordinator", "system_prompt": "You turn research into concrete plans."},
    ],
}

pipeline = PipelineTactic(pipeline_config)
print(pipeline.sub_tactics.keys())   # dict_keys(['researcher'])

session = pipeline("adopting LLM agents in a research lab", return_session=True)
print(session.summary()["sub_tactic_calls"])     # 1
print(list(session.sub_tactic_sessions))         # ['researcher']
  • Assigning a tactic to an attribute after super().__init__() adds it to self.sub_tactics.
  • Every tactic called inside call() is recorded in the caller's session automatically, including calls made through bcall(), acall(), and ccall(). The parent's total_cost includes the sub-tactics' costs.

docs.title: Step 8: Run many tasks
docs.text:
import asyncio

topics = ["topic A", "topic B", "topic C", "topic D"]

# Thread pool; results come back in input order
results = researcher.bcall(topics, max_workers=4)

# Keep going when some tasks fail: exceptions are returned in place of results
results = researcher.bcall(topics, max_workers=4, fail_fast=False)

# One async call, for use inside an async application
result = asyncio.run(researcher.acall("a single async task"))


# Stream results as they complete
async def stream_results():
    async for index, result in researcher.ccall(topics, max_workers=4):
        print(f"Task {index} done: {result[:60]}")

asyncio.run(stream_results())

Each task gets its own fresh agents, so parallel tasks never share dialogs. bcall() also accepts tags=, metadata=, and return_sessions=True.

docs.title: Step 9: Extend a tactic by inheritance
docs.text:
Subclass a concrete tactic to reuse its call() and add stages:

class WritingPipeline(Tactic):
    """Two-agent pipeline: outline, then article."""

    name = "writing_pipeline"
    agent_group = ["outliner", "writer"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        outliner = self.agents["outliner"]
        writer = self.agents["writer"]

        outliner.open("outline")
        outliner.receive(f"Create a concise 5-point outline about: {task}")
        outline = outliner.respond().content

        writer.open("write")
        writer.receive(f"Expand this outline into a short article:\n\n{outline}")
        return writer.respond().content


class EditedWritingPipeline(WritingPipeline):
    name = "edited_writing_pipeline"
    agent_group = ["outliner", "writer", "editor"]   # adds a third agent

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        draft = super().call(task)                     # reuse outline and draft stages

        editor = self.agents["editor"]
        editor.open("edit")
        editor.receive(f"Polish this draft for clarity and concision:\n\n{draft}")
        return editor.respond().content


writing_config = {
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o", "model_args": {"temperature": 0.7}},
    "agent_configs": [
        {"name": "outliner", "system_prompt": "You create concise, structured outlines."},
        {"name": "writer", "system_prompt": "You expand outlines into engaging articles."},
        {"name": "editor", "system_prompt": "You polish prose for clarity and concision."},
    ],
}

print(EditedWritingPipeline(writing_config)("the rise of agentic AI"))

A shared base class can carry helpers without being a usable tactic on its own. Leave name off it:

class WritingBase(Tactic):
    """Shared helpers; never registered because it has no name."""

    agent_group = ["writer"]

    def polish(self, text: str) -> str:
        writer = self.agents["writer"]
        writer.open("polish")
        writer.receive(f"Polish this:\n\n{text}")
        return writer.respond().content


class BlogPostTactic(WritingBase):
    name = "blog_post"
    agent_group = ["writer", "seo_reviewer"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        draft = self.polish(task)
        reviewer = self.agents["seo_reviewer"]
        reviewer.open("seo")
        reviewer.receive(f"Suggest SEO keywords for:\n\n{draft}")
        return reviewer.respond().content

docs.title: Step 10: Register tactics and build them by name
docs.text:
Defining a subclass does not register it anywhere. Register it in a runtime registry, then build it from config by name:

from lllm import Runtime, build_tactic, register_tactic_class

runtime = Runtime()
register_tactic_class(SummarizerTactic, registry=runtime)

summarizer = build_tactic(config, name="summarizer", registry=runtime)
print(type(summarizer).__name__)   # SummarizerTactic
  • With "tactic_type": "summarizer" in the config, build_tactic(config, registry=runtime) needs no name.
  • class SummarizerTactic(Tactic, registry=runtime): ... registers the class when it is defined.
  • Omit registry= to use the default runtime registry.

The tactic's agents resolve registered prompts (system_prompt_path), tools, and proxies from the same registry. In an LLLM package, every tactic class with a name in the package's tactic folders is registered when the package loads. lllm create my-app generates such a project, with prompts, configs, a tactic, and a smoke test (Lesson 1); Lesson 6 covers packages, sharing, and publishing.

docs.title: Step 11: Serve it
docs.text:
Every tactic is also a service-ready unit with typed run / arun methods and an info() description built from its name, docstring, and types, so you can serve it as it is. Put the tactic in a module:

# summarizer_service.py
from lllm import Tactic


class SummarizerTactic(Tactic):
