    """Summarize text in three bullet points."""

    name = "summarizer"
    agent_group = ["writer"]
    input_type = str
    output_type = str

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        writer = self.agents["writer"]
        writer.open("session")
        writer.receive(f"Summarize this text in 3 bullet points:\n\n{task}")
        return writer.respond().content


CONFIG = {
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o"},
    "agent_configs": [{"name": "writer", "system_prompt": "You are a concise technical writer."}],
}

tactic = SummarizerTactic(CONFIG)

From the directory that contains summarizer_service.py, check what will be served, then start the server:

lllm inspect summarizer_service:tactic
lllm serve summarizer_service:tactic --port 8000

lllm inspect prints the tactic's name, runtime, description, and capabilities:

summarizer (native)
Summarize text in three bullet points.
capabilities: acall, arun, call, run

The entrypoint can name a tactic instance, as here, or a factory that returns one: a function with no parameters, or with defaults for all of them and a -> Tactic annotation. Any other function is served as a handler, called once per input (Factories and handlers). Call the service:

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/run \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": "LLLM gives you low-level control of every agent turn.", "context": {"trace_id": "demo-1"}}'

The response carries the tactic's output, a request id, and the tactic name:

{"output": "...", "request_id": "...", "tactic": "summarizer"}

GET /info returns the description and schemas, and GET /health reports readiness. To build the app in Python instead, for example to run it under your own ASGI server:

from lllm import create_tactic_app

app = create_tactic_app(tactic)

Inside call(), self.call_context holds the request's CallContext (request id, trace id, tags, metadata) when the tactic is served, and None when you call it directly; a call() that declares a context parameter receives it there too. NativeTacticAdapter(tactic, ...) remains available when you want to serve a tactic under another name or description, attach a package_ref, or pass fixed keyword arguments to call() with run_kwargs.

For production you can wrap the tactic with call guardrails and logging before serving it:

from lllm import InMemoryProxyLog, ProxyTactic, SandboxPolicy, SandboxedTactic

log = InMemoryProxyLog()
guarded = ProxyTactic(
    SandboxedTactic(
        tactic,
        policy=SandboxPolicy(timeout_seconds=120, max_input_bytes=20_000),
        name="summarizer",
    ),
    sink=log.append,
    name="summarizer",
)
app = create_tactic_app(guarded)
  • SandboxedTactic rejects oversized inputs and outputs and disallowed request metadata keys, and enforces timeout_seconds on async calls, which is how the service runs tactics. It is a call guard, not OS-level isolation.
  • ProxyTactic sends one ProxyRecord per call (request id, state, latency, error) to sink; payloads are captured only with capture_inputs=True or capture_outputs=True.

Lesson 9 covers serving and composition in depth.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Concept API Define a tactic class MyTactic(Tactic): name = ...; agent_group = [...] Implement it def call(self, task), using self.agents["name"] Declare agents config global + agent_configs Call it tactic(task) Typed input and output input_type = Model, output_type = Model Session tactic(task, return_session=True) Compose self.sub = OtherTactic(config) in __init__; sub-calls are recorded automatically Batch and async tactic.bcall(tasks), await tactic.acall(task), tactic.ccall(tasks) Extend subclass and call super().call(task) Register and build register_tactic_class(cls, registry=...), build_tactic(config, name=..., registry=...) Start a project lllm create my-app Serve lllm serve module:tactic, create_tactic_app(tactic)

See the Tactic reference and the Config reference for details.

Next: 6. Packages and the Hub

docs.title: 6. Packages and the Hub
docs.text:
Goal: organise a system as a package: prompts in modules, agents declared in YAML, one lllm.toml that the runtime discovers and the hub publishes. Then validate, serve, and share it.

Everything here runs offline; the last step that calls a model is marked.

docs.title: Step 1: generate a package
docs.text:
lllm create briefs
cd briefs

briefs/
  lllm.toml
  prompts/assistant.py
  configs/default.yaml
  tactics/assistant.py
  main.py
  tests/test_smoke.py
  README.md
  pyproject.toml
  .env.example
  .gitignore

lllm.toml has two halves. The first tells the native runtime what to discover; the second describes the package for the hub:

[package]
org = "local"
name = "briefs"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Briefs"
primary = "tactics.assistant"

[prompts]
paths = ["prompts"]

[configs]
paths = ["configs"]

[tactics]
paths = ["tactics"]

[tactics.assistant]
entry = "main:create_tactic"
description = "A minimal LLLM project: one agent behind a tactic."

[card]
summary = "A minimal LLLM project: one agent behind a tactic."
tags = ["lllm", "minimal"]

[docs.readme]
path = "README.md"
title = "README"

docs.title: Step 2: discover the package
docs.text:
load_runtime reads lllm.toml and registers everything it finds under the package's namespace:

from lllm import load_runtime

runtime = load_runtime("lllm.toml")
print(sorted(runtime.keys()))

['briefs.configs:default', 'briefs.prompts:assistant/system', 'briefs.tactics:assistant']

The prompt in prompts/assistant.py is a plain Prompt with path="system"; its key is the module path plus the prompt path. Agents refer to it by that key, so the prompt text can move or change without touching the code that uses it.

docs.title: Step 3: declare agents in YAML
docs.text:
configs/default.yaml declares the tactic's agents instead of wiring them in code:

tactic_type: assistant

global:
  model_name: "gpt-4o-mini"
  model_args:
    temperature: 0.2

agent_configs:
  - name: assistant
    system_prompt_path: assistant/system

global applies to every agent; each entry in agent_configs names an agent from the tactic's agent_group and can override any global value. A config can also set base: other_config to inherit and deep-merge another config. Resolve it by name:

from lllm import resolve_config

config = resolve_config("default")
print(config["agent_configs"])

[{'name': 'assistant', 'system_prompt_path': 'assistant/system'}]

docs.title: Step 4: build the tactic
docs.text:
build_tactic finds the tactic class named by tactic_type and builds its agents from the config. To run it offline, register a canned invoker:

from lllm import build_tactic, register_invoker
from lllm.runtimes.native import Message, Role
from lllm.runtimes.native.core.const import InvokeResult


class Canned:
    def __init__(self, config):
        pass

    def call(self, dialog, model, model_args=None, **kwargs):
        reply = f"[{model}] {dialog.tail.content}"
        return InvokeResult(message=Message(role=Role.ASSISTANT, content=reply, name="assistant"))


register_invoker("canned", Canned, overwrite=True)
config["invoker"] = "canned"

tactic = build_tactic(config)
print(tactic, "->", tactic("Say hello."))

AssistantTactic(name='assistant', agents=['assistant']) -> [gpt-4o-mini] Say hello.

Drop the invoker line to use LiteLLM and a real model; main.py does exactly that in create_tactic().

docs.title: Step 5: validate
docs.text:
lllm hub validate .

ok

Validation imports main:create_tactic, checks the refs and paths, and reports warnings for anything that would make the package hard to use, such as a missing card. The manifest reference lists the main checks.

docs.title: Step 6: serve it (calls a model)
docs.text:
lllm setup .               # stores any API keys the package declares
lllm serve . --port 8000   # serves the primary tactic: /run, /stream, /info

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/run \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": "Say hello in one sentence."}'

docs.title: Step 7: publish and share
docs.text:
lllm hub publish . --local
lllm hub list
lllm hub card local/briefs
lllm hub agent-card local/briefs

The card is generated for people, the agent card for coding agents that will use the package. Someone else fetches it with lllm hub get local/briefs.

To publish your own read-only hub, write a static catalog any web server can host (see The Hub):

lllm hub index ./site/hub

indexed 1 package(s) into ./site/hub

It writes site/hub/data/catalog.json and the package zip, site/hub/packages/local/briefs/0.1.0.zip.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Step Command or API New package lllm create NAME (or lllm init for an existing folder) Discover resources lllm.load_runtime("lllm.toml") Load agent configs lllm.resolve_config("default") Build the program lllm.build_tactic(config) Check the package lllm hub validate . Serve it lllm setup ., lllm serve . Share it lllm hub publish . --local, lllm hub index

More in Discovery, Configs, and The Hub.

Next: 7. Logging and Cost Tracking

docs.title: 7. Logging and Cost Tracking
docs.text:
Goal: see what LLLM logs, read the session every call produces, track tokens and dollars, persist every tactic call with an observer, tag and query runs, debug failures from their tracebacks, and save full transcripts.

Every turn in LLLM leaves a structured trace. Each respond() produces an AgentCallSession that records every model call, parse repair, tool round, provider retry, and its cost. Each tactic call produces a TacticCallSession that collects the agent sessions, the sessions of sub-tactics it called, the result or the error with its traceback, and the total cost. An observer hook on the tactic lets you persist these traces wherever you keep experiment data.

This matters for research work: runs must be inspectable after the fact, costs must add up across thousands of calls, and a failure in the middle of a batch should leave enough behind to debug it.

Where Pydantic fits: sessions, messages, and costs are Pydantic models, so you can read their fields directly, and session.summary() and Message.to_dict() give JSON-ready views.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Finish Lesson 5. The examples use this tactic:

from lllm import Tactic


class SummarizerTactic(Tactic):
    name = "summarizer"
    agent_group = ["writer"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        writer = self.agents["writer"]
        writer.open("session")
        writer.receive(f"Summarize this text in 3 bullet points:\n\n{task}")
        return writer.respond().content


config = {
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o"},
    "agent_configs": [{"name": "writer", "system_prompt": "You are a concise technical writer."}],
}

docs.title: Step 1: Turn on Python logging
docs.text:
LLLM's native runtime logs through Python's standard logging module under the lllm logger hierarchy. Configure it like any other library:

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s")

tactic = SummarizerTactic(config)
tactic("LLLM records a session for every tactic call.")

INFO lllm.runtimes.native.core.tactic: Tactic 'summarizer' started — session_name=summarizer_<hash>_<timestamp>
INFO lllm.runtimes.native.core.tactic: Tactic 'summarizer' completed — cost=<dollars> agent_calls=1

What each level shows:

Level Messages DEBUG Every tool call with its arguments, successful agent calls, and the traceback of a failed tactic call INFO Tactic start and completion with cost and agent-call count, and one line per failed call (Tactic 'summarizer' failed: ValueError: ...) WARNING Parse repairs ([writer] Handling exception (retry 0/3): ...) and provider retries ERROR An agent call that uses up its tool rounds without a final reply ([writer] Agent call failed)

An agent call that runs out of parse repairs, provider retries, or rate-limit retries logs nothing at ERROR: it raises the last error, and the tactic's INFO failure line reports it.

To see tool calls without turning on debug output for every library:

logging.getLogger("lllm").setLevel(logging.DEBUG)

docs.title: Step 2: Read a tactic call session
docs.text:
return_session=True returns the TacticCallSession instead of the result:

session = tactic("Sessions record every agent call.", return_session=True)

print(session.tactic_name, session.tactic_path, session.state)
print(session.delivery)           # what call() returned
print(session.agent_call_count)   # respond() calls across all agents
print(session.summary())
Field or property Meaning tactic_name The tactic's name (a name= given to the constructor wins over the class name) tactic_path Stable identifier used for filtering (Step 9) state "success" or "failure" ("running" while in flight) delivery The value call() returned error, error_traceback Exception summary and full traceback on failure agent_sessions Agent name to the list of its AgentCallSessions sub_tactic_sessions Tactic name to the sessions of sub-tactics called inside call() (Lesson 5, Step 7) total_cost InvokeCost summed over agent and sub-tactic sessions agent_call_count, sub_tactic_call_count Counts summary() Compact dict with tactic, state, counts, and cost

docs.title: Step 3: Drill into agent calls
docs.text:
Each respond() inside the tactic left an AgentCallSession:

for agent_name, calls in session.agent_sessions.items():
    for call in calls:
        print(
            agent_name,
            call.state,
            "repairs:", call.exception_retries_count,
            "tool rounds:", len(call.interrupts),
            "provider retries:", call.llm_recalls_count,
            "cost:", call.cost.cost,
        )

The dictionaries are keyed by the loop step (one step per tool round):

  • exception_retries[step]: the parse or validation errors that triggered repairs;
  • interrupts[step]: the tool calls requested in that round;
  • llm_recalls[step]: provider errors that were retried;
  • invoke_traces[step]: one InvokeResult per model call, including failed attempts, with the exact model_args sent, any execution_errors, the returned message, and the provider's raw_response.
call = session.agent_sessions["writer"][0]
for step, traces in call.invoke_traces.items():
    for trace in traces:
        print(step, trace.model_args, trace.has_errors, trace.message.content[:60])

call.delivery is the accepted reply, the same Message respond() returned.

docs.title: Step 4: Track tokens and cost
docs.text:
Costs are InvokeCost objects at three levels:

reply = call.delivery
print(reply.cost)                  # one message
print(session.total_cost)          # one tactic call
print(session.total_cost.cost)     # total dollars as a float
print(session.total_cost.prompt_tokens, session.total_cost.completion_tokens)

Printing an InvokeCost gives a readable breakdown:

Tokens: <total> (Prompt: <n> [Cached: <n>], Completion: <n> [Reasoning: <n>])
Cost Breakdown: Prompt: $<x>, Completion: $<y> | Total Cost: $<z>
Field Meaning prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens Token counts reported by the provider cached_prompt_tokens, reasoning_tokens Cached-prompt and reasoning token counts, when reported prompt_cost, completion_cost, cost Dollar amounts input_cost_per_token, output_cost_per_token Per-token rates recorded on individual messages; zero in sums

Dollar amounts come from LiteLLM's model price list. For a model LiteLLM has no price for, token counts are still recorded and dollar amounts are 0.0. A dialog sums its own messages with dialog.cost (Lesson 2).

docs.title: Step 5: Persist every call with an observer
docs.text:
Pass an observer when you construct a tactic. LLLM calls its hooks for every tactic call, passing the session, the task, and the tags and metadata of that call:

  • on_tactic_success(*, tactic, session, task, result, span, tags, metadata)
  • on_tactic_failure(*, tactic, session, task, exception, span, tags, metadata)
  • optionally observe_tactic(*, tactic, session, task, session_name, tags, metadata), a context manager wrapped around the call; whatever it yields is passed to the other hooks as span. Use it for timing or tracing spans.

Every hook is optional, and an exception inside a hook is logged without breaking the call. This observer appends one JSON line per call:

import contextlib
import json
import time


class JsonlRunLog:
    """Append one JSON record per tactic call."""

    def __init__(self, path: str):
        self.path = path

    @contextlib.contextmanager
    def observe_tactic(self, *, tactic, session, task, session_name, tags, metadata):
        yield {"session_name": session_name, "started": time.time()}

    def on_tactic_success(self, *, tactic, session, task, result, span, tags, metadata):
        self._write(session, span, tags)

    def on_tactic_failure(self, *, tactic, session, task, exception, span, tags, metadata):
        self._write(session, span, tags)

    def _write(self, session, span, tags):
        cost = session.total_cost
        record = {
            "session_name": span["session_name"],
            "seconds": round(time.time() - span["started"], 3),
            "tactic": session.tactic_path,
            "state": session.state,
            "tags": tags or {},
            "agent_calls": session.agent_call_count,
            "cost_usd": cost.cost,
            "prompt_tokens": cost.prompt_tokens,
            "completion_tokens": cost.completion_tokens,
            "error": session.error,
            "traceback": session.error_traceback,
        }
        with open(self.path, "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            f.write(json.dumps(record) + "\n")


run_log = JsonlRunLog("runs.jsonl")
tactic = SummarizerTactic(config, observer=run_log)

docs.title: Step 6: Tag runs and query them
docs.text:
Tags are string key-value pairs attached at call time. They reach the observer, so you can filter on them later:

tactic("First document ...", tags={"env": "dev", "experiment": "prompt-b"})
tactic.bcall(["Second document ...", "Third document ..."], tags={"env": "dev", "experiment": "prompt-b"})

metadata={...} works the same way for values that are not strings. Querying the log is ordinary Python:

with open("runs.jsonl", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    runs = [json.loads(line) for line in f]

prompt_b = [run for run in runs if run["tags"].get("experiment") == "prompt-b"]
print(f"{len(prompt_b)} runs, ${sum(run['cost_usd'] for run in prompt_b):.4f} total")

by_tactic = {}
for run in runs:
    by_tactic[run["tactic"]] = by_tactic.get(run["tactic"], 0.0) + run["cost_usd"]
print(by_tactic)

The same observer can write to SQLite, a data warehouse, or an experiment tracker instead of a JSONL file; only _write() changes.

docs.title: Step 7: Debug failed calls
docs.text:
A failing call raises as usual, and the observer still receives the session, with state="failure", the exception summary, and the full traceback:

from lllm import Tactic


class FlakyTactic(Tactic):
    name = "flaky"

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        raise ValueError(f"cannot handle {task!r}")


try:
    FlakyTactic(observer=run_log)("bad input", tags={"env": "dev"})
except ValueError:
    pass

with open("runs.jsonl", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    failures = [run for run in map(json.loads, f) if run["state"] == "failure"]

print(failures[-1]["error"])       # ValueError: cannot handle 'bad input'
print(failures[-1]["traceback"])

The session passed to on_tactic_failure also holds the agent sessions recorded before the failure, so you can see how far the call got.

docs.title: Step 8: Save full transcripts
docs.text:
Sessions keep the accepted replies; the complete dialogs live on the agents of each call. The tactic passed to the observer hooks is the per-call copy, so its agents still hold every dialog they opened:

class TranscriptLog(JsonlRunLog):
    """Also save every dialog of every agent, one JSON file per call."""

    def on_tactic_success(self, *, tactic, session, task, result, span, tags, metadata):
        super().on_tactic_success(
            tactic=tactic, session=session, task=task, result=result,
            span=span, tags=tags, metadata=metadata,
        )
        transcripts = {
            agent_name: {alias: dialog.to_dict() for alias, dialog in agent.dialogs.items()}
            for agent_name, agent in tactic.agents.items()
        }
        with open(f"{span['session_name']}.dialogs.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            json.dump(transcripts, f)


tactic = SummarizerTactic(config, observer=TranscriptLog("runs.jsonl"))
tactic("Save the whole conversation.")

dialog.to_dict() produces JSON-ready data with the messages (including tool calls and parsed output), the dialog's lineage, and its latest prompt. Load a saved dialog with Dialog.from_dict(data) to review it, replay it, or build datasets from it (Lesson 2, Step 9).

docs.title: Step 9: Use stable tactic identities
docs.text:
session.tactic_path identifies the tactic in logs. When a tactic is built from a package registry it has the form "<package>::<tactic name>":

from lllm import Runtime, build_tactic

runtime = Runtime()
runtime.register_tactic("summarizer", SummarizerTactic, namespace="my_project.tactics")

packaged = build_tactic(config, name="my_project.tactics:summarizer", registry=runtime)
print(packaged("Stable ids.", return_session=True).tactic_path)   # my_project::summarizer

Loading an LLLM package registers its tactics this way (Lesson 6). The identifier does not depend on file paths inside the package, so log queries keep working when you reorganize a project; only renaming the package or the tactic's name changes it. A tactic constructed directly uses its name.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Task API See runtime logs logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO); logging.getLogger("lllm") Session of one call tactic(task, return_session=True) Per-respond details session.agent_sessions[name][i]: retries, interrupts, invoke traces Sub-tactic sessions session.sub_tactic_sessions[name] Cost message.cost, dialog.cost, session.total_cost Persist every call MyTactic(config, observer=obj) with on_tactic_success / on_tactic_failure Timing or tracing spans observe_tactic(...) context manager on the observer Tag runs tactic(task, tags={...}, metadata={...}), tactic.bcall(tasks, tags={...}) Debug failures session.error, session.error_traceback in on_tactic_failure Save transcripts dialog.to_dict() for each agent of the per-call tactic Stable identity session.tactic_path, "<package>::<name>" for packaged tactics

See the Logging reference for details.

Next: 8. Advanced Patterns

docs.title: 8. Advanced Patterns
docs.text:
Goal: combine everything so far into patterns for production-grade agentic systems: multi-proxy data analysis, hypothesis exploration with dialog forks, typed multi-stage pipelines, high-throughput batches, streaming, custom repair strategies, image input, and offline tests.

Each pattern leans on a native capability from the earlier lessons: forkable dialogs, prompts as per-turn contracts with parsers and handlers, proxies, the invoker abstraction, and per-call sessions. Pydantic shows up wherever stages hand data to each other: typed tactic inputs and outputs, and models validated from parsed replies.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Finish Lessons 2 to 7. The proxy basics (BaseProxy, exec_env: interpreter, run_python, CALL_API) are in Lesson 4, and the JsonlRunLog observer used in Pattern 4 is defined in Lesson 7, Step 5.

docs.title: Pattern 1: Multi-proxy data analysis
docs.text:
Give one agent several data sources through a shared interpreter, so it can fetch and join data across APIs in Python.

LLLM ships proxies for research data. Importing them registers them in the default runtime:

from lllm.runtimes.native.proxies import load_builtin_proxies

loaded, errors = load_builtin_proxies()
print(errors)   # proxies whose optional packages are missing, e.g. exa needs `exa_py`

Each proxy reads its API key from the environment, for example FMP_API_KEY, FRED_API_KEY, and SEARCH_API_KEY (Google Trends), adds it to its requests, and caches responses on disk by default. Then activate several of them on one agent:

global:
  model_name: gpt-4o

agent_configs:
  - name: research_analyst
    system_prompt: >
      You are a financial research analyst with company data, macroeconomic
      series, and search-interest data. Combine them in your analysis.
    max_interrupt_steps: 12
    proxy:
      activate_proxies: [fmp, fred, gt]
      exec_env: interpreter
      max_output_chars: 8000
      timeout: 90.0

The built-in proxy instructions include the full API directory of every activated proxy; for these three it runs to tens of thousands of characters. Activate only the proxies an agent needs, or set prompt_template (Lesson 4, Step 14) so the agent reads documentation through query_api_doc instead.

The tactic looks like the one in Lesson 4, Step 14: open a dialog, receive the task, and respond; the proxy tools are offered on every turn. A typical session interleaves documentation lookups with Python, calling endpoints by the paths the documentation lists. This is an illustration of the agent's turns, not a script to run:

# Turn 1 (tool call): read the documentation of a data source
query_api_doc("fred")

# Turn 2 (run_python): pull data from several sources
profile = CALL_API("fmp/profile", {"symbol": "AAPL"})
gdp = CALL_API("fred/series/observations", {"series_id": "GDP", "observation_start": "2015-01-01"})
print(profile)
print(gdp["observations"][-4:])

# Turn 3 (run_python): variables from turn 2 are still defined
interest = CALL_API("gt/google_trends_overtime", {"q": "iPhone", "geo": "US"})
print(interest)

The interpreter acts as a scratchpad for the whole call, so a complex analysis can be built up over many run_python rounds; max_interrupt_steps on the agent caps how many.

docs.title: Pattern 2: Explore hypotheses with dialog forks
docs.text:
Fork a dialog to evaluate several hypotheses from the same conversation state, then bring the results back to the main thread:

from lllm import Tactic


class HypothesisTactic(Tactic):
    name = "hypothesis_explorer"
    agent_group = ["analyst"]

    def call(self, task: str, hypotheses: list[str] = ()) -> str:
        analyst = self.agents["analyst"]

        # Establish shared context once
        analyst.open("base")
        analyst.receive(f"Background: {task}\nSummarize the key facts.")
        analyst.respond()

        results = {}
        for i, hypothesis in enumerate(hypotheses):
            analyst.fork("base", f"branch_{i}")   # each branch starts from the shared context
            analyst.receive(f"Evaluate this hypothesis: {hypothesis}")
            results[hypothesis] = analyst.respond().content
            analyst.close(f"branch_{i}")

        # Decide on the main thread, which never saw the branches
        analyst.switch("base")
        summary = "\n".join(f"- {h}: {r[:200]}" for h, r in results.items())
        analyst.receive(f"Evaluations:\n{summary}\n\nWhich hypothesis is strongest, and why?")
        return analyst.respond().content


explorer = HypothesisTactic({
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o"},
    "agent_configs": [{"name": "analyst", "system_prompt": "You are a rigorous analyst."}],
})

print(explorer(
    "Weekly active users dropped 20% in Q3.",
    hypotheses=["a pricing change", "seasonality", "a broken onboarding flow"],
))

Extra keyword arguments to a tactic call, here hypotheses, are passed to call(). Every branch shares the base context without paying for, or being biased by, the other branches.

docs.title: Pattern 3: Typed multi-stage pipeline
docs.text:
Use parsers to pull structure out of one stage and Pydantic models as the interface to the next:

from pydantic import BaseModel

from lllm import Prompt, Tactic
from lllm.runtimes.native import DefaultTagParser


class Plan(BaseModel):
    steps: list[str]
    risks: list[str]


plan_prompt = Prompt(
    path="pipeline/plan",
    prompt=(
        "Create a plan for: {task}\n\n"
        "Write each step as <step>...</step> and each risk as <risk>...</risk>."
    ),
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["step", "risk"]),
)


class PlanAndExecute(Tactic):
    name = "plan_and_execute"
    agent_group = ["planner", "executor"]
    output_type = list[str]

    def call(self, task: str) -> list[str]:
        planner = self.agents["planner"]
        executor = self.agents["executor"]

        # Stage 1: a structured plan (the parser enforces the tags, with repairs)
        planner.open("plan")
        planner.receive_prompt(plan_prompt, {"task": task})
        tags = planner.respond().parsed["xml_tags"]
        plan = Plan(steps=tags["step"], risks=tags["risk"])

        # Stage 2: execute each step in its own dialog
        results = []
        for i, step in enumerate(plan.steps):
            executor.open(f"step_{i}")
            executor.receive(f"Known risks: {plan.risks}\n\nExecute this step: {step}")
            results.append(executor.respond().content)
            executor.close(f"step_{i}")
        return results


pipeline = PlanAndExecute({
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o"},
    "agent_configs": [
        {"name": "planner", "system_prompt": "You plan projects as short, concrete steps."},
        {"name": "executor", "system_prompt": "You carry out one step at a time and report the result."},
    ],
})

for result in pipeline("set up a benchmark for a text classifier"):
    print("-", result[:80])

The plan prompt is sent with receive_prompt() so its parser drives the turn, and output_type = list[str] validates what the tactic returns.

docs.title: Pattern 4: High-throughput batches
docs.text:
Process many items concurrently with bcall() and record every call with an observer:

from lllm import Prompt, Tactic
from lllm.runtimes.native import DefaultTagParser

classify_prompt = Prompt(
    path="classifier/task",
    prompt=(
        "Classify the sentiment of this review as positive, negative, or neutral. "
        "Answer as <label>...</label>.\n\nReview: {review}"
    ),
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["label"]),
)


class ClassificationTactic(Tactic):
    name = "classifier"
    agent_group = ["classifier"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        if not task.strip():
            raise ValueError("empty review")
        classifier = self.agents["classifier"]
        classifier.open("classify")
        classifier.receive_prompt(classify_prompt, {"review": task})
        return classifier.respond().parsed["xml_tags"]["label"][0].strip()


classifier = ClassificationTactic(
    {
        "max_workers": 16,   # default thread count for bcall()
        "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o-mini"},
        "agent_configs": [{"name": "classifier", "system_prompt": "You label sentiment."}],
    },
    observer=JsonlRunLog("batch_runs.jsonl"),
)

reviews = ["Great battery life.", "", "Arrived broken.", "It is fine."]

results = classifier.bcall(reviews, fail_fast=False, tags={"batch": "2026-03-17", "env": "prod"})
for i, result in enumerate(results):
    if isinstance(result, Exception):
        print(f"item {i} failed: {result}")
    else:
        print(f"item {i}: {result}")
  • With fail_fast=False, failures come back as exception objects in place of results and the batch keeps going. The default, fail_fast=True, raises the first error.
  • Every item, successful or not, lands in batch_runs.jsonl with its tags, cost, and traceback, ready for the queries from Lesson 7.
  • Provider rate limits are retried with exponential backoff, up to the agent's max_rate_limit_retries (default 8).

docs.title: Pattern 5: Stream responses
docs.text:
Give an agent a stream_handler to receive text as it is generated:

from lllm import Agent, Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native.invokers import build_invoker
from lllm.runtimes.native.invokers.base import BaseStreamHandler


class PrintStreamHandler(BaseStreamHandler):
    def handle_chunk(self, chunk_content: str, chunk_response) -> None:
        print(chunk_content, end="", flush=True)


storyteller = Agent(
    name="storyteller",
    system_prompt=Prompt(path="storyteller/system", prompt="You are a storyteller."),
    model="gpt-4o",
    llm_invoker=build_invoker({"invoker": "litellm"}),
    stream_handler=PrintStreamHandler(),
)

storyteller.open("chat")
storyteller.receive("Tell me a short story about a robot.")
message = storyteller.respond()   # text prints as it arrives
print()
print(message.usage)              # usage is still recorded for streamed replies

handle_chunk() receives each text delta and the provider's raw chunk object. The complete reply is still assembled, parsed, and appended to the dialog, so parsers, repairs, and sessions behave exactly as without streaming.

docs.title: Pattern 6: Custom repair and tool-result messages
docs.text:
Each prompt carries a handler that writes the messages the agent loop sends on your behalf. Reword them per prompt with DefaultSimpleHandler:

from lllm import Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import DefaultSimpleHandler, DefaultTagParser

strict_answer = Prompt(
    path="strict/answer",
    prompt="Compute {expression}. Reply with only <answer>NUMBER</answer>.",
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["answer"]),
    handler=DefaultSimpleHandler(
        exception_msg="Your reply could not be parsed:\n{error_message}\nReply again using exactly the required format.",
        interrupt_msg="Tool output:\n{call_results}",
        interrupt_final_msg="Stop calling tools now and give your final answer.",
    ),
)
Message Sent when Placeholder exception_msg the reply fails parsing or validation {error_message} interrupt_msg a tool result is fed back {call_results} (keep it, or the result is lost) interrupt_final_msg the tool-round limit is reached none

For strategies that adapt as attempts accumulate, subclass the handler. Each hook receives the prompt driving the turn and the live AgentCallSession:

from lllm import Prompt
from lllm.runtimes.native import AgentCallSession, DefaultSimpleHandler, DefaultTagParser


class EscalatingHandler(DefaultSimpleHandler):
    def on_exception(self, prompt: Prompt, session: AgentCallSession) -> Prompt:
        attempt = session.exception_retries_count
        advice = (
            "Reply with ONLY the required tags and nothing else."
            if attempt >= 2
            else "Please fix the format."
        )
        return prompt.extend(
            path=f"{prompt.path}/repair_{attempt}",
            prompt=f"Attempt {attempt} failed: {{error_message}}\n{advice}",
        )


escalating = Prompt(
    path="escalating/answer",
    prompt="Compute {expression}. Reply with <answer>NUMBER</answer>.",
    parser=DefaultTagParser(xml_tags=["answer"]),
    handler=EscalatingHandler(),
)

The prompt a hook returns drives the next model call, so build it with prompt.extend(...): the copy keeps the parser and tools. The session gives you every earlier exception, tool round, and provider retry, so a handler can change strategy over time; it could even call another agent to diagnose the failure.

docs.title: Pattern 7: Image input
docs.text:
Agents accept images alongside text:

agent.open("vision")
agent.receive_image("chart.png", caption="Q1 revenue chart")
agent.receive("What trends do you see in this chart?")
print(agent.respond().content)

receive_image() accepts a file path, a base64-encoded PNG, JPEG, WebP, or GIF, or a Pillow Image, and raises ValueError for anything else. The model must support image input.

docs.title: Pattern 8: Test tactics offline with a scripted invoker
docs.text:
Invokers are pluggable, so tests can replace the model with scripted replies and run whole tactics without network access or API keys:

from lllm import Message, Role, Tactic, register_invoker
from lllm.runtimes.native import InvokeResult
from lllm.runtimes.native.invokers.base import BaseInvoker


class ScriptedInvoker(BaseInvoker):
    """Return pre-written replies in order, parsing them like a real invoker."""

    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__(config)
        self.replies = list(config.get("replies", []))

    def call(self, dialog, model, model_args=None, parser_args=None, responder="assistant",
             metadata=None, api_type=None, stream_handler=None):
        content = self.replies.pop(0)
        prompt = dialog.top_prompt          # the prompt driving this turn
        parsed, errors = {}, []
        if prompt.parser is not None:
            try:
                parsed = prompt.parse(content, **(parser_args or {}))
            except Exception as exc:        # becomes a repair, as with a real model
                errors.append(exc)
        message = Message(role=Role.ASSISTANT, name=responder, content=content,
                          parsed=parsed, model=model)
        return InvokeResult(message=message, execution_errors=errors)


register_invoker("scripted", ScriptedInvoker)


class SummarizerTactic(Tactic):
    name = "summarizer"
    agent_group = ["writer"]

    def call(self, task: str) -> str:
        writer = self.agents["writer"]
        writer.open("session")
        writer.receive(f"Summarize: {task}")
        return writer.respond().content


tactic = SummarizerTactic({
    "invoker": "scripted",
    "invoker_config": {"replies": ["- first summary", "- second summary"]},
    "global": {"model_name": "gpt-4o"},
    "agent_configs": [{"name": "writer", "system_prompt": "You summarize."}],
})

assert tactic("document one") == "- first summary"
assert tactic("document two") == "- second summary"
  • register_invoker(name, builder) makes a builder available to configs through the top-level invoker key; the builder receives invoker_config.
  • One invoker is shared by all calls of a tactic instance, which is why the replies are consumed in order across calls.
  • For an agent you built by hand, assign agent.llm_invoker directly.
  • lllm create projects ship a smoke test built on the same idea.

docs.title: Architecture at a glance
docs.text:
lllm.toml                  package declaration (Lesson 6)
├── prompts/               Prompt objects
├── configs/               agent configs (YAML)
├── tactics/               Tactic classes
├── tools/                 @tool functions
└── proxies/               BaseProxy classes

Runtime                    registry of prompts, tools, proxies, tactics, configs
Tactic                     the program: call(task) -> result, served as is over HTTP
└── Agent(s)               built from config: model, system prompt and tools, invoker, limits
    └── Dialog(s)          append-only, forkable conversation state
        └── Prompt         template + parser + tools + handlers (+ format), one per turn
Invoker                    talks to the model provider (LiteLLM by default)
TacticCallSession          per-call trace: agent and sub-tactic sessions, costs, errors, sent to the observer

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
When a project outgrows a single file, let LLLM lay it out:

lllm create my-app

my-app/
├── lllm.toml          # [package] name = "my_app", plus the folders to discover
├── prompts/
│   └── assistant.py   # system = Prompt(path="system", ...), registered as assistant/system
├── configs/
│   └── default.yaml   # tactic_type: assistant, plus global and agent_configs
├── tactics/
│   └── assistant.py   # class AssistantTactic(Tactic): name = "assistant"; agent_group = ["assistant"]
├── main.py            # create_tactic(): load_runtime, resolve_config, build_tactic
└── tests/
    └── test_smoke.py  # builds the tactic without calling a model

The other templates (--template pipeline, proxy, research, service) start from richer layouts. A production entry point loads the package, resolves the config, and builds the tactic by name:

from lllm import build_tactic, load_runtime, resolve_config

runtime = load_runtime("my-app/lllm.toml")
config = resolve_config("default", registry=runtime)
tactic = build_tactic(config, registry=runtime, observer=JsonlRunLog("production_runs.jsonl"))

results = tactic.bcall(
    ["first task", "second task"],
    max_workers=20,
    fail_fast=False,
    tags={"version": "1.2", "env": "prod"},
)

load_runtime() reads lllm.toml, registers every prompt, config, and tactic in the package (it also becomes the default runtime), and build_tactic() constructs the class named by tactic_type with its stable my_app::assistant identity. Lesson 6 explains the package layout, configs with inheritance, dependencies, and publishing.

docs.title: What to explore next
docs.text:
• Serving and composition: serve tactics with lllm serve and create_tactic_app (Lesson 5, Step 11), call them remotely, and compose them by reference (Lesson 9).
  • Pydantic AI agents: run Pydantic AI agents as tactics and give tactics to Pydantic AI agents as tools (Lesson 10).
  • Channels: connect tactics through SSSN channels (Lesson 11).
  • Agent skills: the skills config key loads skills that follow the agentskills.io SKILL.md format from .agents/skills/ or .claude/skills/, adds a short catalog to the system prompt, and gives the agent an activate_skill tool that loads a skill's full instructions on demand; like other agent tools, it is offered on every turn. See the Agent reference.
  • Responses API and web search: api_type: response on an agent selects the provider's Responses API, and Prompt(addon_args={"web_search": True}) adds the provider's web search tool for that turn.
  • Custom invokers: wrap any model API behind BaseInvoker and register it with register_invoker (Invokers reference).
  • Computer use: lllm.runtimes.native.tools.cua is an experimental browser-automation agent built on Playwright (install the tools extra).

Next: 9. Serving and Composition

docs.title: 9. Serving and Composition
docs.text:
Goal: put tactics behind HTTP, call them from anywhere as if they were local, and wire a system together by refs instead of hard-coded objects.

Everything here runs offline. Most examples use FastAPI's test client, so they run without a server; Step 4 calls the server that Step 2 starts with lllm serve.

docs.title: Step 1: a tactic worth serving
docs.text:
Any tactic can be served, whether its program is a native call() or the protocol hook _run:

from pydantic import BaseModel
from lllm import Tactic, endpoint


class Question(BaseModel):
    text: str


class Shout(Tactic):
    name = "shout"
    input_model = Question

    def call(self, task):
        return task.text.upper()

    def stream(self, task, **kwargs):
        for word in task.text.split():
            yield word.upper()

    @endpoint.post("/whisper", description="Lowercase instead.")
    async def whisper(self, input_value, *, context=None):
        return input_value.text.lower()

stream adds a streaming surface; @endpoint adds extra routes. Both receive the validated Question, exactly like call.

docs.title: Step 2: serve it
docs.text:
From the command line:

lllm serve tactics:Shout --port 8000

Or build the app yourself:

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from lllm.services import create_tactic_app

client = TestClient(create_tactic_app(Shout()))

client.post("/run", json={"input": {"text": "hello there"}}).json()
# {'output': 'HELLO THERE', 'request_id': '...', 'tactic': 'shout'}

client.post("/whisper", json={"input": {"text": "HELLO"}}).json()
# 'hello'

client.get("/info").json()["capabilities"]
# ['acall', 'arun', 'call', 'run', 'stream']
Route Does POST /run One call: {"input": ..., "context": {...}} → {"output": ...} POST /stream Server-sent events, one per streamed item GET /info Name, description, JSON schemas, capabilities GET /health Liveness your @endpoint routes Custom surfaces on the same tactic

The request context carries trace_id, request_id, tags, and metadata; a call(self, task, *, context=None) signature receives it as a CallContext. Errors come back in one envelope with the error type, message, tactic, and request id. See Services.

docs.title: Step 3: several tactics, one service
docs.text:
from lllm.services import create_service_app


class Count(Tactic):
    name = "count"

    def call(self, task: str) -> int:
        return len(task.split())


service = TestClient(create_service_app([Shout(), Count()]))
service.post("/tactics/count/run", json={"input": "a b c"}).json()["output"]
# 3
[info["name"] for info in service.get("/tactics").json()]
# ['shout', 'count']

Each tactic gets /tactics/<name>/run, /stream, and /info.

docs.title: Step 4: call a service as a local tactic
docs.text:
RemoteTactic speaks the same HTTP API and is itself a tactic, so callers do not change when an implementation moves behind a URL:

from lllm import RemoteTactic

shout = RemoteTactic("http://127.0.0.1:8000")
shout.run({"text": "remote"})          # 'REMOTE'
shout.fetch_info().capabilities        # what the service advertises

arun, astream, and aevents work the same way. Without name=, the tactic is named after the URL: 127.0.0.1-8000 here, or shout for http://127.0.0.1:8000/tactics/shout.

docs.title: Step 5: name things by ref
docs.text:
A ref names a resource independently of where it runs: lllm://org/package/tactics/name. Code asks for the ref; a resolver decides whether it is a local object or a service.

Bind refs to services in .lllm/config.toml:

[refs."lllm://demo/briefs/tactics/shout"]
url = "http://127.0.0.1:8000"

[refs."lllm://demo/briefs/channels/events"]
store = ".lllm/network"

and resolve them with one lllm.Resolver:

from lllm import Resolver

resolver = Resolver.from_config(".")
resolver.tactic("lllm://demo/briefs/tactics/shout")   # a RemoteTactic
resolver.store("lllm://demo/briefs/channels/events")  # a LocalStore

resolver.register("lllm://demo/briefs/tactics/count", Count())
resolver.run("lllm://demo/briefs/tactics/count", "x y")  # 2

Tests register local objects; deployments bind URLs; the code in between never changes. Channel refs resolve to SSSN stores.

docs.title: Step 6: serve a whole package
docs.text:
A package folder serves its primary resource, after checking the API keys it declares:

lllm setup ./briefs
lllm serve ./briefs --port 8000
lllm inspect ./briefs        # what would be served, and which keys are missing

Tactic entries load like module:attribute targets: a factory is called once at load and a handler once per input (Loading entrypoints). A service entry that fails to build stops lllm serve with an error instead of serving its tactic without the service's auth (Services).

To serve everything a package declares (tactics and channels) as one API, mount it in an AAAX strategy: lllm shell serve ./briefs.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
You want Use HTTP for one tactic lllm serve module:attr or create_tactic_app(tactic) Many tactics, one app create_service_app([...]) Extra routes @endpoint.post("/path") on the tactic A remote tactic RemoteTactic(url) Wiring by name lllm:// refs, .lllm/config.toml, lllm.Resolver A package lllm serve ./package, lllm shell serve ./package

Next: 10. Pydantic AI Agents

docs.title: 10. Pydantic AI Agents
docs.text:
Goal: wrap a Pydantic AI agent as an LLLM tactic, keep the runtime features Pydantic AI owns, stream it, serve it over HTTP, package it, and hand an LLLM tactic back to Pydantic AI as a tool.

PydanticAITactic puts a typed tactic boundary around a Pydantic AI agent. The agent keeps owning models, tools, dependencies, model settings, streaming, and instrumentation; the tactic adds validated Pydantic input and output, a published contract, and the same run/stream/serve/package surface every other tactic has.

Steps 1 to 9 use the offline stand-in agents in examples/pydantic_ai_tactic/. They implement the parts of the Pydantic AI Agent interface the adapter calls (run_sync, run_stream_sync, output_json_schema), so everything runs without provider keys. Step 10 swaps in a real pydantic_ai.Agent driven by Pydantic AI's offline TestModel.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
A checkout of the LLLM repository, with the development and Pydantic AI extras:

python -m pip install -e ".[dev,pydantic-ai]"

Run the snippets from the repository root so examples. imports resolve. 9. Serving and Composition covers serving in general; Runtimes is the reference for everything here.

Files used:

examples/pydantic_ai_tactic/
  structured_agent.py      BriefInput, BriefOutput, FakeStructuredAgent, build_tactic
  surrounding_features.py  ConfiguredAgent, run_demo
tests/
  test_pydantic_ai_adapter.py
  test_examples.py

docs.title: Step 1: define typed I/O
docs.text:
The tactic's public contract is two Pydantic models. These are defined in examples/pydantic_ai_tactic/structured_agent.py:

from pydantic import BaseModel


class BriefInput(BaseModel):
    topic: str
    audience: str = "engineers"


class BriefOutput(BaseModel):
    title: str
    bullets: list[str]
    trace_id: str | None = None

They become the tactic's JSON schemas and are checked on every call. They describe the tactic's contract; a real Pydantic AI agent still validates the model's output against its own output_type.

Import them from the example module rather than redefining them. The tactic checks the agent's output against the exact BriefOutput class, and the stand-in agent returns the module's class:

from examples.pydantic_ai_tactic.structured_agent import BriefInput, BriefOutput

docs.title: Step 2: wrap the agent
docs.text:
from lllm import PydanticAITactic


def build_tactic(agent) -> PydanticAITactic:
    return PydanticAITactic(
        agent,
        name="brief-writer",
        input_type=BriefInput,
        output_type=BriefOutput,
        description="Write a short structured brief.",
        run_kwargs={"model_settings": {"temperature": 0}},
    )

run_kwargs are copied into every agent run. Use them for options Pydantic AI owns (model_settings, deps, usage_limits, and so on) instead of turning them into tactic fields. Pass description= too: it is what /info, lllm inspect, and package cards show.

flowchart TD I["BriefInput"] --> T["PydanticAITactic"] T --> K["run_kwargs"] T --> M["CallContext metadata"] K --> A["Pydantic AI agent"] M --> A A --> O["BriefOutput"]

docs.title: Step 3: run it locally
docs.text:
from lllm import CallContext
from examples.pydantic_ai_tactic.structured_agent import FakeStructuredAgent

agent = FakeStructuredAgent()
tactic = build_tactic(agent)

output = tactic.run(
    {"topic": "package refs", "audience": "robotics engineers"},
    context=CallContext(trace_id="trace-brief", metadata={"caller": "tutorial"}),
)
print(repr(output))
print(agent.last_metadata)

assert output.title == "Package Refs for robotics engineers"
assert output.trace_id == "trace-brief"

BriefOutput(title='Package Refs for robotics engineers', bullets=['Define package refs', 'Make it useful for robotics engineers'], trace_id='trace-brief')
{'caller': 'tutorial', 'lllm_request_id': 'c86ee4e7-2e8a-4f6e-8d47-aaa31a7e4c91', 'lllm_trace_id': 'trace-brief'}

The input arrived as a dict, was validated into BriefInput, and reached the agent as JSON text. Because the agent's run_sync accepts metadata, the adapter forwarded the context's metadata with lllm_request_id and lllm_trace_id added; the stand-in agent copies the trace id into its output. An explicit metadata= argument to run() is never overwritten.

docs.title: Step 4: choose input and output modes
docs.text:
The default input_mode="auto" sends a model input as JSON text. Pick another mode when your agent expects a different shape:

dict_tactic = PydanticAITactic(
    agent,
    input_type=BriefInput,
    output_type=BriefOutput,
    input_mode="dict",
)
dict_tactic.run({"topic": "modes"})
print(agent.last_task)

{'topic': 'modes', 'audience': 'engineers'}
input_mode The agent receives auto, json The model as JSON text. dict model.model_dump(mode="json"). python The model instance. text str(value).

By default the adapter returns result.output. result_mode="result" returns the whole run result instead. The result is not a BriefOutput, so without an output_type the output type becomes Any and the result is not validated:

result_tactic = PydanticAITactic(agent, input_type=BriefInput, result_mode="result")
result = result_tactic.run({"topic": "modes"})
print(type(result).__name__, result.output.title)

Result Modes for engineers

Use this mode in process only. A real agent's run result carries its private run state, such as the agent's instructions, which you would not want to serve (Runtimes).

docs.title: Step 5: keep runtime-owned features
docs.text:
The surrounding-features example passes runtime-owned options through the tactic: model settings and deps, stand-ins for an eval hook and a tool-approval policy, and a durable run id and a graph node given at call time:

from examples.pydantic_ai_tactic.surrounding_features import run_demo

output, configured = run_demo()
print(output)
print(configured.seen["kwargs"])

assert output["durable_run_id"] == "durable-1"
assert output["graph_node"] == "plan.step"
assert configured.seen["instrumented"] is True

{'task': 'summarize package refs', 'model': 'fake-provider:small', 'instrumentation': ['logfire', 'opentelemetry'], 'trace_id': 'trace-surrounding', 'durable_run_id': 'durable-1', 'graph_node': 'plan.step'}
{'model_settings': {'temperature': 0}, 'deps': {'vector_store': 'fake'}, 'eval_hook': 'offline-score', 'tool_approval': 'runtime-owned', 'durable_run_id': 'durable-1', 'graph_node': 'plan.step'}

run_kwargs from the constructor and keyword arguments given to run() are merged and handed to the agent unchanged. LLLM forwards them without interpreting them, so with a real pydantic_ai.Agent use arguments its run_sync() and run() accept, such as model_settings, deps, and usage_limits.

docs.title: Step 6: stream
docs.text:
An agent with run_stream_sync() or run_stream() makes the tactic stream:

print(tactic.info().capabilities)
print(list(tactic.stream(BriefInput(topic="refs"))))

('arun', 'run', 'stream')
['topic:refs', 'audience:engineers']

The streaming methods validate the input the way run() does, so tactic.stream({"topic": "refs"}) gives the same chunks, with the default audience filled in.

stream_mode picks the view of the stream result: "output" (the default) reads stream_output(), "text" reads stream_text(), "response" reads stream_response(), and "raw" yields the stream object itself:

raw_tactic = PydanticAITactic(agent, stream_mode="raw")
print(list(raw_tactic.stream(BriefInput(topic="refs"))))

[<examples.pydantic_ai_tactic.structured_agent.StreamResult object at 0x12ed39b28e00>]

When the agent has run_stream_events(), as a real pydantic_ai.Agent does, aevents() wraps each of Pydantic AI's events in a TacticEvent whose kind is the event's event_kind (part_start, ..., agent_run_result) and whose data is JSON, so /stream sends plain JSON events.

docs.title: Step 7: serve it
docs.text:
The example module has a factory, build_tactic(), that wraps a fresh stand-in agent. Its one parameter has a default and it is annotated to return a PydanticAITactic, so lllm serve calls it once at load instead of treating it as a handler (Loading entrypoints). Serve it:

lllm serve examples.pydantic_ai_tactic.structured_agent:build_tactic --port 8000

Call it with the same envelope every tactic uses:

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/run \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input":{"topic":"refs","audience":"engineers"},"context":{"trace_id":"trace-1"}}'

{"output":{"title":"Refs for engineers","bullets":["Define refs","Make it useful for engineers"],"trace_id":"trace-1"},"request_id":"8f69d704-bcd7-4203-ba75-4ce26a4129e0","tactic":"brief-writer"}

The trace_id traveled from the request's context into the agent's metadata and back out in the output. /stream takes the same envelope and validates its input too.

To test the app in-process, build it with create_tactic_app:

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from lllm import create_tactic_app

client = TestClient(create_tactic_app(tactic))
response = client.post(
    "/run",
    json={"input": {"topic": "refs"}, "context": {"trace_id": "trace-1"}},
)
print(response.json()["output"])
print(client.get("/info").json()["description"])

{'title': 'Refs for engineers', 'bullets': ['Define refs', 'Make it useful for engineers'], 'trace_id': 'trace-1'}
Write a short structured brief.

docs.title: Step 8: package it
docs.text:
A package makes the tactic discoverable, servable by path, and publishable to a hub. Create a folder brief-package/ with a factory module and a manifest.

brief-package/brief_tactic.py:

from examples.pydantic_ai_tactic.structured_agent import (
    BriefInput,
    BriefOutput,
    FakeStructuredAgent,
)
from lllm import PydanticAITactic


def create_tactic() -> PydanticAITactic:
    return PydanticAITactic(
        FakeStructuredAgent(),
        name="brief-writer",
        input_type=BriefInput,
        output_type=BriefOutput,
        description="Write a short structured brief.",
    )

brief-package/lllm.toml:

[package]
org = "demo"
name = "brief"
version = "0.1.0"
primary = "tactics.brief"
description = "Structured briefs from a Pydantic AI agent."

[schemas.brief_input]
entry = "examples.pydantic_ai_tactic.structured_agent:BriefInput"

[schemas.brief_output]
entry = "examples.pydantic_ai_tactic.structured_agent:BriefOutput"

[tactics.brief]
entry = "brief_tactic:create_tactic"
input = "brief_input"
output = "brief_output"
runtime = "pydantic-ai"
description = "Write a short structured brief."

Validate it and see what lllm serve would launch:

lllm hub validate brief-package
lllm inspect brief-package

warning: readme_missing: Package should include README.md.
warning: card_metadata_missing: Package should declare [card] metadata for generated cards.
ok
demo/brief:tactics.brief (tactic)
port: 8000
GET /health
GET /info
GET /tactics
GET /tactics/{name}/info
GET,HEAD /docs
GET,HEAD /docs/oauth2-redirect
GET,HEAD /openapi.json
GET,HEAD /redoc
POST /run
POST /stream
POST /tactics/{name}/run
POST /tactics/{name}/stream

The two warnings are about the hub card; add a README.md and a [card] table before publishing. lllm serve brief-package now serves the primary tactic. A package around a live agent declares its provider key, and lllm serve checks for it before starting:

[requirements.api_keys]
OPENAI_API_KEY = "Model access for the brief writer."

Keys belong in the environment, .env.local, or the OS keyring (lllm setup brief-package), never in the manifest.

docs.title: Step 9: expose a tactic as a tool
docs.text:
tactic_as_tool turns any tactic into a plain, typed function:

import inspect
from lllm import tactic_as_tool

tool = tactic_as_tool(tactic, name="write_brief", parameter_mode="kwargs")
print(inspect.signature(tool))
print(repr(tool(topic="refs", audience="engineers")))

(*, topic: str, audience: str = 'engineers') -> examples.pydantic_ai_tactic.structured_agent.BriefOutput
BriefOutput(title='Refs for engineers', bullets=['Define refs', 'Make it useful for engineers'], trace_id=None)

With parameter_mode="kwargs" the function takes one keyword per input field; the default "task" mode takes the whole input as one task argument. Native tactics have the same helper as a method, tactic.as_tool(). The function's annotations match its signature, and Pydantic AI reads them to build the tool schema, so the function registers with a Pydantic AI agent as it is (Step 10).

docs.title: Step 10: use a real Pydantic AI agent
docs.text:
build_tactic works unchanged with a real pydantic_ai.Agent. TestModel keeps it offline by filling the output with placeholder values:

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.models.test import TestModel

real_agent = Agent(TestModel(), output_type=BriefOutput, name="brief-writer")
real_tactic = build_tactic(real_agent)

print(repr(real_tactic.run({"topic": "package refs"})))
print(real_tactic.info().capabilities)

BriefOutput(title='a', bullets=['a'], trace_id=None)
('arun', 'events', 'run', 'stream')

For live calls, give the agent a model name such as Agent("openai:gpt-4o-mini", output_type=BriefOutput) and set OPENAI_API_KEY.

Going the other way, a Pydantic AI agent can call an LLLM tactic as a tool. Register the function from Step 9. Pydantic AI derives the tool schema from its annotations and validates the model's arguments against it:

planner = Agent(TestModel(), tools=[tool])
print(planner.run_sync("Plan a talk about package refs.").output)

{"write_brief":{"title":"A for engineers","bullets":["Define a","Make it useful for engineers"],"trace_id":null}}

TestModel called the tool with topic="a", and the tactic filled in the default audience. The same call hands any tactic to a Pydantic AI agent: a native multi-agent program, a plain function, or a RemoteTactic.

The tool is synchronous and calls tactic.run(), and Pydantic AI does not allow Agent.run_sync() inside a synchronous tool. For a tactic around a real pydantic_ai.Agent, such as real_tactic, write an async tool that awaits arun():

async def write_brief(request: BriefInput) -> BriefOutput:
    """Write a short structured brief about a topic."""
    return await real_tactic.arun(request)


planner = Agent(TestModel(), tools=[write_brief])
print(planner.run_sync("Plan a talk about package refs.").output)

{"write_brief":{"title":"a","bullets":["a"],"trace_id":null}}

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Concept API Wrap an agent PydanticAITactic(agent, input_type=..., output_type=..., description=...) Runtime options run_kwargs={...} and keyword arguments to run() Context run(..., context=CallContext(...)) reaches the agent as metadata Input shape input_mode="auto", "json", "dict", "python", or "text" Full run result result_mode="result", in process only Stream tactic.stream(input), stream_mode=... Serve lllm serve module:factory, create_tactic_app(tactic) Package [tactics.NAME] with entry and runtime = "pydantic-ai" Tactic as a tool tactic_as_tool(tactic); an async tool over arun() for a tactic around a real agent

See Runtimes for the full adapter reference and Services for the HTTP contract.

Next: 11. Channels with SSSN

docs.title: 11. Channels with SSSN
docs.text:
Goal: connect a tactic to a stream of events. You will keep support messages in a channel, triage each one with a tactic through TacticProcessor, serve the store over HTTP, continue the work from another process, and finally mount the tactic, the channels, and the processor in one AAAX strategy.

You need: pip install "lllm-core[server,client]" and curl. Nothing here calls a model, so it all runs offline. Steps 5 to 7 start servers; keep a second terminal open in the same folder.

Work in an empty folder:

mkdir support-desk && cd support-desk

docs.title: Step 1: create a store and two channels
docs.text:
make_store.py:

from lllm.network import ChannelExistsError, LocalStore

store = LocalStore(".lllm/network")

for name, description in [
    ("inbox", "Support messages as they arrive."),
    ("triaged", "One triage result per message."),
]:
    try:
        store.create_channel({"name": name, "form": "log", "description": description})
    except ChannelExistsError:
        pass

print([channel.name for channel in store.list_channels()])

python make_store.py

['inbox', 'triaged']

The whole store is one folder: SQLite for channels, events, and cursors, and a directory for artifact files.

.lllm/network/
  network.sqlite
  artifacts/

Catching ChannelExistsError makes the script safe to run twice.

docs.title: Step 2: append events
docs.text:
Every message is an Event: a payload plus the fields that let other systems route and trace it. send.py:

from lllm.network import Event, LocalStore

store = LocalStore(".lllm/network")

messages = {
    "T-100": "The checkout page is down for every customer",
    "T-101": "How do I change the email on my account?",
    "T-102": "Invoices from March show the wrong tax rate",
}
for ticket, text in messages.items():
    event = store.append_event(
        Event(
            channel="inbox",
            source="web-form",
            kind="message",
            payload={"text": text},
            correlation_id=ticket,
        )
    )
    print(event.cursor, event.correlation_id, event.payload["text"])

python send.py

1 T-100 The checkout page is down for every customer
2 T-101 How do I change the email on my account?
3 T-102 Invoices from March show the wrong tax rate

The store assigns each event a cursor, its position in the store. The correlation_id is the ticket number; it will follow the message into every channel it reaches.

The CLI writes to the same store (.lllm/network is its default):

lllm network append inbox '{"text": "Password reset emails never arrive"}' \
  --kind message --source cli --correlation-id T-103

{"id":"d5339382-115a-4318-a665-b94613f8d575","cursor":4,"channel":"inbox","timestamp":1793846679.3149977,"source":"cli","kind":"message","payload":{"text":"Password reset emails never arrive"},"schema":null,"metadata":{},"correlation_id":"T-103","parent_ids":[]}

docs.title: Step 3: write a tactic
docs.text:
The tactic triages one message. It is plain Python so this tutorial runs offline; a native tactic that calls a model plugs in the same way, because the processor only calls run() (or arun()). tactics.py:

import re

from pydantic import BaseModel

from lllm import Tactic

URGENT = re.compile(r"\b(down|outage|failing|broken)\b", re.IGNORECASE)


class Ticket(BaseModel):
    text: str


class Triage(BaseModel):
    priority: str
    summary: str


class TriageTicket(Tactic[Ticket, Triage]):
    name = "triage"
    description = "Assign a priority and a short summary to a support message."
    input_type = Ticket
    output_type = Triage

    def _run(self, input_value, *, context=None):
        text = input_value.text
        priority = "urgent" if URGENT.search(text) else "normal"
        return Triage(priority=priority, summary=" ".join(text.split()[:6]))

Try it directly:

python -c '
from tactics import TriageTicket

print(TriageTicket().run({"text": "The API is down"}))
print(TriageTicket().run({"text": "Where can I download my invoices?"}))
'

priority='urgent' summary='The API is down'
priority='normal' summary='Where can I download my invoices?'

docs.title: Step 4: run the tactic over the channel
docs.text:
TacticProcessor reads inbox through a named subscription, runs the tactic on each message, and appends the result to triaged. process.py:

from lllm.network import LocalStore, TacticProcessor
from tactics import TriageTicket

store = LocalStore(".lllm/network")
processor = TacticProcessor(
    TriageTicket(),
    store,
    source="inbox",
    sink="triaged",
    kind="message",
)

for event in processor.process():
    print(event.cursor, event.correlation_id, event.payload)

python process.py

5 T-100 {'priority': 'urgent', 'summary': 'The checkout page is down for'}
6 T-101 {'priority': 'normal', 'summary': 'How do I change the email'}
7 T-102 {'priority': 'normal', 'summary': 'Invoices from March show the wrong'}
8 T-103 {'priority': 'normal', 'summary': 'Password reset emails never arrive'}

Run it again and it prints nothing. The processor's subscription, triage-inbox-message-processor (the tactic's name, the source channel, and the kind filter, plus -processor), lives in the store and remembers the last event it finished. The cursor moves only after a result is written, so a run that stops halfway repeats the unfinished message next time:

python process.py
lllm network get-subscription triage-inbox-message-processor

{"id":"triage-inbox-message-processor","channel":"inbox","cursor":4,"consumer":"triage-inbox-message-processor","batch_size":100,"filters":{"kind":"message"},"metadata":{}}

Each result points back at the message it came from. trace.py:

from lllm.network import LocalStore

store = LocalStore(".lllm/network")

result = store.query_events("triaged", limit=1)[0]
origin = store.get_event(result.parent_ids[0])
print(result.source, result.kind, result.correlation_id)
print(origin.channel, origin.payload["text"])

python trace.py

triage-inbox-message-processor result T-100
inbox The checkout page is down for every customer

docs.title: Step 5: serve the store
docs.text:
In the second terminal, from the support-desk folder:

lllm network serve --port 7700

The store API is now at http://127.0.0.1:7700, with interactive docs at /docs:

curl -s -w '\n' http://127.0.0.1:7700/health
curl -s -w '\n' "http://127.0.0.1:7700/events?channel=triaged&limit=1"

{"ok":true}
[{"id":"ea41698d-0f45-4afa-b745-4604de002705","cursor":5,"channel":"triaged","timestamp":1793846681.0239878,"source":"triage-inbox-message-processor","kind":"result","payload":{"priority":"urgent","summary":"The checkout page is down for"},"schema":null,"metadata":{},"correlation_id":"T-100","parent_ids":["381bb4ae-10dc-4c09-846f-15d7f70b4651"]}]

The server opens the same folder, so local scripts and HTTP clients can share the store.

docs.title: Step 6: read it from another process
docs.text:
RemoteStore has the same methods as LocalStore. A dashboard that shows new triage results keeps its own subscription. dashboard.py:

from lllm.network import RemoteStore

store = RemoteStore("http://127.0.0.1:7700")
store.create_subscription("triaged", subscription_id="dashboard")

for event in store.pull_subscription("dashboard"):
    print(event.correlation_id, event.payload["priority"], event.payload["summary"])

python dashboard.py

T-100 urgent The checkout page is down for
T-101 normal How do I change the email
T-102 normal Invoices from March show the wrong
T-103 normal Password reset emails never arrive

Run it again and it prints nothing new. create_subscription with an existing id returns the existing subscription, so the script is safe to rerun.

Now move the worker off the local store. Instead of hard-coding the URL, bind the channels to the server in .lllm/config.toml:

[refs."lllm://demo/support-desk/channels/inbox"]
url = "http://127.0.0.1:7700"

[refs."lllm://demo/support-desk/channels/triaged"]
url = "http://127.0.0.1:7700"

worker.py asks lllm.Resolver for the store behind the ref:

from lllm import Resolver
from lllm.network import TacticProcessor
from tactics import TriageTicket

resolver = Resolver.from_config(".")
store = resolver.store("lllm://demo/support-desk/channels/inbox")

processor = TacticProcessor(
    TriageTicket(), store, source="inbox", sink="triaged", kind="message"
)
print(type(store).__name__)
for event in processor.process():
    print(event.correlation_id, event.payload)

Send a message over plain HTTP, then run the worker and the dashboard:

curl -s -w '\n' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7700/events \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"channel": "inbox", "kind": "message", "source": "curl", "correlation_id": "T-104", "payload": {"text": "Login is down on the mobile app"}}'
python worker.py
python dashboard.py

{"id":"b969625d-89c8-4916-802c-746f9dedd11d","cursor":9,"channel":"inbox","timestamp":1793846688.7259398,"source":"curl","kind":"message","payload":{"text":"Login is down on the mobile app"},"schema":null,"metadata":{},"correlation_id":"T-104","parent_ids":[]}
RemoteStore
T-104 {'priority': 'urgent', 'summary': 'Login is down on the mobile'}
T-104 urgent Login is down on the mobile

The worker processed only T-104. It used the same triage-inbox-message-processor subscription as step 4, and that subscription lives in the store, not in the process, so a worker on another machine picks up exactly where the local one stopped. To point the worker back at the local folder, change the binding to store = ".lllm/network"; the code stays the same.

docs.title: Step 7: mount it all in an AAAX strategy
docs.text:
Describe the folder as a package. lllm.toml:

[package]
org = "demo"
name = "support-desk"
version = "0.1.0"
kind = "app"
description = "Triage support messages."

[tactics.triage]
entry = "tactics:TriageTicket"
description = "Assign a priority and a short summary."

[channels.inbox]
form = "log"
description = "Support messages as they arrive."

[channels.triaged]
form = "log"
description = "One triage result per message."

The shell reads it without starting anything:

lllm shell inspect .

support-desk: Triage support messages.
package support-desk lllm://demo/support-desk
tactic triage lllm://demo/support-desk/tactics/triage
channel inbox lllm://demo/support-desk/channels/inbox
channel triaged lllm://demo/support-desk/channels/triaged

A strategy adds what the manifest cannot say: what /run should do. Here it appends the request to inbox and drains the backlog through the processor. strategy.py:

from pathlib import Path

from lllm.network import TacticProcessor
from lllm.shell import Strategy


def build_strategy() -> Strategy:
    strategy = Strategy("support-desk", description="Triage support messages.")
    strategy.use_package(Path(__file__).parent)  # the tactic and channels in lllm.toml

    processor = TacticProcessor(
        strategy.tactics()["triage"],
        strategy.store,
        source="inbox",
        sink="triaged",
        kind="message",
    )

    @strategy.runner
    async def run(input_value, *, context=None):
        strategy.store.append_event(
            {"channel": "inbox", "kind": "message", "source": "shell", "payload": input_value}
        )
        return [event.payload for event in await processor.aprocess()]

    return strategy

use_package mounts the tactic and both channels and opens the package store, .lllm/network in the package folder: the same store as every step before. With strategy.py present, lllm shell serve . loads it instead of the bare manifest. Stop the store server from step 5 (or leave it running; the two can share the folder) and start the strategy:

lllm shell serve . --port 8400

From the other terminal, run the strategy, call the tactic on its own, and queue a message through the channel shortcut:

curl -s -w '\n' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8400/run \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": {"text": "Refunds are failing for every customer"}}'
curl -s -w '\n' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8400/tactics/triage/run \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": {"text": "Where can I download my invoices?"}}'
curl -s -w '\n' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8400/channels/inbox/events \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": {"kind": "message", "correlation_id": "T-105", "payload": {"text": "Search results are broken"}}}'

{"output":[{"priority":"urgent","summary":"Refunds are failing for every customer"}],"strategy":"support-desk","metadata":{}}
{"output":{"priority":"normal","summary":"Where can I download my invoices?"},"request_id":"db41a404-25e8-446c-be59-aa7345fc76a4","tactic":"triage"}
{"output":{"id":"4f3b1f3f-a0c3-41ba-a9e9-06ba8289f381","cursor":13,"channel":"inbox","timestamp":1793846694.8979056,"source":"lllm.shell","kind":"message","payload":{"text":"Search results are broken"},"schema":null,"metadata":{},"correlation_id":"T-105","parent_ids":[]},"strategy":"support-desk","metadata":{"resource":"inbox","endpoint":"channel"}}

The tactic route ran the tactic without touching the channels. The queued message waits in inbox until the next /run drains it along with the new request:

curl -s -w '\n' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8400/run \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": {"text": "Thanks, all good now"}}'
curl -s -w '\n' http://127.0.0.1:8400/network/subscriptions/triage-inbox-message-processor

{"output":[{"priority":"urgent","summary":"Search results are broken"},{"priority":"normal","summary":"Thanks, all good now"}],"strategy":"support-desk","metadata":{}}
{"id":"triage-inbox-message-processor","channel":"inbox","cursor":14,"consumer":"triage-inbox-message-processor","batch_size":100,"filters":{"kind":"message"},"metadata":{}}

One server now offers the strategy's /run, the tactic at /tactics/triage/, channel shortcuts at /channels/<name>/events, and the full store API at /network/. GET /strategy lists everything that is mounted. Stop the servers with Ctrl+C when you are done.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
You want Use A store on disk LocalStore(".lllm/network"), create_channel To record something that happened append_event(Event(...)) or lllm network append To run a tactic over every new event TacticProcessor(tactic, store, source=..., sink=...).process() To trace a result to its input parent_ids, correlation_id, get_event To share a store between processes lllm network serve, RemoteStore, AsyncRemoteStore To keep URLs out of code .lllm/config.toml refs and lllm.Resolver One API for tactics, channels, and workflows lllm.toml, a Strategy with a runner, lllm shell serve
